facts:
Mr Ian Barnetson was engaged by Framlington in early March 2005 as its Chief Operating Officer. On 7 March 2005 Framlington’s chairman, Lord Douro, orally offered him the role at an annual salary of £172,500 with standard executive benefits. Mr Barnetson understood from that discussion that he would also receive two further significant benefits: an allotment of restricted shares in Framlington (“the Restricted Shares”) and participation in a bonus scheme comprising guaranteed and discretionary elements. He accepted the offer and began work promptly, with the orally agreed terms left to be confirmed in writing.

Mr Barnetson said that, during protracted attempts to obtain written confirmation, disputes arose—particularly about the Restricted Shares and the bonus arrangements—between him and Framlington, and especially with Lord Douro. In March 2005, at least two approaches to Lord Douro did not produce written confirmation. Around 11 April 2005 Mr Barnetson was given two draft contracts which he considered incomplete or inaccurate, notably regarding the Restricted Shares and bonus. He raised concerns at a meeting with Lord Douro two days later, and Lord Douro indicated a further draft would be prepared.

Further meetings followed. On 20 April 2005 Mr Barnetson again raised that he still had no confirmation of his employment terms and mentioned the Restricted Shares; Lord Douro again said he would deal with it. On 25 April 2005 Lord Douro gave Mr Barnetson another document said to confirm the contract terms and asked him to sign. Mr Barnetson refused initially, querying several matters including the absence of any mention of the Restricted Shares. Lord Douro reacted impatiently, threatened to withdraw the offer of appointment, remarked that they would have a difficult working relationship, and said corporate shareholders needed formal confirmation of Mr Barnetson’s role. Under that pressure, Mr Barnetson signed the document, stating he believed Lord Douro would honour what he understood had been agreed orally on 7 March 2005 and that he regarded the document as incomplete.

Mr Barnetson said further attempts at the end of April 2005 to resolve matters with Lord Douro and Mr Alain Dromer (a board member) were rebuffed. Over subsequent months he did not raise the issue again with Lord Douro because of Lord Douro’s overbearing attitude and because Mr Barnetson believed Lord Douro would honour his word. In early August 2005 Mr Barnetson mentioned the issue to the Chief Operating Officer of AXA Investment Managers (the second appellant), which was negotiating to purchase Framlington.

On 26 October 2005 Mr Barnetson wrote to Lord Douro and Mr Dromer seeking resolution. A telephone call on 27 October 2005 followed in which Mr Barnetson expressed dissatisfaction in blunt terms; Lord Douro terminated the call. On 28 October 2005 Framlington’s Chief Executive Officer, Mr Robert Kyprianou, told Mr Barnetson he would be dismissed at the end of the year and sought to discuss terms for his departure.

On 1 November 2005 Mr Barnetson gave Mr Kyprianou a sheet headed “Ian Barnetson-COO Framlington Settlement” setting out terms he would accept for early termination, including what he sought regarding the Restricted Shares and bonus for 2005 and 2006. Negotiations then took place, including: a meeting on 18 November 2005 with Ms Louise McMahon (a human resources executive) where, according to Mr Barnetson, she proposed a bonus figure he rejected and challenged his claim to the Restricted Shares, and she presented a draft compromise agreement which he refused to read and returned, saying he would deal only with Mr Kyprianou; discussions with Mr Kyprianou on 22 and 24 November 2005 including an offer of £175,000 as bonus and Mr Barnetson’s insistence on £200,000; a discussion on 1 December 2005 where Mr Kyprianou asked if Mr Barnetson would accept £200,000 for bonus if it could be agreed internally, and Mr Barnetson agreed conditionally on acceptance of his claims to Restricted Shares and further bonus; and further exchanges up to and including 20 December 2005 proposing changes to the draft compromise agreement and including an offer of £200,000 for bonus.

There was a factual dispute about whether the draft compromise agreement shown on 18 November 2005 was marked “without prejudice” and whether that was drawn to Mr Barnetson’s attention. Ms McMahon said it was and that she drew attention to it; Mr Barnetson denied any mention of “without prejudice” and said he would not have appreciated its significance. The judge at first instance found there was no evidence to support a finding that “without prejudice” was referred to at that meeting.

On 13 December 2005 Mr Barnetson wrote to Framlington threatening proceedings if the dispute was not resolved quickly. Framlington then discontinued negotiations and, by letter dated 20 December 2005, purported to terminate his employment with effect from 31 December 2005 by making payments in lieu of notice under the written contract. Mr Barnetson issued proceedings on 24 April 2006.

The appeal concerned an interlocutory evidential issue: Framlington applied to require Mr Barnetson to re-serve his first witness statement with certain passages removed on the basis that they referred to settlement negotiations said to be protected from use in evidence. The first instance judge refused the application, viewing the discussions as attempts to agree a variation of the employment contract before any dispute existed. The Court of Appeal disagreed, concluding that by late October to mid-December 2005 the parties were already at odds about Mr Barnetson’s contractual entitlements (including Restricted Shares and bonus) in the context of an intended early dismissal, and that the negotiations were conducted against the background of potential litigation if no agreement was reached. The Court of Appeal allowed Framlington’s appeal and directed amendment and re-service of the witness statement and exhibits to omit the passages in question.
claims:
In the underlying action begun on 24 April 2006, Mr Barnetson claimed damages against Framlington for wrongful dismissal from his employment as Chief Operating Officer with effect from 31 December 2005 and for other alleged breaches of his employment contract. His contract was for a fixed term until 1 April 2007, and he challenged Framlington’s early termination and the payments/terms offered.

A central part of his position, as reflected in the factual narrative and the negotiations described in his evidence, was that he was contractually entitled to additional benefits beyond salary and standard benefits—specifically an allotment of Restricted Shares and bonus entitlements (including for 2005 and 2006). He sought resolution of those matters in October 2005 and, when told he would be dismissed at year end, he set out settlement terms he would accept for early termination, including what he sought for Restricted Shares and bonus. He rejected counter-proposals he considered inadequate, insisted on higher bonus figures in negotiations, and maintained that acceptance of a bonus figure was conditional on acceptance of his claims to Restricted Shares and further bonus.

He threatened proceedings in a letter of 13 December 2005 if the dispute was not resolved.

In the interlocutory dispute that reached the Court of Appeal, Mr Barnetson resisted Framlington’s application to remove passages from his witness statement. His arguments (as summarised in the judgment) were that the communications should not be treated as protected settlement communications because, on his case, there was no relevant dispute at the time of the exchanges and the parties were discussing the terms of his departure rather than compromising litigation; alternatively, that if negotiations began on an open basis, Framlington had not signalled any change to make later communications protected; and he relied on the absence of any mention to him that the discussions were on a protected basis. He sought to keep the challenged passages in his witness statement for use in the litigation.

facts:
Mr Day, a businessman and developer, bought the freehold of a substantial residential property in Surrey in March 2008. In August 2009 he borrowed £3,000,000 from Standard Chartered (Jersey) Limited to refinance the property, secured by a mortgage/legal charge in Standard Chartered’s favour.

In October 2010 Mr Day obtained planning permission to demolish the existing house and redevelop the site as a substantial high-quality residence, but he needed further finance. In June 2011 he entered into a loan facility agreement with TIL under which TIL agreed to lend £6,600,000 to refinance existing borrowings (including paying off Standard Chartered and discharging its charge) and a further £6 million to be drawn down in tranches against architects’ certificates to fund redevelopment. Mr Day executed a first legal charge in favour of TIL and received the initial £6,600,000 tranche. About £3,000,000 of that tranche was used to repay Standard Chartered and discharge Standard Chartered’s charge. TIL later advanced further sums, bringing total advances to £7,866,782.70.

Mr Day’s evidence was that TIL’s advances were persistently and systematically late, creating risks of contractors stopping work and causing delays; he said contractors did stop and had to be replaced. He said that on 5 July 2012 TIL went into administration and no further funds were released, leaving the property half-built, exposed to the elements, and incapable of completion because he had no other funding.

Under the loan agreement Mr Day’s debt to TIL became repayable on 9 November 2012. Mr Day did not repay and accepted he lacked the financial means to do so. In January 2013 TIL appointed joint receivers over the property to market and sell it and apply proceeds to reduce the loan. The receivers appointed Savills to market the property. Mr Day took steps to oust the receivers from possession; after the receivers re-entered and changed the locks, Mr Day ousted them again and resumed possession.

In April 2013 Mr Day issued proceedings against TIL, TIL’s administrators, the receivers and others. TIL responded with a defence and counterclaim seeking, among other things, declarations validating the charge and the receivers’ appointment and authority to market the property, and an injunction restraining Mr Day from interfering with the receivers’ possession. TIL applied to strike out parts of Mr Day’s pleading based on set-off and sought summary judgment on parts of its counterclaim. For the purposes of the summary judgment application, TIL accepted Mr Day had arguable unliquidated damages claims for breach of the loan agreement that might exceed the outstanding loan, and therefore did not seek summary judgment for the outstanding loan balance.

At the summary judgment hearing Mr Day also advanced a new allegation (not previously pleaded) that he had been induced to enter into the loan and charge by fraudulent misrepresentations about TIL’s financial status and ability to perform, and that he was entitled to rescind the charge, which would invalidate the receivers’ appointment. TIL argued that even if rescission were available it would be entitled, because it had paid off Standard Chartered’s secured debt, to be treated as having security equivalent to Standard Chartered’s former charge to the extent of the approximately £3 million paid.

The judge struck out the pleaded set-off argument and granted summary judgment for declarations that the receivers were validly appointed and entitled to market the property, and granted an injunction restraining Mr Day from interfering with the receivers’ possession. The judge also ordered that sale proceeds above £3,002,225.51 be paid into court, leaving TIL free to apply proceeds up to £3,002,225.51 (the amount paid to discharge Standard Chartered’s loan/charge). Mr Day appealed against the order. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal.
claims:
Mr Day brought proceedings asserting an unliquidated claim for damages against TIL and contended that this claim could be set off against the secured loan so as to release the property from TIL’s charge and thereby invalidate the receivers’ appointment. On that basis he sought declarations that the receivers’ appointment was void and injunctions to stop all marketing of the property until further court order.

In resisting TIL’s applications, Mr Day advanced two main lines of case.

First, he relied on the set-off contention: that his unliquidated damages claim (arising from alleged breaches of the loan facility, including late advances and the cessation of funding after TIL entered administration) could be set off against the loan debt so that TIL could not enforce its security and the receivers’ appointment should be treated as invalid.

Second, he advanced a rescission case based on alleged fraudulent misrepresentations: he alleged he was induced to enter into the loan and charge by fraudulent misrepresentations made on TIL’s behalf about TIL’s solvency/financial status and its ability to comply with the loan agreement going forward. He argued that he had rescinded, or was entitled to rescind, the charge (and/or loan agreement), and that rescission would invalidate the receivers’ appointment.

On appeal, Mr Day sought to overturn the strike-out and summary judgment orders. His arguments included that TIL should not be able to rely on rights equivalent to Standard Chartered’s former charge unless and until it was determined that TIL had not obtained the security it bargained for; that the receivers could not be treated as properly appointed by reference to Standard Chartered’s former charge because TIL had not appointed them under that charge and the preconditions for appointment under it had not been satisfied; and that equitable principles (including “do equity” and “clean hands”) should defeat any attempt by TIL to rely on security equivalent to Standard Chartered’s former charge where the payment to discharge Standard Chartered was said to have been made under a facility procured by fraud and where Mr Day alleged damages exceeding the amount paid. He also maintained (while accepting the Court of Appeal was bound by existing authority) that the judge was wrong to hold that an unliquidated cross-claim could not prevent enforcement of the security.

facts:
Peter Cruddas was Treasurer of the Conservative Party from May 2011 until 24 March 2012. Jonathan Calvert and Heidi Blake were journalists on The Sunday Times Insight Team, and Times Newspapers Ltd published The Sunday Times.

In late 2011 the two journalists believed that Sarah Southern, a former Conservative Party worker then acting as an independent lobbyist, might be willing to arrange introductions to senior Conservative figures in return for payment. To test this, they created a fictitious Liechtenstein-based company, “Global Zenith” (GZ), with a website claiming it managed two funds totalling £4.11 billion. They adopted false identities (“John Brewster” and “Hayley Harris”) and approached Ms Southern. After meeting her and discussing the possibility of making large donations to the Conservative Party, Ms Southern arranged a meeting with Mr Cruddas.

The meeting took place on 15 March 2012 at Mr Cruddas’s office in Houndsditch, London, attended by Mr Cruddas, the two journalists, and Ms Southern. The journalists covertly recorded the meeting on video and audio, producing a full transcript.

During the meeting the journalists presented themselves as international financiers planning a new UK investment strategy involving buying government assets, and said they wanted high-level contacts within the Conservative government. They discussed making donations to get “noticed,” to have contact with senior figures, to be able to say they had spoken to the Prime Minister, to have their concerns represented, to have a say in policy areas affecting their business, and to pick up “intelligence” about what was going on.

Mr Cruddas welcomed the prospect of donations and produced the Conservative Party’s donor brochure describing donor “clubs,” including the “Leader’s Group.” He stated on a number of occasions that donations did not buy access to the Prime Minister and did not entitle donors to influence government policy. However, he also described donor benefits in ways that tended to contradict those general statements. He spoke about invitations for major donors to events with the Prime Minister and senior ministers, including smaller private dinners; opportunities at such dinners to ask the Prime Minister questions and to “pick up” useful information; the government listening to donors’ concerns and feeding them into a policy committee at 10 Downing Street (while saying donors could not change policy); opportunities at larger events to be seated with senior figures if paying enough; opportunities for photographs with senior ministers; and networking with prominent people.

There was also discussion about how donations could be made given that GZ was foreign. Two possibilities were discussed: donations via a UK subsidiary company, or personal donations by the journalists. Mr Cruddas said they would need to discuss the arrangements with Mike Chattey, head of fundraising at Conservative Campaign Headquarters, whose team handled compliance. The meeting lasted about two hours and ended amicably.

On 25 March 2012 The Sunday Times published four related pieces in print and online, including three articles written by Calvert and Blake: (1) “Tory Treasurer charges £250,000 to meet PM” (pages 1–2), (2) “Cash for Cameron: cosy club buys the PM’s ear” (pages 8–9), and (3) “Pay the money this way and the party won’t pry” (bottom of page 9). A photograph of Mr Cruddas taken during the meeting accompanied the first article. A fourth article (“Rotten to the Core”) was written by a lobbyist, and the newspaper also carried an editorial calling for the Treasurer to be sacked.

Mr Cruddas learned of the articles on the evening of 24 March 2012. After discussions with Conservative Party colleagues, he submitted a resignation letter in terms drafted by them; an extract appeared in later editions of the 25 March paper alongside the first article. On 26 March 2012 the Prime Minister made a speech about the incident, having read the articles but not the transcript. He said what Mr Cruddas had said was wrong, asserted that the party carried out thorough compliance procedures before accepting donations, denied that donors exerted undue influence on policy, and said the party would publish a register of donors attending dinners with the Prime Minister and other senior ministers.

Mr Cruddas was distressed and considered the Sunday Times articles inaccurate and defamatory. He issued proceedings on 24 July 2012 seeking damages for libel and malicious falsehood in respect of the three articles by Calvert and Blake, and an injunction to restrain repetition.

At a preliminary meanings hearing in June 2013, the High Court held the articles bore the meanings pleaded by Mr Cruddas. On appeal later in June 2013, the Court of Appeal confirmed the pleaded meanings for libel, with the qualification that in meaning 1 “corruptly” was to be understood as “inappropriate, unacceptable and wrong,” and it also held that for malicious falsehood some reasonable readers might wrongly interpret the articles as imputing criminal corruption.

After a trial in July 2013, the High Court found for Mr Cruddas on all three meanings, awarded £180,000 damages and granted an injunction. The defendants appealed.

On the appeal, the Court of Appeal held that meaning 1 (as qualified for libel) was substantially true on the transcript: Mr Cruddas was effectively saying that if the journalists donated large sums they would have an opportunity to influence government policy and gain unfair commercial advantage through confidential meetings with the Prime Minister and senior ministers, which was “unacceptable, inappropriate and wrong.” Accordingly the defendants were not liable in libel or malicious falsehood for meaning 1.

However, the Court of Appeal upheld the findings that meanings 2 and 3 (the foreign-donation allegations) were not true: Mr Cruddas had discussed lawful routes, repeatedly indicated any UK company must be a real operating company, and emphasised that compliance staff at Conservative Campaign Headquarters would ensure donations complied with the rules; he also said they could not “sail close to the wind.” The Court of Appeal upheld liability for libel and malicious falsehood on meanings 2 and 3, reduced damages to £50,000, and limited the injunction to restrain repetition of meanings 2 and 3 only.

facts:
JCAM Commercial Real Estate Property XV Ltd was the registered proprietor of warehouse premises in Crewe. Davis Haulage Ltd was the tenant under a lease granted on 28 June 2012.

Davis Haulage fell into substantial rent arrears. A payment plan was agreed in March 2015 to clear arrears by instalments, but the company failed to pay rent due thereafter. By January 2016 the arrears exceeded £261,000 plus interest.

On 18 January 2016 JCAM wrote to Davis Haulage stating it intended to take steps to recover possession if full payment was not received within seven days. On 28 January 2016, with no payment made, JCAM issued possession proceedings in the County Court at Crewe.

Unknown to JCAM, on 22 January 2016 the company’s sole director, Mr Davis, filed in the Manchester District Registry a copy of a notice of intention to appoint administrators (the first notice). The notice was given to Close Brothers Ltd as the holder of a qualifying floating charge. The notice named Steven Muncaster and Sarah Helen Bell of Duff & Phelps Ltd as intended administrators. It was verified by Mr Davis by statutory declaration and was accompanied by a signed record of the director’s decision stating that the company was insolvent and that it was appropriate to seek the immediate appointment of administrators as soon as reasonably practicable, and authorising the steps needed to effect the appointment.

On 2 February 2016, Duff & Phelps emailed JCAM’s agent enclosing the first notice. The email said the notice had been filed in view of JCAM’s proposed possession proceedings and the threat of a winding-up petition by HMRC for unpaid VAT, PAYE and national insurance contributions. Duff & Phelps said it was working with management and the invoice discount provider to find a feasible solution, and intended to undertake a marketing exercise with a possibility of completing a sale of the business and assets as a going concern.

The interim moratorium arising from the first notice expired on 5 February 2016. On 5 February 2016 Mr Davis filed a second notice, starting a further interim moratorium. Duff & Phelps sent it to JCAM’s solicitors, stating the company was not in administration and Duff & Phelps was not acting formally, but was working with management and Close Brothers to secure the business’s survival; one element of the proposal was to settle the rent arrears in full and discuss terms going forward.

On 19 February 2016 Mr Davis filed a third notice, starting another interim moratorium. Duff & Phelps again stated the company was not in administration and that it was working with management and Close Brothers to secure the business’s survival.

No administrators were appointed following the first three notices. The court considered it clear that the notices were given and filed to obtain the automatic moratorium while the company considered the best means of securing its future or the future of its business.

On 23 February 2016 Duff & Phelps told JCAM’s solicitors the company was preparing a company voluntary arrangement (CVA) proposal. On 29 February 2016 Duff & Phelps said a draft CVA would be finalised the next day with a creditors’ meeting planned for 18 March 2016, and said that if the CVA was not accepted, alternative insolvency options would be considered.

On 3 March 2016 the CVA proposal was filed and circulated to creditors under a letter dated 4 March 2016, convening a creditors’ meeting for 23 March 2016. Mr Muncaster and Ms Bell were nominees for the CVA and stated in their report that if the proposal was not approved it was probable the company would have to go into administration or liquidation.

On 4 March 2016 Mr Davis gave and filed a fourth notice of intention to appoint administrators, again triggering an interim moratorium. The notice and accompanying documents were in the same terms as before.

In a witness statement, Mr Davis said that after the CVA proposal was issued, creditors representing more than the minimum voting requirement indicated they would not support it, creating uncertainty as to whether the CVA would succeed. He said the company approached Leonard Curtis for contingency planning if the CVA was not approved, and that advice was that, absent CVA approval, the company should consider a sale of its business to continue trading, avoid redundancies, and achieve the best outcome for creditors. He said consideration was being given to a “pre-pack” sale, and that this would be necessary because the company held haulage operating licences which an administrator could not hold, so the business could not continue to trade in administration. He said the company was under significant creditor pressure from its landlord and subcontractors and that, to preserve value for a pre-pack sale and achieve a better outcome than liquidation, it was appropriate and necessary to have the benefit of a moratorium. He stated that given the real possibility the CVA would not be approved, it was his intention to place the company into administration if the CVA was not approved.

The court found that at the time of the first three notices, appointing an administrator was at most one of a range of possible outcomes; the position at the fourth notice may have been similar, though opposition to the CVA after circulation appeared to move matters towards administration if the CVA failed.

The CVA was approved with modifications at an adjourned creditors’ meeting on 6 April 2016, so no administrator was appointed at that time. The CVA later failed in December 2016 and the company entered administration on 23 December 2016.

JCAM’s application was heard on 14 March 2016. The judge made orders granting retrospective permission for the commencement of the possession proceedings and permission to continue them. The judge reserved judgment on the challenge to the fourth notice and handed down judgment on 31 March 2016, rejecting JCAM’s challenge. JCAM appealed. By the time of the appeal hearing, the company was in administration and did not appear due to lack of funds, though the court had the benefit of a skeleton argument prepared for the company.

The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, concluding that the fourth notice had been invalidly given and filed because the statutory pre-requisite of a settled intention to appoint administrators was not satisfied. It ordered that the copy of the notice filed on 4 March 2016 be removed from the court file.
claims:
JCAM applied (by application issued on 11 March 2016) for an order that the copy of the notice of intention to appoint administrators dated 4 March 2016 (the fourth notice) filed by Davis Haulage be vacated and removed from the court file.

JCAM’s case was that when the company gave the notice and filed a copy with the court it did not have a fixed, genuine, settled intention to appoint administrators. JCAM argued that, at best, the company proposed to appoint administrators only if its CVA proposal was not approved by creditors, and that this conditional or contingent approach was insufficient to justify filing the notice and thereby obtaining the interim moratorium.

JCAM also sought retrospective permission for the issue of its possession claim and permission to continue the possession proceedings. This aspect was not contentious and was granted.

On appeal, JCAM maintained that at the time of giving a notice of intention to appoint administrators the company or its directors must have a fixed and genuine intention to appoint (even if later events might change that intention). JCAM argued that a notice should not be given where alternatives are being considered or pursued and administration would occur only if those alternatives failed. JCAM contended that the relevant wording required a true intention rather than a mere possibility, and argued that otherwise a company could obtain a moratorium indirectly while pursuing a CVA even though a moratorium for a CVA was only available in limited circumstances.

JCAM asked the Court of Appeal to set aside the judge’s decision and to order removal of the filed copy of the fourth notice from the court file. JCAM also submitted that the filing should be characterised as an abuse of process, though the Court of Appeal considered it sufficient to decide the matter on the basis that the notice was invalidly given and filed.

facts:
Germany sought the extradition of Mr Dziedzic to face trial for an alleged offence said to have been committed on 8 August 1991. The alleged conduct was described in the requesting material as burglary and attempting to choke with intent to rob.

The evidence relied on by the German authorities was essentially that Mr Dziedzic’s driving licence was found at the scene. Two witnesses were shown the licence and identified the photograph on it as being the person who committed the offence.

After the alleged offence, Mr Dziedzic left Germany. The German authorities were unable to discover his whereabouts for many years. A domestic arrest warrant was issued on 30 September 1991, followed by an arrest warrant in October 1991. On 2 May 1996 an international arrest warrant was issued, later superseded by a European arrest warrant dated 19 October 2004.

Germany’s explanation for not pursuing a warrant beyond a domestic warrant until May 1996 was that Mr Dziedzic was then known to be in Poland and, at that time, the Polish authorities would not extradite alleged offenders to Germany for trial. The German authorities took steps to enforce the existing warrants only after being notified by Interpol on 6 March 2006 that Mr Dziedzic was in the United Kingdom.

On 17 May 2006 a district judge ordered Mr Dziedzic’s extradition. The judge found that the delay was attributable in significant part to Mr Dziedzic having fled Germany after committing the offence, and concluded that he could not rely on the delay. The judge also indicated that the delay would not in fact cause injustice in the conduct of any trial.

On appeal, it was accepted that the issue was whether the passage of time (now over 15 years) meant Mr Dziedzic could not have a fair trial. The appeal court noted that the question of Mr Dziedzic’s departure from Germany had not been explored in detail in the evidence before the district judge, and that the district judge’s reasons did not clearly explain the basis for finding that Mr Dziedzic was to blame for the delay. However, the appeal court concluded that, on the known evidence and the defence advanced, the delay would not prevent a fair trial in Germany.

Mr Dziedzic’s asserted defence was that he had lost his driving licence and someone else had taken it; he said he was not the person who committed the robbery. He would therefore challenge the witnesses’ identification. The appeal court considered that the witnesses’ identification was made close to the time of the offence and was an identification of the photograph on the licence, so Mr Dziedzic would be in essentially the same position to challenge that evidence now as he would have been shortly after the offence. The court also considered there was nothing to suggest he was in a worse position in proving his asserted absence than he would have been earlier, and that any difficulties caused by delay could be addressed within a properly conducted trial in Germany.
claims:
Mr Dziedzic opposed extradition on the basis that it would be unjust because of the passage of time since the alleged offence (over 15 years). His case before the district judge, and on appeal, was that the delay meant he could not have a fair trial.

In support of that position, he relied on the length of the delay and argued that the district judge had no, or no adequate, material to conclude that the delay was significantly attributable to him fleeing Germany after the offence. He contended that the district judge’s conclusion on responsibility for the delay could not stand.

He also argued that, given the very long lapse of time, the district judge’s further conclusion that the delay would not cause injustice was wrong, and he sought to have the extradition order set aside.

As to the substance of the allegation, Mr Dziedzic’s asserted defence was that his driving licence had been lost and taken by someone else, and that he was not the offender; accordingly he would challenge the identification evidence based on the photograph on the licence. He maintained that the delay undermined the fairness of any trial on those issues.

facts:
Dr Robin Edward Lawrence was a consultant psychiatrist practising privately from 96 Harley Street, London. Patient B, a married woman in her late thirties/early forties, was referred to him in December 2005 after a traumatic miscarriage. Dr Lawrence first saw her on 30 December 2005 and treated her with medication for depression and one-to-one psychotherapy. He also recommended group therapy sessions, which Patient B attended regularly; these were facilitated by Dr Lawrence and colleagues at 96 Harley Street, including Sue Sutcliffe and (in the early days) Kay Dowd.

During 2006 Patient B became aware she was becoming attracted to Dr Lawrence. It was common ground that this was a recognised phenomenon in psychotherapy described as “erotic transference.” Dr Lawrence discussed Patient B’s case regularly in a peer supervision group at 96 Harley Street, which included Ms Sutcliffe and Ms Dowd. Supervisors expressed concern about Dr Lawrence’s vulnerability given Patient B’s persistent erotic transference and advised him to stop treating her; Dr Lawrence explained why he thought it preferable to continue, and his supervisors accepted his reasoning.

In early July 2006 Patient B discovered she was pregnant and was ambivalent about continuing the pregnancy. She discussed this ambivalence in group sessions and in one-to-one sessions with Dr Lawrence. She did not ask to be referred elsewhere and rejected Dr Lawrence’s suggestion that she might see Ms Sutcliffe instead. Dr Lawrence did not stop seeing her for one-to-one sessions and did not refer her to another therapist for counselling about whether to undergo a termination. On 6 September 2006 Patient B underwent a termination performed by the referring obstetrician, Mr Guy Thorpe-Beeston; Dr Lawrence, as her psychiatrist, signed the relevant form stating the procedure was clinically indicated.

On 11 September 2006 Patient B sent Dr Lawrence an email. This email was only discovered by Dr Lawrence after the fitness to practise hearing was well under way and after Patient B had already given evidence. Dr Lawrence relied on it as corroborating his account that he had not reciprocated Patient B’s attraction and had sought to make her realise there was no realistic possibility of a relationship. Patient B was recalled to answer questions about the email.

At some point between December 2006 and April 2007 (no precise date found), Patient B raised with Dr Lawrence that she had searched for him online and found media reports about his previous involvement with the regulator concerning sex with a patient. It was not disputed that in 2000 Dr Lawrence had been found guilty of serious professional misconduct for pursuing an emotional and sexual relationship with a vulnerable female patient and having sexual intercourse with her on three occasions, and that his registration was suspended for a period which ended in May 2002 after later hearings.

Patient B went abroad for around two months between February and April 2007. After returning, she continued to see Dr Lawrence until 25 June 2007, when she left a one-to-one session and did not return. Patient B said that at that session she sought clarification about his feelings and that Dr Lawrence said it was appropriate to continue working together but they had to accept that nothing could happen at the end of therapy; she said he disclosed personal details including his divorce, sole care of four children, and a new partner. Dr Lawrence referred Patient B on 27 June 2007 to Maggie Chapman, a psychotherapist.

On 2 July 2007 Patient B saw her GP, Dr Peter King-Lewis, and complained about allegedly inappropriate behaviour by Dr Lawrence, including suggestions of meeting for a drink outside appointments and having sexual fantasies during sessions. The GP referred her to Dr Jeanie Speirs, a consultant psychiatrist, who saw her on 3 July 2007 and supported referral to a psychotherapist/counsellor, Suzi Barnett. Dr Speirs diagnosed a moderate depressive illness and found no evidence of psychosis or personality disorder.

Patient B then saw Ms Barnett for 37 one-hour sessions from 5 July 2007 to 12 September 2008. One topic addressed was Patient B’s relationship with Dr Lawrence, which Patient B described in detail. Ms Barnett used hypnosis in therapy, but said she did not use it when discussing Dr Lawrence. Ms Barnett later produced typed, structured notes for the regulator after re-reading her handwritten notes and then destroying the originals.

On 25 September 2008, shortly before moving to Australia with her husband, Patient B wrote a complaint letter to the regulator about Dr Lawrence’s alleged treatment.

A Fitness to Practise Panel (FTPP) held a 15-day hearing in September 2010. It allowed Patient B to give evidence by live video link from Australia. It also decided it could have regard to Ms Barnett’s typed, non-contemporaneous, non-chronological notes despite destruction of the originals. The panel heard evidence from Patient B, Ms Barnett, Dr Lawrence, colleagues (including Ms Sutcliffe, Ms Dowd, and Ms Chapman), and expert psychiatrists (including Dr Rodger Kennedy for the regulator and Dr Francesca Denman and Dr Adrienne Reveley for Dr Lawrence). Evidence relating to the termination was heard in private.

At the outset Dr Lawrence admitted that he was a consultant psychiatrist; that Patient B was his private patient; that he told her personal information about himself; that he told her she was attractive; that he continued treating her despite supervisors advising him to stop; that Patient B had a termination; and that he did not refer her to another therapist for counselling about whether to undergo a termination. He denied that his conduct was inappropriate, against Patient B’s interests, an abuse of position, or sexually motivated, and denied attempting to pursue an emotional relationship or encouraging her to believe he wanted one.

After hearing evidence, the FTPP made adverse findings of fact against Dr Lawrence on many allegations (though not all). It found, among other things, that he encouraged Patient B to believe he wanted to pursue an emotional relationship; that he told her of a sexual fantasy about her; that he spoke of meeting her socially; and that he continued psychotherapy after becoming emotionally involved with her. It found the proved conduct sexually motivated in a broad sense and in most respects inappropriate, not in Patient B’s best interests, and an abuse of professional position. It did not find proved that he attempted to pursue an emotional relationship, and did not find proved that he tried to persuade her in June 2007 to continue therapy when she asked for a referral. It also found there was insufficient evidence to find that continuing to treat her despite supervisors’ advice was “inappropriate,” though it left open and later found it was not in her best interests and was an abuse of position.

The FTPP found Dr Lawrence’s fitness to practise impaired by reason of misconduct and directed erasure from the medical register, with immediate suspension pending the erasure taking effect or appeal.

Dr Lawrence appealed to the High Court against procedural decisions (including video-link evidence and admission of Ms Barnett’s notes), factual findings, impairment, and sanction. The High Court upheld the FTPP’s procedural decisions on video-link evidence and admission of Ms Barnett’s typed notes. However, on the factual determination, the High Court found material procedural unfairness and inadequate reasoning in the FTPP’s approach to issues concerning low self-esteem and erotic transference, and also criticised the lack of adequate reasons on key evidence such as the 11 September 2006 email and important parts of Ms Dowd’s and Ms Sutcliffe’s evidence. The High Court concluded the FTPP’s findings on disputed facts and the findings that the disputed allegations were proved were unsafe and should be quashed, and indicated a provisional view that the matter should be remitted for a fresh hearing, with further submissions invited on consequential orders.
claims:
Dr Lawrence appealed against: (1) procedural decisions of the Fitness to Practise Panel, (2) some factual findings, (3) the finding that his fitness to practise was impaired, and (4) the sanction of erasure.

On procedure, he argued that it was wrong and unfair to allow Patient B to give evidence by video link from Australia. He contended that because Patient B was the sole complainant and the allegations concerned private one-to-one sessions with a direct conflict of evidence, careful assessment of her demeanour was required; that she had undergone extensive counselling (including hypnosis) before complaining; that she was willing to travel to the UK; and that the panel was wrong to treat her as a vulnerable witness on mental health grounds when her depression was said to be in remission and wrong to treat the allegations as “sexual” in the absence of sexual touching. He also argued the panel lacked power to permit video-link evidence and criticised the way the video-link arrangements were handled.

He also challenged the admission and use of Ms Barnett’s typed notes, arguing it was unfair to admit a non-chronological, non-contemporaneous typed summary created at an unknown date and based partly on her overall experience, particularly because she destroyed the original handwritten notes, depriving him of the ability to cross-examine by reference to the originals. He further argued that the use of hypnosis in therapy raised concerns about reliability.

On the factual findings, Dr Lawrence mounted a “root and branch” challenge, contending that the panel’s adverse findings were against the weight of the evidence and/or inadequately reasoned. He argued that key evidence strongly supported his account and undermined Patient B’s reliability, particularly the 11 September 2006 email (which he said corroborated that he had not reciprocated her attraction and had sought to show a relationship was unrealistic) and the evidence of Ms Sutcliffe and Ms Dowd from supervision and group therapy. He argued the panel wrongly disregarded or discounted this evidence without proper explanation.

A central strand of his factual challenge concerned the panel’s treatment of erotic transference and its reliance on what it described as its own “expertise.” He argued the panel decided important issues (including whether a woman with low self-esteem would be unlikely to fantasise she was attractive unless encouraged, and whether erotic transference alone would be likely to cause Patient B to believe Dr Lawrence had feelings for her) without those issues being properly raised and tested in evidence and submissions, and without giving him a fair opportunity to address them. He contended the panel’s conclusions were unsupported by, or inconsistent with, the expert evidence and that the panel failed to give adequate reasons, particularly where it appeared to reject expert evidence.

He also argued that certain findings were logically inconsistent, including that the panel could not properly find he encouraged Patient B to believe he wanted an emotional relationship while also finding he did not attempt to pursue such a relationship.

In terms of relief, Dr Lawrence sought to have the panel’s procedural decisions overturned, the adverse factual findings set aside, and the findings of impairment and the sanction of erasure overturned.
