facts:
The proceedings concerned the construction of provisions in the Kenrick & Jefferson Group Pension Plan (the Scheme), a defined benefit “balance of cost” occupational pension scheme. The Scheme was in winding up. Capital Cranfield Trustees Limited (the Trustee) was the sole trustee of the Scheme and submitted a proof of debt in the members’ voluntary liquidation of K & J Holdings Limited (the Company), formerly Kenrick & Jefferson Limited. The Company was the Principal Employer and, in practice, the only participating employer.

On 22 October 1997 the Company served a written notice on the trustees stating (i) an intention to cease contributing to the Scheme with effect from 31 March 1998 and (ii) a wish, as sole employer, that the Scheme be terminated with effect from 31 March 1998. It was common ground that after 31 March 1998 the trustees determined that the Scheme should be administered as a “closed scheme”. During the period as a closed scheme, employer contributions ceased.

The Trustee’s case in the negligence proceedings was that at around the time the Scheme became a closed scheme the Scheme had a “buy-out deficit” (the shortfall between Scheme assets and the cost of securing accrued benefits by purchasing insurance policies) of about £1.246m to £2.3663m.

On 2 November 2001 Capital Cranfield Trustees Limited was appointed trustee of the Scheme. On 11 April 2003 the Trustee resolved to wind up the Scheme. By then, according to the Trustee in the proof of debt proceedings, the buy-out deficit had grown to about £12.2m.

On 15 April 2003 the Company entered members’ voluntary liquidation and joint liquidators were appointed. The Company had been realising assets and distributing substantial sums to shareholders, and had sold its businesses and property. The directors’ declaration of solvency contemplated a surplus after paying debts in full of £4,421,879 and did not identify any liability to the Trustee. A communication to shareholders shortly before liquidation indicated that liquidation would protect shareholders from future deterioration in the pension plan’s funding level and suggested there was no further liability expected on the basis then being considered.

On 30 January 2004 the Trustee lodged its proof of debt in the liquidation. The proof stated that the Scheme had insufficient assets to meet liabilities on winding up and claimed a debt calculated on a “buy-out” basis (initially estimated around £12.2m, later said to have increased). The proof explained that the final buy-out deficit would not be known until benefits were secured in the market and sought the opportunity to provide the best estimate at the adjudication date.

On 8 March 2004 the liquidators rejected the proof insofar as it was based on the buy-out calculation, but indicated willingness to consider an alternative debt if further particulars were provided. The Trustee commenced the proof of debt appeal proceedings on 26 March 2004. Separately, the Trustee brought a professional negligence action against its former solicitors (Pinsent Curtis and successors), in which the solicitors denied negligence. The construction issues common to both matters were ordered to be heard together as preliminary issues.

The court determined, on construction of the Scheme, that the Trustee did not have power on or after 11 April 2003 (after the Scheme had been terminated and administered as a closed scheme and then moved into winding up) to require the Company to pay a contribution equal to any buy-out shortfall. The court also determined that before the effective date of the termination notice (31 March 1998) the Trustee did have power, after taking actuarial advice, to demand a contribution to make good any buy-out deficit then obtaining.
claims:
In the proof of debt proceedings, the Trustee appealed the liquidators’ rejection of its proof of debt calculated on a buy-out basis. The Trustee’s position was that, because the Scheme’s assets were insufficient to secure members’ accrued benefits by purchasing insurance policies, it was entitled under the Scheme to require the Company to pay an “appropriate” contribution equal to the buy-out shortfall. The Trustee contended that the relevant contribution power allowed it, after taking actuarial advice, to determine what contribution was appropriate and that this could include a lump-sum contribution calculated on a buy-out basis. The Trustee argued that although employer contributions ceased while the Scheme was administered as a closed scheme, once the Trustee resolved to wind up the Scheme the Scheme ceased to be a closed scheme and the Trustee’s ability to demand appropriate contributions revived, enabling it to call for the buy-out deficit.

The proof of debt also advanced an alternative claim: if the Trustee was wrong that the Company was liable for the buy-out deficit under the Scheme, the Trustee claimed an alternative debt said to be about £1.9m as at 11 April 2003.

In the negligence action, the Trustee alleged that its former solicitors were professionally negligent in their advice to, or failure to advise, the Trustee, particularly regarding whether the Scheme’s terms gave the trustee an ability at material times to demand the buy-out shortfall from the Company as a contribution. The solicitors’ defence (as relevant to the preliminary construction issues) was that the Scheme did not entitle the Trustee to demand a buy-out shortfall from the Company either before or after the Company’s termination notice took effect. The Trustee sought determination of the construction issues because they were central both to whether its proof of debt should be admitted on the buy-out basis and to whether the solicitors’ advice was wrong.

facts:
In July 1996 ROMAK S.A. (a Swiss company) and FTC “Uzdon” (a foreign trade company based in Uzbekistan) entered into a written contract for ROMAK to sell Uzdon up to 50,000 metric tons of Kazak milling wheat. The contract required Uzdon to open a letter of guarantee or equivalent letter of credit by 10 October 1996 at the latest, with delivery to be completed by 31 December 1996. The contract was issued in Russian and English and contained an agreement to arbitrate disputes in London under GAFTA rules.

Around the time Uzdon signed the contract (by its General Director, Mr Kadyrov), Uzdon, ROMAK and two other organisations (referred to as GAK and ODIL) also entered into a “quadripartite agreement”. The effect of that agreement later became an issue in the arbitration.

ROMAK delivered wheat into Uzbekistan of the right quantity and quality by 31 December 1996; most of the delivery was completed and invoiced by 9 September 1996. On 24 October 1996 Mr Kadyrov signed a letter to ROMAK expressing regret that the required guarantee/credit had not been provided and promising to correct the situation. The court considered this letter to recognise the validity of the contract and Uzdon’s payment liability at a time when delivery was virtually complete. The first-tier award also recorded that Uzdon wrote again in February 1997 referring to the contract as binding.

On 2 April 1997 ROMAK gave notice of arbitration to Uzdon by fax and appointed an arbitrator, asking Uzdon within nine days either to accept that arbitrator as sole arbitrator or appoint its own. Uzdon did not appoint an arbitrator, and on 21 April 1997 GAFTA notified Uzdon that an arbitrator had been appointed on its behalf and that Uzdon could appear in person or by representative or state its case in writing, with written statements and documents to be submitted in accordance with the rules. Further appointments and procedural directions followed, all notified to Uzdon.

Uzdon was given 21 days for submissions (later extended) and served submissions prepared by its Chief Legal Adviser, Mr Tulaganov. Uzdon provided a translation; the tribunal obtained its own translation and supplied copies to Uzdon. ROMAK served reply submissions on 11 July 1997. Uzdon responded on 5 August 1997.

The first-tier tribunal issued its award on 22 August 1997. It rejected Uzdon’s defences, including arguments based on an alleged lack of “quota” and arguments based on the quadripartite agreement, and concluded that Uzdon was responsible to ROMAK for failures connected with delivery/payment. The award ordered Uzdon to pay ROMAK US$10,510,629.12 plus interest. The award and GAFTA’s covering letter notified Uzdon of a right of appeal under the rules and the deadline for doing so.

ROMAK delivered a Russian translation of the award to Uzdon at a meeting in Tashkent on 2 September 1997. Evidence before the court indicated there was discussion at that meeting about the possibility of both sides appealing (ROMAK because it believed penalties had been wrongly rejected), but that both agreed not to appeal. ROMAK later wrote on 30 September 1997 stating the award was final and warning of further steps absent settlement proposals; Uzdon did not respond. GAFTA wrote repeatedly in October and November 1997 and December 1997 about non-compliance and warned it would “post” Uzdon; Uzdon did not respond and was posted on 26 January 1998.

On 9 February 1998 Uzdon wrote stating it could not agree with the GAFTA decision because it lacked a juridical basis. After a visit by Mr Kadyrov to GAFTA on 26 February 1998, Uzdon raised an issue that the award may have named the wrong buyer (Uzdon rather than ODIL). On 13 March 1998 Mr Tulaganov wrote to GAFTA asserting the award should have been against ODIL and asking for reconsideration. Uzdon instructed solicitors on 16 March 1998 and gave notice of intention to appeal on 27 March 1998, seeking permission to appeal out of time. GAFTA’s Board of Appeal refused to extend time in an appeal award dated 31 July 1998.

Uzdon then applied to the High Court on 28 August 1998 to challenge the first-tier award. The application was supported by solicitor affidavits based on information from Mr Kadyrov. ROMAK objected to late additional affidavit evidence served by Uzdon. The court ultimately refused Uzdon’s application and ordered Uzdon to pay ROMAK’s costs on an indemnity basis.
claims:
Uzdon applied to the High Court to set aside or challenge the first-tier GAFTA arbitration award on the basis of serious procedural irregularity. Uzdon’s case was that the tribunal failed to treat it fairly and failed to adopt procedures ensuring fair treatment, and that this caused Uzdon substantial injustice.

Uzdon’s procedural complaints included: that it was an “innocent abroad” and misunderstood the role of the arbitrator appointed on its behalf, expecting that arbitrator to represent Uzdon’s interests; that the time limits imposed on Uzdon were unreasonably stringent and that ROMAK was treated more favourably; that Uzdon did not receive ROMAK’s original claim submissions; that Uzdon was not given time to reply to ROMAK’s reply; that Uzdon was not informed there would be no oral hearing and believed there would be a meeting in London where the dispute would be discussed and oral evidence could be given; and that the tribunal should itself have decided that deciding the case on documents was inappropriate given the nature of the issues (including whether there were binding agreements) and the substantial sums involved.

Uzdon also contended that the alleged procedural failures caused “substantial injustice” in the sense that, had proper procedures been adopted, the tribunal might well have reached an award more favourable to Uzdon.

Although Uzdon’s High Court application was framed as a procedural challenge, its supporting material indicated it disputed liability to ROMAK on the merits. In outline, Uzdon sought to advance arguments that the contract was ineffective or unlawful due to an alleged lack of quota for delivery into Uzbekistan; that certain transport documents referred to contracts other than the contract relied on by ROMAK; that Uzdon never received delivery; and later that the award should have been made against ODIL rather than Uzdon. Uzdon sought relief from the award on these bases by having the court intervene due to the alleged serious irregularity and resulting injustice.

facts:
The father (41) and mother (39) are Australian nationals; the mother is also a Greek national. They married in Australia in October 1991. The father is not the biological father of the older child, JA (born 25 February 1990). The younger child is JE (born 1 April 1992).

In December 1998 the father was posted to Germany for work and the family moved there. In January 2001 the mother moved with the children to England and applied for orders concerning the children. On 15 February 2002 a consent order was made in London providing that the children would live with the father in Germany permanently after March 2002. A residence order was made in the father’s favour on terms that he would not move the children’s residence from Germany for three years without the mother’s permission or a court order. The parents accepted the children should be educated in schools where teaching was predominantly in English. The order set out agreed contact for the mother, including at least two weeks in summer and one week at half-term, with further contact to be agreed.

The mother said she consented to the 2002 order because she lost her job and could not cope financially and believed the father was better able to provide for the children. The father disputed this, saying the children were unhappy living with the mother in cramped circumstances and that she did not lose her employment until about six months after the order.

After March 2002 the children lived with the father in Germany and attended schools in Aachen. They spent summer contact periods with the mother in 2002 and 2003.

The mother said that in summer 2003 JA began complaining about the father’s conduct and was unsettled in Germany. She said the father agreed JA could return to England to live with her, but this did not happen. She also said she was alarmed by a report from JE that she had found JA with a plastic bag over his head.

In October 2003 the mother was due to travel to Germany to collect the children for half-term. Two days before, the father told her there was a court hearing in Aachen the next day. On 17 October 2003 the mother spoke to the judge, who told her the father was apparently seeking sole custody and permission to return to Australia with the two children, with a further hearing expected later. The mother said this was the first she knew of the father’s applications; the father said she already knew and had been served with papers in Greece and he had spoken to her about them.

The mother attempted to locate the father in Germany, returned to England, then went back to Germany when she learned he was at his address. The father was unwilling to let her collect the children and the police became involved. On 23 October 2003 the mother attended a Youth Welfare Office where the children were present. Following that meeting it was agreed the father would allow the children to go with the mother to England for the half-term holiday. The father said he insisted the mother buy return train tickets.

The mother accepted she brought the children to England on 24 October 2003 for half-term and did not return them. On 29 October 2003 she told the father she would not send them back. It was accepted this was an unlawful retention.

The father denied the children were unhappy in Germany with him or with his girlfriend. He accused the mother of instability and compulsive gambling. He said that during the mother’s October 2003 visits to Germany she caused chaos in his flat, involved the police, and behaved aggressively, which he said shocked and scared the children. He said JA told a police officer the mother had planned to keep him in England the year before, and that JA said he wanted to live in Australia with the father.

A German Youth Welfare Officer, Mr Krosch, interviewed the children on 23 October 2003. In his later statement he recorded that JE said clearly she wanted to continue living with her father and was very happy in Germany, and that she only wanted to stay with her mother for the autumn holidays. JA said the situation with his father was difficult at present; he attributed this mainly to the language barrier and to arguments about computer games and television, which Mr Krosch regarded as typical parent-child conflict at that age. Mr Krosch also recorded the mother’s assurance that she would definitely bring the children back at the end of the holidays.

The father said Mr Krosch was aware JA did not know the father was not his true father and recommended JA be told soon but sensitively and after discussion between the parents. The father alleged the mother then told JA (and later JE) in a way that was devastating and insensitive.

A CAFCASS reporter, Mr Hartley, saw the children in London on 19 November 2003. Both children told him firmly they wished to live with their mother and did not want to return to Germany. They said they did not like where they lived in Germany and were not doing well at German-speaking schools. They expressed concern that if they returned their father would not let them see their mother alone and would insist contact be supervised.

JA told Mr Hartley he felt isolated in Germany, was ridiculed at school, and had no positive connection with Germany. He said the plastic bag incident began as a joke. By then JA had learned the father was not his biological father and felt like an outsider in the father’s household. He complained of excessive punishment, shouting, and being hit on the hand with a wooden spoon; he said he loved the father but could not live with him and would be unhappy if ordered to return.

JE told Mr Hartley that JA wished he had never found out about having a different father. She said the atmosphere at home in Germany had been quite nice in the last few months, but she still did not want to return and wanted to live with her mother; her objections focused on school and neighbourhood and she repeated her fear of not being allowed to see her mother. Mr Hartley considered both children had age-appropriate maturity; he noted JE’s attachment to her father and that her objections were based on external factors, while there was a more serious breakdown in JA’s relationship with the father. In evidence, Mr Hartley said he had questioned whether JE’s objections were serious enough, and considered JA’s feelings of isolation and alienation serious.

The mother indicated that if the children were ordered to return to Germany she would feel compelled to go too, though she did not want to. Arrangements were discussed about her position in Germany if she returned: it was agreed she would be entitled to benefits, legal assistance, and housing if the children were with her; the father agreed to pay 600 euros for two months; he would undertake not to initiate criminal proceedings relating to the retention; and it was accepted a German court could arrange a hearing within 2–4 weeks, with a further hearing about 1–2 months later. The father said he had applied earlier in 2003 for permission to relocate the children to Australia because he faced imminent redundancy in Germany and could work in Australia; the mother disputed the redundancy.

The mother alleged the father abused JE orally and JA physically, including locking JA in his room and hitting him. The father denied these allegations. The judge noted the evidence was seriously disputed and not capable of full resolution in the summary procedure.

The court found the children were habitually resident in Germany at the time of the retention. It accepted that JA and JE had expressed objections to returning and were of sufficient age and maturity for their views to be taken into account, but noted the strength of their objections developed after arrival in England and contrasted with what was recorded in Germany on 23 October. The court concluded the mother had not established that return would expose the children to a grave risk of harm, and ordered the children’s return to Germany, relying on the support available to the mother there and the father’s undertaking and financial offer.

The proceedings were brought by Mortgage Agency Services (Number 4) Ltd against Alomo Solicitors (a firm) in relation to what the judge described as a solicitors’ mortgage fraud case. The underlying transactions involved Mr Edwards purchasing four properties in transactions that were, on the claimant’s case, sub-sales: Ellis & Carter Limited had owned the properties for about six months and sold them on in circumstances where Mr Edwards (and another Mr Edwards) were the owners of Ellis & Carter Limited. The lender involved was GMack.

The claimant’s case was that the defendant solicitor, Mr Alomo, failed to notify GMack that the transactions were sub-sales and failed to identify and disclose the involvement of Ellis & Carter Limited and its connection to the borrower. The judge noted that these matters were clearly identifiable from a company search, which Mr Alomo failed to carry out; he admitted this in evidence. The claimant also relied on the fact that the documents showed significant “uplifts” in price on all four properties (approximately 44%), and that Mr Alomo knew of the uplift but did not inform GMack.

The purchase prices paid by Ellis & Carter were substantially lower than the prices stated in the mortgage application forms (figures referred to in the judgment included 309 stated in applications and 215 as the sale price). The case proceeded with particulars of claim of about 12 pages. The defence served on behalf of the defendants was about 66 pages, signed with a statement of truth by the defendants’ solicitors (not by an individual). Mr Alomo confirmed in evidence that he approved the defence.

The judge considered that the defence raised numerous issues and did not narrow the dispute, including challenging matters such as the claimant’s identity, and that it failed to make appropriate admissions on key points. The judge was surprised the matter proceeded to a full trial given the involvement of insurers and the apparent lack of a viable defence. During the trial, it was accepted that there was at least a duty of care, and the judge regarded the failures to disclose the unexplained uplift and to inquire into and disclose the previous seller’s involvement as serious breaches that were almost impossible to defend. The case ultimately “collapsed” when the defendant gave evidence under cross-examination.

The court had undertaken costs management. The claimant’s costs budget was initially around £120,000 and was later increased to £174,000; counsel indicated the costs on detailed assessment were likely to exceed that and be nearer £200,000. The judge attributed the increased work largely to the way the defence was conducted and the lack of cooperation in narrowing issues.

The parties reached agreement following a without prejudice save as to costs offer made by the claimant on 11 August 2011. There were no offers until the week before trial, meaning the case had to be fully prepared for trial before settlement.
claims:
Mortgage Agency Services (Number 4) Ltd claimed that Alomo Solicitors, acting in the relevant conveyancing/mortgage transactions, breached duties owed to the lender (GMack) by failing to disclose material facts about the transactions.

In particular, the claimant’s case was that the transactions were sub-sales involving Ellis & Carter Limited and Mr Edwards, and that the defendant failed to notify GMack of the sub-sale structure and failed to identify and disclose Ellis & Carter Limited’s involvement and its connection to the borrower (including that the borrower was a shareholder/owner of Ellis & Carter). The claimant also contended that there were substantial uplifts in the prices (about 44% across four properties) which were apparent from the documents, that the defendant knew of these uplifts, and that he failed to inform GMack. The claimant’s position was that the true purchase prices and the sub-sale/connected-party features were not revealed to GMack.

The claimant made a settlement offer on 11 August 2011 and, after the case settled following that offer, sought an order that its costs be assessed on an indemnity basis. The claimant’s argument for indemnity costs was grounded in the way the defence was pleaded and conducted: it was lengthy, raised numerous issues without narrowing them, failed to make appropriate admissions on key matters, and caused the claimant to incur substantially increased costs in preparing for a trial that ultimately collapsed during the defendant’s evidence.

facts:
Newcastle City Council applied to commit Carl Murtha Senior for alleged breaches of an injunction made by the County Court on 7 July 2015 within Court of Protection proceedings concerning “P”. P was a 79-year-old man who lived alone and received support services from the local authority; the court had determined (for other purposes) that P lacked capacity. The injunction relevantly forbade Mr Murtha Senior from entering specified premises in Newcastle upon Tyne, referred to in the judgment as P’s home.

Two alleged breaches were before the court. Both were said to have occurred on 24 May 2016 and consisted solely of Mr Murtha Senior attending at P’s home. It was alleged that he attended in the morning accompanied by his son, Carl Murtha Junior, and then returned at about 10 pm alone, when it was said he asked what time it was. There were no allegations about any particular behaviour during the attendances. Mr Murtha Senior denied all allegations and said that since his release from prison (after serving a sentence for previous breaches) he had not been to P’s home at all.

The evidence in the bundle included statements from P’s social worker (Josie Reichart), a police officer (PC Steven Rayburn) who attended on P on 25 May 2016, and a health and social care officer (Clifford Renwick) who had been assisting P for about five years. Miss Reichart and PC Rayburn did not attend for cross-examination; the only live evidence was from Mr Renwick and Mr Murtha Senior.

Mr Renwick’s evidence was that when he attended P on 25 May 2016, P reported that Mr Murtha Senior and Mr Murtha Junior had been to the property in the morning and that Mr Murtha Senior had returned alone later that day. Mr Renwick said he observed smoked cigarette ends on P’s bedroom windowsill, which prompted his enquiry. He described P as reluctant to “cause trouble” within his family and reluctant to discuss events, but said P disclosed that Mr Murtha Senior and Junior had been there in the morning and commented that Mr Murtha Senior was “out of his head” then, and “better” when he returned in the evening. Mr Renwick reported the disclosures to the police.

PC Rayburn attended P on 25 May 2016 and reported P as agitated and distressed, but in the account recorded by the police P mentioned only Carl Murtha Junior and did not mention Mr Murtha Senior. The court noted inconsistencies between Mr Renwick’s contemporaneous note and his later statement, and inconsistencies in accounts about money and about an alleged removal of a bottle of Lucozade from P’s fridge.

Mr Murtha Senior relied on the “out of his head” description, admitting he was a regular (though reduced) heroin user but saying heroin did not make him “out of his head” and instead sent him to sleep; he also said he would not take heroin if he were going to see P. He said he was living in a tent and of no fixed abode, and suggested it would be easier for him to admit the breaches and return to prison where he would be sheltered and fed, but he maintained his denial.

The judge found there was no direct independent eyewitness evidence of Mr Murtha Senior’s presence and that the case depended on hearsay evidence, but accepted Mr Renwick as a truthful witness with no reason to fabricate matters and accepted that his note was an accurate record. The judge concluded, sure beyond doubt, that Mr Murtha Senior was at P’s home in the morning and evening of 24 May 2016 and that the breaches were proved to the required standard.

In considering disposal, the judge noted Mr Murtha Senior had served a significant custodial sentence previously and had been released in February 2016; these were the first allegations since then, and the local authority indicated there were no other outstanding allegations. Mr Murtha Senior’s tenancy near P’s home had been terminated and he had been evicted; he was then based in Felling in a tent. The judge was satisfied Mr Murtha Senior understood his obligations, though he did not admit the breaches and the judge considered he likely had no recollection of the times involved for various reasons. The judge regarded the breaches as at the lowest end of seriousness, with no allegation of wrongdoing such as taking P’s property. The judge decided not to impose an immediate custodial sentence or a suspended custodial sentence, and instead adjourned sentence on the basis it could be brought back and considered if further breaches were proved during the period of the injunction.
claims:
Newcastle City Council sought an order committing Carl Murtha Senior for contempt of court on the basis that he breached the injunction by entering P’s home twice on 24 May 2016 (once in the morning with Carl Murtha Junior and once at about 10 pm alone). The Council’s case was that these attendances, if proved, were breaches of the injunction, and it relied primarily on the accounts reported by P to Mr Renwick and to the police, together with Mr Renwick’s contemporaneous note and evidence. The Council’s application proceeded on the basis that P experienced distress and anxiety when Mr Murtha Senior attended the property.

In response, Mr Murtha Senior denied the alleged breaches and argued that the evidence against him was hearsay and contained inconsistencies, and that it was insufficient in weight to prove the allegations to the required criminal standard.

facts:
The proceedings arose out of appeals by Hutchison 3G UK Limited and British Telecommunications plc against a decision-making process concerning a mobile call termination (MCT) price control set by the Office of Communications (OFCOM) in a statement issued in March 2007 for a four-year period (2007–2011). Telefónica O2 (UK) Limited, T-Mobile (UK) Limited, Vodafone Limited and Orange Personal Communications Services Limited (mobile network operators) intervened.

As a result of BT’s appeal, the Tribunal upheld a determination by the Competition Commission that the level of the MCT price control set by OFCOM was too high. The subsequent dispute concerned the scope of the Tribunal’s powers to direct OFCOM to remedy that error, particularly in relation to parts of the four-year control period that had already elapsed by the time the appeal process concluded.

It was common ground that the Tribunal could direct OFCOM to reduce price control levels for the period after the matter was remitted to OFCOM. The Tribunal’s Final Judgment remitted the matter to OFCOM, and on 2 April 2009 OFCOM issued a new price control. For the remaining future part of the control period (years 3 and 4), the revised rates set on 2 April 2009 applied and were not challenged.

The practical problem concerned what should happen about years 1 and 2 of the control period, which had already passed. In an earlier judgment (the Disposal Powers Judgment), the Tribunal held unanimously that it would have power to direct OFCOM to reset the relevant charge levels for the whole four-year period (a “replacement price control” covering years 1–4). In the Final Judgment, the Tribunal directed OFCOM, among other things, to adopt such a replacement price control.

The interveners sought permission to appeal against the Tribunal’s conclusions in the Disposal Powers Judgment and/or the Final Judgment. The central issue was whether directing a replacement price control was inconsistent with the limitation that the Tribunal could not direct OFCOM to take action that OFCOM would not otherwise have power to take in relation to the decision under appeal. This raised a question of whether OFCOM’s powers should be assessed as at the date of remittal (2 April 2009) or as at the date of the original decision (27 March 2007), and whether OFCOM would be acting “retrospectively” by issuing on 2 April 2009 a price control covering the whole period from March 2007.

The Tribunal also noted a further jurisdiction point previously raised by BT about whether there was power to adjust the charges in years 3 and 4 to take account of the fact that charges complied with in years 1 and 2 were later found to have been set too high (a “future adjusted” approach). The Tribunal had not reached a unanimous conclusion on that point and, for procedural reasons, did not exercise any such power in disposing of the appeal.

The Tribunal further observed that it had not ruled on whether other forms of relief (such as declaratory relief or interim relief) were available within this appeal regime. It also recorded that the appeal did not concern whether OFCOM should compensate BT for having paid too much to the mobile network operators in years 1 and 2, and the Tribunal had rejected the characterisation that the mobile network operators should compensate BT for overpayments.

If the Tribunal did have jurisdiction to direct a replacement price control, Vodafone and T-Mobile also challenged whether it was right, in the circumstances, to direct OFCOM to adopt a replacement price control. That challenge depended on whether the “Appropriateness Question” (whether it was appropriate to adopt a replacement price control) was a matter for the Competition Commission or for the Tribunal. Vodafone contended it was for the Competition Commission and argued the Competition Commission had not properly addressed it; the Tribunal held that, properly read, the Competition Commission had addressed it. The Tribunal also addressed the possibility that, if there had been a failure to address the issue, questions would arise as to the proper remedy (including whether the matter should go back to the Competition Commission, be decided by the Tribunal, or be remitted to OFCOM).

The Tribunal granted permission to appeal on all proposed grounds, considering that the issues were difficult, important to the outcome, and important for clarifying the scope of the Tribunal’s powers in future cases.
claims:
The interveners (Telefónica O2, T-Mobile, Vodafone and Orange) sought permission to appeal against the Tribunal’s rulings that (i) the Tribunal had power to direct OFCOM to adopt a replacement price control covering the entire four-year period (including years 1 and 2 that had already elapsed), and (ii) in the circumstances of this case it was right to direct OFCOM to adopt such a replacement price control.

On the jurisdiction issue, the interveners’ position was that directing OFCOM to reset the price control for the whole period was not permitted because it would require OFCOM to take action it did not have power to take in relation to the original decision, in substance involving an impermissible “retrospective” price control. Their argument turned on whether OFCOM’s powers should be assessed by reference to the position at the time of remittal (when OFCOM issued the new control on 2 April 2009) or by reference to the position at the time of the original decision (27 March 2007).

If the Tribunal did have jurisdiction to direct a replacement price control, Vodafone and T-Mobile further challenged the Tribunal’s decision to exercise that power in this case. A key part of Vodafone’s argument was that the “Appropriateness Question” (whether it was appropriate to impose a replacement price control) was for the Competition Commission to decide rather than the Tribunal. Vodafone contended that the Competition Commission did not properly address that question and effectively moved straight from acknowledging the existence of the power to deciding it should be exercised.

In connection with that contention, Vodafone’s requested relief (as described in the ruling) included, as primary relief in its challenge, an order directing OFCOM not to make any adjustment in respect of years 1 and 2, on the basis that this was the only lawful conclusion. Alternatively, Vodafone sought relief that would result in the matter being remitted with directions so that the task Vodafone said had not been lawfully completed would be completed.

Vodafone also advanced an alternative challenge on the basis that, if the Appropriateness Question was not for the Competition Commission but for the Tribunal, then the Competition Commission’s reasoning would be legally irrelevant and the Tribunal’s own reasoning for directing a replacement price control was said to be legally flawed.

T-Mobile additionally argued that a declaratory order could have enabled the Tribunal to give effect to its decision without the need for a replacement price control, and Orange asserted that interim relief would be available in an appropriate case to address the Tribunal’s concerns about giving effect to its decision.

Overall, the interveners sought appellate review to overturn (or limit) the Tribunal’s conclusions about the existence and/or exercise of the power to require a replacement price control affecting elapsed years, and to obtain a different outcome that would avoid adjustment of years 1 and 2.

facts:
On 5 February 2010 the Office of Communications (OFCOM) issued a determination resolving disputes between British Telecommunications plc (BT) and four mobile network operators (T-Mobile, Orange, Vodafone and O2) about BT’s wholesale termination charges for calls to 0800 and 0808 numbers that terminate on BT’s network (“080 calls”). The disputes arose after BT issued a network charge change notice, NCCN 956 dated 3 June 2009, notifying communications providers (including the mobile operators) that from 1 July 2009 it intended to levy specified charges for terminating 080 calls on BT’s network when those calls originated from non-BT fixed or mobile networks. BT described NCCN 956 as creating a sliding scale of payments between BT and the originating provider depending on what that provider charged its own customers for 080 calls.

T-Mobile asked OFCOM to resolve the dispute in September 2009; OFCOM accepted the dispute on 6 October 2009 and set a deadline of 5 February 2010 for its determination. Vodafone, O2 and Orange made similar requests in October 2009 and OFCOM joined those disputes into the existing BT/T-Mobile dispute. During the dispute process, OFCOM published an update note on 16 November 2009 stating it would not amend the scope of the dispute to consider whether the specific charges introduced by BT in NCCN 956 were fair and reasonable; it said its first task was to consider whether it was fair and reasonable for BT to impose any termination charge for calls to BT-hosted 080 numbers, and that consideration of specific charges would be premature. In email exchanges in December 2009, BT queried why OFCOM was asking about retail charges given BT’s understanding that the 080 charges themselves were not within scope; OFCOM replied that while it was not directly considering 080 charges, the information was helpful to obtain an indicative view of mobile operators’ retention on an 080 call.

OFCOM issued a draft determination on 23 December 2009 and invited comments by 12 January 2010. BT responded on 12 January 2010 indicating it had commissioned independent economic evidence. BT submitted two expert reports dated January 2009 on 27 January 2010, and further expert reports dated 1 February 2010 and 3 February 2010 on 3 February 2010. OFCOM issued its final determination on 5 February 2010.

BT’s evidence for its appeal included multiple reports from two economists (three reports from each), and witness statements from BT personnel including an internal economist and a network strategist, plus a further witness statement. OFCOM and the mobile operators objected to the admissibility of substantial parts of BT’s evidence on the appeal, including (i) material BT had submitted to OFCOM late in the dispute process which OFCOM did not take into account in its determination, and (ii) material not submitted to OFCOM at all but served with BT’s notice of appeal. There were also objections that certain BT witness statements were in substance expert opinion rather than factual evidence, and that parts of one witness statement amounted to argument. A case management conference in May 2010 led to a separate hearing in June 2010 to determine these evidential objections.

The Tribunal concluded that the challenged categories of evidence were admissible on the appeal and should not be excluded. It also held that the BT employee statements in issue were admissible as factual evidence, and that the notice of appeal did not require amendment or further clarification. In discussing the background, the Tribunal noted BT’s contention that it had been misled during much of the dispute process into believing that the specific NCCN 956 charges were outside the scope of OFCOM’s consideration, whereas the draft determination’s summary indicated OFCOM had provisionally concluded that the termination charges set out in NCCN 956 had not been demonstrated to be fair and reasonable and that the parties should revert to the prior trading terms.
claims:
BT appealed OFCOM’s 5 February 2010 determination. In support of its appeal BT relied on expert economic evidence (multiple reports from Professor Ian Dobbs and Dr Dan Maldoom) and witness statements from BT personnel (including Paul Richards, Andrew Reid and Darren Kilburn), together with documentary evidence.

BT’s position on the evidential dispute was that there were no general limits preventing an appellant from adducing evidence on appeal merely because it was not provided to OFCOM during the dispute process or was provided too late for OFCOM to consider. BT argued that, provided the evidence related to the grounds of appeal set out in its notice of appeal, it should be admissible.

BT also advanced an explanation for why some of its economic evidence was submitted late or only on appeal: it said it was taken by surprise by the content of OFCOM’s draft determination and that, until receiving the draft on 23 December 2009, BT believed OFCOM had expressly excluded from the dispute’s scope any consideration of the specific charges in NCCN 956. On BT’s account, it had therefore been addressing only whether it was fair and reasonable for any termination charge for 080 calls to exist, not whether the particular NCCN 956 charges were fair and reasonable.

As to the substance of its appeal arguments (as reflected in the notice of appeal passages discussed in this judgment), BT contended that NCCN 956 was intended to ensure callers using BT’s network to call 080 numbers were not charged, and that economic analysis showed NCCN 956 created clear incentives for mobile network operators to reduce what they charged callers for 080 calls. BT asserted that, viewed through economic analysis, NCCN 956 would benefit consumers and that OFCOM’s analysis could not stand.

In response to objections that two BT employee statements were really expert evidence, BT maintained they were properly served as factual witness statements, but said it was willing to re-serve them as expert reports if necessary. BT also maintained that the Kilburn statement was proper factual evidence and not advocacy. Finally, BT contended that its notice of appeal was properly pleaded and sufficiently clear.

facts:
The respondent, Wykowski, is a European citizen who was the subject of a decision dated 12 December 2012 by the Secretary of State to deport him from the United Kingdom. He appealed that deportation decision to the First-tier Tribunal.

The First-tier Tribunal heard the appeal initially on 29 January 2013 before a panel consisting of a judge and a non-legal member. The hearing concluded on the shared understanding that the Tribunal would later issue a reserved decision. After that hearing, the Tribunal issued directions focused exclusively on the issue of the respondent’s risk of reoffending, invited further evidence, and stated that both parties would be able to make further representations. The Tribunal then reconvened for a second hearing day on 15 April 2013.

At the second hearing, the respondent was permitted to adduce further evidence relating to whether he could relocate to an alternative place of residence, an issue the Tribunal treated as relevant to the risk of reoffending. The Secretary of State’s representative asked two questions of the witness, but the Tribunal did not permit the Secretary of State’s representative to make submissions about the new evidence.

In its determination promulgated on 18 April 2013, the First-tier Tribunal allowed the respondent’s appeal against deportation on the basis that deportation would breach his rights as a European citizen. Although the respondent had also pursued a separate ground based on his private and family life, the First-tier Tribunal did not decide that ground because it considered it unnecessary.

A central factual issue in the case concerned the respondent’s residence status. The First-tier Tribunal stated that the Secretary of State accepted the respondent had acquired a permanent right of residence by being in the United Kingdom for a continuous period of over five years, and repeated this. However, the Secretary of State’s deportation decision letter stated there was no evidence of residence in accordance with the relevant requirements for a continuous five-year period (or ten years) and that the respondent had not acquired a permanent right of residence.

Another central factual issue concerned the respondent’s risk of reoffending and risk of serious harm. Evidence included an OASYS report and, mainly, a probation service report (referred to as the NOMS report). The NOMS report assessed the respondent as presenting a low likelihood of reoffending, but a medium risk of inflicting serious harm if he did reoffend. The medium serious-harm assessment was based on multiple risk factors. The report assessed him as presenting a risk to the victim of his index and previous offences and to the general public. It recorded that he was under the influence of alcohol when he committed the index offence, and that he was capable of aggressive and impulsive behaviour due to his temperament, needing skills to deal with conflict and improve problem-solving and consequential thinking. The report identified employment, stable accommodation, and engagement and compliance with community-based orders as protective factors.

The Upper Tribunal also noted an irregularity in the First-tier Tribunal’s composition: the first hearing day included a non-legal member, but the second hearing day did not, and the final determination was issued in the name of the judge only, without any order regularising the change. The determination’s text mixed references to the judge’s personal views and to combined views of the judge and non-legal member.

The Secretary of State appealed to the Upper Tribunal, which heard the appeal on 14 November 2013 and issued its fuller reasons on 6 January 2014. The Upper Tribunal allowed the Secretary of State’s appeal, set aside the First-tier Tribunal’s decision, and remitted the case to the First-tier Tribunal to be determined afresh by a differently constituted tribunal with no findings of fact preserved.
claims:
Before the First-tier Tribunal, the respondent’s position was that the Secretary of State’s decision to deport him should be overturned. He pursued the appeal on the basis that deportation would breach his rights as a European citizen, and he also advanced a separate ground based on his private and family life, seeking to resist deportation on that basis as well. The First-tier Tribunal allowed the appeal on the European-citizen-rights basis and did not determine the private and family life ground.

Before the Upper Tribunal, the claimant/appellant was the Secretary of State, who sought to overturn the First-tier Tribunal’s decision allowing the respondent’s appeal. The Secretary of State argued that the First-tier Tribunal made fundamental errors about the respondent’s residence status and applied the wrong approach to the case. In particular, the Secretary of State contended that the First-tier Tribunal wrongly stated that the Secretary of State accepted the respondent had acquired a permanent right of residence, when the deportation decision letter had stated the opposite.

The Secretary of State also argued that the First-tier Tribunal failed properly to understand and engage with the evidence about the respondent’s risk of reoffending and risk of serious harm, placing undue emphasis on the respondent’s place of residence and relocation, and failing to appreciate that the probation evidence was not based solely on residence and was not limited to a single potential victim.

In addition, the Secretary of State complained of procedural unfairness arising from the way the First-tier Tribunal conducted the second hearing day: although further evidence was admitted following the Tribunal’s directions, the Secretary of State’s representative was not permitted to make submissions on that new evidence, despite the directions indicating both parties would be able to make further representations.

The Secretary of State’s requested relief in the Upper Tribunal was that the First-tier Tribunal’s decision be set aside. The Upper Tribunal granted that relief and ordered that the appeal be remitted for a fresh hearing with no preserved findings.
uk_statute_references_predicted: Tribunal Procedure (First-tier Tribunal) (Immigration and Asylum Chamber) Rules 2014

facts:
The claimant is a Nigerian national born on 16 October 1989. He entered the United Kingdom on 5 May 2011 with leave to enter as a student. That leave was due to expire on 30 July 2013 but was curtailed on 31 May 2012 following withdrawal of sponsorship. He was later granted leave to remain on the basis of family and private life until 29 May 2013, because he claimed a parental relationship with a British citizen child born in 2012; the decision records that he appears no longer to have any contact with that child.

The claimant later formed a relationship with a British citizen, JO, and they married on 17 November 2015. JO has a child from a previous relationship, and it is said that the child’s father has contact with that child. A child was born to the claimant and JO in 2016.

The claimant applied for leave to remain relying on his relationship with his wife. On 12 January 2016 the Secretary of State refused the application, on the basis that the relationship relied upon was not considered genuine and subsisting, that the relevant requirements were not met, and that there were no exceptional circumstances justifying a grant of leave on human rights grounds.

The First-tier Tribunal heard the claimant’s appeal on 14 December 2016, with both parties represented, and heard oral evidence from the claimant and his wife. In a decision sent on 9 January 2017, the First-tier Tribunal dismissed the appeal. It was not argued before that tribunal that the relevant requirements were met. The tribunal accepted the relationship was genuine, but concluded there was nothing exceptional to justify allowing the appeal outside the relevant framework. It considered it reasonable to expect the claimant to return to Nigeria and seek entry clearance, noting information suggesting such an application would take about 120 days. The tribunal concluded that although the right to respect for family life was engaged, removal would not have consequences of such gravity as to engage that right.

Permission to appeal was granted because it was thought the First-tier Tribunal might have failed to conduct an adequate assessment of the human rights issue and might have failed properly to consider the interests of the child of the marriage. The Secretary of State indicated non-opposition to setting aside the decision. At the Upper Tribunal hearing, the Secretary of State’s representative confirmed that position, and with the parties’ agreement the Upper Tribunal set aside the First-tier Tribunal’s decision. The Upper Tribunal considered that the earlier decision contained an inadequate analysis and too few material findings of fact, and that further evidence and extensive fact-finding would be needed. The case was therefore remitted to the First-tier Tribunal for a complete rehearing, with no findings preserved, to be heard at Manchester before a different judge.
claims:
The claimant appealed against the Secretary of State’s refusal of 12 January 2016 to grant him leave to remain on human rights grounds, relying on his family life with his British citizen wife and their child. His application and appeal sought leave to remain on the basis that removal would unjustifiably interfere with his family life.

Before the Upper Tribunal, the claimant pursued an appeal against the First-tier Tribunal’s dismissal of his human rights appeal. The grounds on which permission was granted were that the First-tier Tribunal may have failed to carry out an adequate assessment of the human rights issue and may have failed properly to consider the interests of the child of the marriage. The claimant did not advance arguments based on any other legal basis beyond the human rights claim.

At the Upper Tribunal hearing, the claimant’s representative asked for the case to be remitted for a fresh hearing, explaining that he did not have all the paperwork and that the claimant had expected the hearing to address only whether there was an error of law. The outcome sought was that the First-tier Tribunal decision be set aside and the human rights appeal be reheard.

facts:
The appellant is an Albanian national born in 1993. He said he left Albania on 17 April 2014, flew to Paris, stayed in France until mid‑2015, then entered the United Kingdom concealed in a lorry. He made a protection claim on 13 August 2015.

His account was that he and his family were associated with the Democratic Party in Albania. He said his father was a long‑time party member and, after the Democratic Party lost the general election on 23 June 2013, his father lost his job at the Post Office, which the appellant attributed to political affiliation.

The appellant said that in early 2014 he was arrested in connection with being near a demonstration outside the Greek embassy in Tirana. He claimed the police recognised him as a Democratic Party member and that a police officer assaulted him with a truncheon, injuring his right ear. He said he already had hearing problems in his left ear and that the assault caused hearing problems in his right ear. He said he was detained at a police station and was released the same day after Democratic Party MPs and/or deputies attended and secured his release. He said there was media coverage of his release and that he gave a statement to the media outside the police station.

He said that after returning to his home area of Kukes he was approached by well‑dressed individuals who threatened him, and that these threats caused him to leave Albania. He also claimed that after he left, his family experienced further problems due to political affiliation and that his brother was arrested in February 2015. He said his family later left Albania.

The Secretary of State accepted his nationality and accepted, based on a membership card, that he had been a member of the Democratic Party since 20 June 2013. The Secretary of State did not accept that he was an active member and rejected his account of detention and threats, relying on matters including perceived gaps in his political knowledge, inconsistencies and implausibilities in his narrative, and the view that he was able to leave Albania without difficulty. The Secretary of State also relied on delay in claiming protection and not claiming in France.

Before the First‑tier Tribunal, the appellant produced documentary bundles and brought a DVD said to contain footage of the assault, but no request was made during the hearing for it to be viewed; it was first raised in closing submissions. The First‑tier Tribunal declined to view it after the hearing. The First‑tier Tribunal identified multiple credibility concerns, including inconsistent accounts of events after release, inconsistencies about his party ID card, implausibility about contact with family after they allegedly left Albania, and lack of supporting evidence (including medical evidence about the alleged injury and evidence from family or party sources). The First‑tier Tribunal did not accept that he had been targeted as claimed, found he was an economic migrant, and dismissed the appeal on protection and human rights grounds. On further appeal, the Upper Tribunal concluded there was no material legal error in the First‑tier Tribunal’s approach and upheld the dismissal.
claims:
The appellant sought international protection and related relief in the United Kingdom on the basis that he faced harm in Albania connected to his and his family’s Democratic Party affiliation.

He claimed that because of his membership and support for the Democratic Party he was targeted by the police and others. He relied on an incident in early 2014 in which he said he was arrested at or near a demonstration outside the Greek embassy in Tirana, assaulted by a police officer with a truncheon causing injury and hearing problems, and detained at a police station until Democratic Party MPs and/or deputies intervened to secure his release. He said his release attracted media attention and he spoke to the media. He further claimed that after returning to Kukes he was threatened by well‑dressed individuals, prompting him to flee Albania. He also asserted that after his departure his family continued to face problems due to political affiliation, including his brother’s arrest in February 2015, and that his family later left Albania.

In challenging the refusal decision and pursuing his appeal, he argued that he was at risk because of his political involvement, and that evidence (including a video recording said to show the assault and a party letter said to support his political activity) supported his account.

In the Upper Tribunal proceedings, his arguments were that the First‑tier Tribunal materially erred by not considering the DVD/video evidence said to show the police attack; by failing to make findings on his claimed arrest and detention; and by making inconsistent findings about a Democratic Party letter (rejecting it as unreliable while accepting he was a party member). He sought the setting aside of the First‑tier Tribunal decision and a successful outcome on his protection claim.

facts:
The appellant is a Sri Lankan national of Tamil ethnicity. He said he comes from a family with past involvement with the LTTE. He claimed that, before leaving Sri Lanka, he was arrested, detained and tortured on at least two occasions. He said his grandmother then made arrangements for him to travel to the United Kingdom as a student. After spending some time in the United Kingdom, he claimed asylum.

The Secretary of State refused his protection claim on asylum and human rights grounds on 18 January 2017. The appellant appealed, but the First-tier Tribunal (Judge Price) dismissed the appeal in a decision promulgated on 12 June 2017. The First-tier Tribunal did not accept that the appellant was telling the truth, did not accept that he had been tortured in Sri Lanka, did not accept that he had a genuine fear of return because of his activities, and did not accept that his mental health diagnosis was caused by the reasons he claimed. The First-tier Tribunal also did not accept that he faced an adverse risk because of activities he had undertaken in the United Kingdom on behalf of Tamil diaspora groups.

In the Upper Tribunal proceedings, the appellant relied on, among other things, a letter from his grandmother sent from Sri Lanka, which on its face supported his account and indicated continuing interest in him by the Sri Lankan authorities. He also relied on a medical report by Dr Izquierdo-Martin describing scars on his back, explaining why they were typical of the treatment alleged, and considering and effectively ruling out other possible causes. There was also material relating to the appellant’s post-flight diaspora activities, including photographs said to have appeared online.

The Upper Tribunal found that the First-tier Tribunal had recorded the existence of the grandmother’s letter but had not addressed its contents. It also found that the First-tier Tribunal had not properly engaged with the scarring evidence in Dr Izquierdo-Martin’s report, despite its potential significance to whether the appellant had been tortured. The Upper Tribunal further found that the First-tier Tribunal had not properly addressed the evidence about the appellant’s diaspora activities, including the nature of the photographs and the unsustainable reasoning about their reach and whether they could come to the attention of the Sri Lankan authorities.

The Upper Tribunal concluded that these failures concerned important issues going to credibility and were material. It set aside the First-tier Tribunal’s decision and remitted the case to the First-tier Tribunal for a fresh determination on all issues, to be heard by a judge other than Judge Price.
claims:
The appellant’s underlying claim for protection was that he would be at risk if returned to Sri Lanka because he is an ethnic Tamil from a family with past LTTE involvement, because he himself had been arrested, detained and tortured on at least two occasions in Sri Lanka, and because there was continuing adverse interest in him from the Sri Lankan authorities. He also relied on his mental health condition as part of his case, contending it was linked to what he said had happened to him.

He further claimed that he would face risk on return due to activities he undertook in the United Kingdom on behalf of Tamil diaspora groups.

In his challenge to the First-tier Tribunal’s dismissal, he argued that the First-tier Tribunal: (1) failed properly to consider and made inconsistent findings about his diaspora activities; (2) failed properly to address the medical evidence from Dr Izquierdo-Martin concerning scarring consistent with his account of torture; and (3) failed to have regard to the evidence in the letter from his grandmother, which supported his account and indicated continuing interest by the Sri Lankan authorities. He sought that the First-tier Tribunal’s decision be set aside and the appeal reconsidered.
uk_statute_references_predicted: Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004

facts:
The appellant, D K, was born on 20 February 1999 and is a national of Albania. Her father is a British citizen. In September 2014, when she was 14 years old, she entered the United Kingdom as a visitor. She had been intending to visit cousins in Dublin but decided she wanted to live with her father and remained in the UK. The appellant stated that her mother left Albania in September 2016 to start a new life in Italy, where she now lives.

On 2 February 2018 the Secretary of State refused the appellant’s protection and human rights claim. The appellant made her claim when she was 18 years old. In support of her case she relied, among other evidence, on a report by Dr Joanna Hanson (a 10-page report with 52 paragraphs). There was also evidence from the appellant and from her father, and reference was made to background materials.

The appellant appealed to the First-tier Tribunal. First-tier Tribunal Judge Black dismissed her appeal in a decision promulgated on 3 October 2018. Permission to appeal to the Upper Tribunal was granted on 5 November 2018.

In the Upper Tribunal’s consideration of the First-tier Tribunal decision, it was noted that the First-tier Tribunal judge described the appellant as giving a consistent account but rejected parts of it due to the quality of documentary evidence and a delay in disclosing an important part of her claim, concluding that she lacked credibility. The First-tier Tribunal judge referred to Dr Hanson’s report but dismissed it briefly, stating it was based on speculation. The First-tier Tribunal judge also concluded there was no evidence showing the appellant faced a real risk of trafficking or gender exploitation beyond that faced by other lone women in Albania. On the human rights aspect, the First-tier Tribunal judge treated the appellant as a 19-year-old student who had lived with her father for four years, but rejected the existence of family life between them.

The Upper Tribunal found material errors of law in the First-tier Tribunal decision, set it aside, preserved none of its findings, and remitted the case to the First-tier Tribunal for a complete rehearing before a different judge.
claims:
The appellant sought international protection and relied on human rights grounds to resist removal to Albania.

Her protection claim was that she had a well-founded fear on return to Albania as a lone young woman, saying she would be vulnerable and unprotected and liable to fall prey to traffickers and other exploitation, including gender-based exploitation. She relied on her own evidence, her father’s evidence, an expert report from Dr Joanna Hanson, and background materials to support the asserted risk.

On the human rights claim, she argued that she had family life with her father in the UK. She relied on the fact that she had lived with him since she was 14 years old and asserted financial and emotional dependency on him. She contended that family life did not end simply because she had turned 18.

In her appeal to the Upper Tribunal, she argued that the First-tier Tribunal had (1) failed to give adequate reasons for placing little or no weight on the expert report, (2) applied the wrong standard when assessing risk, (3) failed to give adequate reasons for rejecting her account and credibility despite evidence from her and her father, and (4) carried out an inadequate assessment of her family life with her father. She asked the Upper Tribunal to set aside the First-tier Tribunal decision and remit the case for a fresh hearing.

facts:
The case concerns Mr Amir Jafar’s appeal against a decision dated 15 January 2019 refusing his human rights claim (said to have been made on 3 July 2017). The refusal relied heavily on an allegation that he had acted dishonestly in relation to an English language test: the Secretary of State stated that ETS records showed he took a TOEIC speaking test on 15 May 2013 at the Manchester College of Accountancy and Management, and that ETS voice verification analysis indicated significant evidence that the certificate had been fraudulently obtained through use of a proxy test taker. The Secretary of State also concluded he did not meet the relevant requirements for leave on private life grounds and that there were no exceptional circumstances such that refusal would breach his right to respect for private and family life.

Mr Jafar appealed to the First-tier Tribunal. His appeal was heard on 19 July 2019 by Judge Talbot and dismissed in a decision dated 6 August 2019. Mr Jafar did not attend the hearing, having asked for the appeal to be decided on the papers. The First-tier Tribunal concluded he did not meet the relevant private life requirements and, when addressing the deception allegation, noted that he denied deception but did not attend to have his evidence tested; the judge stated it was not necessary to make findings on deception. The First-tier Tribunal then dismissed the appeal after assessing the right to respect for private and family life outside the rules.

Permission to appeal to the Upper Tribunal was granted only on the issue that the First-tier Tribunal failed to make a specific finding on deception. In response to Upper Tribunal directions, the Secretary of State filed a skeleton argument dated 8 January 2020 stating that the allegation of deception was withdrawn. At the Upper Tribunal hearing, the Secretary of State confirmed she would not rely on the TOEIC deception allegation relating to 15 May 2013 when deciding any future applications by Mr Jafar. The Upper Tribunal considered that the First-tier Tribunal had erred in law by not determining the deception issue, but concluded that, because the allegation had been withdrawn and would not be relied upon in future, there was no longer any tangible benefit in determining it and the error was not material to the outcome. The Upper Tribunal therefore did not set aside the First-tier Tribunal’s decision, which remained in force.
claims:
Mr Jafar’s underlying application was a human rights claim seeking leave to remain, relying on his private and/or family life. In the refusal decision, the Secretary of State treated the application as falling for refusal on suitability grounds because of an allegation that he had used deception to obtain a TOEIC speaking test certificate in May 2013, and also concluded he did not meet the relevant private life requirements and that refusal would not breach his right to respect for private and family life.

On appeal to the First-tier Tribunal, Mr Jafar challenged the refusal. He denied the allegation that he had used deception in the English language test. He also pursued his human rights appeal on the basis that refusal would breach his right to respect for private and family life.

Before the Upper Tribunal, his permitted challenge was limited to arguing that the First-tier Tribunal erred by failing to make a specific finding on whether he had used deception in obtaining the English language test certificate. The practical relief sought through that ground was a determination of the deception allegation (and, by implication, correction of the First-tier Tribunal’s failure to decide it). During the Upper Tribunal proceedings, the Secretary of State withdrew the deception allegation and confirmed it would not be relied upon in future applications, leaving the deception issue no longer relevant to the outcome of the appeal.

facts:
The appellants are an uncle (first appellant) and his niece (second appellant), both citizens of El Salvador. They sought protection in the United Kingdom based on fear of gang violence in El Salvador.

A central event in the first appellant’s account was an incident on 20 June 2010 when a public bus was set alight by members of the gang Barrio 18. The first appellant said he witnessed the gang kill the driver and pour fuel into the bus. He broke a window and helped three people escape. He said gang members observed him and others helping, and that he was shot at from a distance and fled. The First-tier Tribunal’s preserved findings accepted that the bus incident occurred, that the first appellant did come forward to help people escape from the burning bus, and that gang members at a distance attempted to shoot at him but did not hit him.

After the 2010 incident, the first appellant said gang members came to his home four days later and told his wife he would be killed because he had helped people survive the bus attack. He said gang members then came repeatedly, initially about twice a week, repeating death threats, later less frequently. He described one occasion when he spoke to gang members through a window and they threatened him directly. He said that for years he largely stayed away from the family home, visiting only briefly and at times designed to avoid being seen, and that he was unable to work during this period.

From June 2016, the first appellant said gang members demanded money. He initially refused and contacted the police. He said his wife paid the gang $1,000 on one occasion, after which the gang demanded $5,000 each month. He described an occasion when gang members entered the home and took money themselves. He said he complained to the authorities.

He said harassment continued, including a threatening note in August 2018. He went into hiding. He said his daughters and his niece (the second appellant) were threatened and followed in the street. He said gang members saw him at his home in October 2018, threatened him with death again, and tried but failed to enter the property.

The second appellant lived with the first appellant and his immediate family. She described extortion connected to the first appellant’s wife’s food-selling business run from the garage and family home. She said gang members came to the property around six times in 2016 and that the first appellant reported matters to the authorities twice in 2016 but no police action was taken. She said that although she was not personally threatened between 2010 and 2017, the gang threatened the first appellant that they would take his daughters and that his daughters and the second appellant would be forced into prostitution. She described an incident in September 2018 when men shouted at her and the first appellant’s eldest daughter in the street, referring to forcing them to work as prostitutes. She believed they were members of the same gang. She did not report this to the police and later left her employment, giving notice in mid-October 2018.

The first appellant said that while there, questions were asked by another gang controlling that locality, and the family decided to leave El Salvador. Both appellants claimed protection on the basis that they feared persecution or serious harm from gangs in El Salvador.

He also claimed risk because gang members later extorted money from his household linked to the family’s business activities, and because he refused to continue paying the demanded sums and reported matters to the police. He maintained that these factors meant he would face serious harm if returned.

The second appellant’s claim was linked to the same events and threats affecting the first appellant and his household. She claimed that if returned she would be persecuted by the gang and could be killed, raped, or forced into prostitution because of the first appellant’s actions in 2010 and his later refusal to comply with extortion demands.

In the appeal proceedings before the Upper Tribunal, the appellants argued that the first appellant had a continuing risk profile as a witness/rescuer from the 2010 incident and as a victim of extortion who resisted gang demands, and that the second appellant’s risk followed from her association with him and the threats made against female family members. They relied on an expert report and country materials to argue that gangs can retain long-term interest in targets even after many years, that reporting to the authorities can increase danger due to corruption and information-sharing, and that effective protection would not be available. They also argued that internal relocation would not be safe or reasonable because gangs operate throughout the country, control territory, monitor movement, and newcomers can attract suspicion and checks, making it likely the appellants would be found and harmed.

They asked the Tribunal to allow their appeals and grant protection on the basis that they faced a real risk of persecution or serious harm on return, with no adequate state protection and no safe internal relocation alternative.
