facts:
The appellant is a Somali national born on 1 July 1996. She said she arrived in the United Kingdom and claimed asylum on 16 April 2017. Her initial asylum claim was refused on 25 September 2017 and her appeal against that refusal was dismissed in a decision promulgated on 23 October 2017, after which she became appeal rights exhausted on 6 April 2018. In the 2017 appeal, the tribunal made significant adverse credibility findings and found that she had fabricated her claim. It also found that she had family in Mogadishu and was in contact with them at that time. Although she was living with her father in the UK at the time of the 2017 hearing, he did not give written or oral evidence in support of that appeal.

After becoming appeal rights exhausted, she made further submissions. She asserted that she would be at risk if returned to Somalia because she would be a lone woman, because she was a member of a minority clan, and because of the general security situation. She also relied on family life said to have been established in the UK with her father.

In her later evidence about family in Somalia, she stated in writing that she had no family left in Somalia and that she had been told by a member of the Somali community that her family had fled to Ethiopia, but that neither she nor her father had been able to locate them there. In her oral evidence before the First-tier Tribunal, she said she did not know where her family were (possibly Ethiopia or Kenya), that her father had tried to find them, that she herself had not tried, and that she had not contacted the Red Cross. She said her family fled Somalia in mid-2018.

Her father provided a written statement dated 28 January 2019 (said to be materially identical to his statement before the First-tier Tribunal). He said he fled Somalia in 1998 due to escalated conflict and because of minority clan membership, entered the UK in 1999, and was granted refugee status in 2004. He said that after arriving in the UK he learned his family were in Kenya; he visited them in 2010 and then sponsored their entry to the UK for family reunion. He said that at that time the appellant was not with the family in Kenya and he did not know where she was, as the family had lost contact with her while they were still in Somalia. He said he contacted the Red Cross to find her but received no information, and that they later resumed contact in the UK. He asserted that the appellant had no family left in Somalia.

In his oral evidence before the First-tier Tribunal, the father said he had heard that his family members (the appellant’s mother and siblings) had left Somalia and travelled to either Kenya or Ethiopia, and that he had attempted to contact them through the Somali community. He said he did not know exactly when they left but thought it was the end of 2017 and that he had known they were planning to leave. He said he did not know whether the appellant’s uncles remained in Somalia and had no way of contacting them. He said his contact with the Red Cross was in 2010 and there had been no news.

The First-tier Tribunal treated the 2017 decision as the starting point and found no reason to depart from the earlier adverse credibility findings. It found the appellant not credible and found the father’s evidence lacked detail and did not corroborate her account. It found inconsistencies between the appellant’s and her father’s evidence (including about when the family fled) and noted the lack of detail about efforts to trace family members and the absence of information about the whereabouts of uncles who had previously supported her. It concluded there was no credible evidence to displace the earlier finding that she had family in Mogadishu and would return with family and clan support, and therefore she would not be at risk on return.

On her human rights case, the appellant’s evidence was that after arriving in the UK she re-established a relationship with her father, lived with him and his family (who were British citizens), and took part in family responsibilities including helping her father (who was disabled), assisting with household duties, and helping with the children’s daily needs. She said her father supported her. The father’s evidence on their relationship was limited to saying she lived with him. The First-tier Tribunal found she had established only a limited private life since April 2017, and that her care for her father was no more than would be expected from a child towards a parent; it found the level of care was not substantial enough to show dependence and noted that before the appellant arrived these tasks were carried out by the step-mother. It concluded there was no established family life for these purposes and that removal would not be disproportionate.

The Upper Tribunal upheld the First-tier Tribunal’s decision, concluding it was open to the First-tier Tribunal to find there was no credible evidence to depart from the 2017 findings about family in Somalia, and that the evidence of family life in the UK was very thin and did not establish dependence beyond normal adult child/parent ties.
claims:
In her further submissions (and subsequent appeal), the appellant sought protection and permission to remain in the UK on the basis that she would face harm if returned to Somalia. She argued she would be at risk because she would be a lone woman, because she was a member of a minority clan, and because of the general security situation. She also relied on her relationship with her father in the UK, asserting that she had established family life with him and that removal would breach her right to respect for family and private life.

In challenging the refusal and the First-tier Tribunal’s dismissal, she argued that the tribunal’s approach to the evidence was wrong. She relied on evidence that her father had been granted refugee status, contending this was not before the tribunal in 2017 and supported her claim that she had suffered the same persecution in Somalia. She also argued it was unfair for the tribunal to find her father had not tried to locate family through the community when the Red Cross had been contacted, and she contended there was no proper basis for finding she still had family in Somalia.

On her human rights case, she argued the tribunal made errors in its assessment of her relationship with her father, including applying the wrong approach to whether family life existed and failing properly to recognise the significance of her caring role for him. She also relied on the history of separation from her father due to conflict and the re-establishment of their relationship in the UK since 2017 as part of her case that removal would be unjustified.

She further argued that the tribunal failed to consider up-to-date country information which, she said, supported her claim to be at risk on return because of her clan membership and as a lone woman.

The relief she sought through these claims was the overturning of the refusal of her protection and human rights claim and a finding that she should not be removed to Somalia.

facts:
Mr D Dass brought a complaint to an Industrial Tribunal alleging racial discrimination by Tower Hamlets College. His originating complaint form (IT1) set out the details of his complaint briefly, in about 15 lines. The Industrial Tribunal unanimously dismissed his complaint of racial discrimination.

Mr Dass then appealed to the Employment Appeal Tribunal. His appeal paperwork was extensive: a 17-page notice of appeal, a 13½-page affidavit, and a 5-page skeleton argument. At a preliminary hearing held ex parte on 13 May 1998, the Employment Appeal Tribunal considered that the notice of appeal did not clearly identify the points of law relied upon and contained a large amount of material that was not points of law. The Tribunal decided not to hear the appeal on the basis of the existing documents and instead adjourned the preliminary hearing generally, giving Mr Dass permission to amend his notice of appeal so that it contained only the points of law.

Mr Dass had received some assistance that day from ELAAS, and the Tribunal considered it likely that this would help him produce a proper and concise amended notice of appeal. Mr Dass welcomed the adjournment proposal. The Tribunal warned that if, when the matter returned, the amended notice of appeal still did not comply with the required approach, the appeal might be struck out for non-compliance. The Tribunal therefore adjourned the preliminary hearing with liberty to restore once Mr Dass had amended his notice of appeal accordingly.
claims:
Mr Dass’s underlying claim before the Industrial Tribunal was that Tower Hamlets College had subjected him to racial discrimination. That claim was dismissed by the Industrial Tribunal.

In his appeal to the Employment Appeal Tribunal, Mr Dass sought to challenge the Industrial Tribunal’s decision, but the Tribunal found that his notice of appeal did not clearly identify the points of law forming the grounds of appeal and included extensive irrelevant material. The judgment does not set out the specific legal grounds or the precise order Mr Dass sought on appeal, beyond indicating that he was appealing the dismissal of his racial discrimination complaint.

facts:
Mr Dominic Kelly was a professional oboist who also worked as a “professional fixer” in the music industry, assembling musicians for commercial engagements. He was Managing Director and fixer of the English Session Orchestra. He had been a member of the Musicians’ Union since February 1999. Separately from his union membership, he had also been an approved contractor of the Union under a commercial agreement dated 10 January 2000 (the “Approved Contractor Agreement”).

By letter dated 24 January 2018, the Union’s General Secretary, Mr Horace Trubridge, informed Mr Kelly that the Union had received a number of serious complaints from musicians whom Mr Kelly had booked for work. The complaints alleged sexual harassment, discrimination, bullying and threatening behaviour. The letter stated that the complaints had been investigated under the Union’s disciplinary procedures and that disciplinary charges would be considered by the Union’s Disciplinary Sub-Committee.

It was common ground that the alleged disciplinary offences were said to have occurred more than 28 days before the dates on which the complaints were made to the General Secretary. In response to a request from Mr Kelly, Mr Trubridge wrote on 25 January 2018 that the allegations dated within the last four years, other than one described as historical.

Mr Kelly provided a substantive response by letter dated 9 February 2018 and attended a Disciplinary Sub-Committee meeting on 14 February 2018. By decision letter dated 16 February 2018, the Disciplinary Sub-Committee upheld charges of sexual harassment and of bullying and threatening behaviour, and dismissed a charge of discrimination. It indicated that the sanction would be expulsion from Union membership, with the period to be determined by the Union’s Executive Committee.

Mr Kelly appealed by letter dated 4 March 2018. In a letter dated 8 March 2018, the Union stated that the Executive Committee had decided the expulsion would be for 10 years and that Mr Kelly’s approved contractor status would also be removed for 10 years. The same letter stated that the Union could and did treat his behaviour as a fundamental breach of the Approved Contractor Agreement and that no notice was required in the event of such a fundamental breach.

Mr Kelly did not attend the appeal hearing on 20 April 2018, but he provided further written representations, including a letter dated 13 April 2018 and a letter from his solicitors dated 12 April 2018. By letter dated 24 April 2018, Mr Trubridge informed Mr Kelly that the appeal had been dismissed, confirmed the 10-year expulsion, stated that his approved contractor status had been removed, and that he had been placed on the “Ask us First List” (a placement later removed).

On 14 August 2018, Mr Kelly made a complaint to the Certification Officer about the Union’s disciplinary proceedings and decisions of 16 February, 8 March and 24 April 2018. The Certification Officer treated the issue of whether the Union’s rules permitted disciplinary proceedings where complaints were made more than 28 days after the alleged offences as a preliminary issue.

Evidence before the Certification Officer included that, following the #MeToo campaign, the Union had set up an online “Safe Space” for members to report sexual harassment at work, and that the complaints against Mr Kelly were reported through that system. All alleged incidents were reported to the Union more than 28 days after they occurred. The Union regarded the complaints as very serious and decided it had to institute disciplinary proceedings. It was also said that the disciplinary rules in their current form had been in place since around 2004 and that this was the first time the Union had considered the impact of the 28-day provision.

The Certification Officer decided that the Union’s rules did not permit disciplinary action in respect of complaints made outside the 28-day period and set aside the sanctions imposed on Mr Kelly, including the 10-year expulsion. She also concluded that the Executive Committee had removed Mr Kelly’s approved contractor status as part of the disciplinary process and made an order restricting the Union from removing that status on the basis of the same information used in the disciplinary process.

The Union appealed. The Employment Appeal Tribunal allowed the appeal on the preliminary issue, holding that the Union’s rules, properly construed, gave the General Secretary a discretion to initiate disciplinary proceedings even where the complaint was made more than 28 days after the alleged offence. The Tribunal therefore set aside the Certification Officer’s decision and the enforcement order in its entirety.

The Tribunal also addressed the approved contractor issue. It found that although approved contractor status derived from a separate commercial agreement, the Union had purported to remove that status by way of a sanction imposed through the disciplinary process. The Tribunal considered that imposing that sanction through the disciplinary process was a breach of the Union’s rules and that the Certification Officer was therefore right to treat the matter as within her jurisdiction. However, the Tribunal considered that any order must be clear and, in any event, indicated that if the Union’s appeal on the preliminary issue had failed it would have set aside the particular paragraph of the Certification Officer’s order dealing with approved contractor status because of uncertainty about its effect.
claims:
Mr Kelly complained to the Certification Officer that the Union had breached its own rules by instituting and pursuing disciplinary proceedings against him based on complaints made more than 28 days after the alleged disciplinary offences. He sought to have the disciplinary outcomes set aside on the basis that the Union had no power under its rules to proceed in those circumstances.

In his complaint, he identified the relevant disciplinary steps and decisions as those taken on 16 February 2018 (the Disciplinary Sub-Committee decision), 8 March 2018 (the Executive Committee’s decision on sanction and related communication), and 24 April 2018 (dismissal of his appeal and confirmation of sanctions).

In addition to the time-limit point, Mr Kelly’s particulars also raised complaints of unfairness in the disciplinary process, including: alleged failure adequately to particularise the charges; alleged failure to specify the available sanctions; alleged inadequacy of the appeal procedure; and alleged failure to allow him legal representation before the Disciplinary and Appeals Sub-Committees.

As relief, Mr Kelly sought the setting aside of the sanctions imposed through the disciplinary process, including restoration of his Union membership (he had been expelled for 10 years). He also sought relief concerning his removal as an approved contractor, contending that this removal had been imposed as part of the disciplinary process; he sought an order preventing the Union from removing his approved contractor status on the basis of the information considered in that disciplinary process. The Certification Officer declined to grant the wider form of order sought in relation to the approved contractor relationship, but did make a more limited order aimed at preventing the Union from re-imposing a similar sanction through a Union process arising from his membership and based on the same information.

facts:
HMRC issued two decisions dated 12 December 2002 concerning Class 1 National Insurance contributions in relation to two “specimen” individuals. Each decision treated Goldman Sachs International (GSI) as liable for primary and secondary Class 1 contributions on amounts described as arising from the exercise of “Unapproved Share Options” in the tax years 1997/1998, 1998/1999 and 1999/2000, and stated amounts said to be due and amounts already paid.

The preliminary issue arose because, although HMRC initially treated GSI as the secondary contributor, GSI later contended that another group company, Goldman Sachs Services Ltd (GSSL), was the secondary contributor. HMRC responded that GSSL was outside the relevant jurisdiction for secondary contribution purposes and that GSI, being within the jurisdiction, was liable as the “host employer.”

For the purposes of the preliminary issue, the Tribunal proceeded on a limited evidential basis and made a number of working assumptions (without determining the main dispute about whether the option-related sums were “earnings,” how or when they were paid, or the employees’ own positions). The Tribunal accepted, as the basis on which the issue was argued, HMRC’s understanding that during a first period (from 6 April 1997 to around June/July 1999) the relevant employees (including the two specimen individuals) were contractually employed by GSSL and seconded to work for other Goldman Sachs entities, with most (including the two specimen individuals) seconded to work for GSI in the UK; and that during a second period (around June/July 1999 to 5 April 2000) some employees (including the two specimen individuals) were employed by and worked for GSI.

It was accepted that GSSL was incorporated in the British Virgin Islands, was not registered in England and Wales or Scotland, and was not resident in any part of the UK at the relevant times. It was not disputed that GSI was within the jurisdiction.

The Tribunal found as fact that GSSL did not have a place of business in Great Britain during the relevant period (1997–2000). In reaching that conclusion, it relied on (among other things) GSSL’s earlier stance in the proceedings that it had no place of business in Great Britain; GSSL’s 1991 notice to Companies House that it had ceased to have a place of business in Great Britain; and contemporaneous letters written on GSI notepaper by a senior individual stating that GSSL had no office in London and did not conduct business in the UK.

The Tribunal then considered whether GSSL was nevertheless “present” in Great Britain. It found that GSSL was not present in Great Britain. In particular, it found that GSSL had no office or other specific location in Great Britain, no identifiable address for service in Great Britain, and was not present by reason of UK bank accounts or banking activity. It also found that GSSL was not present by reference to the activities of its employees in Great Britain because they were seconded to other entities (not working for GSSL’s business), and that payroll and related administrative functions for those employees were performed in the UK by GSI under a services agreement under which GSI provided payroll, benefits and related administrative services and was responsible for providing remuneration and benefits (with reimbursement by GSSL). The Tribunal was not persuaded that the presence in Great Britain of a director associated with GSSL was sufficient to constitute GSSL’s presence for these purposes.

On the basis of those findings, the Tribunal concluded that GSSL was a “foreign employer” for the relevant purposes and that, for the period when the two specimen individuals were employed by GSSL and seconded to GSI, their personal service was made available to GSI, was rendered for the purposes of GSI’s business, and began after 6 April 1994. The Tribunal therefore found that GSI was the host employer of the two specimen individuals throughout those parts of the relevant period when GSI was not directly their employer.
claims:
GSI appealed HMRC’s decisions that treated GSI as liable for primary and secondary Class 1 contributions in respect of the two specimen individuals’ option-related amounts. In the preliminary issue, GSI’s position was that GSI should not be treated as the secondary contributor for the period when the individuals were contractually employed by GSSL and seconded to GSI.

GSI argued that GSSL, not GSI, was the secondary contributor because GSSL was “present” in Great Britain at the relevant times, even though it was not resident and (as GSI initially put its case) did not have a place of business in Great Britain. GSI contended that the jurisdictional test for being “present” was not stipulated and could be satisfied without residence or a place of business. In closing submissions, GSI also advanced an alternative contention that, if its main argument on “presence” failed, the Tribunal might instead find that GSSL had a place of business in Great Britain.

Accordingly, the relief GSI sought on the preliminary issue was a determination that GSI was not the secondary contributor by virtue of being a host employer, because GSSL was within the jurisdiction (by presence, and alternatively by having a place of business), so that GSSL should bear any secondary contribution liability for the relevant period.

facts:
Mourne Properties Limited is a Northern Ireland company established in 1976, whose principal activity was described in its accounts as property development. Its business was largely regional: it typically acquired and dealt in land and property within roughly a 30-mile radius of Newry, relying on local knowledge to identify sites and add value (for example through planning and zoning). It had not previously been involved in property or ventures outside the UK.

On 2 July 2007 the company purchased 300 “A” Units in the Anglo Irish Federal Street UK Limited Partnership (the Fund) for a total price of US$3 million. It funded US$1.5 million from cash reserves and borrowed the remaining US$1.5 million from Anglo Irish Bank. The bank’s loan letter described the facility as a loan to assist with the company’s proposed investment in the Fund by becoming a limited partner. The company held about 11% of the units in the Fund.

The Fund was promoted by Anglo-Irish Bank Private Banking and was marketed through a confidential information memorandum (the Prospectus) sent to selected qualified investors. The Prospectus described the opportunity as a potential investment in limited partnership interests and stated the aim was to provide investors with capital growth from an office asset with ground floor retail accommodation in downtown Boston, Massachusetts (the Landmark Building at 160 Federal Street). The Prospectus included risk factors, including that the Fund was not suitable for investors needing liquidity or short/medium-term access to capital, and described it as a long-term investment where investors would not normally be able to access their investment until the underlying property was sold. It indicated an intended cash return after about 5 to 8 years, though the holding period could be shorter or longer.

The tribunal did not see the document establishing the Fund or the company’s subscription agreement, but the dispute proceeded on the basis that the binding terms materially reflected those in the Prospectus. The period of holding and any exit were to be determined by the Fund’s management rather than by the company. The Fund’s term was stated as eight years from the closing date (30 June 2007) but could be varied at the general partner’s discretion, up to a maximum of ten years.

The company’s initial bank loan was extended by a supplemental facility letter signed on 5 June 2008, pursuant to a company resolution of the same date, extending the facility to 30 June 2009. That resolution referred to the company’s “investment” in the partnership.

The Fund itself entered into a further limited partnership arrangement with a Taurus entity under an agreement dated 30 March 2007. The tribunal noted provisions concerning buy/sell mechanisms that could be invoked only in limited circumstances, including after the eighth anniversary of the agreement.

Evidence was given by two directors/shareholders, Mr Craig Best (a chartered surveyor) and Mr Daniel McKevitt Sr (with a construction background). Mr Best was the prime mover behind the purchase. He said the company borrowed additional funds to increase returns and believed value could be added to the Boston building by restructuring tenancies. He said that despite statements in the Prospectus about term, he had discussions with the bank suggesting they did not intend to be involved for eight years and he envisaged involvement for around two years (accepting in cross-examination that two to three years was fair). He said that changing financial conditions in 2008 made disinvestment impossible and the company had no choice but to remain invested. The units were eventually sold in 2014; permission was sought from the general partner to sell, and Mr Best said the company was forced to sell by its bankers.

Mr McKevitt accepted Mr Best led the purchase and said the aim was to “flip” fairly quickly, with an expected duration of about two years, though he would defer to Mr Best’s judgment. He also described the company’s other property holdings and development sites reflected in its accounts.

The tribunal found that, compared with the company’s usual trading stock (property it owned directly and could sell or deal with as it wished), the company could not sell or manage the Boston building and had not inspected it before investing. It was reliant on the Prospectus and its bankers’ recommendation, had no day-to-day control over management, and there was no evidence it was consulted on leasing decisions. The tribunal found the company could not in reality add value to the building and that any return would be the product of putting money into the Fund rather than anything the company did during the holding period. The tribunal also found that from the outset there were real impediments to exiting within two to three years and that an early exit would likely have been very difficult. The units were sold in 2014 by transfer of the units rather than by any sale of the underlying building.
claims: The company appealed HMRC’s decision that the 300 “A” Units it purchased in the Fund were an investment and therefore should not be treated as part of the company’s trading stock. The company’s position was that the purchase was initially and remained, for the relevant periods, trading stock because it was made in the ordinary course of its business as a long-established property company. It argued in substance that it intended a relatively short holding period (around two to three years) and that it expected to make profit by adding value to the underlying property (for example by restructuring tenancies), consistent with its property development/trading activities. The relief sought was for the units to be treated as trading stock for corporation tax purposes, rather than as an investment, so that HMRC’s amendments and assessments/determinations based on investment treatment would not stand.

facts:
The Trustees of the Harbour of Dundee (the Trustees) derived from the town of Dundee rights connected with the harbour of Dundee, described as a free port, based on ancient charters. Those charters set out geographical limits extending several miles on both sides of the River Tay estuary, and it was admitted that Ferry-port-on-Craig lay within those charter limits on the south side of the river.

Ferry-port-on-Craig was a harbour on the opposite side of the firth from Dundee, in the county of Fife, with frequent ferry communication to Dundee. Ferry-port-on-Craig belonged to William Stark Dougall.

The Trustees’ statutory powers referred to “the harbour of Dundee and the precincts thereof” but did not state precise limits. A dispute arose as to whether Ferry-port-on-Craig fell within the “precincts” for the purpose of levying harbour dues.

Dougall did not produce an express grant of a “free port” for Ferry-port-on-Craig; his titles were described as containing a grant of “portus” (and related ferry privileges), and he asserted there was sufficient colour of title. Independently of any such title, Dougall alleged and the Trustees ultimately admitted (as the equivalent of a jury finding on the first issue) that, from time immemorial and for the prescriptive period, vessels had loaded and unloaded at Ferry-port-on-Craig and the Trustees had never levied dues on those vessels. The courts treated this as a use of the harbour inconsistent with the Trustees’ asserted right to levy dues there.

In the proceedings below, two issues had been directed: one concerning the long-standing loading and unloading at Ferry-port-on-Craig without payment of dues to the Trustees, and another concerning whether Dougall had a right himself to levy dues there. After the Trustees admitted the first issue, the Inner House considered it unnecessary to decide the second issue. The result in substance was that Dougall was absolved from the Trustees’ claim to levy dues on ships loading and unloading at Ferry-port-on-Craig. On appeal, the House of Lords affirmed that outcome, while indicating that the judgment should not be taken as deciding that Dougall had a right of free port or a positive right to levy dues, and that the interdict should not be treated as extending beyond the harbour of Ferry-port-on-Craig as covered by the admitted issue.
claims:
The Trustees raised an action of declarator seeking a declaration that they had the sole and exclusive right to levy harbour dues at Ferry-port-on-Craig, and sought to prevent Dougall from resisting their levying of such dues there.

Their case was that Ferry-port-on-Craig was within the area covered by their rights as transferred and confirmed to them, and within the “harbour of Dundee and the precincts thereof,” so that they were entitled to levy the scheduled dues there. They argued that their ancient charters clearly defined limits that included Ferry-port-on-Craig, and that the statutory transfer and scheme confirmed their exclusive right to levy dues within those limits.

They contended that Dougall’s reliance on long non-levy of dues by the Trustees could not defeat their right: (i) mere omission or non-user by a body charged with public duties should not amount to abandonment or dereliction of the right to levy dues at a particular point within the granted limits; (ii) a negative usage (ships loading and unloading without paying dues to the Trustees) could not be used to cut down or interpret an unambiguous grant; and (iii) it was insufficient, as a defence, to show only that dues were not paid to the Trustees—rather, Dougall would need to show a competing positive right in himself (such as an earlier inconsistent grant) or actual enjoyment of levying dues by him.

They also argued that Dougall’s titles did not amount to a grant of a free port or of the right to levy dues, and that his ownership of the landing place or soil did not provide a basis to resist their claim.

In the appeal, the Trustees further sought to challenge the form and breadth of the lower court’s orders, arguing that the interdict and declarator went too far by effectively treating Ferry-port-on-Craig (and its “precincts”) as exempt in a way that could be read as establishing in Dougall a free-port status or a right to levy dues, and by assoilzing him from the whole conclusions of the action. They sought reversal of the interlocutors, or at least narrowing/variation so that any restraint on the Trustees would be confined to what was strictly justified and would not imply that Dougall had a right of free port or a general right to levy dues.

facts:
Patrick Terrance Maginnis was indicted on three drug-related counts. The appeal concerned only count 1 (possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply it unlawfully to another) and count 2 (an alternative count relating to the same drugs, alleging simple unlawful possession). Count 3 related to a different smaller quantity of drugs and was not relevant to the appeal.

At trial in the Inner London Crown Court before a judge and jury, Maginnis pleaded not guilty to count 1 but guilty to count 2. The prosecution did not accept the guilty plea to count 2, and the trial proceeded on count 1.

The prosecution evidence was that, after Maginnis had been arrested in connection with an alleged assault, police searched his car and found a package containing 227 grammes of cannabis resin under the driver’s seat. The cannabis resin was said to have a street value of about £500.

Maginnis told police officers that he did not deal in drugs and that the package had been left in his car the previous evening by a friend. He refused to name the friend and said that he expected the friend to come round and pick the package up.

At the close of the prosecution case, Maginnis’s counsel asked the trial judge to direct the jury that, if they accepted that Maginnis’s intention was merely to return the package to the person who had left it in the car, that would not amount to an intention to supply it to another, and he should therefore be acquitted on count 1. The judge ruled that an intention to return the package to the person who had left it in the car did amount to the requisite intent for conviction on count 1. Following that ruling, Maginnis changed his plea on count 1 to guilty and was sentenced to 12 months’ imprisonment.

Maginnis appealed. The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal and quashed the conviction on count 1. The prosecution then sought and obtained certification that a point of law of general public importance was involved and leave to appeal further.

In the House of Lords, the appeal was brought by the Commissioner of Police for the Metropolis on behalf of the Crown, seeking review and reversal of the Court of Appeal’s order. The House of Lords reversed the Court of Appeal’s order (except as to legal aid) and restored Maginnis’s conviction on count 1. The certified question was amended to ask whether a person in unlawful possession of a controlled drug deposited with him for safe keeping has the intent to supply if his intention is to return the drug to the person who deposited it with him; the House answered that amended question “yes” and remitted the matter to the Court of Appeal to proceed consistently with that judgment.

The House of Lords’ reasoning proceeded on the assumed factual basis that Maginnis had been made custodian of the drugs by an unnamed friend and that Maginnis intended to hand the drugs back to that friend when asked. The judgment noted that these assumed facts had not been tested before the jury because Maginnis changed his plea after the judge’s ruling.
claims:
The appeal to the House of Lords was brought by the Crown (through the Commissioner of Police for the Metropolis) seeking to have the Court of Appeal’s order of 10 March 1986 reviewed and reversed (or varied/altered), and to have Maginnis’s conviction on count 1 restored.

The Crown’s argument was that, for the offence charged in count 1, an intention to return the controlled drug to the person who had deposited it with the defendant amounted to an intention to “supply” the drug to another. In substance, the Crown contended that handing the drugs back to the depositor would constitute supplying them, because it would enable the recipient to use the drugs for the recipient’s own purposes.

Maginnis’s position at trial (advanced through his counsel’s request for a direction) was that if his intention was merely to return the package to the friend who had left it in the car, that intention would not amount to an intent to supply to another, and he should be acquitted on count 1. This reflected the argument accepted by the Court of Appeal when it quashed the conviction: that “supply” should not be treated as satisfied by a mere transfer of physical control, and that returning an item left for safe keeping was not, in ordinary language, an act of supplying it.

Before the House of Lords, the issue was framed by the certified question (as amended) focusing on whether intent to supply is established where a person unlawfully possessing a controlled drug deposited with him for safe keeping intends to return it to the depositor. The Crown sought an affirmative answer; Maginnis’s position (consistent with the Court of Appeal’s decision) was that the answer should be negative.

facts: The complainant made two information requests to the Department for International Development (DfID). The requests concerned (1) what legislation governs DfID’s actions and (2) details about DfID’s published accounts. DfID refused to comply with both requests on the basis that they were vexatious. The Information Commissioner considered the complaint and decided that both requests were vexatious and that DfID was entitled to refuse them. The decision notice records that no further action was required and that the decision was under appeal to the Information Tribunal at the time of the notice.
claims: The complainant sought disclosure of information from DfID about the legislation governing DfID’s actions and about details of DfID’s published accounts. After DfID refused both requests as vexatious, the complainant pursued a complaint to the Information Commissioner, effectively challenging DfID’s refusal and seeking a decision requiring DfID to provide the requested information.

facts: The complainant made a request to Pembrokeshire College for information about the College’s employment of a named individual and about the qualifications of a student. The College disclosed some information in response but withheld other information on the basis that it was third-party personal data. The Information Commissioner considered the complaint and concluded that the College had provided all the recorded information it was able to provide and that the withheld material was correctly withheld as third-party personal data. No further steps were required of the College.
claims: The complainant sought disclosure of information concerning (1) details of the College’s employment of a named individual and (2) the qualifications of a student. The complainant’s complaint to the Information Commissioner, as reflected in the decision, was that the College had not provided all the requested information and that the withheld information should be disclosed rather than withheld as third-party personal data.

facts:
The case concerns a long-running dispute involving Andras Szucs, his former employer, and the UK Intellectual Property Office (UKIPO) about certain patent applications. In October 1989, arising from that wider dispute, Mr Szucs made a complaint alleging misconduct by a patent agent. The complaint was handled under a procedure in which the Comptroller (through an Assistant Comptroller) investigates allegations of misconduct by inviting the patent agent complained about to provide a confidential written response.

As part of the investigation into Mr Szucs’s 1989 complaint, an Assistant Comptroller sent the complaint to the patent agent and invited a response. The patent agent replied by letter dated 21 November 1989. That letter is the specific document at the centre of the later information request and appeal. The investigation proceeded to a decision that there was no evidence of misconduct discreditable to a patent agent; the parties were informed and no further action was taken.

From 1990 onwards, Mr Szucs continued to pursue complaints against the patent agent and the Patent Office/UKIPO in various forums.

On 2 February 2005, Mr Szucs made an information request to UKIPO seeking access to all relevant files on his complaint going back to 1989 (as outlined in earlier correspondence). UKIPO replied substantively on 24 March 2005, disclosing almost all the material but withholding the patent agent’s 21 November 1989 letter. Mr Szucs sought an internal review on 22 November 2005; UKIPO upheld the refusal and communicated the review outcome on 6 December 2005.

Mr Szucs complained to the Information Commissioner on 14 December 2005, asking the Commissioner to investigate UKIPO’s refusal to disclose the patent agent’s statement/letter. The Commissioner investigated and issued a decision notice dated 3 July 2007 concluding that the withheld letter was exempt from disclosure and that UKIPO had handled the request in accordance with the applicable information-access regime.

Mr Szucs appealed to the Tribunal on 30 July 2007. The Tribunal joined UKIPO as an additional party. The appeal was determined on written submissions and an agreed bundle, without an oral hearing. The Tribunal also reviewed the withheld letter itself; it was not shown to Mr Szucs during the appeal process.

The Tribunal found that the 1989 investigation into the complaint was an inquiry conducted by the Assistant Comptroller under the relevant complaint-investigation procedure. It accepted evidence that the patent agent’s 21 November 1989 letter was requested by and provided to UKIPO solely for the purposes of that inquiry, and that the patent agent could reasonably have assumed it would remain confidential unless a further step (a hearing) was ordered. The Tribunal concluded that UKIPO held the letter only because it was contained in a document placed in the custody of the person conducting the inquiry for the purposes of the inquiry, and that later filing arrangements or whether copies existed elsewhere did not alter that characterisation.
claims:
Mr Szucs sought disclosure from UKIPO of all relevant files relating to his 1989 complaint, including the patent agent’s letter of 21 November 1989. After UKIPO refused to disclose that letter, he requested an internal review and then asked the Information Commissioner to investigate UKIPO’s refusal.

In his appeal to the Tribunal, Mr Szucs’s central argument was that the withheld letter did not fall within the exemption relied upon to refuse disclosure. He also argued that the inquiry into his complaint had not been properly conducted and that due inquiry into the patent agent’s conduct and possible removal from the register were not the prime considerations.

Mr Szucs further contended that UKIPO had been inconsistent in its approach: (1) he asserted that UKIPO initially relied only on one basis for withholding the letter and only later raised the inquiry-related exemption; and (2) he argued that because UKIPO had disclosed other documents that, in his view, could also have been withheld under the same exemption, UKIPO should be directed to act consistently and disclose the disputed letter as well.

Overall, the relief he sought through the appeal was that the decision notice be overturned so that UKIPO would be required to disclose the patent agent’s 21 November 1989 letter.

facts:
In December 1997 an incident occurred at a house in Brighton. On 28 November 1998 Stafford Freeborn was convicted of wounding with intent arising from that incident and was sentenced to seven years’ imprisonment. He maintained that he had acted in self-defence and that he had been wrongly convicted. He complained strongly about the way Sussex Police investigated and handled the case and their subsequent conduct. A central issue for him was a tape of a 999 call made by a witness, which he regarded as crucial trial evidence and which he alleged the police had interfered with.

From around 2000 onwards Mr Freeborn made many complaints to Sussex Police and to the police complaints body, and from 2005 he made many information requests to Sussex Police, particularly about the 999 tape and the handling of his complaints. He complained to the Information Commissioner that Sussex Police had not complied with five such information requests. The Commissioner issued a decision notice in October 2007. Mr Freeborn appealed. At a preliminary hearing in February 2008 he agreed not to pursue the third and fourth requests, leaving the first, second and fifth requests for determination.

First request (January/February 2005): Mr Freeborn’s request proceeded on the premise that a sealed “master copy” cassette of the 999 call had been removed from police evidence stores and destroyed before 2000. The Tribunal distinguished between the sealed master cassette copy and the “working copy” derived from the original reel-to-reel recording of 999 calls. The evidence Mr Freeborn relied on for destruction was a letter from his solicitor to another body in 2002 referring to a note of a 2000 telephone conversation with a police officer stating “master tapes-no longer exist,” and a vague recollection of being told on another occasion that original tapes had been destroyed. Sussex Police evidence was that the original reel-to-reel tape of all 999 calls would have been recorded over after relevant parts were copied to cassette, which could have caused confusion. During the hearing Mr Freeborn produced a photograph of a cassette taken while it was in the possession of another body involved in reviewing his case from September 2004; Sussex Police identified it as the master copy. The Tribunal accepted that identification and concluded the master copy had not been destroyed and that the information Mr Freeborn sought about who destroyed it, when, and who authorised it was never held by Sussex Police. Sussex Police had previously told him in February 2005 that the original copy of the 999 tape was in that other body’s possession, which matched the Tribunal’s finding.

Second request (April/May 2005): Mr Freeborn sought copies of all documents relating to the investigation of three complaints he had made about Sussex Police to the police complaints body, and the reasons Sussex Police gave for not recording those complaints. Two complaints were made in 2000 and one in 2003, identified by reference numbers supplied by the complaints body. It was accepted that Mr Freeborn made those complaints and that there must have been written communications between the complaints body and Sussex Police. Sussex Police responded in May 2005 by relying on various grounds for not supplying the information, without suggesting they did not hold it.

Evidence to the Tribunal was that a complaints database (Centurion) had been searched and, apart from two later irrelevant complaints, only a miscellaneous entry in 2000 was found; no 2003 entry was found, and files relating to miscellaneous entries were normally destroyed after three years. The Tribunal accepted that such files were normally destroyed after three years and found that by 2005 Sussex Police may well have destroyed records relating to the two 2000 complaints.

During the hearing, however, Mr Freeborn produced a 2004 letter to him from a senior officer in Sussex Police Professional Standards, said to be in response to the 2003 complaint. The letter bore a Sussex Police reference number. A further search of Centurion by reference to that number revealed an entry relating to the 2003 complaint that had been missed previously, and indicated that the paper file relating to that complaint had been sent to the Information Compliance Manager’s office (under a predecessor). Sussex Police undertook to carry out a detailed search of that office to find the file and to supply Mr Freeborn with a copy under the data protection route without charging a fee. Sussex Police also undertook to make reasonable inquiries of the Chief Constable’s office to see if any relevant files were held there and to supply copies of anything found on the same basis.

Fifth request (January/March 2007): Mr Freeborn sought the exact details and provenance of a cassette tape exhibit in his criminal case (reference FA/216/97). He understood that two bound books held by police would contain such details: a “Major Incident Register” and a “G-83 Book.” He asked for arrangements to inspect these records. Sussex Police responded in March 2007 stating that any G-83 book was no longer held because such books were routinely destroyed after specified periods, and that exhibits in major crime enquiries were logged in the Major Incident Register rather than the G-83 book. Sussex Police referred to two entries in the Major Incident Register relating to FA/216/97 and again relied on various grounds for withholding information. Mr Freeborn was not offered an opportunity to inspect either book.

Before the Tribunal, Sussex Police evidence confirmed that the G-83 book would not have contained any entry relevant to exhibits in Mr Freeborn’s criminal case; Mr Freeborn did not dispute this and the Tribunal found there was no relevant information in that book. As to the Major Incident Register, Sussex Police brought the original to the hearing. The Tribunal inspected it and found it consisted of three slim books recording every item of property seized or created in connection with the investigation, including two entries relating to FA/216/97 (copies of which Mr Freeborn had already seen). Mr Freeborn was allowed to inspect the original briefly at the hearing, which alleviated some of his suspicions about the entries.

The Tribunal invited Sussex Police to copy the whole Register and send it to Mr Freeborn for inspection. Sussex Police indicated they would supply a copy but would consider whether to redact information relating to other individuals. The Tribunal concluded Sussex Police had failed to give Mr Freeborn a reasonable opportunity to inspect the Major Incident Register in response to his request.

Overall, the Tribunal noted unsatisfactory features in Sussex Police handling of the requests, including the late discovery of the 2003 complaint reference and the initial reliance on grounds that were not pursued later, and formed the impression that Sussex Police had tended to supply as little information as possible rather than taking a cooperative approach.

The Tribunal allowed the appeal in part and substituted a decision requiring Sussex Police to conduct further searches for the 2003 complaint file (including in the Information Compliance Manager’s office and the Chief Constable’s office) and to provide Mr Freeborn with a copy of the Major Incident Register for his case with only limited redactions relating to other individuals.
claims:
Mr Freeborn’s underlying position was that he had been wrongly convicted and that Sussex Police had mishandled his case, including alleged interference with a 999 call tape. In the information-rights proceedings, he complained that Sussex Police had not complied with five information requests and sought disclosure/inspection of information connected with the 999 tape and with the handling of his complaints.

In his appeal against the Commissioner’s decision notice, Mr Freeborn argued that the information he had requested should not have been treated as his “personal information” and therefore should not have been withheld on that basis. After dropping the third and fourth requests, he pursued:

1) First request: he sought to be told who removed and destroyed the sealed master cassette of the 999 call, when it was destroyed, and the name and rank of the officer who authorised its destruction.

2) Second request: he sought copies of all documents relating to the investigation of three complaints he had made to the police complaints body about Sussex Police, and the reasons Sussex Police gave for not recording those complaints.

3) Fifth request: he sought arrangements to inspect the Major Incident Register and the G-83 book insofar as they contained information relevant to the provenance and details of a cassette tape exhibit in his criminal case (FA/216/97), and he maintained that inspection of the books themselves was what he was requesting.

Through the appeal he sought a determination that Sussex Police held relevant information and should provide access to it, including by allowing inspection and/or providing copies, rather than refusing on the basis that it was his personal data.

facts:
On 19 February 2001 at Eastern Docks, Dover, Customs stopped a white Citroen BX (registration J248 KLY) owned by Christopher Bowers. He was travelling with Sharon Durkan. Customs seized the car and excise goods found in it. The seized goods comprised 13 kilograms of hand-rolling tobacco, one bottle of whisky, and 55 cigarillos. Mr Bowers valued the car at about £1,700 at the time.

Mr Bowers was interviewed by the stopping officer, Alec James Esposito, who made a handwritten interview record. At the end of the question-and-answer section Mr Bowers wrote and signed a statement that he agreed it was “a near on true account” (dated 19 February, with the year written incorrectly). The officer recorded reasons for seizure including that the quantity exceeded indicative levels, lack of funds for the purchase, and that Mr Bowers was a regular traveller; similar reasons were recorded in relation to Ms Durkan, with notes of her disagreement with two reasons.

Mr Bowers maintained that none of the goods were concealed and that the goods were for personal use. He said that what Ms Durkan imported should be treated separately from his own goods and that he was not responsible for her purchases. He said he had brought in 60 pouches of tobacco, as he had told the interviewing officer, and objected to Ms Durkan’s stated purchases being counted with his.

A disputed issue concerned what Mr Bowers had said about previous travel and purchases. The interview record included that when first stopped he said he had been abroad about a week earlier to France to buy drink for his daughter’s 18th birthday party and had not bought tobacco then, and that he had last been abroad to buy tobacco about six months previously. In the formal interview it was recorded that he said he had travelled two weeks earlier, had tobacco, had been stopped, and there was “no problem,” and that he had personally bought “20 pouches, 30 pouches maximum,” with six pouches left. At the tribunal hearing Mr Bowers insisted he had not said “20 pouches of tobacco” and that the reference should have been to alcohol; the officer was sure the reference was to tobacco and pointed to the recorded follow-up answer about “six pouches.”

Mr Bowers also said that on a previous occasion when he had been stopped he had been told not to return with anything further for six months and that he had complied with this, including not buying tobacco on the trip for wine for the party.

A review officer, David Arthur Leavesley, conducted a further review and on 9 July 2003 decided not to restore the excise goods and to offer only conditional restoration of the car. In his decision letter he treated Mr Bowers as having admitted three trips in three weeks: a trip a fortnight before 19 February 2001 (when he had 20–30 pouches of tobacco), the trip of 19 February (when he acknowledged 60 pouches as his own), and a journey one week before for drinks for the party. The review officer considered that Mr Bowers had initially suggested he had not purchased tobacco for six months but later corrected that, and concluded Mr Bowers was seeking to mask the frequency of his trips. The review officer also noted there was no record of Mr Bowers having been stopped two weeks earlier as claimed.

The review officer examined affordability and compared the cost of the goods with the means of Mr Bowers and Ms Durkan, questioning how they financed the purchases given statements about having no funds shortly before. He also noted discrepancies between their accounts of where they travelled (Mr Bowers saying France for wines and spirits; Ms Durkan saying France and Holland) and when. He concluded their statements lacked credibility and that the importation was not for personal use.

Applying the Commissioners’ policy on restoration, the review officer decided the goods would not be restored (absent exceptional circumstances, which he did not find). He considered factors relevant to vehicle restoration (including the extent to which imports exceeded guidelines, whether it was a first offence, concealment or deceit, the value of the car, and hardship) and offered restoration of the car on payment of a sum equal to the duty not paid on the goods, calculated at £1,249.77.

At the tribunal hearing, the tribunal considered the factual background and concluded that, on the information available to the review officer, it was reasonable for him to decide the importation was not for own use. The tribunal found misleading inconsistencies in Mr Bowers’ evidence about previous travel and discrepancies between his evidence and Ms Durkan’s statement, and considered it reasonable for the review officer to be sceptical about how the purchases were financed. The tribunal was satisfied the review officer had not apportioned the total imports between the two travellers and accepted that approach, concluding on the evidence that this was a joint enterprise organised by Mr Bowers and part of a series of such trips, and that the goods were not readily divisible into separate holdings as Mr Bowers claimed.
claims:
Mr Bowers appealed to the tribunal against the Commissioners’ re-review decision of 9 July 2003. He challenged (1) the refusal to restore the seized excise goods and (2) the decision to offer only conditional restoration of his car.

In support of his appeal, Mr Bowers argued in substance that:

- The tobacco attributed to Ms Durkan should not have been counted together with his own; her imports should have been treated as separate from his, and he was not responsible for her goods.
- The goods were not concealed and were for personal use.
- The interview record was not fully reliable in two respects: he said he was shown it only one page at a time and signed when he just wanted to leave; and he disputed an alleged inaccuracy about what he had imported on a previous occasion, insisting that a recorded reference to “20 pouches” should have been a reference to alcohol rather than tobacco.
- He had complied with an earlier instruction (as he described it) not to return with further goods for six months, and said he did not buy tobacco on the trip for drink for his daughter’s party because it was within that period.

Through the appeal he sought reversal of the review decision so that the goods would be restored and/or the car restored without the condition requiring payment of £1,249.77.

facts:
Jobe Transport Ltd (a small family-run haulage business) owned a DAF tractor unit, registration Y10 KPE (“the Vehicle”). On 2 August 2007 the Vehicle, driven by the company’s employee Mr Richard Ogilvie, was stopped by Customs at Ramsgate dock while towing a trailer belonging to Maenhout Transport. The trailer contained a legitimate load together with 1,087,400 cigarettes (excise duty stated as £164,675.85). The cigarettes were packed in four black shrink-wrapped pallets labelled “Dow Chemicals” and were not accompanied by appropriate paperwork. Customs seized the cigarettes, the Vehicle, and the trailer. No one challenged the legality of the seizure and the goods and vehicles were treated as forfeit. Mr Ogilvie was arrested on 2 August 2007 and later charged, but the criminal charges were subsequently dropped.

On 7 August 2007 the Appellant asked for restoration of the Vehicle. On 9 August 2007 the Appellant’s director and transport manager, Mr Brian Boccius, voluntarily attended at Dover, was arrested, and was interviewed under caution about the seizure (with his solicitor present). From that interview, the Tribunal recorded that Mr Boccius had received an enquiry from a person named Mevlot Ferati at an address in Dagenham, confirmed by fax, to collect six pallets from an address in Bruges, Belgium and deliver them to Dow Chemicals at King’s Lynn for an agreed price of £900 including ferry fees. Mr Boccius had not dealt with Mevlot Ferati before. Later, the delivery address was changed by telephone from Dow Chemicals to BMH Freight in Basildon, Essex. Mr Boccius arranged for the load to be collected in Maenhout Transport’s trailer despite Maenhout’s express instructions. Mr Ogilvie could not find the stated collection address, but was directed by someone waving and then collected four pallets rather than the six expected. Mr Boccius expected the consignment paperwork to be provided with the load and hoped the contact might lead to regular work. He denied that he or Mr Ogilvie knew the load was cigarettes. After the seizure, Mr Boccius made no effort to contact Mevlot Ferati.

On 13 August 2007 the trailer was restored to Maenhout Transport free of charge. Customs asked the Appellant for proof of ownership and for information about employment documentation, anti-smuggling measures, checks on consignor/consignee, physical checks of loads, and any written procedures. On 20 August 2007 Mr Boccius provided ownership documents and stated that the company believed the collection was legitimate because it had a fax/phone number, collection and delivery addresses, and the pallets were marked for the stated address; he said they only learned what was in the pallets when stopped by Customs. He also said the company crossed the Channel once or twice a week and had not previously had problems.

Customs initially offered restoration of the Vehicle for £19,650 (agreed to be 100% of the Vehicle’s trade value). The Appellant sought a review and provided further details, including that Dow Chemicals was known to be a legitimate business, delivery details often change, the enquiry appeared normal, confirmation was received by fax and followed up by telephone, the caller used a landline that seemed to be a genuine business, the replacement delivery address appeared to be a freight company, the pick-up point was a warehouse on an industrial estate, and the shrink-wrapped pallets could not realistically be inspected without interfering with the wrapping. The Appellant also said it was suffering serious hardship: the Vehicle was on finance at £595 per month while unusable, and the company was losing between £1,000 and £2,000 per week in income.

On review, Customs reduced the restoration fee to £9,825 (50% of the Vehicle’s trade value). The Appellant paid that amount to obtain restoration, while continuing to challenge the fee. It was common ground that neither the Appellant nor Mr Ogilvie was responsible for or complicit in the smuggling attempt. The dispute focused on whether “basic reasonable checks” had been carried out to confirm the legitimacy of the load and detect any illicit load. The Tribunal found that sufficient basic reasonable checks had not been carried out: there was no consignment documentation with the load; the Appellant did not have systems requiring the driver to obtain such documentation or otherwise confirm legitimacy (by inspection or enquiry); and the Appellant did not have systems encouraging the driver to be alert to irregularities such as difficulty locating the collection address and the discrepancy between the expected six pallets and the four collected.
claims:
The Appellant appealed against the review decision that restoration of the Vehicle should be conditional on payment of £9,825 (50% of the Vehicle’s trade value). The Appellant’s case was that this restoration fee was unreasonable because it was disproportionately large. It argued that if any restoration fee could properly be required, it should not exceed 25% of the Vehicle’s trade value; it suggested that 25% would be at the high end of what could be reasonable, that restoration without any fee would also be reasonable, and that around 10% would be a “median” reasonable fee.

In support of reducing the fee, the Appellant argued that it had taken reasonable precautions to establish the legitimacy of the job: the original consignee (Dow Chemicals) was known to be legitimate; changes of delivery address were not unusual in haulage; the initial enquiry and order appeared normal; confirmation was received by fax and followed up by telephone; the caller used a landline that appeared to be associated with a genuine business; the replacement delivery address appeared genuine; the collection point did not raise suspicion; and the pallets were addressed to Dow Chemicals. It also contended that the driver could not realistically inspect the shrink-wrapped pallets without interfering with the wrapping.

The Appellant further relied on hardship and proportionality: it said it was a small family business operating on tight margins; loss of the Vehicle caused serious hardship; it remained liable for monthly finance payments of £595 while the Vehicle was out of use; it was losing between £1,000 and £2,000 per week in income; and it did not have the resources to pay the higher fee originally demanded. It argued that a fee set at 100% of trade value (and, by implication, the reduced 50% fee) was disproportionate to the degree of fault involved.

The Appellant also challenged aspects of the reasoning used to justify the 50% fee. It submitted that the breach of the agreement with Maenhout Transport (using Maenhout’s trailer contrary to instructions) should carry little or no weight because it was irrelevant to whether basic reasonable checks were carried out to prevent an illicit load. It argued that more credit should have been given for Mr Boccius’s cooperation in interview. It also argued that the expected haulage fee of £900 should have been taken into account when fixing the restoration fee. Finally, it contended that Customs had wrongly focused only on whether hardship was “exceptional,” rather than considering hardship more generally when setting the fee.

facts:
The parties married in 1974, having lived together for some years beforehand. At the time of marriage the husband was 27 and the wife 37. There were no children. They separated on 2 January 1987 after about 12½ years of marriage, and the husband went to live with another woman.

The wife began proceedings for judicial separation and obtained a decree of judicial separation on 11 April 1989. Both parties applied for financial orders. In July 1991 a district judge made financial orders on the basis that he had not been given the full facts by the wife. The district judge ordered that the matrimonial home (“Torcello”) should be transferred to the wife, with the wife to pay the husband £15,000. The wife was also ordered to pay £4,000 costs within 12 months. A nominal maintenance order for the wife was made (5 pence per year), and it was common ground at that time that there would not be a substantial order for ongoing maintenance. The wife remained living in Torcello thereafter, but she never paid the £15,000 or the £4,000 costs.

The wife filed an appeal application the day after the 1991 hearing, but for years did not pursue it to a hearing. By March 2000, nearly nine years later, she still had not brought that appeal before the court.

On 2 March 2000 a circuit judge dealt with multiple matters, including a defended divorce based on five years’ separation (which the wife contested), and the husband’s application to set aside the wife’s long-unpursued appeal application. The wife sought an adjournment shortly before the hearing; the judge refused to adjourn. The wife did not attend court. The judge made orders intended to achieve a complete final separation of the parties’ affairs, including granting a decree nisi, striking out the wife’s notice of appeal against the 1991 financial order, directing payment to the wife of about £20,000 plus interest held by the husband’s solicitors, ordering a nominal lump sum of £1, making an order intended to prevent either party bringing a further claim on death, and ordering the wife to pay the husband £10,000 costs.

There had also been a maintenance order made about a year after the 1991 order for £30 per week to the wife, which continued (with applications to vary) until the March 2000 hearing, when the circuit judge ended it as part of his attempt to create a clean break.

Permission to appeal was later refused in relation to most matters, but the issue of financial relief after decree nisi proceeded because of concern about how the maintenance issue had been dealt with. When the matter came before the Court of Appeal, it emerged that the husband’s side did not consider the circuit judge’s “clean break” to have disposed of sums the wife still owed under the 1991 order and later costs orders. The Court of Appeal was concerned that substantial unpaid liabilities (including the £15,000 and costs) might still hang over the wife.

The husband, through counsel, obtained and offered an undertaking that if all proceedings were finished he would not pursue further claims against the wife for the substantial sums she owed him (including sums connected with the house). The practical effect was that the 1991 order would stand, the wife would keep the house, the husband would not receive the £15,000, and the wife would not receive further maintenance.

The Court of Appeal considered the parties’ financial positions as described: the husband’s income was around £24,000–£25,000 per year; the wife’s income was about £8,000 per year. The wife had had the major benefit of the family assets through retaining the home. The husband, a retired police officer, had received a gratuity, much of which had been spent on the costs of the prolonged litigation. The only identified money potentially available was about £20,000 held by the husband’s solicitors.

Ultimately, the Court of Appeal refused the wife permission to appeal, treating the 1991 order as governing the capital position, subject to the husband’s forbearance under his undertaking not to enforce the sums owed. The application was refused on that basis.
claims:
The wife sought permission to appeal against the circuit judge’s March 2000 orders insofar as they concerned financial relief, in particular the ending of her maintenance. Through counsel, she argued that the financial issues should be reconsidered following the divorce and that the circuit judge’s approach was flawed.

Her arguments included that there had been no proper assessment of the husband’s ability to pay a lump sum and that relevant financial matters had not been explored, including the husband’s interest in his new partner’s property and his ability to contribute to other mortgages. She contended that the judge made mistakes, including failing to set out an adequate balancing exercise and giving a deficient judgment. She also argued that the case was not fairly heard because the judge proceeded when she was not present.

In terms of outcome sought, her position was directed to obtaining further financial provision from the husband, particularly ongoing maintenance (and, as advanced by counsel, consideration of a lump sum), relying on the disparity between her income and the husband’s income and the husband’s partner having her own pension. She sought the opportunity for the financial issues to be heard again on the permission-to-appeal application and, if successful, for the matter to be sent back for a further hearing.

facts:
The appellant parents have seven children. About a year before this appeal, six of the children were removed from the parents’ day-to-day care following an application by the local authority, and their long-term future was being determined in ongoing proceedings under the control of Kirkwood J.

On 23 October 2001 Kirkwood J made an order by consent listing a final hearing for 11 February 2002 and giving the parents permission to disclose the case papers to the Legard Family Support Centre so that it could consider whether it could assess the family.

At an internal local authority meeting on 30 October 2001, the local authority decided to exclude the possibility of rehabilitating the six children to the parents. The meeting minute also recorded a consensus that the local authority would take the same approach to a seventh child whom the mother was then expecting. This decision was communicated to the parents the next day.

On 15 November 2001 the parties returned before Kirkwood J. The parents’ counsel raised issues about the unborn child and asked that, if the local authority sought removal after birth, the issue should be referred to Kirkwood J. Concern was also raised that an emergency order might be sought before the matter could be referred. The judge indicated he would expect “fresh evidence” for removal rather than relying on evidence predating 23 October 2001, and stressed the importance of ongoing consultation between the parties and the local authority. The order of 15 November 2001 permitted the local authority to instruct Dr Eyre for a further report and gave directions for a report from Mr Maggs (instructed for the parents). It also directed that any proceedings relating to the unborn child be immediately transferred to the High Court to be listed before Kirkwood J.

The consultation envisaged by the judge did not develop. On 30 November 2001 the guardian proposed that a residential placement be found for the mother and baby; the local authority rejected this on 5 December 2001. The local authority adhered to its 30 October policy decision and did not engage in meaningful consultation with the parents about their wish to care for the baby. It also appeared that Dr Eyre did not meet the parents again to assess any change following the threshold findings made on 23 October 2001.

The baby (D) was expected around 21 January 2002 but was born early on 30 December 2001. The local authority promptly applied for an interim care order to implement its policy of separating mother and baby. The application came before Judge Curl on 2 January 2002 and was adjourned to 8 January 2002 before Judge Tyrer. Kirkwood J was unavailable during the last week of the Christmas vacation, and the hospital required discharge of mother and baby.

Judge Tyrer heard the matter over 8 and 9 January 2002. During cross-examination on 9 January it emerged that the local authority’s search for a residential placement had proceeded on an erroneous basis that the mother was a teenage, inexperienced mother. Once corrected to reflect that she was an experienced mother, the local authority identified an available placement: Beacon Lodge in East Finchley. This was geographically convenient because the Legard Centre was in Highbury. The guardian supported the proposal that mother and baby move from hospital to Beacon Lodge, and the judge considered it a sensible arrangement.

The local authority sought time to consider but returned the next day stating it would not agree to placement at Beacon Lodge and instead sought an interim care order with the intention of separating mother and baby and placing D with a foster mother in Dagenham. The identified foster mother was not prepared to allow parental contact in her home. The judge considered that once an interim care order was made the local authority could dictate management, and that he could only grant or refuse the interim order without imposing terms. He granted an interim care order until the hearing listed before Kirkwood J, directed “maximum possible contact” between parents and D at the foster parent’s home (details to be agreed or referred back), directed a pre-residential assessment by the Legard Centre, permitted disclosure of papers to Dr Freedman at the Portman Clinic for assessment, granted permission to appeal, and stayed the interim care order until noon the following day.

On appeal, additional information was available. The Legard Centre explained it would not offer immediate residential placement given the history, but would offer a pre-residential assessment of about six weeks involving sessions with the parents and observation of contact. It stated that, in its experience, bonding and attachment are promoted when there is contact at least five times a week for around five hours per day with opportunities for parents to be actively involved in day-to-day care; later information indicated an optimum of five days a week for about five hours per day if the baby was not living with the mother, and a minimum of three times a week for two to three hours per day. It was also clarified that Legard’s residential placement is for an entire family, whereas Beacon Lodge could accommodate only the mother and baby.

A brochure for Beacon Lodge showed it accepted local authority referrals for assessment of parenting skills, could admit women during pregnancy or after birth, and provided ongoing assessment with regular key-worker sessions, focusing on the mother’s ability to learn and develop parenting and (where appropriate) independent living skills, recognising that addressing the mother’s needs may be necessary to meet the child’s needs.

During the appeal hearing, the local authority indicated it would arrange contact six days a week for two hours per day at a family centre in Newham, near the foster placement in Dagenham, and argued this would allow the Legard Centre to carry out its pre-residential assessment even if mother and baby were separated.

The Court of Appeal concluded that the judge had been wrong to regard himself as constrained to accept the local authority’s decision to separate mother and baby once an interim care order was made, and allowed the appeal by adding a direction for a residential assessment at Beacon Lodge pending the listing before Kirkwood J.
claims:
The parents appealed Judge Tyrer’s decision to make an interim care order that enabled the local authority to separate the newborn baby (D) from the mother and place D in foster care.

In the court below, the parents’ case was that the judge’s welfare balancing was wrong: they argued that the disadvantages of removal outweighed the advantages, and that it was preferable to consolidate the mother–child relationship under professional supervision rather than separate them.

On appeal, the parents advanced additional arguments seeking an outcome that would keep mother and baby together in a supervised residential setting. They contended that the judge should have recognised and exercised the ability to make the interim care order while also directing that mother and baby reside at Beacon Lodge as part of the assessment process. They argued that the judge had an opportunity to couple the interim care order with such a direction, and that he was wrong to treat the local authority’s stance as dictating separation.

They also argued more generally that the court could impose terms and conditions on how an interim care order was implemented, and further contended that the judge could have directed the Beacon Lodge placement by relying on broader judicial powers. In addition, they relied on human rights arguments, seeking a declaration of incompatibility or, alternatively, an order directing placement of D and the mother at Beacon Lodge.
