The relief sought through the appeal was to overturn the practical effect of the interim care order (separation and foster placement) and to secure a direction that mother and baby be placed together at Beacon Lodge pending further hearings, so that assessment could proceed in that setting.

facts:
The case concerned Thomas Gibson’s occupation of a house in the Wirral owned and occupied by Lillian Douglas. Mr Gibson had lived at the property for about four or five years. He began living there after meeting Mrs Douglas around 2008/2009. They had an arrangement under which Mr Gibson claimed housing benefit and made payments to Mrs Douglas for his use of part of the premises. Mr Gibson said they initially lived in separate bedrooms and that the relationship was at first a platonic friendship, later becoming closer after 2010.

Towards the end of 2012 Mrs Douglas’s health deteriorated and she went into hospital. While in hospital she made disclosures (the truth of which the trial judge did not need to decide) about Mr Gibson’s behaviour towards her, including allegations of violence, and she indicated she did not want to return to the property while Mr Gibson was living there.

In early January 2013 the hospital contacted Mrs Douglas’s son, Ian Douglas, as next of kin. Mr Douglas came to the area and on 7 January 2013 approached Mr Gibson to find out what was happening; at that stage relations were reasonably amicable and Mr Douglas stayed overnight with Mr Gibson. The next day Mr Douglas went to the hospital, spoke to his mother, and established that on discharge she did not want to go back to the property while Mr Gibson remained there. Mr Douglas contacted the police after being told about the emerging revelations.

On 9 January 2013 police attended at or near the property, with Mrs Douglas nearby but a little distance away. There was a fracas between the police and Mr Gibson. Mr Douglas was present and moved into the property immediately, said to be to assist his mother. Mr Gibson was forcibly ejected from the property by the police, taken away in a police car, and thereafter lived in other rented accommodation until his relationship with Mrs Douglas resumed.

The claim was heard in March 2014. Between the alleged eviction and the hearing, in summer 2013, Mrs Douglas married Mr Gibson. By the time of the hearing she lacked capacity to litigate and was suffering from advanced vascular dementia; she acted through a litigation friend. On the morning of the hearing Mr Gibson’s claim against Mrs Douglas was compromised for a nominal payment of £5, and he pursued the claim only against Mr Douglas.

At trial, the judge concluded Mr Gibson was not a tenant but a licensee, and treated him as an excluded licensee. The judge found that the physical removal was carried out by the police, that Mrs Douglas had communicated through the authorities that she wanted Mr Gibson to leave, and that Mr Douglas’s role was no more than conveying his mother’s wishes. The judge held there was no evidence that Mr Douglas played a sufficient part in the eviction to make him liable, and also found there was a lack of evidence supporting the claimed losses for missing items.

On appeal, it was common ground that Mr Gibson was a licensee and not a tenant, and that his occupation was an excluded licence. The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal on the basis that, on the trial judge’s findings, Mr Douglas did not take an active role in the eviction and there was nothing to show he did anything at the property during the eviction that could make him jointly responsible for the police’s actions.
claims:
Mr Gibson brought a claim alleging he had been unlawfully evicted from the Wirral property on 9 January 2013 by Mrs Douglas and her son, Ian Douglas. By the time of trial the claim against Mrs Douglas had been settled for £5, so the claim proceeded only against Mr Douglas.

As described by the trial judge, Mr Gibson’s claims against Mr Douglas were two-fold:
1) damages on the basis that Mr Douglas played an instrumental role in evicting him on 9 January 2013; and
2) damages for Mr Gibson’s possessions which he alleged were appropriated, destroyed, or otherwise disposed of by Mr Douglas.

In argument before the trial judge, Mr Gibson contended that a person is entitled to notice before being required to leave and that it was contrary to human rights for someone to be turned out without being given several days’ opportunity to leave.

On appeal, permission was granted only on the issue whether a licensee may lawfully be evicted without notice, including the related point that the trial judge had made no finding that Mr Gibson was given notice before eviction. Mr Gibson’s appeal therefore sought to overturn the dismissal of his claim against Mr Douglas on the basis that eviction without notice (and/or without adequate time to pack up and leave) was unlawful and should sound in damages against Mr Douglas.

facts:
The case concerns an attempt by Cyril Nicol to appeal to the Employment Appeal Tribunal (EAT) out of time.

An Employment Tribunal made an original decision in Mr Nicol’s case in August 2016. He applied for reconsideration. That reconsideration application was heard on 30 January 2017 and was dismissed, with reasons given orally. The formal judgment recording the dismissal was not issued until 31 March 2017, after which Mr Nicol became entitled to request written reasons. He requested written reasons, and they were sent to the parties on 2 May 2017. The delays in producing the formal judgment and the written reasons appeared to be connected with the Employment Judge’s ill-health.

From 2 May 2017 Mr Nicol had 42 days to institute an appeal to the EAT, with the deadline expiring at 4.00 pm on 13 June 2017. On 12 June 2017 he lodged a notice of appeal and most of the required accompanying documents, but he omitted the Employment Tribunal’s written reasons. After the EAT drew the omission to his attention, he supplied the written reasons the next day, but not until 4.33 pm. As a result, the appeal was treated as having been instituted 33 minutes late.

Mr Nicol applied for an extension of time. The EAT Registrar refused the extension. Mr Nicol appealed that refusal to an EAT Judge. The appeal was heard on 24 November 2017 by HH Judge Katherine Tucker. Mr Nicol appeared in person and the respondent was represented by a solicitor. The Judge dismissed the appeal.

Mr Nicol then sought permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal. The Court of Appeal was concerned that the EAT Judge may have treated her role as limited to reviewing the Registrar’s decision rather than deciding the matter afresh. At the rolled-up hearing before the Court of Appeal, the respondent accepted that the appeal from the Registrar should proceed by way of rehearing. The Court of Appeal concluded that the EAT Judge had misdirected herself by adopting a review approach.

The Court of Appeal considered whether the misdirection was immaterial. It noted that missing the deadline by minutes can still be fatal, even where only an ancillary document is missing. However, it also noted the explanation advanced by Mr Nicol: his mother died on 19 April 2017 in Nigeria, and he said he had to return to Nigeria and remained there until 10 June 2017, leaving only a few days before the deadline to complete the appeal paperwork. The Court of Appeal accepted that, in those particular circumstances, it was arguable that the discretion to extend time could properly be exercised in his favour, though it did not decide that it should be.

The Court of Appeal granted permission to appeal, allowed the appeal, and remitted to the EAT for a further hearing the question whether an extension of time should be granted. It expressed no view on the merits of any underlying appeal from the Employment Tribunal decision.
claims:
Mr Nicol sought an extension of time to institute his appeal to the EAT after his appeal was treated as 33 minutes late because he had omitted the Employment Tribunal’s written reasons from the documents lodged before the deadline and only supplied them after 4.00 pm on the final day.

In support of an extension, he relied on his explanation for the late compliance: his mother died in Nigeria on 19 April 2017, and he said he had to travel to Nigeria and remained there until 10 June 2017, leaving him only a very short period (about two or three days) before the deadline to prepare and lodge the appeal documentation. His position was, in substance, that given those circumstances it was understandable that a single required document was overlooked and then supplied shortly after the deadline.

Before the Court of Appeal, his challenge to the EAT Judge’s decision included the argument that the Judge had approached her task incorrectly by treating the appeal as a review of the Registrar’s refusal rather than determining the extension application afresh. He sought permission to appeal, an order allowing the appeal, and a remittal so that the EAT could reconsider at a further hearing whether time should be extended.

facts:
Mr Kemal Yildiz was the secure tenant of a four-bedroom house at 35 Victorian Grove, Yorkshire Grove Estate, London, let by the London Borough of Hackney. He died on 4 September 2014. His son, Mr Yavuz Yildiz, succeeded to the tenancy after his father’s death.

On 28 January 2015 the Council told Mr Yildiz that he was under-occupying the four-bedroom property and would be required to move to alternative accommodation. Mr Yildiz did not accept one or more offers of one-bedroom accommodation.

The Council then served Mr Yildiz with a notice dated 23 June 2015 stating that it intended to apply to the court for an order requiring him to give up possession of 35 Victorian Grove. The notice stated that proceedings would not be begun until after 20 July 2015 and also stated that proceedings could be begun at once after that date or at any time during the following twelve months, after which the notice would lapse and a new notice would have to be served before possession could be sought.

Because of what was described as a clerical error, the Council did not issue possession proceedings until 8 August 2016, which was a few weeks more than twelve months after 20 July 2015.

Mr Yildiz defended the possession claim, including on the basis that the 23 June 2015 notice had lapsed. The Council responded by applying for an order dispensing with the requirement to serve a notice.

On 5 December 2016, Deputy District Judge Harris decided it was just and equitable to dispense with the requirement to serve a notice and made an order to that effect. Mr Yildiz appealed, but on 13 July 2018 His Honour John Hand QC (sitting as a Deputy Circuit Judge) dismissed the appeal. Mr Yildiz then appealed to the Court of Appeal, which concluded that the Council was not entitled to rely on the under-occupation ground in the circumstances because the proceedings were issued neither within twelve months of the relevant date nor while the June 2015 notice was still in force, and allowed Mr Yildiz’s appeal.
claims:
Mr Yildiz resisted the Council’s possession claim and appealed against the order dispensing with the notice requirement.

His case was that the Council’s notice dated 23 June 2015 had lapsed before proceedings were issued, because the Council did not start the possession claim until 8 August 2016, more than twelve months after the date stated in the notice after which proceedings could begin. He argued that, once the notice had expired, the Council could not rely on it to bring possession proceedings.

He further argued that allowing the Council to proceed by dispensing with the notice requirement would undermine the time limits built into the under-occupation ground relied on by the Council, because it would remove any effective longstop and could permit the Council to seek possession long after the relevant period had passed.

Accordingly, Mr Yildiz sought to have the earlier decision upheld by the lower court overturned, contending that the Council was not entitled to rely on the under-occupation ground on the facts of this case and that the possession claim should not be allowed to proceed on the basis of a lapsed notice combined with dispensation.

facts:
Etihad Airways PJSC provided financial support to Air Berlin PLC over a number of years after acquiring a minority shareholding in 2011. In April 2017, as part of a further support package, Etihad and Air Berlin entered into a €350 million facility agreement dated 28 April 2017 under which Etihad was the lender and Air Berlin the borrower.

The facility agreement contained an asymmetric jurisdiction clause. It stated that the courts of England had exclusive jurisdiction to settle any dispute arising out of or in connection with the facility agreement (including non-contractual obligations and disputes about existence, validity or termination). It also stated that the clause was for the benefit of Etihad only, and that Etihad was not prevented from bringing proceedings relating to a dispute in any other court with jurisdiction and could take concurrent proceedings in multiple jurisdictions. The effect was that Air Berlin was bound to litigate disputes in England, while Etihad retained flexibility to sue elsewhere.

Air Berlin had longstanding financial difficulties and in 2016 began work on a restructuring. Its external auditors identified going concern and funding as significant issues for the audit of its 2016 financial statements. During March and April 2017, Air Berlin sought additional support from Etihad so that the auditors would sign off the accounts on a going concern basis. Etihad was unwilling to agree to all requests, but it was agreed that, alongside the facility agreement and other commitments, Etihad would provide a comfort letter.

Etihad issued a comfort letter dated 28 April 2017 addressed to Air Berlin’s directors. It stated that, for the purpose of finalising Air Berlin’s 2016 financial statements and having seen forecasts to the end of 2018, Etihad confirmed its intention to continue to provide the necessary support to enable Air Berlin to meet its financial obligations as they fell due for the foreseeable future and in any event for 18 months from the date of the letter, referring to Etihad’s historic support. The comfort letter did not contain a jurisdiction clause and did not cross-refer to the facility agreement.

In summer 2017 Air Berlin encountered severe operational difficulties affecting revenues, costs and liquidity. It applied to the Berlin court to open insolvency proceedings on 15 August 2017 and ceased operations on 27 October 2017. Professor Dr Lucas Flöther became Air Berlin’s insolvency administrator.

On 24 July 2018, Professor Flöther, as insolvency administrator, commenced proceedings against Etihad in the Regional Court of Berlin. Those German proceedings related to the comfort letter and were pleaded in a lengthy document, with a preliminary estimate that the amount in dispute was at least €2 billion.

On 22 January 2019, Etihad commenced proceedings in England against Professor Flöther as sole defendant, seeking declarations that would mirror and negate the relief sought in Germany. It was common ground that the Berlin court was first seised and the English court second seised.

Air Berlin (through the insolvency administrator) applied in April 2019 disputing the jurisdiction of the English Commercial Court. The High Court dismissed that application, concluding there was a good arguable case that the facility agreement’s jurisdiction clause applied to the comfort letter and related non-contractual claims and that the German claim fell within its scope. Permission to appeal was granted only on the issue whether the English court should stay its proceedings in favour of the first-seised German court or whether the special rule giving priority to the chosen court applied to this asymmetric jurisdiction clause.

Separately, Etihad applied in Germany for a stay of the German proceedings. In May 2020 the Berlin court stayed the German proceedings until the English High Court gave a final decision on its jurisdiction, and in December 2020 the Berlin appeal court dismissed Air Berlin’s appeal against that stay.

The Court of Appeal dismissed Air Berlin’s appeal, holding that the priority rule applied to the asymmetric jurisdiction clause and therefore the English proceedings were not required to be stayed in favour of the German proceedings.
claims:
In the German proceedings, the insolvency administrator (Professor Flöther on behalf of Air Berlin) brought claims against Etihad arising out of the comfort letter, advancing two alternatives under German law: (1) a claim for breach of the comfort letter on the basis that it was legally binding; and (2) alternatively, if the comfort letter was not legally binding, a pre-contractual claim based on the allegation that Etihad used its negotiating power to avoid giving a clearly binding statement while inspiring Air Berlin’s trust that it would adhere to the commitment expressed in the comfort letter.

In the English proceedings, Etihad sought declaratory relief aimed at defeating the German claims and relocating the dispute to England. Etihad asked for declarations that: (1) the claims and declarations sought in the German proceedings were subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the English court because, properly construed, they fell within the scope of the facility agreement’s jurisdiction clause; (2) the claims and declarations sought in the German proceedings were governed by English law on the proper construction of the facility agreement’s governing law clause; (3) Etihad was not liable for breach of the comfort letter because, properly construed, it did not create a legally binding promise to provide financial support; (4) Etihad was not liable on the alternative pre-contractual basis alleged in Germany because the facts relied on did not give rise to a cause of action known to English law; and (5) in any event, Etihad was not liable to Air Berlin as alleged in the German proceedings.

On the jurisdictional challenge and appeal, Air Berlin’s position was that because the German court was first seised, the English court was obliged to stay its proceedings, and that the rule giving priority to a chosen court did not apply to the facility agreement’s asymmetric jurisdiction clause. Air Berlin argued that the priority rule applied only where the parties had conferred exclusive jurisdiction in a way that required all parties to bring proceedings only in the designated court, whereas the clause here allowed Etihad to sue in other jurisdictions and therefore was not an agreement conferring exclusive jurisdiction for these purposes. Air Berlin also argued that the English court was not “seised on the basis of” an exclusive jurisdiction agreement because Etihad had chosen to sue in England despite being free to sue elsewhere.

facts:
On 15 October 1998 at Oxford Crown Court the appellant, John Keyes, was convicted by a jury of attempted robbery on count 3 of an indictment and later sentenced to a combination order of 36 months’ probation and 40 hours’ community service. He was acquitted on counts 1 and 2. The events underlying the indictment occurred on 20 April 1998 in central Oxford between about 1.45 pm and 2.15 pm, when the appellant went into three different banks.

Count 1 concerned Lloyds Bank at about 1.45 pm. A cashier, Julie Ward, said the appellant ignored the queue and demanded money. She asked if he had an account and, receiving no response, gave him paper to write details. She noticed he smelt of alcohol. The appellant then said he had a gun. She described him as quiet, not aggressive, slurring his words, and appearing drunk; she did not take him seriously and found it humorous. The police were not called and she did not follow robbery procedures; she said she was not in fear. A supervisor, Jane Butler, said the appellant was drunk and incoherent. He followed her to the customer service area, asked if she would give him money, put his face close to hers, and then fell over. She escorted him out and told him to return when sober. She said she was not frightened. She also said the appellant gave his proper name and asked her to tell the police he had “done a robbery,” and that he spoke like someone drunk and not aware of what he was saying.

Count 2 concerned Barclays Bank at about 2.10 pm. A cashier, Teresa Addison, said the appellant interrupted her while she was serving another customer (Mr Cooper), refused to queue, and repeatedly demanded money. He carried a cloth bag in the crook of his arm and said he had a gun, pushing his arm toward the glass; she thought there was something in the bag about six to nine inches long. He said, “This is a stick up,” repeated that he had a gun, and told her not to press the button; she pressed it. She initially thought it was a joke but then panicked; she did not smell alcohol and did not think his speech was slurred, though she thought he might be “mad.” She described his tone as not aggressive but threatening. Mr Cooper said he heard the appellant ask for money and say he had a gun. He was shocked but did not feel threatened. He saw the appellant’s hand in his jacket pocket and could see it was fingers being pointed through the lining, not a gun. He thought the appellant was seeking attention and not seriously trying to rob the bank. He could not recall smelling alcohol but thought the appellant might be mentally ill. He moved the appellant away from the counter and ushered him out; he did not treat the matter as serious and did not contact the police at that time.

Count 3 concerned National Westminster Bank at about 2.15 pm. A bank employee, Sarah May, said the appellant stumbled to her counter and demanded, “Give me your money.” She thought he was pointing something under his jacket but could not see anything. She did not initially think it was a serious robbery. She and a colleague followed procedure by dropping to the floor, shouting “raid,” and pressing the alarm. They then heard the appellant say, “Call the police. I’ve done it. This is great.” When they got up he was sitting with the manager; he seemed jovial and she thought he might be drunk, noticing he swayed when walking. Another cashier, Miss Thorne, thought he had pointed something at them; she thought he was drunk, laughing, and treating it as a joke, and said he repeated, “I did it. I did it. Call the police.” A customer, Mr Powell, saw the appellant with his hand in his pocket pointing it and saying “Give me money,” and also saying “I’m not going to hurt you.” Mr Powell grabbed him from behind and felt there was nothing in the pocket. The appellant did not struggle but ranted and laughed about a robbery; he smelt of alcohol. Mr Powell thought the appellant wanted to be arrested and wanted attention. The bank manager, Mr Talbot, heard the appellant say, “I’ve robbed the bank. Arrest me. Please arrest me. I’m not well. I am an ill man.” Mr Talbot thought the appellant appeared drunk and not “all there,” and said the appellant produced his benefits book to prove his identity.

A police officer, WPC Murphy, arrived and said the appellant told her, “I want to be arrested. Look at all this excitement. I love it.” She arrested him and thought he could understand the seriousness of what was happening. The police treated the incident seriously, calling a firearms team and a helicopter. An inspector gave evidence that the next morning, when cautioned, the appellant said he had left a public house and wanted money but did not really mean it, had not hurt anyone, and it was only a joke; he said he had been into two banks and been put out, and was arrested in the third, then asked, “Am I in trouble?” In a later interview with a solicitor present, he changed his story somewhat but continued to say he had not thought he was scaring people and was playing a joke and trying to make people laugh.

At trial the appellant’s defence was that he lacked the necessary intent because he was drunk, or because he was carrying out a drunken joke, or because he was a pathetic individual seeking attention. In his evidence he said he could remember going into one bank but then remembered nothing until waking in a police cell, with the other two bank visits blanked from his memory.
claims: The appellant appealed against his conviction on count 3 (attempted robbery). His argument, advanced on appeal, was that the conviction on count 3 was unsafe because the jury had acquitted him on counts 1 and 2, and there was no discernible reason why the evidence on count 3 should have been sufficient to prove the necessary intent when the evidence on counts 1 and 2 had not. In substance, he sought to have the conviction on count 3 set aside on the basis that the verdicts could not safely stand together given that the only real issue across all three counts was whether he had the necessary intent.

facts:
David Michael Shayler was a member of the Security Service (MI5) from November 1991 to October 1996. At the start of his employment he signed a declaration acknowledging the confidential nature of security and intelligence material that might come into his possession and also acknowledged a contractual obligation not to disclose such information without authority. When he left MI5 he signed a further declaration acknowledging that the confidentiality obligations continued after his employment ended.

By about August 1997 Shayler was in contact with journalists from The Mail on Sunday. He appears to have handed over to the newspaper a collection of documents that had been removed from MI5. In March 1998 the newspaper returned about 30 different documents to the Treasury Solicitor; most appeared to relate to security or intelligence matters and were classified at levels ranging from “classified” up to “Top Secret”. Some documents included material obtained by, or relating to, the interception of communications under warrants.

On 24 August 1997 The Mail on Sunday published an article attributed to Shayler (by by-line) and other articles by journalists said to be based on information he provided. He was paid a substantial sum of money by the newspaper for these activities. The prosecution’s position was that the information in and referred to in the articles related to security and intelligence matters to which Shayler could only have had access because of his MI5 employment.

The day before publication Shayler left the United Kingdom for Holland. On 21 August 2000 he voluntarily returned from France, arrived at Dover, and was arrested. He was cautioned and made no reply. He was not interviewed, but was taken to London and charged the same afternoon. In response to being charged he said he had returned voluntarily to face charges, to clear his name, and to challenge what he described as “cover-ups and complacency” following his disclosures. He admitted he had been a Crown servant as an MI5 officer from November 1991 to October 1996, but did not admit making disclosures contrary to the criminal law, asserting that any disclosures were made in the public and national interests.

He faced three counts alleging unauthorised disclosure: two counts concerning disclosure of documents or information relating to security or intelligence said to have been in his possession by virtue of his MI5 position, and one count concerning disclosure of information obtained under interception warrants.

Before trial, at a preparatory case management hearing, the trial judge ruled on what the prosecution had to prove and on the availability of certain defences. The judge ruled that the prosecution needed to prove Shayler’s status as a member/former member of the security and intelligence services, that he disclosed the relevant documents or information that he had by virtue of that position (including interception-warrant material), and that he did so without lawful authority. The judge also ruled that the offences did not permit a defence based on the disclosure being necessary in the public interest to avert threats to life or limb or serious damage to property, and that the statutory scheme provided routes for authorised disclosure (including disclosure to specified officials and the possibility of seeking authorisation), with refusal of authorisation capable of challenge by judicial review.

On appeal, the Court of Appeal dismissed Shayler’s appeal against those rulings. The court concluded that, although a defence of duress/necessity of circumstances can in principle apply to these offences, Shayler’s stated justification (as revealed by the material before the court) could not satisfy the requirements of that defence because he could not identify an imminent, specific threat to life or serious injury that his disclosures were necessary to avert, and there was no close nexus between the disclosures and any such imminent harm. The court also concluded that the offences were not subject to a general public interest defence based on freedom of expression, and that the statutory scheme’s restrictions were justified given the availability of authorised channels for raising concerns and the importance of protecting national security.
claims:
Shayler’s position, as stated when charged and as advanced on appeal through his counsel, was that he had not committed criminal offences because any disclosures he made were made in the public and national interests. He said he returned to the United Kingdom to clear his name and to challenge what he described as “cover-ups and complacency” that followed his disclosures.

He contended that he should be entitled to rely on freedom of expression (including under common law principles and the right to freedom of expression) as a defence or justification for the disclosures. In substance, he argued that the offences should not be treated as absolute and that there should be scope for a defence where disclosure was necessary in the public interest, including (a) to avert threats to life or limb or serious damage to property, and/or (b) to expose serious and pervasive illegality or iniquity in the obtaining of warrants and surveillance.

He also sought to rely on the common law defences of duress and necessity of circumstances in an extended form, arguing that the jury should be allowed to consider whether he was (or might have believed he was) compelled by circumstances to disclose in order to prevent grave harm to others. He argued that the developments in the law on necessity/duress of circumstances should be available to him at trial and that the jury should decide, on the evidence, whether his disclosures were justified on that basis.

In addition, he challenged the appropriateness of the trial judge making binding rulings at the preparatory hearing that effectively removed these defences and arguments from the issues to be explored at trial, contending that such rulings should not have been made at that stage even if the judge’s legal conclusions were correct.

facts:
A fire occurred on 11 May 2012 at 18 Victory Road, Derby, in the home of Michael and Mairead Philpott, in which six of their children died. Michael and Mairead Philpott, together with Paul Mosley, were charged with manslaughter and were later convicted after a jury trial at Nottingham Crown Court.

A key prosecution witness was Lisa Willis, described as the mother of five children, four of whom were fathered by Michael Philpott. For several years she had lived with Michael and Mairead Philpott at the same address, but she left several months before the fatal fire. After she moved away, a dispute arose between her and Michael Philpott about arrangements for the children. The judgment states that Philpott’s involvement in the fatal fire stemmed from a determination to demonstrate that Lisa Willis was unfit to care for the children, and that the fire was started the night before a listed hearing with the intention that she should be blamed.

Before these events, the lifestyle of Michael Philpott and the women in his life, and his large number of children, had attracted extensive media coverage. Photographs and images of Lisa Willis and her children had appeared on television and in newspapers. Lisa Willis had appeared in three television programmes discussing her relationship with Michael Philpott and the family’s living arrangements, and she and her children were filmed and shown.

The trial attracted worldwide coverage and international interest. Media coverage included images of Lisa Willis, which remained widely available on the internet, including on websites outside the jurisdiction.

Before the trial began, the prosecution applied for special measures for Lisa Willis when giving evidence. The measure granted was the use of protective screens in court. The application relied on a statement from Lisa Willis and oral submissions describing her fearful state of mind. She was willing to give evidence but was concerned her physical identity would be revealed at court. She had taken steps to avoid anyone connected to Philpott knowing her whereabouts or what she looked like. She was living with her children at an unknown location, had changed their surnames, and had altered her appearance. She feared that if she gave evidence openly someone might see her and then locate and follow her to where she lived with her children. She said it would be easier if she could not see Michael Philpott and if he and his family and friends could not see her. She did not want to give evidence by video link; she wanted to give evidence in court but behind screens.

On 12 February 2013, during the trial, the judge made an order prohibiting publication of photographs of Lisa Willis or any of her five children until 5 March 2013. The judge then addressed whether, despite that order, media could publish photographs that evening or before she gave evidence. The judge’s concern was the integrity of the criminal trial. It was submitted that publication of photographs just as she was about to give evidence would undermine the purpose of the special measures. The judge accepted that public focus on her and her children would undermine her ability to give evidence and that publication would reinforce her fears and undermine her attempts not to be recognised. The judge therefore postponed publication of photographs of Lisa Willis or her children and ordered that any photographs already published during the hearing be withdrawn. The judge considered the impact on reporting and concluded written and verbal reports were sufficient and saw no public interest in publishing photographs; she also noted that publishing photographs of Lisa Willis would immediately identify the children.

On 13 February 2013, after reconsideration, the judge revoked the previous order and replaced it with a new order made under a different power. The new order prohibited publication of any photograph, pseudo-photograph, or other image of Lisa Willis or her children in any way that connected them to the case. The media were given liberty to apply to amend or revoke the order on 24 hours’ notice. Lisa Willis then gave evidence in open court behind screens; her evidence was widely reported, and it was not suggested that the media were prevented from reporting her evidence in detail by the order.

The media postponed applying to revoke the order until later in the trial to avoid disruption. On 3 April 2013 the media application to revoke was heard and dismissed. The judge stated she could not see the purpose of publishing photographs or film of Lisa Willis and her children, and concluded that publication would have a very damaging effect on them. She decided the order should remain despite the existence of images available online outside the jurisdiction.

A number of media organisations then applied to the Court of Appeal for leave to appeal against the order restricting publication of images. The Court of Appeal granted leave and ultimately dismissed the appeal, concluding that the order was appropriately made and that reference to the children in the order was integral because publication of photographs of the children would be likely to lead to identification of Lisa Willis and affect the quality of her evidence.
claims:
The appellants (media organisations) sought leave to appeal and asked the Court of Appeal to revoke (or amend) the Crown Court order that prohibited publication of any photograph, pseudo-photograph, or other image of Lisa Willis and/or her children in any way connecting them to the criminal case.

Their arguments, as summarised in the judgment, included:

- The principle of open justice required strong justification for restricting publication, and the order interfered with open reporting.

- The Crown Court had no power at common law to make such an order; any power had to come from statute.

- The fact that special measures (screens) had been granted for Lisa Willis did not itself justify a reporting restriction, and a reporting restriction should not automatically follow from a special measures direction; it required a separate decision.

- Protection of the children of an adult witness did not arise under the relevant reporting-restriction power and was said to be a matter better addressed in family courts.

- Lisa Willis had already been identified through previous publications, television programmes, and the internet; her name and her status as the mother of children fathered by Philpott were effectively common knowledge, and she gave evidence under her own name. On that basis, the appellants contended that the reporting restriction was not within the scope of the relevant power and/or should be revoked.

facts:
The proceedings concerned a boy aged about 10 months. Since birth he had been placed in foster care, where he was described as a happy and content baby with an established routine. He was undergoing assessment for delayed motor development, plagiocephaly and torticollis, and his vision was being monitored. The local authority said a paediatric overview needed to continue without further delay because uncertainty about his development could affect matching him with future carers.

The mother was in her early 20s and had two older children by different fathers. Those children no longer lived with her: one had been the subject of earlier care proceedings and was adopted in 2007, and the other was subject to a special guardianship order made in 2009. There was no contact with either child. The father in these proceedings (in his late 20s) was not involved in the earlier proceedings. He had one other child (born in 2009) who lived with that child’s mother, and he had no contact with that child.

In the current case, paternity was initially in question but was confirmed. Both parents were legally represented throughout, as were the local authority and the child’s guardian. Although both parents had large extended families and the local authority made exhaustive enquiries, no family members came forward or were identified as potential kinship carers.

The local authority had previously been extensively involved with the mother. In earlier proceedings the court had made findings that children were at risk because of parents’ inability to learn and develop necessary skills to prevent the children being placed at risk of harm. The judgment records that similar concerns arose again. The parents were described as having low intellect and as regularly failing to engage with professionals, to whom they displayed hostility. Both had experienced chaotic childhoods and were said to have unrealistic views about their ability to parent a young child. The mother had a history of mental health difficulties and self-harm. She was also described as failing to address her own health needs, including not protecting herself from the sun despite an acute medical condition requiring this, and failing to follow up medical and eyesight appointments. The father was described as having been brought up in the care system, which was said to raise concerns about his ability to parent.

Before the child’s birth, there were child protection conferences and some progress was noted in parental cooperation. To assist the parents, the local authority funded an initial four-week residential assessment at an independent parent-and-baby centre, with the possibility of extending funding for a further eight weeks if successful. In August 2009 both parents stayed for one night and then did not continue with the assessment. The limited report from the centre stated that neither parent had the ability or knowledge to meet the child’s very basic needs; although they showed love and affection, this was insufficient, and the centre believed the child would be at risk if left in the community.

By the time of the final hearing, the parents had had no contact with the child for about four and a half months, after the parents terminated contact. Earlier contact had been inconsistent despite efforts by the local authority to promote it both at the residential unit and in the community. The court accepted evidence that the parents showed little commitment to contact and had not shown they were prepared to put the child’s needs above their own.

The mother filed no formal evidence other than a handwritten statement. She said she could not bring herself to agree to the orders sought but did not actively oppose them, stating it was a difficult decision because she loved the child but believed the outcome was in the child’s best interests. The father filed three statements opposing the orders. Shortly before the hearing he admitted he had had no contact with the child for about four and a half months. Neither parent attended the final hearing, despite having been given notice and being represented.

Independent expert evidence included psychological reports indicating that, although both parents had learning difficulties, these were not at such a level that they would be unable to care for a child; however, the conclusion was that the child would be at risk of physical harm and neglect due to the parents’ lack of parenting skills and their refusal to engage with professionals who could assist, and that neither showed the will to learn or cooperate. An independent social worker noted some positive practical features (a clean and tidy home and a well-stocked fridge) but considered it extremely doubtful these skills could be translated into caring for a child. Concern was expressed about the father’s aggressive manner and short fuse and his ability to tolerate normal challenges presented by babies. The parents’ rejection of the residential assessment and failure to commit to contact were said to raise serious concerns about genuine motivation to adapt to parenthood.

The guardian reported that the parents failed to prioritise the child’s needs and failed to attend arranged contact without good reason, despite finding contact emotionally difficult. The guardian accepted that alternative options had been explored and, with regret, agreed with the local authority’s plan as the only option available to meet the child’s best interests.

The court found the threshold for intervention was met on the evidence and noted that neither parent attended the final hearing to oppose the orders. The court decided an order had to be made and that the only realistic option was a care order, approving the local authority’s plan for the child.
claims:
The applicant local authority sought public law orders in relation to the 10-month-old child. It applied for a care order and advanced a care plan for the child to be placed with a substitute family by way of adoption.

To support its application, the local authority asked the court to make findings that: both parents were vulnerable (with the mother having mental health problems and having attempted self-harm); both had been brought up in or partly in the care system and had been poorly parented as children; they lived and continued to live chaotic lifestyles and were unable to budget; neither was realistic about their ability to parent a young child; and the mother displayed hostility to professionals attempting to assist her and the child and to ensure she took proper care of her own health.

The local authority’s case, as reflected in the evidence relied upon, was that the parents lacked the ability and knowledge to meet the child’s basic needs, had rejected and failed to participate in a residential parent-and-baby assessment, had not engaged with professionals who could help them develop parenting skills, and had shown little commitment to maintaining contact with the child. It contended that, if the child were in their care, he would be at risk of physical harm and neglect, and that adoption was necessary to secure the child’s welfare given the absence of suitable family carers and the need for timely planning in light of the child’s developmental uncertainties.

facts:
The proceedings arose out of an earlier Court of Protection application concerning Mrs N, who had been receiving life-sustaining treatment in the form of clinically assisted nutrition and hydration delivered via a percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube. In November 2015 the court heard four days of evidence about Mrs N’s medical condition and her best interests. The judge considered medical evidence and the family’s evidence about Mrs N’s wishes, feelings, character and values. The judge found the family’s evidence to be notably candid and unshaped by their preferred outcome, and described Mrs N as a complex person who was proud of her family, jealous of her privacy, feisty, and loyal to her children. The judge concluded that it was in Mrs N’s best interests for life-sustaining treatment to be withdrawn and granted a declaration to that effect.

On 2 November 2015, during Mrs N’s lifetime, the judge made a reporting restriction order prohibiting identification of Mrs N and the first respondent in press reporting during her lifetime, and continuing for seven days after her death. Mrs N died on 16 December 2015.

On 17 December 2015, M (Mrs N’s daughter and the applicant) applied to vary the reporting restriction order to extend it until 14 days after a forthcoming judgment in another case addressing the scope of reporting restriction orders after the death of the person concerned. On 13 January 2016 the judge varied the order as requested; no party opposed that variation.

After the later judgment was delivered in April 2016, M applied again on 4 May 2016 to extend the reporting restriction order “until further order of the court.” The application was made on notice to the parties and to the press. On 5 May 2016 the judge refused to deal with it on paper and listed it for consideration on 22 June 2016. The court considered written submissions only. The Press Association filed detailed written submissions opposing any further extension.

The judge contrasted this case with another case that had attracted adverse and “prurient” media attention. Here, the judge noted that reporting had been largely confined to issues of capacity and serious medical treatment. The judge also observed that this case had been significant to legal and medical professionals because it represented an evolution in the court’s approach to declarations concerning withdrawal of clinically assisted nutrition and hydration for a person in a minimally conscious state.

The Press Association argued that births and deaths are public events and that reporting a death is not, of itself, a disclosure solely within the private sphere. It also argued that the application was effectively for an open-ended interim order, and emphasised the importance of open justice and the burden on the applicant to justify restrictions. It submitted that, given the sad but not exceptional circumstances, and given press standards about handling grief, significant media intrusion into the family’s life was unlikely. It pointed to an industry scheme enabling families to request that journalists leave them alone.

M became anxious about the outcome and the costs and asked the judge to decide the application on the documents and a short written submission from counsel; no party attended.

In considering the balance, the judge referred to factual material from the earlier best-interests judgment about Mrs N’s history, including that decades earlier she had pursued paternity litigation in court which required discussion of intimate matters and would have been heard in a courtroom open to the press. The judge also noted that, in the present case, there was no evidence of press intrusion in recent months and no indication from the facts that significant intrusion was likely in the future. The judge considered that people close to the family would likely have identified Mrs N from the facts already reported, and that for those beyond that circle, naming the individuals would make the story more real and sharpen public engagement with the issues.

The judge concluded that, in this case, the balance favoured freedom of expression and open justice over continuing anonymity, and refused to extend the reporting restriction order on an open-ended basis. The judge also addressed (though it had not been raised by the Press Association) whether the court had power to deal with such an application after Mrs N’s death, and stated that he was considering the application as a judge of the High Court as well as a judge of the Court of Protection.
claims:
M sought to vary the existing reporting restriction order so that the prohibition on identifying Mrs N and the family would continue after Mrs N’s death on an open-ended basis, namely “until further order of the court.”

In support of that relief, M argued that the family’s privacy interests remained engaged despite Mrs N’s death, because the earlier judgment contained intimate details about Mrs N’s life and her relationships which would not otherwise have been public. M contended that identifying Mrs N would significantly interfere with the privacy of M, her brother and her father, and that any intrusion would have a significant impact because they were a private Jewish family well known in their wider community.

M further relied on evidence that the family had been distressed by their involvement in the proceedings and by press interest. She said that after the judge’s decision there had been significant press interest and requests to the family for publicity, and that the family’s consistent wish had been for their privacy to be respected.

M also argued that the Press Association had not explained why the public interest in reporting would be engaged or enhanced by naming Mrs N or the family. She maintained that the public interest in the medical issues and in understanding the court’s practices and procedures could be widely disseminated without identifying them, and that the privacy considerations and harm from identification outweighed the countervailing interest in publication. On that basis, she submitted that the appropriate duration of the reporting restriction order was “until further order.”

facts:
JMK was born on 18 April 1936. She was married; her husband died in August 2014. There were at least two children from the marriage.

On 8 September 2014 JMK apparently signed a document headed “Continuing Power of Attorney for Property” (an Ontario, Canada document) appointing her daughter SH and son-in-law PH as her attorneys, with authority to act jointly and severally. The document stated that the attorneys were authorised to act even if JMK became mentally incapable. The document contained no other information about JMK’s capacity to execute the instrument or to manage her property and affairs.

On 22 July 2015 JMK moved into DO Care Home in Canada. A letter dated 20 October 2015 from the care home’s Director of Care stated that JMK required assistance with activities of daily living provided by 24-hour personal support workers and registered nursing care; that due to lack of insight and poor judgment she was considered an elopement risk and therefore required 24-hour security in a secure home area; that she was under medical supervision; and that her diagnoses included dementia, depression, osteoporosis and hypertension.

PH told the court that managing JMK’s affairs included a legal dispute with one of JMK’s children who was suing her for funds he believed were his. PH later stated that this dispute was settled in December 2017, on the recommendation of the Canadian public authority involved, in a way that ended the lawsuit but left JMK’s funds nearly exhausted.

SH and PH applied to the Court of Protection on 2 March 2017 seeking recognition in England and Wales of the Canadian continuing power of attorney. A certified copy of the instrument was provided. On 31 August 2017 the application was dismissed on paper. PH applied on 30 October 2017 for reconsideration. The matter was listed for an attended hearing on 13 March 2018, but there was no attendance and no oral submissions; PH filed a written skeleton argument dated 25 February 2018.
claims:
SH and PH (as applicants) sought an order/declaration from the Court of Protection to recognise in England and Wales the Canadian “Continuing Power of Attorney for Property” made by JMK, so that it would be treated as a measure capable of recognition by the court.

In support of recognition, PH argued in writing that the Canadian power of attorney should be treated as a measure directed to protecting JMK and/or her property because it enabled him and SH to represent and otherwise help JMK in managing her financial affairs. He contended that the instrument was designed to operate protectively in the management of JMK’s finances, and he referred to Canadian law as treating the power of attorney as a legal document. He stated that, as attorney, he was legally (and felt morally) obliged to act responsibly in administering, conserving, or disposing of JMK’s property to ensure her wellbeing.

PH also relied on the practical use of the document, stating that it had been used and recognised by Canadian and British institutions and corporations to allow him to represent JMK in matters including disposal of her house and car, settling significant debts, insurance claims, Canadian pensions, UK pensions (including government and Ministry of Defence pensions), and Canadian taxes. He argued that both the power of attorney and their ongoing actions under it were undertaken with the sole intent of protecting JMK’s health, wellbeing, and personal and financial interests, and therefore should qualify for recognition.

In earlier correspondence, PH also asserted that there was no requirement in Canada for such documents to be registered and that the government did not keep a registry, and he explained that the power of attorney had been obtained to allow them properly to help with household finances by having JMK’s authority.
