facts:
The appellant (SR) had been a registered childminder since 14 November 2000. On 15 September 2003 she began caring for JA, then aged 16 months, the son of Ms O.

Ms O said she chose SR because SR did not do school runs and did not have pets. When Ms O first visited SR on 13 September 2003, she said she made clear she did not want JA taken out in the cold and that this was why it mattered to her that SR did not do school runs. Ms O normally collected JA between 4.00pm and 4.30pm, but on one occasion arrived shortly before 3.15pm and found SR dressed and ready to go out while JA was asleep. This caused Ms O concern that SR might be doing school runs and raised questions in Ms O’s mind about what happened to JA if SR went out while he was asleep. Ms O suspected JA might be left with a neighbour if he did not accompany SR.

On Monday 20 October 2003, Ms O finished college early and deliberately arrived at SR’s first-floor flat at 3.18pm. She rang the bell and knocked at the letter box but got no response. She sat on the stairs to wait. After a short while, SR arrived with her own son and two other children, but not JA. Ms O said SR stated she had only been gone five minutes (Ms O thought it had been longer). Ms O said SR did not let her into the flat; Ms O took the pushchair downstairs and SR brought JA out to her. Ms O said she did not hear SR speak to anyone as SR went into the flat, did not notice anyone pass her while she was putting JA into the pushchair, and SR did not tell her anyone was in the flat. Ms O heard SR call out of the kitchen window to her son. Ms O was very upset and cried on the way home. After discussing it with JA’s father, they concluded JA had been left alone in SR’s flat. Ms O decided to find a new childminder and, after being advised to do so, reported the matter to OFSTED on Wednesday 22 October 2003. Ms O said that on the same day SR visited her and told her that the mother of another child had been with JA in the flat while SR was at the school.

OFSTED’s evidence was that on 30 October 2003 there was a strategy meeting and a joint investigation by the local social services department and the police was established. On 31 October 2003 two OFSTED inspectors visited SR to deliver a document informing her of a complaint and inviting her to telephone for further information; the inspectors were instructed not to discuss details of the complaint. The letter raised the possibility of SR voluntarily suspending her childminding and asked for a decision by the following Monday. SR contacted parents of children she cared for and decided not to suspend voluntarily. On 3 November 2003 OFSTED delivered a decision to suspend SR’s registration. SR appealed on 5 November 2003.

Ms O was interviewed by a police officer and a social worker and repeated her account, stating she did not want criminal charges. On 11 November 2003 SR was interviewed by the police in the presence of a solicitor; a transcript was before the tribunal.

SR’s account was that on 20 October 2003 JA was not left alone but was left with Ms U (the mother of another child SR was minding). SR said her own child was usually brought home from school by Ms W, but Ms W was sometimes unable to do so, particularly on Mondays. SR said she had put the boys (JA and Ms U’s son) in their cots and they fell asleep; SR also dozed. Around 3.00pm Ms U arrived to collect her son. SR had not heard from Ms W and so had to go to the school. Both children were still asleep. Ms U suggested SR go to the school while Ms U woke her own son, got him ready to leave, and kept an eye on JA. SR said JA had been coughing and she decided to leave him asleep under Ms U’s supervision while she went to collect her son. SR said she told Ms U not to open the door or answer the telephone. The school was close and SR expected to be out for ten to twelve minutes. While at the school SR arranged to bring home two of her son’s friends. SR said she returned to find Ms O waiting and asked how long she had been waiting; SR said Ms O replied “five minutes.” SR said she apologised and told Ms O she had left JA with another child’s mother and Ms O said that was all right. SR said Ms O had previously preferred not to go up to the flat because she found the stairs difficult. SR said she brought JA to Ms O and, while Ms O was putting JA into the pushchair, Ms U left the flat with her son and Ms O would have seen Ms U. SR said she said goodbye to JA and Ms U’s son from the window. SR said Ms O did not bring JA during the next two days; SR visited Ms O on the Wednesday evening to find out what was happening, and Ms O told SR of her suspicion that JA had been left alone. SR said she asked why Ms O had not raised it at the time and Ms O said she did not wish to be disrespectful.

SR accepted that leaving JA with Ms U (if that is what happened) was wrong, but said it seemed reasonable at the time. SR produced a letter from Ms U supporting SR’s account, and Ms U gave evidence to the same effect.

OFSTED’s evidence was that on 13 November 2003 a further strategy meeting reviewed the position; it was thought unlikely the police or social services would take action, but it was resolved to speak to Ms U and other parents and to consider speaking to JA. By the hearing, the tribunal was told SR’s son had been interviewed with no concerns raised; other parents had said they had no concerns; and Ms U had told the police she had been looking after JA at the relevant time. At a strategy meeting on 21 November 2003 it was decided to end the child protection investigation, but OFSTED should consider whether SR should continue to be registered. OFSTED wished to interview Ms U and SR before deciding whether to cancel SR’s registration.

The tribunal considered whether further investigation by OFSTED was reasonable and whether there might be a risk of harm. It found Ms O was probably honest, and that her complaint required investigation when made. Although SR and Ms U presented a credible alternative account, it was not so compelling as to exclude the possibility that Ms O was right that JA had been left alone. The tribunal considered that further investigation was required, including because new issues and discrepancies arose (including information obtained from the school suggesting SR frequently collected her son herself, which merited investigation).

The tribunal did not decide what actually happened on 20 October 2003, but was satisfied JA may have been left alone and that there was credible evidence from which that inference might be drawn. It considered that if a 17-month-old child is left alone asleep in a cot there is a risk the child may wake and come to serious harm. The tribunal concluded there may be a risk of harm if SR were allowed to continue childminding while the matter was further investigated, and that the potential risk was sufficiently serious to justify continuing the suspension despite the financial loss to SR and inconvenience to parents. The tribunal confirmed OFSTED’s suspension decision and continued the suspension until 15 December 2003, expressing hope investigations would conclude before then.
claims:
SR appealed OFSTED’s decision of 3 November 2003 to suspend her registration as a childminder and sought to have the suspension lifted so she could resume childminding.

In support of her appeal, SR’s central argument was factual: she denied leaving JA alone on 20 October 2003 and maintained that JA was supervised by Ms U (the mother of another minded child) while SR briefly went to collect her own child from a nearby school. SR explained the circumstances leading to this arrangement (Ms W not collecting SR’s child that day; both children asleep; JA coughing; Ms U offering to stay and watch JA) and said she instructed Ms U not to open the door or answer the telephone and expected to be away for only ten to twelve minutes. SR asserted she told Ms O at the time that JA had been left with another child’s mother and that Ms O indicated this was acceptable. SR relied on Ms U’s supporting letter and Ms U’s oral evidence.

SR also relied on the impact of the suspension, referring to the financial loss she was suffering and the inconvenience caused to parents who used her services, and presented supportive evidence from parents (including oral evidence from Ms N, who wanted SR to be allowed to care again for her child).

facts:
The applicant local authority sought interim protective orders for six siblings: J (9), D (8), C (6), Jo (5), F (2) and B (11 months). The children’s mother is LN and their father is RM. The father did not attend the hearing and was unrepresented. The children were represented through a guardian. The family had a long history of involvement with multiple children’s services departments across different areas, with repeated moves.

Historically, concerns recorded by agencies included: the mother’s depression with suicidal ideation; the father’s personality disorder and aggressive behaviour (and he was serving a suspended sentence for public order offences); a history of substance misuse (alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and heroin); significant domestic violence with a pattern of the mother leaving and reconciling with the father, with the children regularly caught up in parental conflict; sporadic school attendance; and lack of engagement with children’s services alongside multiple moves when services became involved.

In 2009, when the parents had three children, proceedings were issued by Hertfordshire following a period of involvement with the children as children in need. Those proceedings concluded after the birth of the fourth child (Jo) in 2010, when, after a period of residential assessment, the parents were considered capable of providing “good enough” care; the concerns at that time related to drug use, mental health and domestic abuse.

The family later moved to Spain and returned around the end of 2013 after the birth of their fifth child (F). By July 2014 they were living in Barnet and the children were again subject to child in need plans. They moved to Croydon in October 2014, after which the sixth child (B) was born. Records noted the mother complaining to an independent domestic violence adviser that the father went on drug and alcohol binges and sold household items to fund his habit, and that the mother was socially isolated in Croydon.

During May and June 2015 the family moved between Hertfordshire and Croydon. In June 2015 the children became subject to child protection plans in Croydon due to reports of domestic violence. A particularly serious incident was recorded as occurring on 4 June 2015: it was alleged (and recorded as witnessed by a member of the public who called police) that the father strangled the mother and held her off the ground by her neck, pushed her to the ground, slammed a double buggy into her, dragged her by the hair, took her keys, and told her to sleep “with one eye open.” The father’s account was that he was trying to get the children away from the mother and that the mother assaulted his sister. The incident appeared to have occurred in front of the children.

Following this, the mother applied for protective orders against the father, stating he had sought to remove the children from her care and had retained the cases of J and D at the time of the application. A hearing took place on 13 July 2015 before a judge in Watford County Court, who ordered a report because the children may have been at risk of significant harm. On 14 July 2015 the father was arrested after making threats to the judge and security, was charged with public order offences, and later received an eight-month prison sentence suspended for 12 months.

After the children were returned to the mother’s care, they made disturbing allegations about the father, including that he had held their heads under water and made them knock on doors and run away and drink vodka. In mid-August 2015 a multi-agency risk assessment meeting assessed the risk of domestic violence as high.

Croydon reported difficulty undertaking direct work with the family. On 27 August 2015 Croydon issued a missing person alert for all six children because their whereabouts were unknown; it was alleged the mother refused to provide details to the social worker. The family had in fact moved to Ealing in early September 2015, and the older children were enrolled in school there. The accommodation in Ealing was said to have been arranged on the basis that the mother was fleeing domestic violence from the father.

On 16 September 2015 the private law proceedings in Watford County Court were dismissed and the earlier direction for a report was discharged. That hearing was attended by social work representatives from Croydon, Ealing and Hertfordshire, and by the mother’s solicitor and counsel for Croydon; neither parent attended. Hertfordshire said it could not undertake the report because the family had moved to Croydon. Croydon informed the court it was considering issuing care proceedings. It was believed the parents had resumed their relationship, and further attempts to engage the mother failed. After delay while agencies decided who should act, Croydon issued these proceedings, in consultation with Ealing, because of the family’s transient lifestyle.

At the time of this hearing, the father was at the mother’s property caring for the children, despite that property having been provided to assist the mother in fleeing him; the parents had reconciled and presented as a couple. The mother had been served with the proceedings only after 4pm the previous day.

The court accepted there were reasonable grounds to believe the children were at risk of significant harm attributable to parental care, particularly due to ongoing risks from domestic abuse and the chaotic and volatile lifestyle. The court was not satisfied the mother could reliably exclude or “police” the father’s absence from the home, given her position that he posed no risk and her history of reconciliation. The court therefore made the interim orders sought and listed an early return date for fuller challenge by the parents.
claims:
Croydon applied for interim care orders for all six children. Croydon’s case was that, given the family’s history and the current situation, the children needed to be separated from both parents and placed in safe care pending further assessments to determine whether the parents could care for them in the longer term. Croydon relied on the history of domestic violence, instability and lack of engagement with services, and contended that the domestic abuse was ongoing and serious, creating a volatile and chaotic environment that placed the children at risk of significant harm.

Croydon’s application was supported by Ealing (which attended anticipating an argument about which authority should be designated) and by the children’s guardian.

The mother opposed the interim care orders and opposed separation. She argued she had insufficient notice and time to prepare, challenged much of the recent history presented, and asserted the father did not pose a threat to her or the children. She contended that domestic abuse between her and the father had ended in 2009 and said that her more recent allegations and steps (including obtaining housing on the basis she was fleeing domestic violence and seeking protective orders) were not truthful and were made to “get her own back” after the father went off with someone else. She asked the court not to proceed with Croydon’s application at that hearing and sought time for a fully contested hearing where she could respond properly. She also emphasised that the father had had no opportunity to put his case to the court.

As an alternative to removal, the mother offered (reluctantly) to exclude the father from the home pending a full determination at a later hearing, proposing that the children remain with her in the meantime.

facts:
Reading Borough Council, through its Licensing Applications Committee, decided on 18 June 2003 to grant 30 additional hackney carriage (taxi) licences, increasing the number in circulation from 138 by just over one fifth. The decision followed a commissioned unmet-demand study by Transport Planning (International) Limited (TPI), whose final report was issued in January 2003.

TPI’s stated objectives were to determine whether there was significant unmet demand for hackney carriage services in Reading Borough and, if so, how many licences would be required to meet that unmet demand. The study was said to cover the entire licensing area. TPI described difficulties in defining unmet demand (including variable demand) and adopted a three-stage approach: identifying the demand profile, estimating passenger and cab delays, and comparing delays to the demand profile. TPI also considered potential or latent demand.

TPI’s methodology included observations at taxi ranks (each of the 138 licensed vehicles was observed at least once), a pedestrian survey of about 500 people, queue analysis, comparisons with other districts, consultation with hackney and private hire operators and other bodies, and observation of informal ranks. The pedestrian survey found that only a small proportion of respondents cited waiting time/availability as a reason for not using hackney carriages; most suggested lower fares, and smaller proportions suggested more ranks or more licences.

TPI’s detailed delay analysis focused on peak periods at Reading Station on 31 October 2002 and 2 November 2002. TPI concluded that eliminating observed passenger delays at peak delay conditions would have required 20 additional vehicles but would have substantially increased cab waiting time; bringing passenger delays under one minute would have required 8 additional vehicles, and further improvements beyond that were described as marginal for passengers and disproportionate in disbenefit to the trade.

TPI reported consultation feedback including from the Reading Taxi Drivers’ Association (represented by Mr Johnson), who emphasised the need for “balance,” warning that a large increase would cause hardship for those who had invested in vehicles and might lead drivers to work unsafe hours, and raising concerns about parking, congestion, service standards, and confrontation with illegal private hire activity.

TPI also addressed informal ranks and was told of private hire vehicles potentially plying for hire. TPI treated this as evidence of unmet hackney demand and suggested rank improvements to attract hackney cabs into areas where they were reluctant to operate. TPI’s conclusions were that there was significant unmet demand and that an increase of 8 licences (to 146) would eliminate that significant unmet demand; it also recommended consideration of rank relocations/expansions and suggested the survey’s useful life was three years.

After the report, a meeting on 14 May 2003 involving representatives of the association, councillors, and the council’s licensing officer (Mr Mortlock) discussed that the survey indicated unmet demand; it was said that the survey recommended a minimum of 8 but that the number issued would be for elected members to decide. The council received an unsigned letter (around 21 May) referring to premiums on plates and suggesting a plate was worth £50,000. A trade union letter of 23 May 2003 stated a general feeling that the council intended to issue more licences than recommended.

On 10 June 2003 Mr Johnson wrote to a councillor urging adoption of the study’s recommendations and stating the trade could absorb 8 new licences, while stressing financial pressures on owners and drivers and asking that no more than 8 plates be issued unless wider impacts were considered. On 16 June 2003 there was a meeting between the report’s author (Mr McKee), Mr Mortlock, and Mr Johnson.

For the Licensing Applications Committee meeting on 18 June 2003, Mr Mortlock prepared an officer report to allow the committee to consider the survey and decide whether any increase was necessary. He referred to problems with private hire cars illegally plying for hire and suggested issuing more hackney licences could help curb illegal activity, though there was strong resistance from the taxi association. He stated that demand on Fridays and Saturdays was exceptionally high and that current hackney numbers could not meet demand, and noted bus services had increased since the survey. He presented four options: (1) issue the minimum 8 licences; (2) move towards market forces determining numbers, phased over several years, with an officer view that 30 per year would be appropriate as part of that approach; (3) issue more than 8 without moving towards de-limiting; or (4) disregard the survey (with a risk of challenge if applications were refused). He appended the survey summary and responses including from the taxi association and the police.

At the committee meeting on 18 June 2003, representatives of the taxi association attended and addressed the committee. Notes record that Mr Mortlock summarised his report and options and that the private hire association’s chairman was said to be happy with 30 to 40 additional licences. Mr Johnson expressed reservations about the survey, said it would be irresponsible to issue too many licences, and referred to financial implications for drivers. Councillors discussed issues including whether unmet demand existed beyond the station, rank facilities, the possibility that the council’s ability to limit numbers might be removed, requests for licences, and the prevalence of private hire vehicles illegally plying for hire around town. The chair indicated that the survey’s quantitative data showed 8 new plates would deal with unmet demand in the station area, but that illegal plying for hire suggested unmet demand for circulating vehicles, and that the committee needed to consider issuing more than 8.

The chair proposed adopting the option to issue more than 8 without moving to de-limiting and proposed 30 new licences. An amendment proposing 15 was moved but the proposal for 30 was carried. The minutes recorded that the committee took into account the unmet demand identified by the survey, the taxi association’s representations, the likelihood of future removal of local control balanced against the trade’s expectations, representations from others seeking more than 8, and the committee’s view that there was unmet demand throughout the town (not just at the station) evidenced by high instances of private hire vehicles plying for hire. The committee considered 30 not unreasonable and noted it would review the impact after 12 months.

In later proceedings, the court upheld the decision as lawful and not irrational. After judgment dismissing the claim, there was argument about costs and the judge ordered the claimant to pay the defendant’s costs, with some reductions on specific items in the costs schedule.
claims:
The claimant (Mr Johnson, on behalf of the Reading Taxi Drivers’ Association) sought judicial review challenging the lawfulness of the council’s decision of 18 June 2003 to grant 30 additional hackney carriage licences.

The claimant’s central argument was that the council misinterpreted the TPI unmet-demand report. The claimant contended that the council wrongly treated TPI’s recommendation of 8 additional licences as addressing only unmet demand at Reading Station and assumed that issuing only 8 would leave unmet demand elsewhere in Reading. The claimant argued that TPI had been commissioned to assess unmet demand across the whole borough without geographical restriction and that TPI’s conclusion and recommendation were not limited to the station.

The claimant further argued that TPI did not rely solely on rank-delay observations but also considered anecdotal evidence, and that the pedestrian survey showed rank delay was only a minor deterrent to hackney carriage use.

The claimant submitted that it was irrational for the council to conclude that unmet demand would remain if only 8 licences were issued, because that conclusion was said to be unsupported by evidence. To the extent councillors relied on their own observations, the claimant argued those were improper and irrelevant considerations. To the extent the council relied on observations of informal rank activity by private hire vehicles, the claimant argued this was wrong and/or a misinterpretation of the report, because (as the claimant put it) the report treated private hire presence as a consequence of hackney carriages being reluctant to operate in those areas.

The claimant also argued that selecting 30 additional licences was irrational because the figure was taken from the officer’s “option 2” (a phased move towards de-limiting) and was not justified as an appropriate number in the context of issuing more than 8 without moving to de-limiting. The claimant argued that even if the report were read as limited to the station, there was no proper basis for concluding that a further 22 licences (beyond the 8 recommended) were required, given that the greatest demand was at the station.

Finally, the claimant argued that the committee’s intention to monitor the impact after 12 months would not remedy the problem because, by then, the harm would already have occurred and the council would not be able to cancel licences at that stage.

After losing on the merits, the claimant sought a costs order that each party bear its own costs, arguing that before issuing proceedings the claimant had proposed alternative dispute resolution and that the council did not engage meaningfully until after permission was granted; the claimant said settlement discussions foundered on the council’s insistence that the claimant pay some of the council’s costs. The court rejected the request for no order as to costs and ordered the claimant to pay the defendant’s costs, with limited reductions to certain claimed items.

facts:
Karen Murphy was convicted by Portsmouth Magistrates’ Court of two offences said to have been committed on 19 August 2006 and 25 September 2006 at her public house, the Red White and Blue in Southsea, Hampshire. The convictions related to the reception and showing in the pub of live Premier League football matches (Bolton Wanderers v Tottenham Hotspur, and Portsmouth v Bolton Wanderers). The Premier League owned the relevant intellectual property rights in the live screening of Premier League matches and granted exclusive territorial licences to broadcasters. At the relevant time, the exclusive licensee for the United Kingdom and Ireland was BSkyB, and the exclusive licensee for Greece was a Greek provider, NOVA.

The matches were filmed using crew, cameras and equipment provided by BSkyB at the grounds. The live feed of visual images and ambient sound was sent to the BT Tower and then to BSkyB and to the Premier League at Chiswick. BSkyB added additional material (including commentary) and its logo in real time and uplinked the resulting broadcast to its satellite for transmission to its subscribers. Separately, at Chiswick the Premier League added an English commentary to the feed, encrypted it, and sent it to NOVA in Greece. NOVA then added its own material (including an optional Greek commentary, its “Live S7” logo, and sometimes advertisements) and uplinked the broadcast to the NOVA (Hotbird) satellite for reception by NOVA subscribers.

Both BSkyB’s and NOVA’s satellite transmissions had footprints extending beyond the territorial limits of their respective licences. Anyone within a satellite footprint with the appropriate dish, decoder box and decryption card could technically view the broadcasts. NOVA used conditional access technology requiring a decoder card; such cards were authorised for use in the licensee’s territory. BSkyB also used conditional access technology and supplied decoder cards to subscribers, retaining ownership of the cards and restricting their use to the licensed territory.

When the two matches were shown in Ms Murphy’s pub, she did not have a BSkyB subscription, having cancelled it on grounds of expense when she became licensee of the pub. She did have a satellite dish, a decoder box and a NOVA viewing card enabling her to receive and view NOVA satellite programmes. The television pictures of the matches carried the “Live S7” logo, indicating the signals came via NOVA.

For the purposes of this appeal, it was common ground that the decoder card used by Ms Murphy was not a “pirate” card manufactured and marketed without the authorisation of the NOVA card issuer; it was treated as a genuine NOVA card, though the respondent contended it was being used outside the area for which it was authorised (outside Greece).

Additional material was placed before the court from related proceedings, including that NOVA subscriptions and decoder cards were available through retail outlets in Greece; that subscribers were required to provide a name, Greek address and Greek telephone number; that private subscriptions were contractually limited to personal use at home or workplace and purported to prohibit use in places such as coffee shops and hotels and other commercial exploitation; and that there was evidence in those proceedings of NOVA cards being procured and activated using false names and addresses and then supplied for use in the UK. There was also material indicating NOVA did not consent to the sale or use of NOVA cards outside Greece, and evidence about differing prices for private and commercial subscriptions and the approximate price paid by the supplier associated with Ms Murphy’s equipment.

Ms Murphy’s appeal to the Crown Court at Portsmouth against conviction was dismissed, though her sentence was reduced to a £1,000 fine for each offence and she was ordered to pay £5,000 towards prosecution costs. A first stage of her further appeal by case stated was determined in December 2007, with the court answering questions posed by the Crown Court but leaving open further arguments based on European law. In this second stage, the High Court decided to refer questions to the European Court of Justice for a preliminary ruling, noting that the dishonesty finding against Ms Murphy was based on an allegation that she knew of and deliberately infringed a geographical restriction on the use of her NOVA card, and that if that restriction were unlawful the dishonesty finding would have to be set aside (as conceded by the respondent).
claims:
Ms Murphy sought to overturn her convictions. She pursued arguments that, even if the domestic offence provisions would otherwise apply, her prosecution and conviction were incompatible with European law principles concerning cross-border provision and receipt of services and the movement and use of conditional access devices, and with European competition principles. She asked the High Court to make a reference to the European Court of Justice so that these European law issues could be authoritatively determined, and contended that success on any one of her European law arguments would remove the basis for her convictions.

First, she argued that European measures concerning conditional access were directed only at “pirate” devices (devices manufactured and marketed without the broadcaster’s authorisation) and did not extend to genuine decoder cards marketed with the issuer’s consent but used in another Member State contrary to contractual or territorial stipulations. On that basis, she contended that the domestic offence provision could not lawfully be applied to her circumstances because her card was genuine and not a pirate device; applying the offence to her would unlawfully restrict the cross-border provision of protected services and/or the movement of conditional access devices.

Second, she argued that prosecuting her for using a genuine decoder card obtained from another Member State deterred or prevented the importation and use in the UK of such cards and deterred or prevented her from receiving satellite broadcasts from another Member State. She contended that any such restriction was not justified or proportionate, and that the domestic offence provision should therefore be disapplied in her case.

Third, she argued that the domestic offence provision was discriminatory because it protected broadcasts provided from within the UK but did not provide equivalent protection to broadcasts provided from other Member States, thereby favouring domestic services and disadvantaging cross-border services. She contended that this discriminatory feature prevented the restriction from being justified and required disapplication of the offence provision in a cross-border context such as hers.

Fourth, she argued that the territorial export restriction underpinning the claimed exclusivity of the UK broadcaster’s rights (and the asserted prohibition on the Greek broadcaster’s service being used in the UK) was an unlawful restriction of competition affecting trade between Member States and therefore void. She contended that if the export restriction was unlawful and ineffective, then the asserted absolute territorial exclusivity relied on by the prosecution would not exist. In that event, she argued, the subscription charge of the UK broadcaster would not be “applicable” to the programme she received from the Greek broadcaster, so the element of the offence requiring intent to avoid payment of an applicable charge would not be made out and her convictions would fall away.

In summary, Ms Murphy’s requested relief was that her convictions be quashed on the basis that the domestic offence provision could not lawfully be applied to her receipt and showing of the Greek satellite broadcast using a genuine decoder card, and she sought a reference to the European Court of Justice to resolve the European law questions central to that outcome.

facts:
Thanaleduchumy Sivapalan (“the mother”) arrived in England on 15 February 2001 with her two daughters, Abiramy and Meera Sivapalan, then aged 15 and 16, and claimed asylum for herself and them based on fear of persecution in Sri Lanka. Permission to enter was refused and the mother’s appeal failed in a decision promulgated on 21 March 2002. The daughters later made their own claims.

The daughters were born and lived in Chundukuli, Jaffna (northern Sri Lanka) until October 1995, when the family left because of fighting. Between 1995 and late 1996 they moved between places and then settled briefly in Skanthapuram.

According to Abiramy, on 12 January 1997, while living at Kanagapuram, their father disappeared. The disappearance was reported to an LTTE camp at Viluthankulam, where they were told not to worry and that the LTTE would look into it. The next day two men in LTTE uniform came to their home, accused them of spying for the army, hit and beat Abiramy, and threatened to return.

Both daughters described an incident the following day when men in some form of military uniform arrived in three trucks, entered their house, and assaulted their mother. Abiramy tried to run away but was chased, slashed on the shoulder with a bayonet, and brought back. The men produced a hooded man who was badly injured and then shot him dead in front of them, though they were not allowed to see his face. Abiramy said the men told them they had shot their father and said it was because he was spying for the Tigers. Abiramy said she was burned with cigarettes and told she deserved to be killed, leaving scars on her legs. Meera also said she suffered cigarette burns on her thighs and legs in the same incident.

After this, the daughters described further harassment by the same troops, including sexual harassment, leading their mother to decide after several months to move somewhere safer. They then began to attract the attention of the LTTE. Meera said that in July 2000 she was abducted by the LTTE and taken to a camp where they tried to recruit her; she described being made to do tasks such as cutting bunkers and jumping through obstacles. She said that after a day or two she escaped by attaching herself to a group of children who were being released.

After Meera’s abduction, their mother decided they must move to a safer part of Sri Lanka. Their departure from the north was arranged by a teacher whose son (an LTTE member) had recently been killed. They paid 2,000 rupees each for passes provided by the LTTE. On 25 January 2001 a man collected them and led them through the jungle to avoid roads, but they encountered an army patrol and were arrested as suspected LTTE sympathisers. They were taken the following evening to a camp or jail at Kolikudi. Abiramy said they were photographed there. Abiramy said she was questioned about the location of an LTTE camp and accused of being a Tiger spy; she said the authorities searched her and saw her burn marks and bayonet scar. Meera said that at the camp she was locked in a room with several men who abused and touched her; one began removing her clothes and she was hit when she resisted, but she managed to shout for help and was released when the door was unlocked.

Their mother contacted a cousin/uncle, Sokkalingam, who owned a press and was well known locally. The daughters said he arranged what was necessary to secure their release, and on 4 February 2001 they escaped and travelled by train to Colombo. Their accommodation in Colombo was arranged by Sokkalingam, who told them to stay indoors and not go out. On 11 February 2001 they flew from Colombo to Singapore and then travelled to England.

In the mother’s earlier appeal, the adjudicator did not find her credible on several matters. The adjudicator was not satisfied that the mother’s husband had been shot, rejected the mother’s account of Meera’s LTTE abduction, and found that photographs were not taken during detention (a finding treated as casting doubt on the daughters’ later allegation that they were photographed).

The daughters made asylum and human-rights-based claims in their own right on 12 October 2006, were interviewed on 17 October 2006, and their claims were refused on 25 October 2006 with certification that they were clearly unfounded. Judicial review proceedings were started on 2 November 2006. Permission was granted on 2 March 2007 because there was new material not available at the original decision. The Secretary of State reconsidered but maintained certification in letters dated 12 April 2007. Further materials were submitted in May 2008, including references, academic certificates, and testimonials describing the daughters’ integration into their Glasgow community and their studies in Accounting and Finance at Strathclyde University. The Secretary of State maintained the earlier position in a letter dated 21 August 2008.

It was accepted in the Secretary of State’s approach that the relevant assessment focused on the daughters’ position in Colombo (rather than asserting they would be safe in the north or east). The decision letters noted that the daughters spoke Tamil and English fluently, presented as young westernised women, and did not speak Sinhala. The daughters asserted they had no relatives in Colombo and would face serious difficulties there, including problems obtaining identification documents and vulnerability during security operations.
claims:
Each claimant sought judicial review of the Secretary of State’s certification that her asylum and human-rights claims were “clearly unfounded,” because the effect of certification was that they could not appeal while in the United Kingdom and would be removed to Sri Lanka unless the certification was quashed.

At the hearing, the claimants focused on (i) protection-based claims centred on risk of serious harm on return, and (ii) interference with their private life.

On the protection-based case, the claimants argued that, if returned (with the assessment focused on Colombo), they would face a real risk of serious ill-treatment. They relied on risk features including: a previous record of being suspected of LTTE involvement; their prior detention and alleged escape from custody; the presence of scarring (including cigarette burns and Abiramy’s bayonet scar); lack of an identity card or proper identification; and alleged LTTE connections through their father. They also contended that without ID cards and without Sinhala they would be vulnerable to being rounded up and detained during routine security measures, and that as young women they would be particularly vulnerable if detained.

On the private-life claim, the claimants argued that removal would disproportionately interfere with their established private lives in the UK. They relied on: their ages on arrival (15 and 16); residence in the UK for over seven years during which they were educated and transitioned from childhood to adulthood; strong integration into their Glasgow community with extensive participation in communal activities and volunteering; current university studies with prospects of qualifying as accountants; lack of relatives in Colombo; and the practical and safety difficulties they said they would face in Sri Lanka, including deprivation associated with conflict conditions and vulnerability to detention and mistreatment.

They sought quashing of the certifications so that they would not be removed without an in-country right of appeal.

facts:
The Export Credits Guarantee Department (ECGD) is a government department whose role includes facilitating UK exports and insuring overseas investment by UK entities, including by providing financial guarantees and export insurance. In complex or sensitive cases it seeks comments from other government departments on projects it is asked to support.

One such project was a scheme to develop offshore oil and gas fields off the north-east coast of Sakhalin Island (the Sakhalin LNG project). In 2003 the project was to be undertaken by a consortium in which Shell had a majority stake; by early 2007 the consortium arrangements changed so that Gazprom held a 50% interest. ECGD was asked to support approximately US$650 million of project finance. The project was expected to have potentially great environmental impacts, including on the habitat and feeding grounds of the Western Grey whale, a species whose survival is endangered; the project’s side effects might prove terminal to it. The project attracted adverse interest from environmental groups including Friends of the Earth (FoE).

On 28 February 2003 ECGD notified several government departments that an application (or prospective application) was being treated as potentially sensitive and invited responses by 14 March 2003. Three responses were received, from the Foreign and Commonwealth Office, DEFRA, and the Department of Trade and Industry.

On 11 March 2005 FoE requested from ECGD (1) the correspondence/notification by which ECGD notified relevant government departments that the application was potentially sensitive and requested comments, and (2) all information received from those departments in response, in relation to the Sakhalin LNG project. On 4 July 2005 ECGD said the request involved internal government communications and refused to disclose the three departmental responses, although it did disclose its own request for information. FoE sought an internal review and ECGD maintained its refusal. During that process it became apparent that a response had been received from DEFRA, which FoE had not identified in its original request.

On 24 November 2005 FoE applied to the Information Commissioner for a decision. On 6 September 2006 the Commissioner upheld ECGD’s refusal. FoE appealed to the Information Tribunal, which on 20 August 2007 allowed the appeal and ordered disclosure of all the information requested, concluding that ECGD had not shown a sufficiently demonstrable public interest in withholding the interdepartmental responses to outweigh the public interest in disclosure.

ECGD appealed to the High Court on a point of law. The High Court identified aspects of the Tribunal’s reasoning that appeared to suggest an incorrect requirement to prove specific harm before weighing the public interest, and criticised the Tribunal’s description of certain general “good government” considerations as “ulterior.” However, the High Court held that, read as a whole, the Tribunal had applied the correct test because it had examined the actual documents and concluded that disclosure of at least one response was highly unlikely to cause prejudice to candour or collective responsibility and might improve the deliberative process, and that another response was not particularly sensitive. The High Court dismissed ECGD’s appeal. The court ordered ECGD to pay FoE’s costs (subject to detailed assessment if not agreed). The judgment also records that no decision on ECGD support for the project had been made and that the application was withdrawn on 29 February 2008, so no decision would ever be made.
claims:
Friends of the Earth sought disclosure from ECGD of environmental information relating to the Sakhalin LNG project: (1) ECGD’s correspondence/notification to government departments treating the application as potentially sensitive and requesting comments, and (2) all information received from those departments in response. FoE challenged ECGD’s refusal to disclose the interdepartmental responses and pursued review and appeal routes, contending that the information should be disclosed and that the public interest favoured disclosure.

In the Tribunal proceedings (as reflected in the High Court judgment), FoE’s position included that there was a strong public interest in the public being acquainted with the exchanges between ECGD and other departments, and specifically in enabling the public to see whether ECGD had been properly advised and whether departments with relevant responsibilities had properly fulfilled them.

In the High Court proceedings, FoE’s requested relief was that ECGD’s appeal be dismissed and the Tribunal’s disclosure order upheld. FoE also applied for its costs of the appeal.

facts:
MN and KN are siblings. At the time of Hackney’s decision on 16 March 2012, MN was aged 3 and KN was aged 13. The family are Jamaican nationals present in the UK unlawfully. The father entered the UK in June 2000 on a short visitor visa and did not leave. The mother and KN joined him in July 2001 on visitor visas and also remained. MN was born in the UK in September 2008 and was diagnosed in May 2011 with an atypical form of autism.

The family did not seek to regularise their status until March 2010, when they applied for leave to remain. That application was refused in November 2010. In March 2011 their solicitors asked for the refusal to be reconsidered or, failing that, for removal directions to be set so that an appeal could be brought. No removal directions were made and the refusal was not reconsidered.

From their arrival until March 2011 the family lived without seeking social services assistance. They stayed with relatives or friends who provided accommodation and financial support, sometimes in exchange for childcare and domestic help. For some period the father earned money selling pirated DVDs at a street market.

In March 2011 the mother approached Hackney saying she was about to become homeless; Hackney refused housing assistance because of immigration status. In January 2012 she again approached Hackney stating she faced homelessness. Hackney again refused assistance but commissioned an assessment of whether the children were “in need” (a Children Act assessment). On 5 March 2012 the mother’s solicitors said the family would be street homeless from 16 March 2012. A letter before action dated 14 March 2012 said the family were temporarily staying with a friend but had been asked to leave before 17 March 2012 and would then be homeless and destitute unless Hackney provided accommodation and financial assistance.

Hackney’s social worker, Donald Brown, met the family on four occasions and made enquiries. Hackney completed two documents: (1) the Children Act assessment (sent 15 March 2012), concluding the children were not “in need”; and (2) an assessment addressing whether refusing support would breach human rights (sent 16 March 2012), concluding there would be no breach if support were refused.

A recurring feature of the assessments was the family’s limited disclosure about how they had supported themselves over more than 10 years in the UK and who had provided past accommodation and financial help. Mr Brown recorded that the parents relied on friends and family but gave scant information, did not explain why that support had ceased, and did not provide contact details for those who had helped them. Mr Brown stated it had not been possible fully to assess the family’s means because of insufficient information. In the Children Act assessment he noted the family “presented as destitute” but said it was “difficult to consider them as destitute” given their current (overcrowded but comfortable) accommodation, though it might end after 16 March 2012. He concluded there was no responsibility for Hackney’s children’s services at that stage and that the family could either continue to support themselves as before or, if not possible, be assisted to return to Jamaica.

On the basis of the assessments, Hackney decided on 16 March 2012 to refuse accommodation and support to the claimants and their parents. Proceedings were issued on 19 March 2012. On the same day, the court ordered Hackney to provide temporary accommodation and support pending the litigation, which Hackney continued to provide while maintaining its position that the family were not in fact destitute.

The court found the assessments did not contain a clear, consistent finding that the family were not destitute; rather, the thrust of Hackney’s reasoning was that, given the family’s long history of surviving without public funds and their failure to provide requested information about past and potential sources of support, Hackney was not satisfied that the family would be homeless and destitute after 16 March 2012 if Hackney did not assist. The court held Hackney had taken reasonable steps to investigate and that it was not irrational for Hackney to decline to accept that the children were “in need” on the information provided. The claim for judicial review was dismissed.
claims:
MN and KN (through representatives) brought a judicial review challenge to Hackney’s decision dated 16 March 2012 refusing to provide accommodation and support to them and their parents. They sought a declaration that Hackney acted unlawfully in making that refusal.

Their case was advanced on the basis that Hackney did not properly determine whether the family were destitute and instead treated the situation as one where Hackney could discharge any obligation by supporting the family to return to Jamaica. They argued that this approach was unlawful and advanced five main grounds:

1) Hackney failed to consider, or to give proper consideration to, whether the children’s needs would be met in Jamaica.

2) Hackney failed to recognise a duty to support the family so they could remain in the UK until a decision was taken to remove them and any appeal on private-life grounds was determined.

3) Hackney failed properly to consider the impact of refusing support (and the consequent return to Jamaica) on the children’s right to respect for their private life, including their ties to the UK.

4) Hackney failed to consider whether the children’s best interests would be served by returning to Jamaica.

5) Hackney failed to comply with its public sector equality duty in relation to MN’s disability.

They also initially raised a further ground relating to a separate duty to accommodate, but did not pursue it at the hearing.

In addition, as a fallback position, the claimants argued that if Hackney’s decision was treated as a conclusion that the children were not “in need,” that conclusion was irrational given the asserted risk of homelessness and destitution.

facts:
Ace Airport Parking Limited sought planning permission from Tandridge District Council for development described as a change of use of buildings to provide storage of cars for airport parking (a storage use) and the relocation of an “In Autos” car facility (a business/industrial use). Tandridge District Council refused the application. Ace appealed that refusal to an inspector appointed by the Secretary of State, and the inspector dismissed the appeal.

In the inspector’s decision letter, the main issues were identified as: (1) whether the proposal would result in the use of sustainable modes of transport and minimise private car mileage to Gatwick Airport; and (2) the effect of the proposal on the use of Church Lane and Bridleway route number 520 in relation to highway safety.

In addressing sustainable transport and private car mileage, the inspector considered the relevant local planning policy in the area and also took into account an objection from Crawley Borough Council (a neighbouring authority). The inspector acknowledged that Crawley’s local plan was not part of the development plan for the appeal site, but treated Crawley’s comments as a relevant material planning consideration. The inspector concluded that the proposal conflicted with the sustainable transport aims and objectives of relevant local policies, and also found harm to Gatwick Airport car parking and sustainable transport aims as outlined in Crawley’s policy.

On highway safety, the inspector concluded that, subject to planning conditions, the proposal would accord with highway safety aims and objectives of relevant local policies and transport planning documents. The inspector also found that, compared with an existing permission for storage use, the proposal would have no worse than a neutral impact on traffic movements, and that use by predominantly cars rather than larger vehicles would likely lead to some relative highway safety improvements. These matters were treated as weighing in favour of allowing the development.

Despite those highway-related findings, the inspector concluded overall that the proposal was fundamentally at odds with the car parking and sustainable transport aims applicable to the area. The inspector also found, on the evidence before him, that required airport car parking could be met within Gatwick Airport itself, which he regarded as a more sustainable location, and he did not find a compelling reason to allow the proposal. He concluded that allowing the proposal would result in non-sustainable transport modes and would unacceptably increase private car mileage to the airport, and that these concerns were overriding and not overcome by the highway safety findings or by the fact that some private vehicle mileage would be associated with the existing permitted storage use.

Ace then brought a renewed application to the High Court for permission to appeal (challenge) the inspector’s decision. The High Court refused permission and dismissed the application. The Secretary of State sought costs for preparing the acknowledgement of service in the sum of £2,479, and Ace did not oppose that costs order.
claims:
Ace Airport Parking Limited sought permission from the High Court to appeal (challenge) the inspector’s decision dismissing its planning appeal.

Ace advanced two grounds. First, it argued that the inspector made an error of law by treating Crawley Borough Council’s local plan policy as a basis for finding conflict, even though that plan was not part of the development plan for the appeal area. Ace relied in particular on the inspector’s statement that allowing the appeal would mean there would be conflict with Crawley’s policy.

Second, Ace argued that the inspector failed to refer to the development plan and failed to reach an express or implicit conclusion on whether the proposal accorded with the development plan.

Ace’s requested relief was permission to appeal on the basis that these were arguable errors of law. Ace did not oppose the Secretary of State’s application for costs in the amount sought for preparing the acknowledgement of service.

facts:
In September 2007 a collision incident occurred in the Gulf of Mexico during a seismic survey operation being conducted by the seismic survey vessel WESTERN NEPTUNE. WESTERN NEPTUNE was towing a very large seismic spread consisting of ten streamers and six gun arrays. Each streamer extended about 8,030 metres (about 4.34 miles) astern, with the streamers spaced about 120 metres apart, giving a total spread width of about 1,080 metres. The streamers were being towed at about 12 metres depth. Buoys were fitted at the aft end of every streamer and at the forward end of the outer six streamers; each buoy had a high-intensity blue strobe light and a radar reflector. There were no lights along the length of the tow between the vessel and the tail buoys over four miles astern.

The survey was being carried out in the Green Canyon area about 150 miles south of New Orleans. Survey lines were planned on reciprocal courses and were long legs; at the material time WESTERN NEPTUNE was on a south-westerly leg on about 225° true at about 4–5 knots. WESTERN NEPTUNE was supported by two other seismic vessels, OCEAN ODYSSEY and GECO TAU, positioned off her port side and proceeding on the same course and speed, and by a chase/guard vessel FURORE positioned between one and three miles ahead. FURORE’s role included contacting approaching vessels on VHF on behalf of WESTERN NEPTUNE. A second chase boat that was usually present was unavailable and was not replaced.

WESTERN NEPTUNE was displaying normal navigation lights and a towing light, and also lights indicating she was restricted in her ability to manoeuvre. Her lack of manoeuvrability was substantial: significant course alterations would take hours if the array was to be maintained, and material speed changes risked damaging or sinking the array.

Information about WESTERN NEPTUNE’s operations was promulgated by a local notice to mariners issued by the US Coast Guard stating that WESTERN NEPTUNE would be towing ten cables five nautical miles long and requesting other vessels to keep clear by specified distances forward and astern, and that WESTERN NEPTUNE would monitor VHF channels. WESTERN NEPTUNE’s AIS information also indicated restricted manoeuvrability and that she was towing a long cable.

The other vessel involved was the container ship ST LOUIS EXPRESS, inbound to Houston on a course of about 292° true at about 20 knots, displaying normal navigation lights and equipped with radar and AIS. A voyage data recorder on ST LOUIS EXPRESS provided a recorded radar/AIS picture and audio from the bridge, including VHF exchanges.

As the vessels approached, AIS data showed WESTERN NEPTUNE on ST LOUIS EXPRESS’s starboard bow at long range. Another vessel, EAGLE SUBARU, was also on ST LOUIS EXPRESS’s starboard bow and developed into a close-quarters concern for ST LOUIS EXPRESS. FURORE had earlier contacted EAGLE SUBARU and recorded that EAGLE SUBARU agreed to pass three miles “behind” the seismic convoy.

At about 0221 FURORE contacted ST LOUIS EXPRESS by VHF, advising that a seismic convoy was ahead on ST LOUIS EXPRESS’s starboard bow, that WESTERN NEPTUNE was towing ten seismic cables five nautical miles long, and requesting a wide “safety box” clearance and that ST LOUIS EXPRESS alter course to port to give a specified passing distance. ST LOUIS EXPRESS initially responded that she was altering to port. Shortly thereafter EAGLE SUBARU contacted ST LOUIS EXPRESS and requested that ST LOUIS EXPRESS alter to starboard first to avoid a close-quarters situation with EAGLE SUBARU; ST LOUIS EXPRESS agreed and altered substantially to starboard, then later altered back toward port.

By about 0250 ST LOUIS EXPRESS entered the requested safety zone around the seismic convoy and then steadied on a heading that resulted in her passing about four miles astern of WESTERN NEPTUNE. While this passing distance was measured from WESTERN NEPTUNE herself, it did not take account of the four-mile-long array astern. ST LOUIS EXPRESS crossed the path of the towed array about four miles astern of WESTERN NEPTUNE and cut through or otherwise damaged almost the entirety of the streamers. The point of initial contact with the outer streamer was found to have been very close to the tail buoy (about 20 metres forward of it). After the impact there were VHF exchanges in which WESTERN NEPTUNE referred to the cables being four and a half nautical miles long and asked whether ST LOUIS EXPRESS had seen the flashing lights; ST LOUIS EXPRESS responded affirmatively. The third officer of ST LOUIS EXPRESS later indicated he had seen flashing lights but believed them to be associated with an oil rig and said he had not been told about lights.

The tail buoys’ radar reflectors were not picked up as echoes on ST LOUIS EXPRESS’s radar, with the judgment indicating a likely explanation being radar anti-clutter settings and the presence of heavy rain clutter on part of the radar picture.

The court found that ST LOUIS EXPRESS created the dangerous situation by failing to keep out of the requested exclusion zone and by altering course so as to cross the path of the array, and that her navigation involved poor visual and radar lookout and failures in use of available information. The court also found that WESTERN NEPTUNE (directly or through FURORE) failed to act with reasonable care in several respects: after ST LOUIS EXPRESS altered to starboard to accommodate EAGLE SUBARU, WESTERN NEPTUNE/FURORE did not re-contact ST LOUIS EXPRESS to confirm the exclusion zone and intentions; they did not draw attention to the presence and significance of the tail buoys; they did not continue to monitor ST LOUIS EXPRESS’s movements as she progressively altered to port toward danger; they did not take steps to warn ST LOUIS EXPRESS by VHF or other means once it became apparent she was standing into danger; and they did not dive the streamers as a last-resort measure, even though the streamers could have been dived from 12 to 25 metres in about five minutes and doing so would probably have avoided some of the subsequent damage (though not all). After the collision, WESTERN NEPTUNE’s practices were changed to require more systematic monitoring and a multi-step VHF contact procedure including advising approaching traffic about tail buoys and marking lights, and later to place a second guard vessel astern when available.

The losses claimed by the claimants were said to be very substantial, in the region of $25 million, arising from the damage to the seismic array.
claims:
The claimants (owners, demise charterers and time charterers of WESTERN NEPTUNE and associated interests) brought an action arising out of the September 2007 incident in which ST LOUIS EXPRESS crossed and severely damaged WESTERN NEPTUNE’s towed seismic streamers and associated equipment. They sought recovery of very substantial losses said to be around $25 million.

On liability, the claimants contended that ST LOUIS EXPRESS was at fault and that the defendants’ admitted faults did not represent the full extent of ST LOUIS EXPRESS’s culpability. Beyond the defendants’ acceptance that ST LOUIS EXPRESS should bear the preponderance of blame for entering the exclusion zone, making an improper alteration of course that crossed the array, and failing to see or appreciate the significance of the buoy lights, the claimants argued that ST LOUIS EXPRESS also:

- failed to make effective use of AIS information (including the details available about WESTERN NEPTUNE’s status and tow) as a navigational aid; and
- failed to maintain a proper radar lookout.

The claimants also resisted the defendants’ contention that WESTERN NEPTUNE was to blame for the collision. The defendants alleged contributory fault by WESTERN NEPTUNE in failing to provide adequate warnings and communications (including about the tail buoy lights), failing to monitor and challenge ST LOUIS EXPRESS’s developing approach into danger, failing to use warning measures such as VHF/lights/flares, and failing to dive the streamers. The claimants’ position, as reflected in the judgment, was that ST LOUIS EXPRESS’s navigation and lookout failures were the dominant cause of the incident and that any alleged shortcomings on WESTERN NEPTUNE’s side did not justify a substantial reduction of ST LOUIS EXPRESS’s responsibility.
