facts:
The claimant, Lancelot Shadwell, was the nephew of Charles Shadwell (the deceased). On 11 August 1838 Charles Shadwell wrote and signed a letter to the claimant from Gray’s Inn stating that he was glad to hear of the claimant’s intended marriage with Ellen Nicholl and, as he had promised to assist him “at starting,” he would pay the claimant £150 yearly during Charles Shadwell’s life and until the claimant’s annual income derived from his profession as a Chancery barrister should amount to 600 guineas. The letter stated that the claimant’s own admission would be the only evidence Charles Shadwell would receive or require as to whether the claimant’s professional income had reached that level.

The claimant subsequently married Ellen Nicholl. The claimant’s annual income derived from his profession as a Chancery barrister never amounted to 600 guineas, and he was always ready and willing to admit and state that fact to Charles Shadwell.

After the marriage and during Charles Shadwell’s lifetime, the time for payment of eighteen yearly sums of £150 each elapsed. Charles Shadwell paid twelve of those yearly sums in full and paid £12 towards the thirteenth yearly sum, but did not pay the remainder of the thirteenth sum and did not pay the last five yearly sums. Those unpaid amounts remained in arrear at Charles Shadwell’s death. The defendants were sued as executor and executrix of Charles Shadwell’s estate.

In response, the defendants asserted (among other points) that the marriage had already been intended and agreed between the claimant and Ellen Nicholl before the letter, without any request by Charles Shadwell, and that there was no consideration for the promise beyond what appeared in the letter. They also asserted that the promise was made on terms that the claimant would continue to practise as a Chancery barrister and not abandon that practice, but that the claimant later voluntarily abandoned that practice and instead practised only as a revising barrister.

The court was not unanimous on whether the letter disclosed a sufficient consideration connected with the marriage, but the majority concluded that the promise was enforceable and that there was no condition requiring the claimant to continue practising at the bar as a prerequisite to payment. It was noted that the claimant died shortly after judgment and that his representatives compromised the matter rather than continue the litigation.
claims:
The claimant sought to recover arrears said to be due under Charles Shadwell’s written promise to pay £150 per year during Charles Shadwell’s life and until the claimant’s professional income as a Chancery barrister reached 600 guineas. He alleged that the promise was made in consideration of his marrying Ellen Nicholl, that he did marry her relying on the promise while it remained in force and unrevoked, and that his professional income never reached (and was never admitted by him to have reached) 600 guineas.

He pleaded that all conditions necessary to entitle him to payment had occurred, that eighteen annual payments fell due after his marriage and during the testator’s lifetime, and that although twelve annual sums and £12 of the thirteenth were paid, the balance of the thirteenth and the last five annual sums were unpaid and in arrear. He claimed £1,000.

In answer to the defendants’ contention that there was no consideration beyond the letter and no request by the testator to marry, the claimant maintained that the written letter itself contained the agreement and that his subsequent marriage, entered into in reliance on the promise, supplied the consideration for the undertaking.

In answer to the defendants’ contention that he forfeited entitlement by abandoning practice as a Chancery barrister, the claimant argued that any alleged term requiring him to continue practising was not part of the written promise and was not a condition precedent to his right to receive the annual payments; the only stated limitation was that payments would cease if his professional income reached the specified level.

facts:
The proceedings arose out of a dispute connected with the purchase and sale of a property. A freezing order had previously been made, and steps were required to provide information and disclosure so that the freezing order could be properly policed and, in due course, properly released.

On 21 June 2013 an “unless” order was made requiring the defendants to provide specified information and documents. The judge in the present hearing had to decide whether the defendants had complied with that order and, if not, whether they should be relieved from the sanction for non-compliance.

The defendants accepted that in a number of respects they had not complied with the order, though they criticised the claimant’s presentation of alleged deficiencies (said to be divided into 39 points) as overstated. The court identified several significant instances of non-compliance.

First, there was a failure to provide charge documentation from five financial institutions. Letters seeking the documentation were prepared by the claimant’s solicitors and sent to the institutions. In reality, none of the charge documents had been made available. The defendants attributed this to a lack of cooperation by the London office of the Bank of Cyprus, through its recoveries manager, Mr Andrew Fouli. The court reviewed correspondence and was not persuaded that strained relations or bank wariness adequately explained the failure; earlier email traffic suggested a close and informal relationship and no apparent difficulty in providing what was required.

Second, there was a failure to provide proper detailed disclosure about how the defendants’ litigation was being funded and the source of that funding. The court considered that the required details had not been provided, and that such disclosure was needed so that the claimant and the court could be satisfied that funds came from a disclosed source and were being used consistently with the freezing orders.

Third, the court noted a late disclosure of an HSBC account statement. The defendants had suggested in evidence that the account was not in the name of any company identified in the relevant part of the unless order, but it became clear that it was an account of Prestige Properties Limited, which was the first company identified as a target of the order. The court regarded this as a troubling development.

Fourth, although the approved letters to financial institutions specified that responsive documents should be returned to the claimant’s solicitors (not to the defendants), documents were instead returned to the defendants, insofar as there was any compliance at all.

Taking these matters together, the court concluded there had been substantial and serious failures to comply with the unless order, not merely minor or technical defaults. The court also noted that the unless order had been made after five previous applications.
claims:
The claimant sought enforcement of the unless order made on 21 June 2013 and contended that the defendants had failed to comply with it in material respects. The claimant relied on multiple alleged deficiencies in compliance (said to be set out as 39 points) and argued that the failures were serious rather than trivial.

In particular, the claimant’s position (as accepted by the court in substance) was that the defendants had not produced charge documentation from financial institutions as required; had not provided proper disclosure of the funding arrangements and source of funds used to fund the defendants’ litigation; and had otherwise failed to provide information necessary to police and enable the proper release of the freezing order.

The claimant opposed any attempt by the defendants to avoid the consequences of non-compliance and argued that relief from the sanction should not be granted, including on the basis that the defendants’ position had not improved since the unless order and had in some respects worsened (for example, their stance had shifted from denying any enforceable contractual relationship to admitting the contract while disputing its interpretation and effect).

facts:
JSC BTA Bank is a major Kazakh bank that was effectively nationalised on 2 February 2009 following the global financial crisis. Until then, the first defendant, Mukhtar Ablyazov, was the beneficial owner of a majority of the bank’s shares and chairman of its board. The second defendant, Mr Zharimbetov, was a close associate and the first chairman of the management board. Both later fled to England. Criminal prosecutions were said to be pending against them and others in Kazakhstan, and multiple civil proceedings were pending in England involving them and alleged associates.

These proceedings concern an alleged scheme in late 2008 by which more than US$1 billion was extracted from the bank. The bank’s case was that the scheme operated through the first to fourth respondents (said to be “borrowers” from the bank) and the fifth to ninth respondents (said to be “intermediaries” and direct recipients of the bank’s advances). The bank’s advances were transferred to accounts at a Latvian bank pursuant to letters of credit opened by the bank on behalf of the borrowers in favour of the intermediaries, on the stated basis that the intermediaries were supplying oil machinery and equipment. The bank alleged there was no genuine underlying trade and that the scheme was a sham carried out by and for the benefit of Mr Ablyazov, using Mr Zharimbetov as an assistant and using the respondent companies as vehicles. Mr Ablyazov’s position was that the loans were made to substantial financial entities and that he had no connection with the borrowers or intermediaries. No defence had yet been filed.

On 9 June 2010, a deputy judge granted without-notice worldwide freezing orders against the respondents, finding at least a good arguable case of fraud and a real risk of dissipation, influenced by the lack of transparency about the respondents’ assets, dealings, ownership/control, and accounts, and by the absence of any sign of the equipment said to justify the payments. The freezing order required each respondent, within five working days of service and after reasonable enquiries, to disclose worldwide assets over £10,000 (with value and location), to answer detailed written questions (including what became of US$1,031,263,000 paid out by the bank), and to provide supporting documents; the information was then to be verified by affidavit within seven days after service.

Permission was given to serve respondents outside the jurisdiction. Foreign-based respondents were served at their registered offices: certain respondents in the British Virgin Islands and others in the Seychelles. The sixth respondent was served in England and Wales. Disclosure was due by 1 July 2010 and affidavits by 5 July 2010.

A similar freezing order was obtained in the British Virgin Islands on 11 June 2010 against the BVI respondents and, after an inter partes hearing on 5 July 2010, they were ordered to provide the disclosure forthwith; they did not do so.

On 2 July 2010, the English freezing order was continued inter partes. Only the fourth and seventh respondents were represented. No extension of time for disclosure was sought, and no application was then made to discharge or vary the order.

On 14 July 2010, solicitors acting for the fourth and seventh respondents requested a four-week extension. On 15 and 22 July 2010, acknowledgements of service were filed for the Seychelles and BVI respondents indicating an intention to challenge jurisdiction. The sixth respondent did not acknowledge service and was not represented.

The bank’s solicitors maintained that the freezing order remained binding despite the stated intention to challenge jurisdiction and sought proposals for compliance. The bank issued the present application on 4 August 2010. The respondents (other than the sixth) issued an application on 12 August 2010 to challenge jurisdiction and to set aside the freezing order on the basis that England was not the convenient forum and Kazakhstan was.

On 9 August 2010, solicitors for the first four respondents sent a letter purporting to provide the ordered information; none of the other respondents provided any information then or thereafter. The bank considered the information from the first four respondents seriously deficient and identified alleged deficiencies by letter dated 10 August 2010.

On 13 August 2010, the court adjourned the bank’s application and directed the respondents to serve further evidence, including responses to the alleged deficiencies, by 18 August 2010, effectively giving a final opportunity to comply. No further evidence was served. On 18 August 2010, the first to fourth respondents sent a fax with further information which the bank said added almost nothing, and indicated an intention to provide an affidavit dealing with asset disclosure by 3 September 2010. The bank responded on 19 August 2010 that the information remained inadequate.

The court noted particular apparent gaps in compliance to date, including lack of any asset valuations, lack of information about when money left the Latvian bank accounts and where it went, and whether any equipment was delivered. The intermediaries had provided no information at all.

The court decided to make an order requiring compliance by 4 p.m. London time on 3 September 2010, with specified drafting clarifications. The order allowed the bank to enter or apply for judgment against any respondent who failed to comply with the disclosure obligations applicable to it, but provided that (except with permission) any judgment against respondents other than the sixth would not be enforced pending determination of their jurisdiction challenge; if the jurisdiction challenge succeeded, the judgment would fall away. A further provision was made that if an application for permission to appeal was made by 4 p.m. on 27 August 2010, the bank would not be at liberty to enter or apply for judgment under the order until that permission application was determined.
claims:
The bank alleged that in late 2008 a fraudulent misappropriation scheme extracted over US$1 billion from it. It contended that the first to fourth respondents were used as purported borrowers and the fifth to ninth respondents as purported intermediaries who received the bank’s advances at a Latvian bank under letters of credit said to relate to supplies of oil machinery and equipment, but that the transactions were a sham. The bank’s case was that the scheme was carried out by and for the benefit of the first defendant, with assistance from the second defendant, using the respondent companies as vehicles.

In the proceedings, the bank asserted proprietary claims to the sums advanced and sought compensation from the first and second defendants (as bank officers) for breach of duty, and compensation from the borrower and intermediary respondents for participating in that breach.

In the present application, the bank sought an “unless” order debarring the respondents from defending and entitling the bank to enter (or apply for) judgment unless they provided the information and documents required by the disclosure provisions attached to the freezing order. The bank argued that the respondents had failed to comply with disclosure obligations (including disclosure of worldwide assets over £10,000, answers to detailed questions aimed at tracing what became of US$1,031,263,000, and supporting documents), that the limited information provided by the first four respondents was seriously deficient, and that the other respondents had provided nothing. It contended that prompt and effective disclosure was necessary to police the freezing order and to trace and preserve assets, particularly given the scale of the alleged fraud, the asserted proprietary claims, the time already elapsed since disclosure was due, and the risk that assets would be dissipated or put beyond reach.

The bank also sought an order structured so that, while non-compliance would trigger the sanction of judgment/debarring, enforcement of any judgment against respondents who were challenging jurisdiction would be stayed pending determination of that jurisdiction challenge, so that the challenge would not be rendered nugatory.

facts:
Hitachi Capital (UK) plc is a financial services company active in, among other areas, dental and medical consumer finance. Medenta Finance Ltd operates in the UK dental and medical consumer market and, since it began trading in 2006, worked exclusively for Hitachi, earning commission when patients entered into Hitachi finance agreements.

The parties’ relationship began in late 2005. Under an initial arrangement recorded in an “Approved Supplier Agreement” dated 1 November 2005, Medenta acted as Hitachi’s agent to set up and administer schemes through dental and medical practices so that patients could obtain Hitachi finance to pay for treatment. Medenta did not deal with patients; it dealt with dental/medical practices (“Suppliers”). Setting up a scheme involved Medenta persuading practices to enter into standard-form Supplier Agreements with Hitachi and then administering those agreements on Hitachi’s behalf.

Under a Supplier Agreement, the practice was appointed as Hitachi’s agent to introduce Hitachi retail finance products to patients. Credit applications were made and processed through a website (“CreditMaster”) to which the practice had access. Approved credit agreements were completed and signed by the practice on Hitachi’s behalf, creating direct contractual relationships between patients and Hitachi. The practice received payment for its services less a “subsidy”; Hitachi could review the subsidy level but had to give 30 days’ notice before implementing changes.

In 2010 the parties replaced the earlier arrangement with a letter agreement dated 15 September 2010. Hitachi agreed to provide finance for sales by practices to patients, and Medenta agreed to act as Hitachi’s agent in setting up and administering the scheme. Medenta’s responsibilities included collecting registration documentation, training staff, handling queries and complaints, distributing sales data, ensuring compliance matters, and renewing licences and insurance. Medenta’s commission depended on the value of concluded finance contracts.

On 3 October 2011 Medenta was acquired by Practice Plan Ltd for about £1 million (with potential additional consideration). Practice Plan’s business was to help dental practices run membership plans, and it saw synergy in cross-selling membership plans and consumer finance. On the same day, Medenta and Hitachi entered into a new agreement (recorded in a letter dated 27 September 2011 and signed on 3 October 2011) replacing the 2010 agreement. Both parties knew Practice Plan would wish to promote its products to Suppliers and patients. The 2011 agreement was largely identical to the 2010 agreement but included additional provisions in clauses 15 and 17, including (in summary) an acknowledgement about Suppliers/customers introduced by Medenta remaining Medenta’s customers/clients and a restriction on Hitachi marketing certain products, and a post-termination restriction for 24 months on solicitation/marketing to Suppliers/customers introduced by Medenta. The 2011 agreement had an initial five-year term expiring on 2 October 2016 and thereafter was terminable on six months’ written notice.

In 2013 Practice Plan was acquired by Wesleyan Assurance Society; another Wesleyan subsidiary is Wesleyan Bank. The 2011 agreement was amended in 2014 and 2015 in ways not material to the dispute. After the initial term expired, the parties discussed a new relationship but did not reach agreement.

By 2018 Medenta brokered over £28 million of dental consumer finance products (about 28% of the market) and earned gross commission of over £900,000.

At a meeting on 15 November 2018 Medenta told Hitachi it intended to terminate the 2011 agreement and thereafter broker financial products for Wesleyan Bank, proposing an exit agreement. On 26 November 2018 Hitachi told Medenta that if Medenta proceeded with the Wesleyan Bank tie-up, Hitachi would terminate the 2011 agreement and contact the dental practices in the scheme to offer direct funding arrangements. On 10–11 December 2018 Hitachi said it would serve termination notice and begin contacting practices shortly thereafter; an email on 11 December 2018 explained Hitachi intended to offer practices a “direct to funder option” while allowing continuation of the current joint offer for a period if Medenta wished.

On 12 December 2018 Hitachi gave notice terminating the 2011 agreement, so it would end on 12 June 2019. Termination would end the parties’ relationship and (as common ground) Medenta’s entitlement to commission from the termination date. However, termination would not end existing Supplier Agreements, which were of indefinite duration and terminable on at least 30 days’ notice; therefore Supplier Agreements could continue for many years. As a result, Hitachi’s contractual relationships with existing Suppliers would continue, including Hitachi’s first right of refusal on relevant credit business and Suppliers’ authority to introduce Hitachi finance products to patients and sign agreements on Hitachi’s behalf. This meant Hitachi and Suppliers would inevitably remain in regular contact.

In response to Hitachi’s stated intention to contact practices, Medenta made an urgent without-notice application on 14 December 2018 for an interim prohibitory injunction. The court granted an interim injunction restraining Hitachi from soliciting persons listed in a schedule, later varied by consent to allow previously agreed work and accompanied by undertakings from Medenta. On the return date (18 January 2019) the injunction was continued to an expedited trial.

At trial, the court determined issues including the meaning of the disputed provisions, whether clause 15 should be rectified, whether a restrictive term should be implied, whether any restraint was unreasonable, and whether Medenta’s supplier list was confidential. The court concluded, among other things, that “third party products” meant products of persons other than Hitachi and Medenta; that “Supplier” in the relevant clauses meant current Suppliers with existing Supplier Agreements; that “solicitation” and “marketing” connoted positive, targeted initiative; that Medenta’s rectification and implied-term claims failed; and that Medenta’s supplier information was not confidential to Medenta and could be used by Hitachi to service existing Supplier Agreements.
claims:
Medenta sought to restrain Hitachi from contacting and competing for the dental practices (Suppliers) and related customers that Medenta had introduced into Hitachi’s scheme.

After Hitachi indicated it would offer practices a “direct to funder option” and begin contacting them, Medenta applied urgently for an interim prohibitory injunction. Medenta’s case was that Hitachi’s proposed conduct would breach (i) an undertaking said to arise from the 2011 agreement not to market/solicit dental practices and customers introduced by Medenta during and for 24 months after termination, alternatively (ii) an implied term to similar effect. Medenta sought an order preventing Hitachi (whether by itself, employees, agents, or by instructing/encouraging others) from soliciting or marketing to any clients and customers introduced to Hitachi by Medenta.

In the expedited proceedings Medenta advanced, in substance, the following claims/arguments:

1) Construction of clause 15: Medenta argued that the phrase “third party products” in clause 15 meant products not brokered by Medenta, so that Hitachi was restricted during the term from actively marketing competing finance arrangements to Medenta-introduced Suppliers/customers.

2) Rectification (if its construction failed): Medenta sought rectification of clause 15 so that it would instead contain a broader restriction preventing Hitachi from becoming engaged (directly or indirectly) in solicitation or marketing to any Supplier or customers introduced by Medenta during the term.

3) Implied term (if construction and rectification failed): Medenta contended that a term should be implied into the 2011 agreement that Hitachi would not become engaged (directly or indirectly) in solicitation or marketing to any Supplier or customers introduced by Medenta during the term.

4) Confidentiality: Medenta asserted that the supplier information it held (its compiled list and related details) was its work product and confidential; that it had been shared with Hitachi in circumstances importing an obligation of confidence; and that Hitachi could not use that information for its own purposes without committing a breach of confidence.

Although the judgment records that relief would be addressed after liability findings, Medenta’s requested relief, as reflected in its injunction application and case theory, was to prevent Hitachi from soliciting/marketing to Medenta-introduced Suppliers (and, in its broader formulation, customers) in order to protect Medenta’s relationships and business as it transitioned away from Hitachi.

facts:
In 1843 the Earl of Eglintoun was a steward of the Doncaster races. Tickets for admission to the Grand Stand and the surrounding enclosure were sold in Doncaster for one guinea each. It was understood that these tickets entitled the holder to enter the stand and the surrounding enclosure and to remain there on each day of the races, which lasted four days. The claimant (Wood) bought one such ticket and entered the enclosure on a race day while the races were in progress.

The defendant (Leadbitter), an officer of police, acted on Lord Eglintoun’s order. While the claimant was in the enclosure during the races, the defendant told him to leave and warned that force would be used if he did not. The claimant refused to go. The defendant then took the claimant by the arm and forced him out of the enclosure, using no unnecessary violence. The claimant was not refunded the guinea. For the purposes of the legal argument, it was assumed that the claimant had not misconducted himself at the time and that, if he had not been required to leave, his presence would have been justified by his purchase of the ticket.

The action was brought as trespass for assault and false imprisonment. The defendant’s position at trial was that the claimant was on Lord Eglintoun’s land and that the defendant, as Lord Eglintoun’s servant acting under his command, used only such force as was necessary to remove the claimant. The claimant’s response was that he was in the enclosure by Lord Eglintoun’s leave and licence. The trial judge directed the jury that, even if the ticket had been sold with Lord Eglintoun’s sanction, Lord Eglintoun could order the claimant to leave without refunding the guinea and without giving a reason; and that if notice to leave was given and a reasonable time to depart had elapsed before the removal, then the claimant was not on the land by leave and licence at the time he was removed. The jury found for the defendant on that issue. The claimant then sought a new trial on the basis that this direction was wrong; the court ultimately upheld the trial direction and discharged the application.
claims:
The claimant sued the defendant in trespass for assault and false imprisonment arising from being physically removed from the Doncaster racecourse enclosure. The claimant’s case, as pleaded and argued, was that at the time he was removed he was lawfully in the enclosure by the leave and licence of Lord Eglintoun, because he had purchased a one-guinea ticket that was understood to entitle him to enter and remain in the stand and surrounding enclosure during the race days.

After the jury verdict for the defendant, the claimant applied for a new trial on the ground of misdirection. He argued that, in the circumstances, the permission given upon purchase of the ticket to enter and remain during the races was not revocable during the races, or at least was not revocable without returning the price of the ticket. On that basis he contended that he remained in the enclosure by Lord Eglintoun’s leave and licence at the time of the alleged trespass, so that the defendant’s removal of him amounted to an actionable assault and false imprisonment.

facts:
The dispute arose from the use of the brand name “LUMOS” on different types of beauty products. Lumos Skincare Ltd (the claimant) sold “anti-ageing” skin care products under the name LUMOS. The defendants were involved in the manufacture and UK distribution of nail care products sold under the trade mark LUMOS.

The second defendant manufactured the nail care products in the United States. It appointed the first defendant as UK distributor, and the first defendant made its first UK sales on or after the end of October 2010. On 30 November 2010 the first defendant’s business was transferred to the third defendant, which then became the UK distributor.

At trial, the passing off claim was rejected on the basis that there was no likelihood of confusion among the relevant public. On appeal, the Court of Appeal reversed that decision, holding that the trial judgment contained errors in its treatment of the evidence, particularly by focusing on trade customers rather than end users. The Court of Appeal found a likelihood of confusion among end users of the claimant’s skin care products: seeing the same brand name used for nail care products, they would likely assume the nail care products came from the same source or an economically associated source.

The second defendant accepted at trial that it was jointly liable with the first and third defendants for the activities found to constitute passing off.

Following the Court of Appeal’s final order (14 June 2013), the defendants served witness statements disclosing income, costs of obtaining the products, and gross profit. The claimant sought inspection of underlying records and a direction that the second defendant comply with the Court of Appeal order; that application was dismissed, the court considering the witness statements adequate for the required disclosure.

The claimant ultimately elected for an account of profits. Directions were given identifying issues for the account, including whether the second defendant must account for profits from supplying the products to the UK distributors, the revenues derived, the purchase/manufacturing costs, and what expenses/overheads could be deducted.

On the account, the court determined that the first and third defendants’ total sales revenue was £79,783.66, but £6,012.76 related to sales to customers elsewhere in Europe (mostly Ireland and Spain). The court excluded those non-UK sales, leaving UK revenue of £73,770.90.

For the second defendant’s revenue from supplying the products to the UK distributors, there was a discrepancy between figures advanced by the second defendant and by the first/third defendants. The parties agreed the precise choice did not matter so long as the same figure was used consistently for revenue and corresponding purchase cost; the court adopted £39,000 and then reduced it to exclude the non-UK sales element, resulting in £33,085.82.

The court rejected an argument that an August 2010 invoice should be excluded because it pre-dated the agreed October 2010 date for commencement of the complained-of activities. It was accepted that the goods invoiced in August 2010 were not put on the UK market until after the end of October 2010 and were used as part of the common design to commit passing off in the UK.

As to costs, the court treated the first/third defendants’ purchase cost as £33,085.82. For the second defendant’s manufacturing costs, the claimant challenged the adequacy and precision of the evidence. The second defendant provided accounting software printouts showing gross profit calculations based on average costs. Despite late provision and limited explanation, the court accepted the evidence and found total manufacturing costs of $23,413, converted to £14,577.

On allowable deductions, the first and third defendants sought to deduct proportions of trade show and catalogue costs on the basis that LUMOS was promoted among other products. The court disallowed those deductions because the business was not shown to be operating at capacity, there was no clear evidence of foregone alternative sales, and the trade show and catalogue costs would have been incurred anyway. The court allowed deductions for advertising specifically promoting LUMOS, allowed certain freight costs (including additional freight costs agreed to relate to LUMOS orders totalling £1,314.59), and allowed the cost of Mrs Nordstrom’s airfare (£666.16) as supported by evidence of direct promotional purpose, but disallowed the cost of Mr Nordstrom’s ticket due to lack of evidence.

The court concluded that the profits to be disgorged were £24,461.48 for the first and third defendants (based on revenue £73,770.90 less purchase costs £33,085.82 and allowable additional costs £16,223.50) and £17,842.66 for the second defendant (based on revenue £33,085.82 less manufacturing costs £14,577 and allowable additional costs £666.16). The court did not allocate liability between the first and third defendants and proceeded on the basis that they would be jointly and severally liable.
claims:
The claimant brought a passing off action complaining that the defendants’ nail care products were sold in the United Kingdom under the name “LUMOS,” which was the same name under which the claimant sold its anti-ageing skin care products. The claimant’s case (as ultimately accepted on appeal) was that use of the same brand name on nail care products would lead end users of the claimant’s skin care products to assume the nail care products came from the claimant or from an economically associated source.

After the Court of Appeal found passing off and ordered financial disclosure, the claimant sought further relief in relation to the financial consequences of the passing off. It applied for inspection of the first and third defendants’ underlying records and for a direction that the second defendant comply with the Court of Appeal’s disclosure order; this application was refused.

The claimant then elected to pursue an account of profits rather than an inquiry into damages, seeking disgorgement of profits made by the defendants by reason of the passing off.

In the account proceedings, the claimant contended that the second defendant should be required to account for profits arising from its supply of the LUMOS products to the UK distributors because it was jointly liable as part of a common design.

The claimant argued that revenues from sales to Ireland and other European customers should be included in the account on the basis that those sales were likely generated by marketing activities in the United Kingdom (such as trade shows) that amounted to passing off.

The claimant challenged the adequacy of the second defendant’s evidence of manufacturing costs, arguing that the evidence was too vague to test and that the second defendant had not discharged the burden of proving its costs; the claimant invited the court to disregard the cost evidence and treat manufacturing cost as zero.

The claimant also resisted certain deductions claimed by the defendants, including (initially) some late-added advertising invoices, sought to exclude some freight costs on the basis that a shipment included a small quantity of another product, and objected to deduction of Mr Nordstrom’s airfare due to lack of evidence of the purpose of the trip.

facts:
Mrs Vivien Harrison and Mr John Harrison married on 16 July 1988 and divorced in 2002, with decree absolute on 14 November 2002. Their divorce included ancillary financial relief proceedings tried in July 2002, with judgment handed down on 30 September 2002. The resulting order provided, among other things, that Mrs Harrison retained the former matrimonial home, Mr Harrison was to pay her a lump sum of £600,000, periodical payments were ordered for the children and for Mrs Harrison, and Mrs Harrison was to transfer her shares in UA Importers Limited to Mr Harrison. No costs order was made in those proceedings and there was no appeal.

In January 2007 (and on amendment in July 2007) Mrs Harrison commenced this High Court action seeking to challenge the 2002 ancillary relief outcome. On 26 July 2007, without notice to Mr Harrison, she obtained a freezing injunction restraining Mr Harrison from removing assets up to £2 million and specifically including certain property and assets connected with The Interchange Organisation Limited (trading as “Interchange”). The terms of the injunction, as made, effectively prevented Interchange from carrying on business because it did not permit disposal of assets in the ordinary course of business. On 31 July 2007 the injunction was varied to remove the provisions affecting Interchange’s assets. On 17 September 2007 the injunction (as varied) was discharged by consent, with costs relating to the injunction reserved.

Mr Harrison then applied to strike out the claim or obtain summary judgment and sought costs (including costs arising from the freezing injunction) and an enquiry into damage caused by the injunction. Shortly before the hearing, Mrs Harrison (then acting in person) applied to transfer the action to the Family Division and sought third-party disclosure from the Metropolitan Police of an unredacted crime report relating to an alleged burglary at Interchange in May 2002.

The court examined the factual bases advanced by Mrs Harrison for alleging fraud in the 2002 proceedings. One allegation concerned a Royal Bank of Scotland account said to have been undisclosed. The evidence showed the account was described as an “RBS Re Interchange Organisation” account, was opened by a £25,000 transfer from an Interchange account, and had no transactions in 2002 other than interest. Mr Harrison’s evidence was that it was a bank account of the bank used as a deposit/treasury account connected with foreign exchange business, and that while the account number was not identified during the 2002 proceedings, the existence of the £25,000 “treasury account” was disclosed in balance sheets and the transfer was visible on disclosed statements. The court also noted that the 2002 judge’s approach to Interchange did not depend on treating it as saleable or valuing it by profits; instead she treated Mr Harrison’s investment in it as the relevant figure, so the £25,000 would not have affected the outcome.

Another allegation concerned an asserted fabrication of a break-in at Interchange’s offices to undermine “daily reconciliation statements” (documents Mrs Harrison had received anonymously and used in the 2002 proceedings). The 2002 judge had already considered the circumstances in which Mrs Harrison obtained those documents, declined to make findings as to their source, and accepted evidence denying involvement by Mr Harrison’s employee. The 2002 judge also concluded the documents did not reveal undisclosed assets and did not add to knowledge of Mr Harrison’s wealth.

Further allegations included: that Mr Harrison misstated the status of a tax investigation; that he misled the court about the level of his drawings/personal expenditure; that stock in UA Importers Limited (opal panels) had been undervalued; and that a business known as Cash on Cars continued trading after it was said to have ceased. The court found there was no worthwhile evidence that any tax investigation resulted in payments or that any misstatement would have materially affected the 2002 judge’s credibility findings; the expenditure allegation relied on an unexplained accountant’s schedule which Mr Harrison criticised as misleading and which was not properly supported; the opal panel valuation issue had been canvassed in 2002 and the later materials relied on did not demonstrate that the panels were undamaged in July 2002 or that Mr Harrison knew that; and there was no evidence that Cash on Cars continued trading as alleged.

The court concluded Mrs Harrison had no real prospect of succeeding in setting aside the 2002 order on the basis advanced. It entered summary judgment for Mr Harrison, dismissed Mrs Harrison’s application to transfer the case and her application for police disclosure as serving no purpose given the claim’s failure, and addressed costs and consequences of the freezing injunction. The court found the without-notice freezing injunction application had been made with serious failures of frankness and disclosure and had misled the judge who granted it on important matters (including the nature and significance of the bank account, the relevance of the alleged break-in to the 2002 judgment, and an incorrect assertion that Mrs Harrison had been ordered to pay Mr Harrison’s costs in 2002). The court ordered Mrs Harrison to pay Mr Harrison’s costs of the action on the indemnity basis and directed an enquiry into damages suffered by Mr Harrison and by Interchange as a result of the freezing injunction.
claims:
Mrs Harrison sought relief to set aside the 30 September 2002 ancillary relief judgment/order on the basis that it had been obtained by fraudulent misrepresentations and/or material non-disclosures made by or on behalf of Mr Harrison during those proceedings, particularly concerning the parties’ financial affairs, the affairs of Mr Harrison’s companies, and the value or likely value of joint assets.

In support, she alleged that Mr Harrison (or those acting for him) represented in the 2002 proceedings that full disclosure of Interchange’s bank accounts and statements had been provided, that the “daily reconciliation statements” she received were unreliable because of a break-in and tampering, that a tax investigation was limited and resolved, that his annual drawings were limited to specified amounts, that UA Importers’ stock (opal panels) had a low value because it was damaged, and that Cash on Cars had ceased lending/trading and was only recovering outstanding loans. She claimed she later discovered these representations were untrue, including that an Interchange-related bank account containing about £25,000 existed and was concealed; that the break-in was fabricated and the police report was made only after developments in the 2002 litigation; that the tax investigation continued and extended to other matters; that his personal expenditure over about 18 months exceeded £220,000; that the opal panels were in good condition and worth over £100,000; and that Cash on Cars continued trading under the name Logbook Loans during 2002 and 2003.

She contended the 2002 judge relied on these misrepresentations and non-disclosures in reaching conclusions and in assessing credibility. She asked for the 2002 judgment to be set aside and also sought an order that Mr Harrison repay to her both her own and his legal costs of the ancillary relief proceedings, together with interest.

In addition, within this action she applied to transfer the proceedings to the Family Division and sought an order requiring the Metropolitan Police to disclose an unredacted crime report relating to the alleged May 2002 burglary at Interchange, apparently to support her contention that the break-in narrative was false.

facts:
American Express Services Europe Ltd brought proceedings against Talib Jafar K Al‑Shabrakah for unpaid sums on two American Express accounts held by him at the relevant time: a Gold Account and a Centurion Account. The defendant applied shortly before trial to vacate the trial date on the basis of ill health, relying on medical letters recommending bed rest and stating he was unfit to attend court or give instructions. The court refused to vacate the trial, noting the application was made very late despite the health issues being longstanding, that the defendant had not served any witness statement despite directions to do so, and that an adjournment would waste court time and cause further delay. 

The claimant served notices indicating it would rely as hearsay on witness statements from two Saudi Arabia–based witnesses (a merchant, Mr Al‑Tayyar, and a jeweller, Mr Al‑Hamoud/Abdul Sammad). The defendant opposed reliance on the written statements and sought to cross‑examine them, but the court allowed the statements to be admitted as hearsay because the witnesses were abroad and unwilling to attend, and an order to cross‑examine would not secure their attendance. The defendant was permitted to rely on an affidavit he had sworn in June 2013 (made in response to an earlier freezing order application), but it was not treated as a substitute for a trial witness statement.

On the Gold Account, the claimant said US$56,790.59 remained outstanding. The defendant’s pleaded position was that the Gold Account matters were part of a fraud described as the “UFX Bank Scandal” and that the claimant had been notified and had accepted that position months earlier. The court found no supporting detail was provided about this alleged scandal and accepted the claimant’s evidence that it had not been notified of such a dispute until the defence was served and had not agreed the charges were not due.

On the Centurion Account, the claimant said US$617,961.57 was outstanding, reflecting disputed transactions in late 2012. The evidence described the transactions as being processed using manual “record of charge” slips produced via a zip‑zap machine, with purchase details written by hand and signed, and with telephone authorisation obtained from American Express for each transaction. The merchant shown on the slips was Mr Al‑Tayyar, an American Express merchant in Riyadh at the time (later no longer trading and with his merchant agreement terminated). The court reviewed the charge slips and accepted they matched the dates and amounts on the account and bore signatures that corresponded, to a lay observer, with signature samples held by American Express (noting the defendant used two signatures).

The defendant admitted three of the transactions (numbers 17, 18 and 20), which were with the same merchant and occurred at the end of the sequence (20–21 December 2012). He had also confirmed by email on 5 December 2012 that two earlier transactions (numbers 8 and 10) were his, writing that he confirmed them. On 22 January 2013 he emailed American Express disputing the Al‑Tayyar charges and asking that all such transactions from 1 October 2012 be disputed and the account brought into credit, asserting he had not received goods/services and suggesting the merchant used a manual machine and rented it to others.

American Express asked the defendant on 7 February 2013 to complete a fraud declaration form in relation to the disputed transactions. The defendant refused by email and reiterated his refusal after his bank forwarded the request and warned that credits might be reversed if the form was not completed. The court characterised the defendant’s responses as unhelpful and found his explanations for refusing to complete the form (including alleged poor English and irritation) were not credible.

The defendant’s case on the facts was that the remaining transactions were fraudulent and that he had not signed the relevant charge slips. He attached to his defence an undated document purporting to comment on the signatures, but the court placed no reliance on it. The court found the defendant’s position internally inconsistent and not credible, including because he both denied doing business with the merchant while admitting some transactions with that merchant, and because he had confirmed two transactions in writing and later sought to retract that confirmation. The court accepted the claimant’s investigator’s evidence and considered the hearsay statements from the Saudi witnesses consistent with the documentary record: they said the defendant attended in person at Abdul Sammad’s shop, produced his American Express card, the transactions were processed using Mr Al‑Tayyar’s machine with telephone authorisations, and goods were handed to the defendant.
claims:
The claimant sought judgment for unpaid sums said to be due under the defendant’s American Express card agreements, together with contractual interest and late payment charges.

For the Gold Account, the claimant claimed US$56,790.59 outstanding and sought interest and late payment charges calculated at the contractual rate, stated in the judgment as totalling US$28,111.38.

For the Centurion Account, the claimant claimed US$617,961.57 outstanding arising from transactions in late 2012, and sought contractual interest stated as US$305,890.86.

The claimant’s case was that the transactions were properly charged to the defendant’s accounts under the applicable account terms: the charge slips and authorisations evidenced the transactions; the defendant had expressly confirmed two of the disputed Centurion transactions by email; he had admitted three further Centurion transactions; he had failed to raise disputes within the time expected after receiving statements; and he had refused to complete a requested fraud declaration form when disputing transactions. The claimant also relied on the Saudi witnesses’ statements (admitted as hearsay) to support that the purchases were made by the defendant in person and the goods were handed over to him.

facts:
The applicant, Mrs Dhamwanti Tirath Kshatriya, is the registered proprietor and long-term occupier of 20 Winchmore Hill Road, Southgate, London. In 1973 she and her husband, Mr Tirath Kisharam Kshatriya (a director of G.T.K (Southgate) Limited, a clothing company), executed a second registered charge over the property in favour of Standard Chartered Bank. The charge was collateral security for the company’s liabilities to the bank.

Mr Kshatriya had a close professional and personal relationship with Choithram International SA, a Panama-incorporated business trading from Dubai which, among other activities, provided commercial lending and had financially backed the company for years. Mr Kshatriya died in 1979 and his son, Mr Gul Kapur, became managing director of the company.

By 1980–1982 Choithram withdrew financial support, the company could not proceed with a potentially lucrative supply contract, and it was agreed the company would cease trading. At that time the company owed Choithram substantial sums on unsecured instruments and also owed money to three banks (including Standard Chartered). Choithram had guaranteed the company’s Standard Chartered overdraft up to £10,000, making Choithram and Mrs Kshatriya co-sureties in respect of that overdraft.

Mr Kapur’s evidence was that discussions took place among him, the bank, and Choithram about how to resolve matters. He said the company discharged liabilities to other banks and that the Standard Chartered overdraft was, as far as he recalled, below £10,000 at the relevant time. He described an arrangement under which Choithram would pay off the Standard Chartered overdraft and, in return, Choithram would take all remaining unsold stock from the company and keep the proceeds for its own benefit. Choithram collected the stock in March and April 1982; a credit note dated 7 June 1982 valued it at £13,800 inclusive of VAT, though Mr Kapur maintained the stock was worth nearer £30,000. Mr Kapur’s firm recollection was that the understanding with Choithram was that returning the stock would settle the company’s liabilities to Choithram “once and for all,” and that he would not have agreed to any arrangement that left his mother exposed to continuing security over her home.

Unknown to Mr Kapur, Choithram negotiated directly with Standard Chartered to pay the company’s entire liability to the bank (in excess of Choithram’s guarantee) in exchange for a transfer of the charge. Documentation showed that by 15 November 1982 Standard Chartered acknowledged receipt from Choithram of £14,374.19 (covering the full overdraft balance plus interest/charges) and closed the company’s account. On 15 December 1982 Standard Chartered executed a transfer of the charge to Choithram, and Choithram was registered as chargee. Mr Kapur said neither he nor his mother received notice of this transfer and they were unaware of it and of the sums paid.

Mrs Kshatriya continued to occupy the property throughout. In 2001, when she considered moving due to ill-health, a title search revealed the charge still registered. From late 2002 to spring 2005, discussions occurred between Mr Kapur and Choithram’s directors. Mr Kapur was given the clear impression that Choithram was willing to release the charge; a director even signed a letter to the Land Registry requesting discharge, but it was not sent (an unsigned copy was sent to Mr Kapur). In summer 2005 Choithram changed position and refused to release the charge.

At the hearing, the only witness with direct knowledge of the early 1980s events was Mr Kapur; Choithram’s current director who gave evidence had no direct knowledge of events before 2002. The adjudicator found Mr Kapur to be a reliable and truthful witness and accepted his recollection. The adjudicator found that there was an agreement in 1982 under which Choithram discharged the bank liability in consideration of taking the company’s remaining stock, and that the arrangement was intended as a “clean break” ending all liability arising from the company’s dealings with the bank and Choithram, necessarily including disposal of the charge. The adjudicator also noted that Choithram appeared to have been unaware of the charge’s existence until it was raised in 2002, could not produce records showing any alleged liability under it, and could not identify what sum it claimed was secured.
claims:
Mrs Kshatriya applied (by application dated 26 September 2005) for cancellation/removal of the registered charge from the property’s title.

Her case, advanced through her son Mr Kapur, was in substance that the charge should not remain because the 1982 arrangements were intended to settle matters finally and to end any liability connected with the company’s debts, so Choithram had no right to keep security over her home. Mr Kapur’s evidence was that there was an understanding that, in exchange for the company handing over its remaining stock to Choithram, Choithram would settle the company’s liabilities and there would be a final settlement; he maintained that there was no agreement that Choithram could retain the charge and that he would have ensured the bank was paid directly if he had known Choithram intended to take a transfer of the charge.

In addition, the application proceeded on the basis that the charge was no longer effective because the underlying bank debt had been paid off in full in 1982 and no payments or acknowledgments had been made thereafter, so there was no subsisting secured liability. The issues explored included whether the charge was time-barred and whether the 1982 settlement prevented Choithram from relying on the charge. The relief sought was an order directing the Land Registry to cancel the charge entry.

facts:
The case concerns the rateable value in the 2005 rating list of a modern distribution warehouse occupied by Hankook Tyre UK Ltd at Fawsley Drive, Heartlands Business Park, Daventry. The property lies in a mixed industrial/warehousing area northwest of Daventry town centre, with access to major roads including the A361 and the M1 via nearby junctions. Heartlands Business Park is one of several major industrial and warehousing estates in Daventry and includes a cluster of larger distribution warehouses built mainly between 1999 and 2004.

The hereditament comprises a large steel-framed warehouse (three bays) with internal blockwork to about three metres and insulated cladding above, predominantly metal-clad externally with some brickwork. The warehouse has 11.0m eaves height, is unheated, has fire detection, some natural light via roof lights, and suspended halogen lighting. It is divided into two linked sections and is partially racked. There are nine raised loading docks and three level loading doors on the south-east elevation. Ancillary accommodation includes a two-storey administrative office annexe and link building to the south-east, built with brick and glazed elevations, with suspended ceilings and typical office finishes, a lift, air-conditioning/comfort cooling, heating, and smoke alarm system. Within the warehouse there is a part single/part two-storey block containing mess/rest/locker and store areas of lower specification, and a small two-storey office block in the despatch bay. Externally there is hardstanding for car parking (59 spaces) and for lorries, trailers and storage; mains services are connected.

The building was constructed in 2004 by MAG Estates Limited under a design-and-build contract to the tenant’s specification, with an agreement that the tenant would take a lease on completion. Hankook Tyre UK Ltd, a UK subsidiary of a Korean company, uses the premises for delivery, storage and distribution of tyres across the UK and as its UK headquarters.

The property is held on a 15-year lease from 26 November 2004, with terms agreed on 1 March 2004 and rent reviews every five years. The tenant is responsible for repairs and for reimbursing insurance and paying rates, water and service charges. The commencing rent was £421,930 per annum, with no rent-free period and no premium. The tenant carried out relatively minor additional fitting-out works relating to works offices and toilets.

The valuation officer appealed a valuation tribunal decision that had reduced the assessment in the 2005 list from £462,500 to £410,000. The ratepayer did not participate in the appeal. The valuation officer relied on rental evidence from the subject property and multiple comparable warehouses (including both new lettings and rent reviews) and also on assessments of comparable properties in Daventry. He analysed rents using a factorised approach that adjusted different types of accommodation and attributes to a main-warehouse-space basis, and he also checked results using an overall analysis. He concluded that the market in the area was generally static between late 2001 and April 2005, and that the weight of comparable rental and assessment evidence indicated a main-space level around £50 per m² for modern distribution warehouses of broadly similar size in this location at the antecedent valuation date. The passing rent on the subject property, when analysed, produced a materially lower figure, which he attributed to the tenant having negotiated a “good deal” rather than it representing the reasonably expected rent.

The tribunal accepted the valuation officer’s evidence and concluded that the agreed rent for the subject property was well below market value. The tribunal directed that the assessment be amended to £462,500 with effect from 1 April 2000, increasing to £470,000 with effect from the date of the valuation tribunal’s decision (11 July 2007).
claims:
The valuation officer appealed against the valuation tribunal’s decision that reduced the property’s assessment in the 2005 rating list from £462,500 to £410,000. He sought an increase in the assessment to £470,000.

In support of that outcome, he argued that the passing rent agreed for the subject property (a new lease commencing 26 November 2004, with terms agreed 1 March 2004) was not the most reliable indicator of the property’s value for rating purposes because, when analysed, it produced a main-space figure significantly below the level indicated by other evidence. He contended that the weight of comparable rental evidence (particularly open-market lettings close to the antecedent valuation date and for properties with similar characteristics) and the pattern of comparable assessments in the locality established a consistent level of value for modern distribution warehouses in Daventry. He maintained that the market was broadly static over the relevant period and that differences in some rents reflected market vagaries rather than a genuine trend.

He further contended that the subject rent’s low analysed level could not be explained by the property’s size, specification, location, or letting date, and was best explained by the negotiating positions of landlord and tenant producing a below-market deal. He therefore asked the tribunal to prefer the broader rental and assessment evidence and to adopt a valuation based on a main-space price of £50 per m² (with adjustments for eaves height, lack of heating, and office air-conditioning), producing a rateable value rounded to £470,000.

facts:
The proceedings concerned a male child, A, aged about four months at the time of the hearing. A’s mother was G; A’s father was not known. The local authority issued proceedings on 13 July 2009 following a negative pre-birth assessment of the mother. That assessment raised concerns about the mother’s ability to care for A in light of historical concerns of neglect relating to her three older children and concerns about her ability to form emotional attachments.

The mother’s three older children had previously been made subject to care orders and placed for adoption; two had been adopted by the time of this hearing. Proceedings concerning another sibling concluded on 21 August 2009 and that child had not yet been placed for adoption. The local authority relied on a schedule of findings which set out concerns of neglect and physical and emotional harm, reflecting findings made in the earlier proceedings concerning A’s sibling.

The court considered the documents in the local authority’s bundles, including statements from the social worker, a residential assessment report, and a report from an independent social worker. The independent social worker had withdrawn a recommendation for a residential assessment at a hearing on 2 November 2009 because the mother had not accessed recommended domestic violence group work, and the mother was given permission to withdraw her application for such an assessment.

The Children’s Guardian filed a final analysis and recommendations dated 18 November 2009 supporting the local authority’s plan for a care order and a placement order. The court found that A was likely to suffer significant harm in the form of emotional harm, physical harm and neglect if he remained in his mother’s care, and noted that the mother conceded the concerns raised. The court accepted that the mother loved A but concluded she was not in a position to care for him in the foreseeable future. The court also found there were no family members able to care for A.

In relation to permanence planning, the local authority had already approached its adoption department and an adoption panel had considered A suitable for adoption on 7 October 2009. The local authority had approached the adopters of A’s older children, but they did not feel able to be assessed to care for an additional child. Placement with the sibling who had not yet been placed for adoption was considered inappropriate due to that sibling’s psychological needs. The court considered that A needed a permanent, stable and loving home and that early permanence would assist him in forming new attachments. The court noted that adoption would mean A would not be brought up in his birth family and might have limited contact with half-siblings, but accepted the arrangements in the care plan and the use of a life story book to address A’s need for information about his biological family as he grew older.
claims:
The local authority applied for a final care order and a placement order in respect of A, contending that the orders were necessary to secure A’s safety and wellbeing. It sought findings that A was likely to suffer significant harm (including emotional harm, physical harm and neglect) if he remained in his mother’s care, relying on the schedule of findings drawn from the earlier proceedings concerning A’s sibling and the mother’s concession of the concerns.

The local authority’s case was that the mother was not able to care for A in the foreseeable future and that there were no suitable family members to care for him, so that the local authority needed to assume parental responsibility to meet A’s emotional and physical needs without delay. It further sought a placement order on the basis that A required a permanent, stable home and that this could only be achieved through adoption.

Because the mother did not consent to the placement order, the local authority asked the court to dispense with her consent on the ground that A’s welfare required it. The Children’s Guardian supported the local authority’s plan for both orders.

facts:
The defendant, F C Frost Limited, was incorporated in 1971 by Frederick Charles Frost and his wife. It has traded in the UK since then, supplying drainage products and also washroom products. Its business model is that it markets primarily to architects and interior designers who specify its products for building projects; contractors (often sub-contractors) then purchase the specified products to fulfil their contracts. Over many years the defendant used signs and names including “FC Frost”, “Frost”, and (until about 2004) “Watrous” (used as a product line descriptor for washroom products). The defendant operated two divisions: one for drainage products and one for washroom/architectural products. Evidence accepted by the court was that the defendant had supplied washroom products under the “Frost” branding for decades, including since at least 1980, and had supplied products for numerous major UK projects. The defendant maintained websites and issued brochures and marketing materials using “Frost” as its trading name and logo, with various evolutions of the logo over time.

The claimant, Frost Products Limited, is a Canadian corporation based near Toronto. It said it began trading in 1929 (formerly known for many years as Frost Metal Products Limited) and has long used the trading name “Frost”, often shown inside an oval on its products. The claimant made attempts to enter the UK market from the 1970s onwards, but its UK sales were modest. Historic dealings included contacts with Bowater Scott in the 1970s/early 1980s, but the claimant could not produce invoices and the evidence suggested limited activity. In January 2005 the claimant entered a sales representation agreement with Robert Sherwood Agencies (purportedly covering the UK, Ireland and Europe), but sales were small and some shipments were to Canadian addresses or to entities linked to Canada. In September 2008 the claimant approached Perrem Design Hardware in Dublin about acting as its representative/distributor in Ireland; before filing its trade mark application it appears to have fulfilled only one non-sample order for Perrem of modest value. Perrem remained the claimant’s agent in Ireland.

On 16 October 2008 the claimant applied to register a Community trade mark for the word “Frost” covering various washroom-related goods (including dispensers, receptacles, holders and other items). The mark was granted on 7 August 2009. In June–July 2009 the claimant corresponded with Perrem about “aggressively expanding” its distribution network and presence in the UK and Europe.

After the claimant’s registration, on 18 December 2009 the defendant applied to register a series of UK trade marks incorporating “Frost” with additional words (such as “start”, “signature”, “washroom”, “vision”, “bespoke”), and in January 2010 launched new marketing materials using “Frost”.

The claimant issued proceedings in July 2012 alleging infringement of its registered mark and seeking to invalidate the defendant’s later UK marks. The defendant defended and counterclaimed, asserting earlier common law rights in “Frost” in the UK washroom products market and alleging the claimant’s registration was improper. The claimant relied on several instances where third parties contacted the claimant with enquiries referencing the defendant’s product numbers or products; the court considered these incidents to show people mistaking the claimant for the defendant (reverse confusion). The court found the claimant’s witness, Mr James (“Jay”) Biggar, to be unreliable on key points, including his asserted lack of knowledge of the defendant’s washroom products business before 2010. The court accepted the defendant’s evidence that it had a substantial reputation and goodwill in “Frost” for washroom products in England and Wales, that its use was not merely local, and that the claimant’s use of “Frost” in that market would have misrepresented an association with the defendant and caused likely damage. The court also found that the claimant, through Mr Biggar, applied for the mark intending to use it as a platform to expand into the UK while knowing of (or deliberately turning a blind eye to) the defendant’s established “Frost” business, and that this conduct amounted to bad faith.
claims:
The claimant’s claim was that it owned a registered Community trade mark for the word “Frost” covering specified washroom-related goods, and that the defendant was infringing that mark by using “Frost” in the course of trade in relation to goods within the scope of the registration and in a way that caused confusion in the marketplace. The claimant sought relief to stop the defendant’s use of “Frost” for washroom products (an injunction and related remedies were implicit in the infringement claim).

The claimant also sought to have the defendant’s later-filed UK trade marks incorporating “Frost” (including “Frost start”, “Frost signature”, “Frost washroom”, “Frost vision”, and “Frost bespoke”, including word-and-device versions) declared invalid on the basis that they conflicted with the claimant’s earlier registered “Frost” mark for identical or similar goods and created a likelihood of confusion.

In support of its infringement case, the claimant relied on asserted instances of marketplace confusion, where third parties contacted the claimant seeking information or pricing using the defendant’s product numbers or images, and contended that the defendant’s use of “Frost” for washroom products would create confusion and damage the claimant’s brand-building efforts in the UK and Ireland.

In response to the defendant’s counter-allegations, the claimant argued (in substance) that mere knowledge of the defendant’s trading position was not enough to amount to bad faith in filing its trade mark application, and pointed to its own (albeit modest) trading history and its long-standing use of “Frost” as part of its position that its registration and enforcement were legitimate.

facts:
The appellant is a Kenyan citizen born on 13 September 1969. He applied for entry clearance to the United Kingdom as a partner of his wife (the sponsor), who has indefinite leave to remain, is settled in the UK, and is employed.

The Entry Clearance Officer in Nairobi refused the application because the appellant did not satisfy the financial requirements, specifically due to deficiencies in the documentary evidence about the sponsor’s employment and salary.

In the First-tier Tribunal, the judge found that the appellant could not succeed under the Immigration Rules because key specified evidence was missing or did not match: the sponsor’s contract of employment was not provided, and the bank statements did not cover the same period as the wage slips (the later months shown on wage slips were not covered by bank statements, while earlier months were covered by bank statements but there were no wage slips for those earlier months). The First-tier Tribunal also addressed accommodation and resolved that issue in the appellant’s favour within the broader assessment.

Although the First-tier Tribunal allowed the appeal on the basis that refusal would be a disproportionate interference with family life, the Entry Clearance Officer appealed to the Upper Tribunal. The Upper Tribunal concluded that, at the date of decision, the appellant did not meet the financial requirements and that it was not certain the application would have been granted even under later evidential provisions because those involved an element of discretion. The Upper Tribunal set aside the First-tier Tribunal’s decision on the family life issue and dismissed the appeal on that basis, while leaving in place the dismissal under the Immigration Rules.

The Upper Tribunal noted that the appellant could make a fresh entry clearance application with the correct specified financial documents. This would involve some expense and delay, but the prior application had been decided in about five weeks.
claims:
The appellant’s case before the First-tier Tribunal was an appeal against refusal of entry clearance as a partner. He sought to overturn the refusal and obtain entry clearance.

Under the Immigration Rules, the appellant relied on the sponsor’s employment income to meet the financial requirement, but the First-tier Tribunal found the specified evidence was incomplete and inconsistent (missing employment contract and mismatched wage slips and bank statements), so the appeal could not succeed on that basis.

The appellant also relied on family life grounds, arguing in substance that refusal would disproportionately interfere with his family life with his wife in the UK. The First-tier Tribunal accepted that it would not be reasonable to expect the sponsor—who is settled and employed in the UK—to leave the UK to live with him in Kenya, and accepted that the evidence showed she earned considerably more than the minimum financial threshold, with the failure under the Rules arising from missing specific documents. The First-tier Tribunal further reasoned that dismissing the appeal would only require the appellant to make a fresh application, and on that basis found refusal disproportionate.

Before the Upper Tribunal, the Entry Clearance Officer argued that the decision was not disproportionate because the appellant could make a further application for entry clearance. The Upper Tribunal agreed and dismissed the appeal on the family life ground.

facts:
Pratigyan Kepchhaki is a Nepalese national born on 29 April 1989. Following earlier appeal proceedings (IA/15819/2011), she succeeded on private life grounds. In that earlier decision, the tribunal noted she had experienced “unhelpful officialdom” and indicated that, while the length of leave to be granted was for the Secretary of State, it envisaged a period that would enable her to complete the proposed course of study.

After that earlier successful appeal, she was granted discretionary leave to remain from 13 June 2012 until 28 December 2012. The grant of leave occurred more than nine months after the earlier tribunal decision.

On 20 December 2012, shortly before her discretionary leave expired, she applied to vary her leave to remain so that she could complete her studies in the UK. The Secretary of State refused that application by a refusal letter dated 10 January 2014 and, on the same date, also made a decision to remove her.

The First-tier Tribunal allowed her appeal on private life grounds. In doing so, it treated as significant that, despite the basis on which she had previously succeeded, she had been granted only six months’ discretionary leave rather than leave comparable to what a student would ordinarily have after a successful appeal; that the delay in granting leave contributed to her situation; that she was unable to obtain a CAS because she had discretionary leave rather than student leave; and that as a result she could not continue her studies in the manner contemplated by the earlier tribunal decision. The First-tier Tribunal also noted that it took about 13 months for the Secretary of State to decide her December 2012 application.

The Secretary of State appealed to the Upper Tribunal. The Upper Tribunal upheld the First-tier Tribunal’s decision, finding no legal error and leaving the appeal allowed.
claims:
Ms Kepchhaki appealed against the Secretary of State’s refusal (dated 10 January 2014) to vary her leave to remain and against the accompanying removal decision. Her case, as accepted by the First-tier Tribunal, was that she had established a private life in the UK and that removal would be disproportionate in light of the particular history of her case.

In particular, she relied on the circumstances following her earlier successful appeal: although the earlier tribunal had envisaged leave enabling her to complete her course, she was granted only six months’ discretionary leave and the grant was delayed by over nine months; because she held discretionary leave rather than student leave she could not obtain a CAS; consequently she was unable to continue her studies as previously contemplated; and these circumstances led her to make the further application in December 2012. She also relied on the lengthy delay (about 13 months) in the Secretary of State determining that application.

On that basis, she sought that the refusal and removal decision be overturned and that she be permitted to remain in the UK, contending that removal would unjustifiably interfere with her private life.

facts:
The claimant is a Ugandan national born on 27 March 1962. He applied for entry clearance as a family visitor to the United Kingdom. The sponsor was his niece, who had been living in the UK since about 1991 and married there in 1993. The sponsor’s husband died on 1 March 2014.

The claimant’s stated purpose for visiting was to support his niece and her three children following the husband’s death, and to say prayers at a service during Ramadan. The visa application was made on 8 July 2014. Entry clearance was refused by the Entry Clearance Officer (ECO) in Nairobi on 21 July 2014.

The claimant appealed. The First-tier Tribunal allowed the appeal, finding the claimant to be a genuine visitor who intended to return at the end of his stay. The Upper Tribunal noted that there was no clear evidence before the First-tier Tribunal about the prior nature of any family or private life between the claimant and the sponsor, whether any such relationship had been maintained over time, or whether there had been any hiatus and for how long. There was also no adequate factual basis to assess the nature and closeness of any relationship between the claimant and the sponsor’s deceased husband. The Upper Tribunal concluded that the First-tier Tribunal had not made necessary findings on these matters and had treated the refusal as disproportionate largely because the visit purpose was legitimate and the claimant intended to leave.

On remaking the decision, the Upper Tribunal found that, on the evidence presented, there was not a necessary family or private life relationship shown, nor a demonstrated attempt to maintain or re-establish such connections arising from the bereavement. The Upper Tribunal therefore found that the relevant human rights were not engaged and dismissed the claimant’s appeal.
claims:
The claimant sought entry clearance to visit the UK as a family visitor. He argued, in substance, that he was a genuine visitor coming for a limited period, that his purpose was to support his niece and her three children after the death of her husband, and to attend prayers during Ramadan, and that he would return to Uganda at the end of the visit.
