In his appeal against the refusal, the claimant’s case (as accepted by the First-tier Tribunal) was that he met the visitor requirements and that refusal of entry clearance was not justified given the compassionate and family-support purpose of the trip and his intention to leave. The appeal was pursued on the basis that the refusal interfered with his ability to visit and support family in the context of bereavement, and that the decision should be overturned and entry clearance granted.

facts:
The appellant is a Sri Lankan Tamil born in 1987. He said that in July 2007 the LTTE came to his parents’ home looking for his older brother, and when the brother was not there the LTTE abducted the appellant and his younger sister. They were taken to an LTTE training camp, separated after about two weeks, and the appellant remained at the camp for about a year, receiving training in communications.

He said that in 2008 he was sent to Colombo and worked for about eight months in communications. He lived in LTTE-arranged accommodation with others. He described being used to handle money: the LTTE opened a bank account for him, paid money into it, and instructed him to withdraw and deposit money into other accounts or hand it to others. He also said he collected money from shops and delivered it to a person referred to as “S”, and received calls directing him where to deposit money and to pass on parcels.

He said that in March 2009 the instructions stopped. After he contacted “S” at the end of March, “S” told him not to contact him again. The appellant said he then hid at his Colombo address and lived off money he had been holding.

He said that in about August 2009 he asked his father for help because his money had run out. His father came to Colombo, moved him to a different address, and told him the younger sister had been sent to the United Kingdom. The appellant said that from August 2009 to May 2012 he lived with people his father introduced him to and studied English.

He said that in May 2012 he met someone he knew from the LTTE camp and gave that person his address. A few days later he was abducted at gunpoint by four men in civilian clothes, interrogated about his LTTE activities, and then taken to Homangna. He said the abductors were part of the Karuna Group. He said he was taken to a CID office where he was fingerprinted and then returned to Homangna, detained for about a week, and tortured, including being burned with cigarettes and a heated spoon. He said the men referred to “S” by name and told him the authorities had raided his room and taken LTTE documents.

He said his father arranged his release through contacts, and that the CID required him to leave the country and in the meantime to stay at an address they controlled. In June 2012, because his wounds were infected, he said CID officers took him to hospital for two days. He said his father was allowed to see him after paying a bribe and took photographs of him.

He said that in August 2012 he applied for a visa with CID assistance, and that in December 2012 he again went through the process and obtained a visa. He said that on 23 January 2013 CID officers told him his journey to the UK had been organised; he was taken to the airport, met an agent, used a specific check-in desk, and left Colombo. He arrived in the UK on 24 January 2013 and was met by his older sister. He claimed asylum on 4 April 2013.

He said that after he arrived in the UK he remained in contact with his father, who told him police had attended the family home and required the father to attend the police station for investigation about the appellant; the father contacted a lawyer who arranged for the questioning date to be extended so the lawyer could attend.

In the First-tier Tribunal, the judge heard oral evidence from the appellant and his older sister and considered documentary evidence including hospital photographs, a scarring report, a GP letter, letters from a Sri Lankan attorney, a letter from the father, an affidavit from the younger sister, and statements from siblings. The First-tier Tribunal found significant problems with the appellant’s account, including inconsistencies about the nature of his 2012 detention and when and how his identity documents were taken; concerns that his description of his LTTE role developed in a piecemeal way; and inconsistencies between his account and information recorded in connection with his student visa interview. The First-tier Tribunal also treated his delay in claiming asylum as adverse to credibility. The judge concluded the evidence did not establish a real risk that he was on a stop list or watch list or that he would be perceived as presenting a current risk, and rejected his health-based claim as not meeting the relevant threshold.

On appeal to the Upper Tribunal, the appellant argued procedural unfairness, including that his father was not allowed to give oral evidence by video link and that the First-tier Tribunal failed to apply a concession in the refusal letter about his LTTE involvement. The Upper Tribunal found there was no procedural unfairness: the tribunal had notified the parties that video link facilities were unavailable and the appellant’s representatives proceeded with a witness statement; and the concession accepted only that he was forcibly recruited and worked for the LTTE until 2009, not the later events or that he was a willing participant. The Upper Tribunal upheld the First-tier Tribunal’s decision and dismissed the appeal.
claims:
The appellant sought to overturn the Secretary of State’s refusal to recognise him as a refugee or as otherwise entitled to international protection or human rights protection.

His protection claim was based on his account that he had been forcibly recruited by the LTTE, later performed communications and money-handling tasks for the LTTE in Colombo until 2009, and that in 2012 he was abducted, detained and tortured by men linked to the Karuna Group and then held under CID control, with the authorities allegedly recovering LTTE-related documents from his room. He asserted that his release was secured only on condition that he would leave Sri Lanka and remain under control at an address dictated by the authorities, and that he was assisted by CID officers to obtain a visa and depart the country. He also relied on claimed continuing interest by the Sri Lankan authorities after his departure, said to be shown by police attendance at his family home and demands that his father attend for questioning.

He relied on supporting material including photographs taken in hospital, a scarring report, a GP letter, correspondence from a Sri Lankan attorney, and statements/affidavit from family members.

Before the Upper Tribunal, his arguments focused on alleged errors of law/procedural unfairness in the First-tier Tribunal decision. He contended it was unfair that his father was not permitted to give oral evidence by video link, and that the First-tier Tribunal then made adverse findings about the father’s evidence without the father being cross-examined. He also argued that the First-tier Tribunal failed to recognise and apply a concession in the refusal letter accepting that he was forcibly recruited and worked for the LTTE until 2009, and that this failure led to unfair adverse credibility findings about his LTTE role. He further argued it was unfair for the First-tier Tribunal to criticise him for inconsistencies connected with his visa application information, and complained that insufficient weight was given to medical evidence and photographs in assessing credibility.

He also advanced a health-based human rights claim, relying on GP evidence, although the First-tier Tribunal found that evidence insufficient to establish the necessary severity.

facts:
Umar Farooq is a citizen of Pakistan, born 8 August 1989. He arrived at Glasgow Airport on 24 January 2015 returning from abroad. At the airport an Immigration Officer served him with a notice refusing him leave to enter and cancelling his leave. The refusal and cancellation were based on information from English Testing Services (ETS) alleging that he had used a false ETS English-language certificate in an earlier application, and that this application had resulted in him being granted Tier 1 leave on 15 June 2012.

In the First-tier Tribunal, Judge Fox allowed Mr Farooq’s appeal in a decision promulgated on 5 August 2015. The judge found that the respondent had produced no evidence directly or indirectly implicating Mr Farooq in fraudulently obtaining an ETS certificate; that the affidavits relied on by the respondent were generalised; and that there was no evidence that Mr Farooq had not attended the test centre and taken the test as he said he had done. The First-tier Tribunal also allowed the appeal on the basis that refusal would be a disproportionate interference with Mr Farooq’s private life.

The Immigration Officer sought to challenge that outcome. The application for permission to appeal from the First-tier Tribunal was made 22 days late, with the stated reason that it would be unfair not to admit a late application when permission had been granted in numerous other cases on similar arguments; no explanation was given for how the delay occurred. A First-tier Tribunal judge refused permission, finding no circumstances to explain or excuse the delay and also considering there was no arguable error of law. The respondent then sought permission from the Upper Tribunal, which extended time and granted permission.

Before the Upper Tribunal, the respondent relied on the usual general ETS evidence and also on a second spreadsheet produced in the First-tier Tribunal (provided late and after the appellant pressed for disclosure). The respondent argued this spreadsheet linked an identification number to the ETS certificate relied on by Mr Farooq and established the certificate was invalid. Mr Farooq’s representative argued the respondent’s evidence was deficient, including that the spreadsheet matched only part of the reference number and was incomplete, and that the respondent had long been on notice to produce the evidence relied upon. The respondent suggested the spreadsheet reference was incomplete due to a computer “drop down box” not being fully expanded and said fuller evidence existed but had not yet been produced; the respondent asked for it to be admitted if the decision were remade. The Upper Tribunal refused that attempt to introduce improved evidence at that stage, holding it was far too late given the appellant’s repeated requests and the expectation of prompt disclosure.

Mr Farooq’s representative also relied on a record of a Border Force credibility interview conducted at the airport on 24 January 2015, which recorded that Mr Farooq answered fluently, was credible at interview, and was fluent in English; this was said to be consistent with his account throughout.

The Upper Tribunal concluded that, although the First-tier Tribunal’s reasons were very brief, they were sufficient; the First-tier Tribunal had not found the match to be proved and the respondent’s evidence was at best incomplete, and the judge must have found Mr Farooq credible. The Upper Tribunal was not persuaded there was an error of law and dismissed the Immigration Officer’s appeal, leaving the First-tier Tribunal decision allowing Mr Farooq’s appeal in place.

After the Upper Tribunal’s March 2016 decision, there was a further hearing about whether the Upper Tribunal should make a recommendation or direction. It was accepted that the Upper Tribunal had no statutory power to make a recommendation. The respondent argued an informal recommendation was unnecessary and that there was no reason to think the respondent would not act lawfully and fairly to give effect to the decision. The Upper Tribunal recorded broad sympathy with Mr Farooq’s position that, having succeeded, the respondent should offer a remedy that as nearly as possible returned him to the position he would otherwise have been in, but the Tribunal did not go further or make any prescriptive recommendation.
claims:
Mr Farooq appealed against the refusal of leave to enter and the cancellation of his leave, which were based on an allegation that he had used a false ETS certificate in a prior application that led to Tier 1 leave being granted in June 2012. His case in the First-tier Tribunal was that he had attended the test centre and taken the ETS test himself, and that the respondent had not produced evidence showing he had used deception or that his certificate was fraudulently obtained. He relied on his oral evidence to that effect.

In resisting the respondent’s challenge in the Upper Tribunal, Mr Farooq argued that the respondent’s evidence was inadequate and incomplete to link him to any ETS fraud, including that the second spreadsheet relied on by the respondent did not fully match the reference number on his certificate. He also argued that the respondent had been repeatedly put on notice to disclose the evidence relied upon and should not be allowed to improve the case late by producing fuller material at the Upper Tribunal stage. He maintained that the First-tier Tribunal’s brief reasoning was sufficient because, if there was no evidence implicating him, it was enough for the judge to say so, and the judge’s acceptance of his account was the clear inference.

Mr Farooq also relied on the contemporaneous airport interview record from 24 January 2015 as supporting his credibility and English fluency, consistent with his position that he took the test himself.

Following his success on the merits, Mr Farooq (through counsel) sought the Upper Tribunal to make a direction or recommendation aimed at securing a practical remedy. The submissions were said to depend on his immigration history, business history, transitional issues, and the outcome of the appeal. Ultimately it was accepted that the Upper Tribunal had no power to make a recommendation, and the Tribunal did not issue any direction; it only recorded sympathy with the proposition that, having succeeded, he should be offered a remedy that as nearly as possible restored him to the position he would otherwise have been in.

facts:
The appellant, Emmanuel Abiodun Osisanya, was born in January 2000. He applied for entry clearance to come to the United Kingdom to join his father, who is settled in the UK. On 10 May 2016 the Entry Clearance Officer in Sheffield refused the application. The appellant appealed that refusal to the First-tier Tribunal, but on 1 August 2017 Judge Bart-Stewart dismissed the appeal.

The appellant then sought and obtained permission to challenge the First-tier Tribunal’s decision in the Upper Tribunal. In the Upper Tribunal proceedings, the respondent indicated in a written response dated 27 November 2017 that the respondent did not oppose the appeal. At the hearing, both representatives agreed the Upper Tribunal could re-make the decision without a further hearing, and the respondent’s representative did not resist the appellant’s request that the appeal be allowed.

In re-making the decision, the Upper Tribunal proceeded on the basis of findings accepted by the First-tier Tribunal: that the appellant met the relevant requirements for entry as a child to join a parent settled in the UK; that the father (the sponsor) could maintain and accommodate the appellant without recourse to public funds; and that there was existing family life between the appellant and his father.
claims: The appellant challenged the refusal of entry clearance to join his father in the UK. In the Upper Tribunal, his principal argument was that the First-tier Tribunal made an error when assessing his family-life circumstances by failing to give any weight to the fact that he met the relevant requirements for entry. He sought the setting aside of the First-tier Tribunal’s dismissal and an outcome allowing his appeal so that entry clearance would be granted on the basis that refusal was an unjustified interference with his family life with his father.

facts:
Shazia Waseem applied on 26 March 2018 for an EEA residence card as the spouse of an EEA national said to be exercising treaty rights in the United Kingdom. The Secretary of State refused that application on 13 November 2018 on the basis that the marriage was a marriage of convenience. The marriage was said to have taken place in Pakistan on 8 April 2015.

Before this application, there had been three applications for entry clearance which were refused on the same basis (that the marriage was one of convenience). In July 2017, an appeal against one of those refusals was dismissed, with the judge finding that the marriage was indeed one of convenience.

After those refusals, the appellant entered the United Kingdom illegally via Ireland, thereby circumventing the refusal of entry clearance.

The refusal of the March 2018 residence card application relied on the appellant’s failure, in that application, to address the concerns about the genuineness of the marriage that had been raised in the earlier refusals and in the earlier appeal decision.

The appellant appealed the refusal to the First-tier Tribunal. First-tier Tribunal Judge Moxon dismissed the appeal (decision promulgated 21 June 2019), treating the earlier tribunal decision as a starting point and considering the evidence and submissions from the appellant, who was unrepresented. The Upper Tribunal later found that the First-tier Tribunal had made an error of law in its approach to the relevant test and to the burden and standard of proof, set aside the First-tier Tribunal decision, and remitted the case for a fresh hearing with no findings preserved.
claims:
The appellant’s case, as reflected in the decision, was an appeal against the refusal of her application for an EEA residence card as the spouse of an EEA national. In substance, she sought to overturn the refusal that was based on an allegation that her marriage was a marriage of convenience, and to obtain recognition of her entitlement to a residence card as a family member.

The Secretary of State’s refusal relied on the position that the appellant had not addressed earlier concerns about the genuineness of the marriage. The First-tier Tribunal treated the issue as whether the appellant had shown the marriage was genuine and subsisting and concluded adversely to her. On appeal to the Upper Tribunal, the appellant challenged the First-tier Tribunal decision, and the Upper Tribunal accepted that the First-tier Tribunal had applied the wrong approach to the issue and misapplied the burden and standard of proof, leading to the requested relief being the setting aside of the First-tier Tribunal decision and a fresh determination. The Upper Tribunal granted that relief by setting aside and remitting the appeal for a new hearing.

facts:
The appellant, SIJ, is a Pakistani citizen born on 25 November 1981. He arrived in the United Kingdom in 2011 with leave as a student.

His account was that he is a gay man. He said that in Pakistan he had a relationship with a man called Ali for around ten years. He later moved to Kuwait at about age 25. After returning from Kuwait, he said he discovered Ali had decided to marry a woman and that their relationship could not continue, which he said left him devastated.

After arriving in the UK, he met a woman, referred to as D, through an online dating agency. They began a heterosexual relationship which later culminated in marriage. He said he entered that relationship and marriage in an attempt to “cure” himself of his homosexuality. He also said he could not maintain a sexual relationship with D and found attempts at sexual relations repulsive. By the time of the First-tier Tribunal hearing he said he was estranged from D and could not contact her.

At the First-tier Tribunal hearing, D did not attend to give evidence. The First-tier Tribunal judge considered there were credibility concerns about the explanation for her non-attendance, because earlier correspondence from the appellant’s solicitors seeking an adjournment had suggested they were in contact with D and that she was expected to be available on a future date, with the only issue being an unavoidable commitment on the listed hearing date.

Medical evidence before the First-tier Tribunal included a medico-legal report from Dr Hussain, a consultant psychiatrist. As summarised in the decision, the report reviewed the appellant’s claimed sexual history and concluded the appellant suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder and depression with suicidal ideation. This was attributed in the report to the appellant’s attempts to suppress his homosexuality and to “cure” himself.

The First-tier Tribunal dismissed the appeal, primarily on credibility grounds, including the judge’s view that it was implausible the appellant was gay given his heterosexual relationship and marriage to D. On appeal to the Upper Tribunal, it was accepted that the First-tier Tribunal’s approach to assessing the appellant’s claimed sexuality was flawed because it relied on the judge’s own subjective expectations about how a gay man would behave, and because the medical evidence was not considered holistically as part of the overall credibility assessment. The Upper Tribunal set aside the First-tier Tribunal decision and remitted the case for a fresh hearing before a different judge, with no findings preserved.
claims:
The appellant sought asylum, humanitarian protection, and related human rights relief on the basis that he is a gay man and cannot safely return to Pakistan. His case was that if returned he would feel compelled to conceal his homosexual identity in order to avoid persecution.

In support of his protection claim, he relied on his account of a long-term same-sex relationship in Pakistan, his subsequent attempt in the UK to enter a heterosexual relationship and marriage as a means of trying to “cure” himself, and his asserted inability to sustain sexual relations with his wife. He also relied on psychiatric evidence (Dr Hussain’s report) describing mental health conditions including post-traumatic stress disorder and depression with suicidal ideation, said to be linked to his attempts to suppress his sexuality.

Before the Upper Tribunal, his challenge to the First-tier Tribunal decision (as reflected in the grounds on which permission was granted and the Upper Tribunal’s discussion) was that the First-tier Tribunal wrongly assessed his credibility by applying the judge’s own expectations and assumptions about how a gay man would behave and what relationships he would form in the UK, and that the judge failed to give proper weight and reasoning in relation to the medical evidence by not integrating it into the overall credibility assessment. He sought the setting aside of the First-tier Tribunal’s dismissal and a fresh assessment of his claim.
uk_statute_references_predicted: Asylum and Immigration (Treatment of Claimants, etc.) Act 2004

facts:
The case concerns a Nepalese woman (the claimant before the First-tier Tribunal) who claimed international protection in the UK on the basis of her sexual orientation. The First-tier Tribunal accepted that she is a gay woman and that she is actively and openly living in accordance with that sexuality. It was also accepted that, if returned to Nepal, she would not seek to deny or hide the active expression of her sexuality.

The First-tier Tribunal’s decision (later challenged) stated that her fear of persecution and ill-treatment would be well founded because of the presence of her family and her ex-husband, and that this was a significant risk factor for her on return. The First-tier Tribunal allowed her appeal, recognising her as a refugee and also allowing the appeal on human rights grounds.

On appeal by the Secretary of State, the Upper Tribunal noted that the Secretary of State did not challenge the First-tier Tribunal’s findings that the claimant is a gay woman, that she openly expresses her sexuality, and that she would not conceal it on return. The Upper Tribunal’s concern was that the First-tier Tribunal had not completed its analysis of whether protection would be available to her in Nepal and whether she could safely relocate within Nepal.

During the Upper Tribunal proceedings it was also recorded that, on the day of the First-tier Tribunal hearing, the Secretary of State had served a Nepal country background note (described as unpublished) which included material on sexual orientation and/or gender identity and which was said to conflict to some extent with other country material relied on in the appeal.
claims:
The claimant’s protection claim was that she faced a real risk of persecution and ill-treatment in Nepal because she is a gay woman who actively and openly expresses her sexuality and would not conceal it on return. Her case, as accepted by the First-tier Tribunal, was that the risk on return arose in particular from her family and from the family of her ex-husband.

She sought recognition as a refugee and also relied on human rights grounds, contending that removal would expose her to serious harm contrary to her fundamental rights.

In submissions before the First-tier Tribunal (as noted by the Upper Tribunal), her representatives also addressed the issues of whether adequate protection would be available to her from the Nepalese authorities and, in the alternative, whether she could reasonably and safely relocate within Nepal.

facts:
Miss Margaret Walsh had a dispute with the London Borough of Hammersmith & Fulham arising from her dismissal. In an earlier Industrial Tribunal decision dated 9 February 1993 (reasons sent 3 March 1993), the Tribunal found that she had been unfairly dismissed but also found that she had contributed to her dismissal to the extent of 80%. Miss Walsh did not appeal the contributory fault finding, and the Council did not appeal the unfair dismissal finding.

The 1993 decision indicated that the parties should try to agree compensation, and if they could not do so within 28 days they should return to the Tribunal for compensation to be assessed. The matter was not brought back promptly; it returned to the Tribunal for a further hearing on 15 December 1994. The Tribunal noted concern that the case had not been returned earlier after the failure to resolve matters within the 28-day period, and it was aware that correspondence had passed between the parties.

At the December 1994 hearing, Miss Walsh represented herself (whereas she had been represented by counsel at the earlier hearing). The Tribunal recorded that she sought to re-open matters already dealt with in the earlier decision, particularly issues concerning disciplinary hearings that took place before the Industrial Tribunal proceedings. The Tribunal found it difficult to keep her focused on the reasons she was seeking reinstatement or re-engagement.

The Tribunal unanimously decided that it was unreasonable to reinstate or re-engage Miss Walsh and dismissed her application for such an order. It then assessed compensation and awarded her £3,588.80, reflecting the earlier 80% contributory fault finding.
claims:
Miss Walsh applied to the Industrial Tribunal for an order that she be reinstated or re-engaged by the London Borough of Hammersmith & Fulham following the finding that she had been unfairly dismissed. At the December 1994 hearing she attempted to revisit matters previously determined, including aspects of the prior disciplinary process, in support of her position.

After the Tribunal refused reinstatement or re-engagement and awarded compensation reduced to reflect 80% contributory fault, Miss Walsh appealed that decision. Her appeal sought to challenge the refusal to order reinstatement or re-engagement (and expressed dissatisfaction with the Tribunal’s decision).

facts:
Mrs Kumud Patel was employed by the London Borough of Brent from 26 May 1992 as a word processor in the Council’s Ad Shop. A redundancy situation developed in the Ad Shop. As a result, on 17 July 1995 she accepted alternative employment within the Council as an information officer in the One Stop Shop. She then asked to be made redundant, and her employment ended on 25 August 1995. She received an enhanced redundancy payment, and the Council’s correspondence stated that her last day of service “for all other purposes” was 25 August 1995.

Following an offer made in September 1995, Mrs Patel returned to work for the Council on 16 October 1995 as a temporary administrative officer in the Language Shop. She remained employed there until she was dismissed in May 1996.

When she brought a complaint of unfair dismissal, the Industrial Tribunal decided it could not hear the complaint because it found she had not been continuously employed for two years or more at the time of her dismissal in May 1996. The continuity issue turned on whether the gap between 25 August 1995 and 16 October 1995 counted as an absence “on account of a temporary cessation of work.” The Industrial Tribunal concluded it was not a temporary cessation, relying in particular on its view that at the end of the employment on 25 August 1995 the Council did not envisage the cessation as temporary, that Mrs Patel had no solid basis for envisaging it as temporary, and that her later work in the Language Shop was different from her earlier work and was only a temporary position.

On appeal, the Employment Appeal Tribunal held that the Industrial Tribunal had not approached the “temporary cessation” issue in the legally correct way because it did not properly apply the required backward-looking assessment of the whole history of events, and it had given disproportionate weight to factors such as the employer’s intention at the time and the change in job. The appeal was allowed and the case was remitted for the continuity issue to be reconsidered afresh by a differently constituted tribunal, with all arguments available to both sides to be deployed.
claims:
Mrs Patel’s underlying claim was a complaint of unfair dismissal arising from her dismissal in May 1996. To pursue that complaint, she contended that she had the necessary continuous employment, arguing that the period between 25 August 1995 and 16 October 1995 should not break continuity because it was an absence caused by a temporary cessation of work.

In the appeal, she argued that the Industrial Tribunal had erred in law by failing to take the correct approach to deciding whether the gap was due to a temporary cessation of work. Her case was that the tribunal should have looked back over the whole history of the employment and assessed the gap in that context, and that the tribunal instead gave undue weight to matters of only limited relevance—particularly the Council’s intention on 29 August 1995 that the cessation should be permanent, and the fact that the job she took up in October 1995 was different and temporary.

She also argued, in the alternative, that the Industrial Tribunal’s conclusion was perverse and invited the Employment Appeal Tribunal to substitute a finding that the absence was on account of a temporary cessation of work.

The relief she sought on appeal was that the Industrial Tribunal’s decision be overturned so that her unfair dismissal complaint could proceed. The Employment Appeal Tribunal allowed the appeal but did not substitute its own finding; instead it ordered that the continuity issue be reheard by a differently constituted tribunal.

facts:
Mr P Coughlan worked for Moon Furniture & Toy Centre as a delivery driver for about four months, delivering furniture to customers’ homes and collecting cash to take back to work. On 10 October 1997, money (said by Mr Coughlan to be £600) went missing from the delivery van while he and his delivery partner were working. When they returned to the workplace they explained what had happened to the manager and were told to continue with deliveries. Later that evening, when they were finishing, the manager dismissed them and refused to pay their wages. Mr Coughlan presented a claim dated 24 October 1997 and received by the Industrial Tribunal on 29 October 1997.

The employer’s response stated that Mr Coughlan had been banned from driving and had an invalid licence, which the employer said came to light when police arrested him on the employer’s premises. The employer said Mr Coughlan was told that if he was banned from driving he would be dismissed, but that he could continue working as a driver’s mate (helping with deliveries but not driving) until his criminal matter was resolved. The employer alleged that, knowing he would be dismissed, Mr Coughlan devised a plan with the other driver to steal £654 from the company. The employer asserted that both men were responsible for collecting money on delivery and that they returned with a story that the money had been left in the glove compartment of an unlocked van and stolen. The employer said that further questioning revealed the missing money had been in a sealed envelope, while £120 in unsealed cash from an earlier delivery remained, and that neither man could explain why the sealed envelope was taken but the £120 cash was not. Police were called and questioned both men, who gave the same response.

The Industrial Tribunal heard the case in the employer’s absence, although the employer had lodged a notice of appearance. The Tribunal concluded there had been an unlawful deduction from wages and awarded Mr Coughlan £220. The employer appealed. At the preliminary hearing, the Employment Appeal Tribunal noted that although the Tribunal stated it had considered the notice of appearance, its written reasons did not address the points raised in the employer’s response, and the EAT considered it arguable that the Tribunal had failed to deal with the employer’s case as set out in the IT3. The EAT therefore allowed the matter to proceed to a full hearing on the issues raised.
claims:
Mr Coughlan’s claim was that after the incident in which money went missing from the delivery van, the manager dismissed him and refused to pay his wages. He said he was owed two weeks’ wages and had tried unsuccessfully to obtain payment. The Industrial Tribunal treated the matter as a claim for unlawful deductions from wages and awarded him £220 in respect of those deductions.

On appeal, the employer’s position (as reflected in its response and the grounds advanced to the EAT) was that the Tribunal’s decision did not deal with the employer’s case set out in the IT3. The employer contended that it was entitled to deduct the missing money from wages, asserting that employees were employed on the basis that shortfalls would be deducted and that this had been communicated to staff. The employer also advanced factual allegations challenging Mr Coughlan’s integrity and alleging he had been involved in the disappearance of the money. The employer sought to overturn the Tribunal’s decision on the basis that the Tribunal failed to address these points.
uk_statute_references_predicted: Employment Tribunals (Constitution and Rules of Procedure) Regulations 1993

facts:
Mr S A Edwards was employed by Marconi Corporation plc. He was appointed a Justice of the Peace for Central London and sworn in before the Senior Judge.

In November 1999 a company officer wrote to Mr Edwards confirming that the company would offer reasonable time off for those duties if he was accepted.

A dispute later arose about time off for a mandatory two-day training course scheduled for 20 and 21 February 2001. Mr Edwards said the company’s current officer did not wish to permit time off and told him he could not attend the course. Mr Edwards had written to that officer on 22 and 23 November 2000. He said the officer told him on 27 November 2000 that he could attend the course, but then withdrew that on 23 January 2001.

Mr Edwards presented his tribunal application on 16 February 2001 (received on 19 February 2001), before the course dates. The Employment Tribunal found that at the time the claim was submitted there had been no breach because Mr Edwards had not yet attempted to attend the course. The Tribunal also considered events after submission and found there had been confusion in the instructions given to Mr Edwards and confusion on the part of a manager (Mr Cooper) about whether permission had been given. However, the Tribunal found that Mr Edwards did in fact take the time off work, was not prevented from attending the course, and no disciplinary action followed. Shortly after his return to work on 23 February, he was told by another manager (Mr Baldwin) that he could have reasonable time off to pursue his duties. On those findings, the Tribunal concluded he had been permitted to take time off even if explicit permission had not been granted, and dismissed the claim.

Mr Edwards appealed. The Employment Appeal Tribunal dealt with the matter at a preliminary ex parte hearing and dismissed the appeal, concluding that Mr Edwards had not identified an error of law and that his criticisms were, in substance, disagreements with factual findings.

The Employment Appeal Tribunal noted that Mr Edwards said he had other ongoing disputes with Marconi, including complaints about not being paid when he sat as a Justice of the Peace and about not being permitted to take time off during working hours for that purpose, but those matters were not determined in this appeal.
claims:
Before the Employment Tribunal, Mr Edwards complained that his employer was not permitting him reasonable time off to perform his duties as a Justice of the Peace. He relied on his appointment and the employer’s earlier written confirmation that reasonable time off would be offered. He alleged that the company’s officer refused to allow him to attend the mandatory two-day training course on 20 and 21 February 2001, after initially indicating in November 2000 that he could attend and then withdrawing that permission in January 2001. His requested relief, as presented, was effectively a finding that the employer had failed to permit him to take time off for those judicial duties/training.

On appeal, Mr Edwards argued that the Tribunal had incorrectly applied or interpreted the relevant right to time off and that there were various errors in the Tribunal’s reasons and extended reasons. The appeal materials, as summarised in the judgment, did not clearly identify a specific legal error beyond asserting misinterpretation and errors in the Tribunal’s reasoning.

Separately (but not part of the claim decided in this appeal), Mr Edwards indicated he had other complaints against the employer, including that pay had been wrongly withheld when he sat as a Justice of the Peace and that he was not permitted time off during working hours for sitting as a Justice of the Peace.

facts:
Mr Whiley began working for Christopher Clarke Workshops Ltd on 16 July 1995 as a sprayer in the respondent’s furniture workshop. The job involved frequent heavy lifting of furniture.

In June 2000 he injured his back and experienced pain at work, which he reported to the general manager, Mr King. Mr Whiley said he asked for assistance with lifting and that help was usually provided, though sometimes no help was available when he needed to lift furniture he was spraying.

On 6 September 2000 Mr Whiley found it impossible to continue working and went off sick with medical certification. He remained absent. A medical certificate dated 23 October 2000 recorded a diagnosis of a prolapsed intervertebral disc; earlier certificates had described his condition as sciatica and later as back pain.

During his absence Mr Whiley telephoned Mr King weekly. Mr King formed the impression that Mr Whiley spent most of his time lying down. At the managing director Mr Clark’s request, and with Mr Whiley’s consent, Mr King spoke to Mr Whiley’s general practitioner. The GP’s notes recorded that it might be up to another three months before Mr Whiley would be fit enough for work. Mr King relayed to Mr Clark that Mr Whiley might be unfit for three to six months, possibly longer, and possibly would not be able to work again. The tribunal found that Mr King had inaccurately reported the GP’s opinion to Mr Clark.

Relying on the information he received from Mr King, Mr Clark decided to dismiss Mr Whiley and did so by letter dated 2 November 2000, with effect the next day. Mr Clark did not speak to Mr Whiley before dismissing him.

Mr Whiley initially started an internal appeal but, after advice from his trade union, withdrew it and instead brought tribunal proceedings complaining of unfair dismissal. The proceedings were later amended to add a complaint of disability discrimination.

The employment tribunal found that the reason for dismissal related to capability but that the dismissal was procedurally unfair because, although there was some medical evidence, a reasonable employer would have discussed the matter with the employee and there had been no consultation.

On disability, the tribunal found that Mr Whiley had a physical impairment (a degenerative back condition) which had a substantial adverse effect on normal day-to-day activities and was long-term (likely to last, and in fact having lasted, 12 months), so that he was disabled. The tribunal also found he was dismissed for a reason related to his disability.

After the tribunal delivered its decision, the parties discussed settlement. The written reasons recorded that the parties informed the tribunal the case was settled on payment of £2,000 and the tribunal ordered the case adjourned generally on agreed terms or until further order. The settlement was not reduced to writing; it was concluded by a handshake. There was later a dispute about whether the payment settled only the outstanding remedy for unfair dismissal or also settled any further litigation including an appeal on disability discrimination. The appeal tribunal concluded the payment settled only the outstanding remedy issue for unfair dismissal and did not bar an appeal on the disability discrimination claim.
claims:
Mr Whiley brought tribunal proceedings against his former employer complaining of unfair dismissal and, after amendment, disability discrimination.

In relation to disability discrimination, he advanced two bases:

1) He contended that by dismissing him the respondent treated him less favourably than it treated or would treat others who were not disabled.

2) He contended that the respondent failed to make reasonable adjustments.

On appeal, Mr Whiley sought to challenge the tribunal’s dismissal of his disability discrimination complaint. His appeal arguments (as presented for him) were that the tribunal had rejected his disability discrimination claims on the wrong basis by treating the employer’s lack of knowledge of the long-term nature of his condition at the time of dismissal as determinative. He argued that this was an error and that the tribunal had not properly addressed whether the employer could reasonably have been expected to know he was disabled and whether he was placed at a substantial disadvantage, including by failing to analyse whether it was reasonable for the employer to obtain its own medical evidence and what could reasonably be concluded from the prognosis that had been communicated within the company.

He sought an outcome that would allow his disability discrimination case to be reconsidered, rather than being finally dismissed on the basis adopted by the tribunal.

facts:
The claimant was employed from 3 October 2005 as the manager of The Eagle Hotel public house in Rochdale, owned by the respondent company (a subsidiary within a wider brewery/pub group). The pub was one of around 50–60 pubs owned by the respondent in the north-west. The claimant initially ran the pub with his partner, but they separated around June 2007.

After the separation, the respondent became concerned about a significant drop in revenue and profitability. Over time, what had been a modest profit turned into losses. Figures cited included takings of £45,039 for the five months to 3 October 2009 compared with £63,511 for the five months to 1 October 2005. The tribunal found that various adverse trading factors existed by December 2008 and that there was no evidence of further adverse trading factors after that date.

The adverse factors included local business closures reducing customer numbers (including closures of a wood-yard and retail stores, and reduced working at a local engineering firm), reduced opening hours after the claimant’s separation, and the respondent’s policy restrictions at the pub (no entertainment, no television, and no gaming). The pub had no marked price advantage over competitors and faced competition from supermarkets, alongside a national decline in pub trade. There was also no pool table in use due to a disagreement about who would pay for re-covering it.

On 20 February 2009 the claimant met the area manager, who highlighted a 28.5% reduction in turnover over three years and a loss for the financial year. The claimant was advised to take a more active role in promoting games and was set a weekly takings target for March 2009, which he narrowly missed. On 15 May 2009 he received a verbal warning for poor trade performance; his appeal was unsuccessful.

Around May 2009 a new area manager, Mr Humphrey Smith, visited and expressed concern about continuing falls in takings and the movement from profit to loss. The claimant was told not to expect a salary increase and was set a target of a 10% increase in takings over the previous year. On 12 November 2009 Mr Smith visited again; the claimant had not met the target, with decreases in takings in several months compared with the previous year.

A disciplinary meeting was arranged for 3 December 2009 but was adjourned due to the claimant’s holiday and then sickness. The claimant was absent from work with stress and anxiety from 8 December 2009 until 6 May 2010. During his absence a non-residential relief manager ran the pub and turnover continued to fall compared with the previous period (with one month showing a modest increase). The claimant attributed this to the relief manager not living on site.

After the claimant returned, he was invited by letter dated 27 May 2010 to a rearranged disciplinary meeting, being told there was no satisfactory explanation for continued poor performance and that it might result in a formal oral warning recorded on his file. The meeting took place on 8 June 2010 and was conducted by Mr Humphrey Smith. Mr Smith compared the pub’s performance with two other respondent-owned pubs in the locality that were doing better; the claimant responded by pointing to limitations affecting The Eagle and said he had tried to encourage custom by setting up darts and pool teams. Mr Smith said the claimant had responsibility to create a welcoming atmosphere, described the claimant as having a negative attitude, and issued a written warning (which the claimant objected to because the invitation letter had referred only to a possible oral warning). The claimant appealed and the appeal failed.

A new target was set from 8 June 2010 to 31 July 2010: takings were to remain at the current level until the end of the World Cup, then increase by 10%. Instead, takings reduced significantly up to 11 July 2010 and then showed a modest increase later in the month. The claimant was invited to another disciplinary hearing on 8 September 2010. He rejected comparisons with other pubs due to local difficulties and referred to efforts to increase trade, including establishing a fantasy football club.

On 29 September 2010 Mr Smith concluded the continued fall in takings was unsustainable and issued a final written warning. The claimant appealed unsuccessfully. A further target for September and October was set: a 10% increase, with a warning that failure could lead to dismissal. Takings instead declined.

On 15 November 2010 the claimant was invited to a further disciplinary meeting held on 23 November 2010. He attended with a trade union representative, again pointing to the difficulties of managing the pub and the efforts he had made to attract customers. Mr Smith considered the position untenable and dismissed the claimant on five weeks’ notice on 26 November 2010, with an effective termination date of 31 December 2010. The claimant appealed against dismissal and the appeal was unsuccessful. It was accepted at the tribunal hearing that the dismissal was for capability.

The respondent’s position throughout was that pub managers/landlords were responsible for creating successful trade by creating a pleasant and comfortable “mein host” atmosphere. The respondent considered the claimant unable to create that atmosphere and to have shown a negative attitude. The claimant had been assisted by a freeze in beer prices and by the respondent providing decent premises.

After the claimant left, management changed. Initially the same relief manager became resident and turnover increased. Subsequently a couple were appointed as new managers and turnover increased significantly (reported as 59.4%). The tribunal considered that post-dismissal performance could not be used to decide fairness based on information available at the time, and also found that comparisons with other managers/pubs were affected by differences such as breaches of the respondent’s policies (entertainment/discos, later serving, poker evenings) and increased opening hours due to higher staffing levels under the new managers.

The employment tribunal found the claimant unfairly dismissed, applied a 40% reduction to reflect the chance of dismissal in any event, and awarded total compensation of £13,014.98. On appeal, the Employment Appeal Tribunal allowed the respondent’s appeal on the basis that the tribunal had impermissibly substituted its own view for that of the employer rather than properly applying the range of reasonable responses approach, and indicated the matter should be remitted to a freshly constituted tribunal.
claims:
The claimant brought a complaint of unfair dismissal, contending that his dismissal for alleged lack of capability in running the pub was not justified or reasonable in the circumstances.

From the tribunal’s findings and the claimant’s case as presented in the disciplinary process and at the hearing, the claimant’s central arguments were that the decline in takings was materially explained by external and structural factors affecting The Eagle rather than by his personal capability. He relied on matters such as local business closures reducing the customer base, reduced opening hours after his separation from his partner, and limitations arising from the respondent’s policies at the pub (including the absence of entertainment, television, and gaming), as well as competitive pressures. He also disputed the fairness of comparing The Eagle’s takings with other pubs that drew customers from different areas and/or operated under different conditions.

The claimant argued that he had made efforts to improve trade, including establishing a darts team, a pool team, and a fantasy football club, and that the respondent’s reliance on takings as the sole or primary measure of his capability was too crude and did not properly assess whether he had the skills and aptitude required.

In support of his unfair dismissal claim, the claimant (through his representative) argued that a fuller analysis and investigation should have been undertaken before dismissal. The proposals advanced included: placing the claimant in another pub for a period to assess his performance; arranging an anonymous assessment of his “mein host” qualities; appointing another manager to monitor and advise him; or providing additional staffing support to allow longer opening hours comparable to those operated by successors, followed by a further assessment. The claimant’s requested relief was a finding of unfair dismissal and compensation for loss arising from dismissal.
uk_statute_references_predicted: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992

facts:
Mrs B Teal was employed by Chelmsford College Corporation as a fixed-term lecturer on what the College described as a “zero hours” contract, meaning she was paid for hours actually worked rather than a fixed salary.

On 30 November 2009 her line manager told her he would not pay her for overtime hours she had claimed for the academic year. That same day she wrote a letter stating she resigned “with immediate effect.” The College treated her letter as raising a grievance.

On 2 December 2009 a Human Resources Officer, Ms Rachel Jessen, wrote to Mrs Teal inviting her to a grievance hearing on 8 December 2009 and stating that the College could not accept her resignation until the grievance had been resolved. The grievance hearing took place on 8 December 2009. On 16 December 2009 Ms Jessen wrote to Mrs Teal confirming the College would pay her for 77.5 hours she had claimed but not been paid (to be paid in January), and that the College would allow her to rescind her resignation, while warning that the College could not be placed in a position where she “walk[ed] out on the students” again.

By a further letter dated 6 January 2010 Ms Jessen referred to drawing a line under the process and said she looked forward to Mrs Teal’s return and continued successful employment.

Mrs Teal returned to work on 11 January 2010. On 14 January 2010 Ms Jessen emailed Mrs Teal stating that because she had a zero hours contract and had not worked since 30 November 2009, she would not be paid for the period 30 November 2009 to 11 January 2010, explaining that the College could not pay for hours not worked.

In response, Mrs Teal raised a further grievance on 1 February 2010. This grievance was rejected on 9 February 2010.

On 12 February 2010 Mrs Teal resigned again. In her resignation letter she said that after the December 2009 grievance outcome (when overtime was to be paid and her earlier resignation was rescinded), she was then told she would not be paid for December 2009, which she said was a breach of contract and an unlawful deduction from wages. She said the rejection of her further grievance was the “final straw,” that there had been a fundamental breach of contract and a breakdown of mutual trust and confidence due to the College’s actions and treatment of her, and that her position had become untenable.

Mrs Teal presented her Employment Tribunal claim on 20 April 2010. The Employment Judge decided that her first resignation had been withdrawn with the College’s consent and that her employment continued until the second resignation on 12 February 2010, so time ran from that later date. On appeal, the Employment Appeal Tribunal agreed that the first resignation was clear (not “conditional”) but held it had been withdrawn by consent, and upheld that the effective termination date was 12 February 2010, meaning the claim was in time.
claims:
Mrs Teal brought a claim that depended on establishing that she had sufficient continuity of employment and that her complaint was presented in time by reference to the correct termination date.

Her case, as accepted by the Employment Judge and upheld on appeal, was that although she resigned on 30 November 2009, that resignation was later withdrawn with the College’s agreement (the College “allow[ing]” her to rescind it), so her employment did not end on 30 November 2009 and instead continued until her later resignation on 12 February 2010.

In her 12 February 2010 resignation letter, she asserted that the College’s refusal to pay her for December 2009 after agreeing to pay overtime and to rescind her earlier resignation was a breach of her contract and an unlawful deduction from wages. She contended that the College’s actions caused a fundamental breach of contract and a breakdown of mutual trust and confidence, making her employment untenable and leading to her resignation.

She therefore sought to pursue an unfair dismissal claim on the basis that the effective termination date was 12 February 2010 and that her tribunal claim presented on 20 April 2010 was within time.

facts:
Mr Lee Knight was employed as a gardener under a detailed written contract dated 11 November 2004. His employment transferred to Robert Bates Wrekin Landscapes Ltd (RBW) in February 2011. RBW was a small family-run business; about 40% of its work came from a contract providing gardening and grounds maintenance at a secure MOD site at Donnington operated by Babcock. Mr Knight had worked at that site for some years, had attended site inductions, and had been given the site rule book. The rule book stated that vehicles entering or leaving were liable to security checks and that no property was to be removed from the site without an appropriately completed property pass signed by a Babcock host. The Employment Judge found Mr Knight understood the importance attached to this rule, given the presence of many metal items that might be stolen.

On 11 October 2011 Mr Bates (RBW’s director) received a tip-off from someone at Babcock that something untoward had been seen in Mr Knight’s van as he left the site. Mr Bates looked in the van and saw a bag of bolts on the dashboard. He returned the bolts to Babcock and was asked to investigate how this had happened. RBW carried out an investigation and suspended Mr Knight on full pay.

Mr Knight’s explanation was that he found the bag of bolts while litter-picking, put them to one side and then on the dashboard of his van, intending to hand them in. He said it had been a difficult day because a van window had been shattered by a stone and there had been a puncture on the mower, and he forgot to hand the bolts in. He intended to return them to the site when he next went to work.

After the investigation, RBW prepared a suspension letter setting out the allegations and enclosing witness statements and the rule book, but it was sent to the wrong address. Mr Knight did not receive it until some days after the disciplinary hearing on 20 October 2011. Mr Bates then summarily dismissed Mr Knight on 26 October 2011, characterising the reasons as theft and removing goods from the site contrary to MOD protocols. Mr Knight appealed and raised a number of points in response to the documentation he had by then received, but Mr Bates heard the appeal himself and rejected it.

The Employment Judge accepted Mr Knight’s evidence that he had simply forgotten to hand the bolts in and that his conduct was not deliberate. The Judge noted evidence supporting this: the bolts were openly visible on the dashboard as Mr Knight left the premises; Mr Knight took the van to a secure yard for the night and did not remove the bolts; the bolts were still on the dashboard when Mr Bates looked; Mr Knight later produced a co-worker’s statement that Mr Knight had said he intended to hand the bolts in when he put them on the dashboard; the scrap value of the bolts was said to be only about £1–£2; and Mr Knight had an unblemished employment record. Mr Knight obtained other employment at a similar rate of pay starting 7 November 2011.

Mr Knight’s contract contained a clause listing circumstances in which RBW said it could terminate employment without notice, including a provision referring to breach of the employer’s or customer’s security rules. The Employment Judge found Mr Knight was not guilty of theft, but was guilty of failing to comply with Babcock’s and RBW’s requirements by removing the bolts without written permission; however, this occurred because he forgot the bolts and was not deliberate. The Judge concluded this was not a fundamental breach entitling RBW to terminate without notice. On unfair dismissal, the Judge found RBW’s investigation and decision-making were reasonable in substance and dismissal was not outside the range of reasonable responses, but the procedure was unfair because Mr Knight was not given advance information and a proper opportunity to represent himself, and the appeal was also procedurally unfair because it was conducted by Mr Bates. The Judge assessed there was a 50% chance Mr Knight would have avoided dismissal with a fair process, and found Mr Knight contributed to his dismissal by one third, reducing the awards accordingly.
claims:
Mr Knight brought claims arising from his summary dismissal. First, he pursued a contractual claim for notice pay (wrongful dismissal), contending RBW was not entitled to terminate his employment without notice because his conduct did not amount to a fundamental breach of contract. His case, accepted by the Employment Judge, was that he did not steal the bolts and did not deliberately remove them for personal gain; he had intended to hand them in but forgot.

Second, he brought a claim for unfair dismissal, challenging the fairness of RBW’s decision to dismiss and, in particular, the fairness of the disciplinary process. On the facts found, his position included that he was not provided with the relevant allegations and supporting material in advance of the disciplinary hearing (because the suspension letter and enclosures were sent to the wrong address and arrived after the hearing), which deprived him of a proper opportunity to respond, and that the appeal was unfair because it was heard and decided by Mr Bates himself rather than independently.

Through these claims Mr Knight sought findings that he had been wrongfully dismissed (entitling him to notice pay) and unfairly dismissed (entitling him to statutory remedies), with any compensation assessed on the basis that he would have had a chance of avoiding dismissal had a fair procedure been followed.

facts:
Brook Partners Limited applied for regulatory approval for David Thomas to perform controlled functions (investment adviser and corporate finance adviser) for Brook Partners under a contract for services. The application was made on 30 June 2003 and received by the regulator on 3 July 2003. Thomas had worked in financial services for over 30 years. From 1996 he was an investment analyst and head of an investment trust corporate finance department at Brewin Dolphin Securities Limited in London. Brewin acted as a corporate broker and was active in the split capital investment trust sector between 1998 and 2001. While at Brewin, Thomas was approved to perform controlled functions as a consultant and worked on modelling, promotion and marketing of a number of split capital investment trusts and on restructuring others. He dealt with investment corporations and managers, not with the public or Brewin’s individual clients.

In February 2002 the regulator announced enquiries into aspects of the split capital investment trust market. In May 2002 it published a report stating it planned to investigate activities around marketing materials, alleged collusive behaviour within or between managers, and possible mis-selling by advisers. In October 2002 and January 2003 investigators were appointed to investigate activities of fund managers and other firms active in the sector between 1998 and 2001. In January 2003 Brewin stopped carrying out in London the type of investment trust work Thomas had been doing. Thomas agreed he would no longer carry on controlled functions for Brewin and instead took a part-time paid consultancy role from 16 January 2003 to help resolve issues relating to Brewin’s historic investment trust business; after that he no longer needed approval to perform controlled functions for Brewin.

As the investigations progressed, the regulator became concerned that practices connected with launching or restructuring split capital investment trusts might have involved misleading statements or practices, market abuse, or breaches of applicable standards and rules. In late June 2003 it appointed investigators to review additional firms and the conduct of specific individuals employed by firms under investigation. On 27 June 2003 investigators were appointed in respect of Thomas. Overall, investigators were appointed in respect of 21 firms (including Brewin) and 30 individuals (including Thomas). Thomas was included because, given his role at Brewin and involvement in the sector, the regulator considered he was knowledgeable of and/or involved with practices surrounding launches of new split trusts or restructuring of existing ones. The stated reasons for appointing investigators in relation to him were that there were circumstances suggesting he may have committed offences relating to misleading statements or practices, that market abuse may have taken place, and that he might not be a fit and proper person to perform functions in relation to regulated activities.

The regulator’s concerns about Thomas’s activities included whether a group of individuals agreed (expressly or impliedly) to support the sector by supporting restructuring of troubled funds; whether lack of transparency around such practices potentially produced a false and misleading impression of the performance of the sector and/or particular split trusts at a time when investment decisions were being made; and whether Thomas knew of and participated in these activities and through his actions contributed to a false and misleading impression.

Brook Partners’ intention was that Thomas would work on designing new investment trusts, converting old structures, and promoting investment trusts to institutional investors, with no intended contact with private or intermediate customers. The regulator issued a warning notice on 31 October 2003 indicating it was minded to refuse the application. Thomas made written representations. The regulator then issued a decision notice dated 10 January 2004 (also described as issued on 16 January 2004) refusing the application on the basis that it was not satisfied Thomas was fit and proper. In reaching that decision it took into account that Thomas was the subject of an investigation that might lead to disciplinary, criminal, or market-abuse proceedings. In July 2004 investigators interviewed Thomas. By the time of the preliminary hearing it was over a year since the application and Thomas had been unable to pursue his chosen career during that period; there was no evidence before the Tribunal about the progress of the investigations. The Tribunal determined preliminary issues including that the regulator had missed the three-month deadline for deciding the application or issuing a warning notice (the warning notice was issued on 31 October 2003 rather than by 3 October 2003), but that this delay did not invalidate the warning notice or decision notice, and that the mere appointment of investigators did not by itself require a conclusion that Thomas was not fit and proper.
claims:
Thomas referred the refusal decision to the Tribunal and sought determination of preliminary issues. He contended that the regulator breached the three-month time limit for deciding whether to grant the application or issue a warning notice, and argued that this breach should have legal consequences. He submitted that the time limit was mandatory and that, if the regulator did not decide to issue a warning notice within the period, the application should be treated as granted. He invited the Tribunal to conclude that the late warning notice and the subsequent decision notice were void and to determine that the appropriate action was to allow him to commence work as an approved person.

On the Tribunal’s powers, he argued that the Tribunal could direct the regulator to approve the application notwithstanding the regulator’s refusal, and suggested that if the regulator later considered public protection required it, it could take further steps after approval. He also suggested the Tribunal could direct an interim approval pending the outcome of the ongoing investigation, while acknowledging there was no express provision for interim approval.

In response to the regulator’s position that the existence of an investigation justified refusal, Thomas argued that the assumptions underlying that position were hypothetical and would need to be proved, and that the regulator was obliged to take a proper decision capable of being reviewed by the Tribunal rather than saying it had not yet made up its mind. He also argued that he was being treated differently from other individuals under investigation who remained in employment, because they could continue working while he could not take up the Brook Partners role without approval.

facts:
On 1 November 2006 the Financial Services Authority issued a First Supervisory Notice to Mr Virendra Rai Agarwala, a sole trader trading as Abbex Insurance. The Notice varied his permission by removing all regulated activities with immediate effect. Mr Agarwala was an insurance intermediary and was not permitted to hold client money or assets.

Mr Agarwala had a regulatory history predating his later general insurance business. On 6 September 1993, while practising as Abbex Insurance Brokers, he was erased from the Register of Practising Insurance Brokers by the Insurance Brokers Registration Council following disciplinary action.

In relation to investment business, he was monitored by the Personal Investment Authority (PIA). After a monitoring visit in December 1995, a report sent in March 1996 identified a number of rule breaches, including failures to keep sufficient, accurate and up-to-date records (including records of investment business, recruitment and training, complaints, and financial records). He was asked to carry out remedial action and provide monthly progress reports. On 15 November 1996 the PIA issued an intervention notice stating that it appeared he might not be fit and proper because he had not met the deadline for remedial action and progress reports, had failed to respond to letters, had failed to supply quarterly returns required for the pensions review, and had failed to pay administrative surcharges. The intervention notice prohibited him from conducting or soliciting investment business and from disposing of or dealing with his assets, with immediate effect. Disciplinary proceedings were initiated to revoke his authorisation. The PIA Disciplinary Committee decided to expel him; he initially referred the matter to the PIA Membership and Disciplinary Tribunal but withdrew his appeal, admitted the charges, and the proceedings were settled on the basis that he was expelled. On 30 July 1997 the PIA issued an order expelling him from membership, meaning he was no longer authorised to give investment advice. After that expulsion he practised as a general insurance broker, for which authorisation was not required until January 2005.

A complaint was made to the Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS) by a client about pension advice given in April 1989. On 30 September 2003 the FOS sent Mr Agarwala a reasoned preliminary view that the advice to opt out of a pension scheme in favour of personal pension arrangements was unsuitable and that he should establish whether the client suffered loss and, if so, pay redress, preferably by reinstating the client’s pension benefits by paying the current cost of restoring lost service. On 15 December 2004 the FOS issued a final decision upholding the complaint and ordering Mr Agarwala to carry out a loss assessment and, if loss was established, to pay to the trustees of the pension scheme the current amount needed to make good the shortfall for the period the client remained opted out due to his advice. On 5 January 2005 the FOS confirmed it had received the client’s acceptance, making the decision binding on Mr Agarwala.

On 12 July 2004 Mr Agarwala applied to the Authority for authorisation for general insurance business, submitting a High Street Firms application form and a controlled function/individual controller form. In the High Street Firms form he answered “No” to questions asking whether the firm had ever had revoked any licence/membership/authorisation/registration or other permission granted by a financial services regulator, and whether there were any other significant events that might adversely affect the application. In the controlled functions/individual controller form he answered “No” to questions asking whether he had ever been refused, restricted in, or had suspended the right to carry on a trade/business/profession requiring permission, and whether he had ever been refused/revoked/restricted/terminated permission by a regulator, been disciplined/suspended/expelled or subject to intervention action, or resigned while under investigation.

After receiving the July 2004 applications, the Authority discovered that Mr Agarwala had been erased from the insurance brokers register and was therefore aware of that non-disclosure, but did not consider it sufficiently material to prevent authorisation. On 14 January 2005 the Authority authorised him to carry on specified regulated activities limited to non-investment insurance contracts.

Mr Agarwala did not comply with the binding FOS final decision. On 22 December 2005 the FOS warned that failure to provide documentary evidence of steps being taken would be reported to the Authority. On 9 January 2006 Mr Agarwala wrote to the pension scheme seeking the reinstatement value for the missing years, but the matter did not proceed; the Tribunal understood the scheme asked for a fee for the information and Mr Agarwala was reluctant to pay it. On 5 June 2006 the Authority wrote requiring compliance by 20 June 2006, failing which the matter would be referred for enforcement action. On 17 July 2006 the Authority wrote stating that by failing properly to comply with the FOS decision he was in breach of obligations to treat the customer fairly and to conduct business with integrity, and that a recommendation would be made that his permission be cancelled.

On 27 July 2006 Mr Agarwala’s advisers told the Authority that the firm that gave the pension advice was not the same as his current firm, and that the earlier firm had been regulated by the PIA and de-authorised in 1994. This was the first time the Authority had been informed of the previous PIA authorisation. The Authority then made enquiries and discovered the 1996 intervention notice and the 1997 expulsion.

On 1 November 2006 the Authority issued the Supervisory Notice removing all regulated activities with immediate effect and requiring Mr Agarwala within 14 days to notify all clients for regulated activities that he was no longer permitted to carry on regulated activities, and to provide the Authority with a copy of the notification and a list of clients to whom it had been sent. By the date of the Tribunal hearing on 20 December 2006, this had not been done.

At the hearing the Tribunal heard oral evidence from Mr Agarwala. The Tribunal accepted his evidence that he had been in insurance for thirty-five years and that in earlier years a colleague (later an employee) undertook independent financial adviser work including pensions advice, and that employee left in or about the early 1990s.

The Tribunal concluded it was not satisfied that suspending the Notice would not prejudice consumers’ interests. It noted that incorrect replies had been given on the application forms, that the Applicant had always been a sole trader trading as Abbex Insurance, and that he accepted the FOS final decision was his personal liability. The Tribunal also noted that the FOS final decision had not been complied with. The Tribunal was satisfied it was necessary for the Notice to take effect immediately and that removing all permissions immediately was proportionate. The application to suspend the Notice was dismissed, and a timetable was set for a speedy substantive hearing fixed for 5 February 2007.
claims:
Mr Agarwala referred the Supervisory Notice to the Tribunal and applied for a direction suspending the effect of the Notice until the reference was finally disposed of, so that the removal of all regulated activities would not take effect pending the substantive determination.

In support of suspension, he argued (through his representative) that although there had been problems in the past, they arose when he acted as an independent financial adviser and occurred before his expulsion from the PIA in July 1997, and that the expulsion did not involve dishonesty. He accepted that his answers on the Authority’s application forms contained errors, but contended they were not intended to mislead. He said he regarded his independent financial adviser business (to 1997) and his general insurance broker business (1997 to 2005) as two separate businesses and believed he only needed to disclose matters relating to the general insurance business. He asserted there had been no complaints relating to his general insurance business and that there was no real immediate risk to consumers if the Notice were suspended.

He further argued that the FOS decision was not given to his current business and related to advice given in 1989 when his firm was acting as an independent financial adviser and was authorised by the PIA. While accepting the FOS final decision was binding on him personally, he contended he was finding it difficult to comply because he lacked the necessary technical competence and did not have the financial resources. He suggested the client should have been referred to the compensation scheme.

He also argued that the procedure adopted by the Authority did not comply with the right to a fair hearing because he had been given no opportunity to make representations to an independent tribunal before the Notice took effect. He contended that if the Notice were not suspended he could not carry on his business and would have no resources to meet the FOS award.

facts:
The appellant was a married woman in her twenties registered as a childminder from 8 July 2008. Her registration included conditions limiting the number and ages of children she could care for, and allowed overnight care for one child under eight. At registration she lived with her husband and baby daughter. She did not begin childminding immediately for personal reasons, but after moving house in April 2009 she started childminding.

On 20 August 2009 a parent complained to the respondent after the appellant had provided three nights of overnight care for the parent’s two children aged five and two. The parent alleged that during the period of care the appellant repeatedly telephoned demanding full payment and threatened to report the parent to social services because the parent had forgotten to leave an asthma inhaler. The parent said the appellant’s husband was abusive during these calls. The parent also said that when she arrived at about 10am to collect the children she was kept waiting for five minutes, heard one child distressed in a downstairs room, and found the children not properly dressed and their belongings not packed. The parent further reported that the older child later said the appellant had hit the children on the face, told them she hated them, and had thrown them from a sofa to the floor. The parent also said the older child reported sleeping in a cot rather than a bed despite the parent’s request for a bed.

That day the respondent referred the matter to social services. A strategy meeting took place on 21 August 2009 attended by social services, police and a representative of the respondent. It was confirmed at that meeting that social services had information indicating the complaint should be treated with caution. However, it was also noted that the appellant was known to social services and the police due to significant domestic violence by her husband against her.
