Her husband had received a police caution for criminal damage in January 2009 when it was believed he broke down the front door, and social services had records of other domestic violence incidents. Police and social services were also aware that the husband was a cannabis user. It was agreed the police would investigate the complaint, and both police and social services supported suspension of the appellant’s registration while investigations were carried out.

Later on 21 August 2009 the respondent conducted an internal case review and decided to suspend the appellant’s registration for six weeks until 2 October 2009. The reasons given included: domestic violence at the property in January 2009 and more generally with the husband still living at the address; the husband’s cannabis use; the specific concerns raised by the parent; the appellant’s failure to notify the respondent of her husband’s police caution; and that the appellant had provided overnight care to two children between 16 and 19 August 2009 in breach of her registration condition permitting overnight care for only one child.

The appellant appealed on 22 August 2009. At the tribunal hearing, the respondent’s witness explained that although social services and police were not taking further action on the original complaint, the respondent intended to continue its own investigation. The respondent planned to speak to the complainant parent and to the appellant and her husband, and was awaiting minutes and confirmatory paperwork from social services and police about the domestic violence and cannabis-related incidents. The respondent had considered alternatives to suspension. The appellant offered not to provide overnight care and to care for children only when her husband was not on the premises, but the respondent considered this insufficient because the husband lived at the premises.

The husband gave evidence acknowledging past cannabis use and incidents of domestic violence. He described financial and personal stress, said he was ashamed of his behaviour, and stated that after the January 2009 incident he sought help from his GP and began drug counselling in July 2009, due to finish at the end of September 2009. He said he had stopped using cannabis but relapsed in July 2009. He said the family’s move in April 2009 was a fresh start and their relationship had improved. He denied that he or the appellant had threatened the complainant parent and said they were concerned about the missing asthma inhaler.

The appellant confirmed her appeal letter and gave detailed evidence about domestic violence incidents, disclosing more incidents than she had previously declared. She said she sought legal advice after the January 2009 incident and considered leaving her husband, and that the last incident was in February 2009. She said things improved after the move. She denied making threats to the complainant parent and denied smacking or ill-treating the children; she denied that the older child slept in a cot and said instead that the older child had hit her own young daughter.

The tribunal accepted that both sides gave honest evidence. A majority concluded that continuing the suspension was proportionate given the seriousness of the allegations, the relatively recent domestic violence (as recently as February 2009), the husband’s incomplete counselling, and the need for the respondent to complete further investigations into the complaint and to verify domestic violence and cannabis-related information with police and social services records. The appeal was dismissed and the suspension upheld, with the tribunal expressing the view that the investigation should be completed within the six-week period if possible. There was a dissenting view that the complaint appeared dubious, that police and social services were taking no further action, that the husband had addressed cannabis use, and that continuing suspension was disproportionate.
claims:
The appellant sought to overturn the respondent’s decision of 21 August 2009 suspending her childminder registration for six weeks.

In her written appeal and oral evidence, she denied the substance of the parent’s complaint, including denying that she or her husband threatened the parent, denying that she hit or ill-treated the children, and disputing the allegation that the older child slept in a cot. She maintained that the incident had been misrepresented and gave her account of events, including that her concern related to the parent leaving an asthmatic child without an inhaler.

She argued that domestic problems had been resolved and described steps and changes since early 2009, including the family moving house and an improvement in the relationship. She relied on the efforts she said she had made to provide a good and safe childminding service.

She also raised the adverse impact of the suspension on parents who planned to use her childminding service.

As an alternative to suspension, she offered to stop providing overnight care and to care for children only when her husband was not on the premises, presenting this as a way to address any concerns while allowing her to continue childminding.

facts:
Mr Slavomir Kutcha was a director and employee of R A Cowen & Partners Ltd (the Company). Over several years while Mr Kutcha’s sons, David Kutcha and Stefan Kutcha, attended university, the Company made payments to them. HMRC treated those payments as scholarships and assessed them for the tax years 2002–03 to 2005–06 as taxable on Mr Kutcha as a benefit provided by reason of his employment. As a consequence, HMRC also assessed the Company to Class 1A national insurance contributions in respect of those benefits.

At the hearing, the appellants’ representative initially contended that no scholarships had been paid and that HMRC had simply assumed scholarships existed; he said the sons’ amounts had been treated as salary, reported on their self-assessment returns and on P60s, with PAYE and national insurance dealt with in the normal way. However, a schedule produced by the appellants showed certain years marked “S” for each son, with annotations aligning with academic terms, and the amounts paid (for example, £6,999.96 in 2003–04) appeared set just below a stated ceiling for scholarship-type payments. The P60 figures for the relevant years showed no or minimal PAYE deducted. After taking instructions during the hearing, the appellants accepted that the payments to David and Stefan were structured to obtain the tax exemption available for scholarship income.

The appellants relied on written statements from two Company executives (Mr Williams and Mr Chaplin), who did not attend the hearing, stating that the payments were made to secure the future success of the business and to “lock” the sons into the Company. HMRC argued that Mr Kutcha had taken the opportunity to fund his sons’ education through the Company in a tax-efficient way, and also contended that neither son was a genuine employee during the periods at university, asserting their employment ceased when they left for university and restarted after graduation.

The Tribunal found that the sons’ employment contracts were valid and that their employments continued throughout the period they received the payments. The Tribunal also found that the Company’s payroll and PAYE treatment was consistent with an intention that the payments were scholarships expected to qualify for exemption: payments during the university courses were made without tax deductions, tax was deducted once the course finished (and in Stefan’s case before he started), and the amounts appeared tuned to remain within the relevant financial limits.

The Tribunal concluded that, notwithstanding the scholarship exemption for the recipients, the benefit-in-kind charge applied to Mr Kutcha in respect of scholarship payments made by the Company to members of his family. The Tribunal rejected the appellants’ arguments seeking to avoid that result and dismissed Mr Kutcha’s appeal against the income tax assessments and the Company’s appeal against the national insurance assessments. The Tribunal noted that it had not heard argument on the detailed figures and left the parties to agree them or return to the Tribunal if they could not.
claims:
Mr Kutcha and the Company appealed against HMRC’s assessments. Mr Kutcha sought to overturn income tax assessments that treated the Company’s payments to his sons during their university attendance as a taxable benefit on him. The Company sought to overturn the associated Class 1A national insurance contribution assessments.

The appellants’ arguments, as presented, were:

1) Initially, that there were no scholarships paid to David and Stefan and that HMRC had wrongly “latched onto” the description following a meeting; the payments were said to have been ordinary salary properly reported through payroll (P60s) and on the sons’ self-assessment returns, with PAYE and national insurance accounted for.

2) After accepting the payments were structured to obtain the scholarship exemption, the appellants argued that HMRC was wrong to assess the amounts as a benefit-in-kind on Mr Kutcha because the payments were not made by virtue of Mr Kutcha’s employment. They contended the payments were made for commercial reasons connected with the sons’ roles and the Company’s business interests—namely to secure the future of the business and retain the sons—rather than because of Mr Kutcha’s employment.

3) The appellants also argued that where the scholarship recipients were themselves employees, the benefit-in-kind charge should not fall on Mr Kutcha, and they relied on the proposition that the relevant provisions should be read so that the charge did not arise on him in these circumstances.

4) They further argued that the “normal course” concept supported their position because, on their case, the payments arose from normal commercial arrangements rather than personal or family relationships.

The relief sought was the cancellation (or reduction) of the disputed income tax assessments on Mr Kutcha and the cancellation (or reduction) of the related national insurance assessments on the Company for the years in question.

facts:
Stephen West appealed against HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) and, by a tribunal casting vote, his appeal was allowed in a decision released on 3 August 2016. The decision notice stated that any application for permission to appeal had to be received within 56 days, so the deadline expired on 28 September 2016.

On 28 September 2016 at 16:28 (towards the end of the final day), HMRC emailed HM Courts & Tribunals Service (HMCTS) applying for a 14-day extension of time, to 12 October 2016, to apply for permission to appeal to the Upper Tribunal. HMRC’s extension request was not immediately communicated to the judge. HMCTS copied HMRC’s extension request to Mr West or his adviser to allow comment, but no comments were provided.

On 5 October 2016 HMRC lodged its application for permission to appeal, including the application form and a separate document setting out its grounds of appeal. That permission-to-appeal application was not copied to Mr West or his adviser under the usual procedure. HMCTS forwarded HMRC’s extension request and the permission-to-appeal application to the judge on 25 October 2016.

The judge considered only whether to extend time, not the merits of HMRC’s proposed appeal. The judge noted that HMRC’s stated reasons for needing more time were that the issues were complicated and potentially wide-ranging, HMRC needed input from multiple operational and policy stakeholders, and the decision was released during the summer holiday period when relevant stakeholders were on leave. The judge considered that HMRC, as a large and well-resourced organisation, should be able to deal promptly with tribunal decisions at any time of year and that HMRC’s explanation did not amount to adequate reasons for the delay.

The delay in lodging the permission-to-appeal application was seven days beyond the normal deadline (it was lodged on 5 October 2016). The judge considered the likely consequences for both parties. Mr West could not properly assume the matter was final until after the appeal period expired, and the judge considered that granting the extension would not materially affect Mr West’s position. If the extension were refused, HMRC would be unable to pursue an appeal and would have no prospect of seeking to recover the PAYE income tax it contended Mr West was personally liable for.

The judge observed that HMRC’s email suggested it wished to treat Mr West’s case as a form of test case, and that this appeared to differ from the way HMRC had conducted the appeal hearing, where both tribunal members had formed the impression that HMRC did not pursue its arguments with much vigour. The judge also considered evidence given by Mr West at the appeal hearing that he was on benefits, and the risk that refusing an extension might lead to further proceedings about the refusal, potentially putting Mr West to additional expense or leaving him unable to participate.

Taking all circumstances together, and particularly the view that Mr West should not be unduly disadvantaged by allowing HMRC to pursue its permission-to-appeal application, the judge granted HMRC an extension of time to lodge the permission-to-appeal application and stated that the permission-to-appeal application would be considered separately.
claims:
HMRC sought procedural relief: an extension of time to apply for permission to appeal the tribunal’s 3 August 2016 decision to the Upper Tribunal. In its email of 28 September 2016, HMRC requested a 14-day extension (to 12 October 2016), explaining that it needed additional time because the issues were very complicated and had broad impact, requiring consultation across multiple HMRC operational and policy areas; the tribunal decision had been split with a dissenting opinion highlighting wider impact and policy considerations; and the decision was released during the summer holiday period when relevant stakeholders were on leave, delaying HMRC’s ability to reach a full policy decision on whether and how to appeal. HMRC also indicated it had instructed counsel to consider grounds for an application for permission to appeal and argued it would be unfair and contrary to justice for HMRC not to be able to apply for permission in these circumstances.

In substance, HMRC’s position was that it should be allowed extra time so it could properly decide and formulate an application for permission to appeal, and thereby pursue an appeal aimed at overturning the decision that had allowed Mr West’s appeal and at enabling HMRC to pursue recovery of PAYE income tax which it contended Mr West should be personally liable to pay.

facts:
Eileen Mary Garland was a married woman employed by British Rail Engineering Limited (BREL). BREL was wholly owned by the British Railways Board, a public authority responsible for providing railway services in Great Britain.

During employment, BREL employees of either sex received valuable concessionary travel facilities, allowing free or reduced-rate travel on British Rail and certain foreign railways. These facilities were extended not only to the employee but also to the employee’s spouse and dependent children.

After retirement, BREL treated former employees differently depending on sex. Former male employees continued to receive (on a reduced scale) travel facilities for themselves, their wives, and dependent children. Former female employees received (on a similarly reduced scale) travel facilities for themselves, but no such facilities were granted for their husbands or dependent children.

The post-retirement travel facilities were not enjoyed as a contractual right. However, employees had a legitimate expectation that they would continue after retirement, and it would be difficult in practice for BREL to withdraw them unilaterally without agreement from the relevant trade unions.

On 25 November 1976 Mrs Garland complained to an industrial tribunal that BREL was discriminating against her. The industrial tribunal held that the post-retirement concessionary travel facilities fell within an exception for “provision in relation to retirement,” so the prohibition on discrimination did not apply. The Employment Appeal Tribunal disagreed, taking the view that the exception should not be construed so widely as to include a privilege that existed during employment and was allowed to continue after retirement. The Court of Appeal restored the industrial tribunal’s decision, treating the exception as wide enough to include any provision about retirement.

The case ultimately reached the House of Lords. The House of Lords referred questions to the European Court of Justice about whether the discriminatory post-retirement travel facilities were contrary to the principle of equal pay and whether that principle applied directly. The European Court of Justice ruled that providing special travel facilities after retirement to former male employees, where former female employees did not receive the same facilities, constituted discrimination, and that the relevant principle applied directly where a national court could establish discrimination using the criteria of equal work and equal pay.

In light of those answers, BREL conceded that the Employment Appeal Tribunal’s construction was correct. The House of Lords reversed the Court of Appeal’s order, restored the Employment Appeal Tribunal’s order, awarded Mrs Garland her costs in the courts below and on the appeal, and remitted the case back to the Employment Appeal Tribunal to proceed consistently with the judgment.
claims:
Mrs Garland’s complaint was that BREL discriminated against her on grounds of sex in relation to concessionary travel facilities after retirement. In substance, she challenged the practice under which retired male employees continued to receive reduced travel facilities not only for themselves but also for their wives and dependent children, whereas retired female employees received reduced travel facilities only for themselves and did not receive corresponding facilities for their husbands or dependent children.

In her appeal to the House of Lords, she sought review of the Court of Appeal’s order and asked that it be reversed, varied, or altered, or that she be granted other appropriate relief. Her position, as ultimately accepted, was that the statutory exception for “provision in relation to retirement” should not be interpreted so broadly as to exclude her complaint where the benefit was a travel privilege that existed during employment and was allowed to continue after retirement.

As part of the proceedings before the House of Lords, questions were raised (and referred for a ruling) as to whether the discriminatory provision of post-retirement travel facilities was incompatible with the principle of equal pay and whether that principle conferred enforceable rights in these circumstances. The outcome sought by Mrs Garland was that the discriminatory practice be treated as unlawful and that the earlier decision rejecting her complaint be overturned.

facts: The complainant made a request to Wolverhampton City Council for a copy of an internal audit report concerning a property owned by the Council, the Tettenhall Institute. The Council refused to provide the report, relying on an exemption and stating that the public interest favoured keeping the report withheld. The Information Commissioner reviewed the Council’s position and concluded that the Council’s arguments were not sufficient to show that the exemption had been correctly applied. The Commissioner therefore required the Council to disclose a copy of the internal audit report. The Commissioner also found that the Council had failed to comply with its duties in relation to responding to the request and issuing an adequate refusal response.
claims: The complainant’s position was that the Council should provide a copy of the internal audit report relating to the Tettenhall Institute. By complaining to the Information Commissioner, the complainant sought a decision requiring disclosure of the report after the Council refused the request on public interest grounds.

facts: The complainant made a request to Spelthorne Borough Council for information about the proposed development of Kempton Park. The Council provided some information in response but withheld parts of three documents by redacting them. The Council relied on exceptions under the environmental information regime to justify the redactions. The Information Commissioner reviewed the matter and accepted that the redacted information was exempt from disclosure on the basis of two of the exceptions relied upon by the Council, and found that the public interest favoured maintaining those exceptions. The Commissioner also found that the Council failed to respond to the request within the required time limit.
claims: The complainant sought disclosure of information held by the Council concerning the proposed development of Kempton Park, including the information contained in the parts of three documents that the Council had redacted. By bringing the complaint to the Information Commissioner, the complainant challenged the Council’s decision to withhold that information and, in effect, requested that the redacted information be disclosed.

facts: The complainant made a request to North East Lincolnshire Council for information about actions the Council had undertaken in response to a specific complaint reference. The Council initially refused to comply with the request, stating that disclosure would involve exempt information. During the Commissioner’s investigation, the Council clarified that it had cited the wrong exemptions in its original response and that its position was instead that it should neither confirm nor deny whether it held any information falling within the scope of the request. The Commissioner concluded that the Council was entitled to refuse to confirm or deny whether it held relevant information and required the Council to take no further steps.
claims: The complainant sought disclosure of information about what actions the Council had taken in response to a particular complaint reference. By bringing the matter to the Commissioner, the complainant effectively challenged the Council’s refusal to provide the requested information and sought a decision requiring the Council to comply with the request (or otherwise address the refusal).

facts:
The case concerned Wolverhampton City Council’s proposed use of compulsory purchase powers to enable redevelopment of a semi-derelict site at Raglan Street, just outside the Wolverhampton Ring Road. Sainsbury’s owned or controlled about 86% of the Raglan Street site and Tesco controlled most of the remainder. Both companies wanted to develop the site and each promoted a redevelopment scheme. Outline planning permission was granted for Tesco’s Raglan Street proposal, and the Council had resolved to grant outline planning permission for Sainsbury’s proposal. Both schemes were regarded as acceptable in planning terms and both were said to bring economic, social and environmental benefits.

Separately, Tesco controlled another large city-centre site known as the Royal Hospital site, about 850 metres away. The Royal Hospital site contained listed buildings in poor condition. The Council had for years sought regeneration of that site. Tesco’s position was that developing the Royal Hospital site in accordance with the Council’s aspirations (including refurbishment of listed buildings and provision for a Primary Care Trust facility) was not financially viable and would involve a substantial loss. Tesco proposed that it would undertake the Royal Hospital site redevelopment if it were able to develop Raglan Street, describing this as a cross-subsidy from the Raglan Street development. The Council accepted that, on its preferred requirements, the Royal Hospital site was unlikely to attract development for the foreseeable future unless Tesco’s proposals were brought forward with such a cross-subsidy.

Historically, Sainsbury’s had obtained outline planning permission in 2002 for a mixed-use redevelopment of Raglan Street. In early 2005 Sainsbury’s told the Council it no longer intended to develop Raglan Street because it had agreed to sell its interests to Tesco; sale documentation was prepared and Tesco also acquired other third-party interests. In June 2005 the Council considered Tesco’s proposed scheme and contemplated linking permission to obligations relating to the Royal Hospital site, and approved in principle the use of compulsory purchase powers if needed to assemble the site (then thought to be only for minor interests). In November 2005 Tesco entered into a conditional agreement with the Council concerning the Council’s interest in Raglan Street and the Council’s use of compulsory purchase powers if necessary to acquire outstanding interests; the agreement also required Tesco to carry out demolition and repairs at the Royal Hospital site before commencing works at Raglan Street. Later, Sainsbury’s changed position again, decided it wished to redevelop Raglan Street itself, and submitted a fresh planning application.

Tesco submitted planning applications for both the Royal Hospital site (April 2006) and Raglan Street (July 2006). Sainsbury’s submitted its own Raglan Street application in October 2006. Both Raglan Street applications proposed a supermarket with parking and a petrol filling station, flats, sheltered housing and small commercial units; Tesco’s supermarket was more than 50% larger, while Sainsbury’s scheme included retail warehouses and a leisure centre. The Council’s Planning Committee resolved in March 2007 to grant both applications subject to requirements. In the officer report on Tesco’s Raglan Street application, it was recorded that Tesco had initially wanted to link Raglan Street permission to Royal Hospital redevelopment, but no legitimate linkage was identified and the Raglan Street application was considered without reference to Royal Hospital benefits.

Because Sainsbury’s and Tesco could not agree how the Raglan Street site should be developed, the Council considered using compulsory purchase powers to resolve the impasse. In June 2007 the Council invited both companies to demonstrate how their proposals met the Council’s objectives and encouraged negotiation. In January 2008 a report to the Council’s Cabinet concluded that both Raglan Street schemes met the basic statutory purpose and would promote well-being, but recommended Tesco’s scheme because it would enable the Royal Hospital site redevelopment to be brought forward consistently with the Council’s objectives, through the proposed cross-subsidy. The Cabinet approved in principle making a compulsory purchase order over Sainsbury’s land at Raglan Street to facilitate Tesco’s Raglan Street development and also the Royal Hospital site mixed-use redevelopment, subject to conditions including evidence of Tesco’s commitment to the Royal Hospital works. The decision was noted by the Council’s Scrutiny Board.

Sainsbury’s brought judicial review proceedings challenging the Council’s decision-making. The High Court dismissed the claim and the Court of Appeal dismissed Sainsbury’s appeal. Sainsbury’s then appealed to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court majority allowed Sainsbury’s appeal and declared that the opportunity for redevelopment of the Royal Hospital site was not a lawful consideration in deciding whether to make a compulsory purchase order in relation to the Raglan Street site.
claims:
Sainsbury’s challenged, by judicial review, the Council’s resolution approving in principle the making of a compulsory purchase order over Sainsbury’s land at Raglan Street to facilitate Tesco’s development. Sainsbury’s position was that it was illegitimate for the Council, when deciding to make a compulsory purchase order affecting Sainsbury’s land, to take into account Tesco’s commitment to redevelop the separate Royal Hospital site and the benefits said to flow from that redevelopment.

In particular, Sainsbury’s argued that the Council could not lawfully treat the Royal Hospital site redevelopment (and the claimed cross-subsidy arrangement linking it to Tesco’s Raglan Street scheme) as a relevant benefit when deciding whether to exercise compulsory purchase powers in relation to Raglan Street. Sainsbury’s contended that any well-being benefits relied upon to justify compulsory purchase had to flow from the redevelopment of the land being compulsorily acquired (the Raglan Street site), and that benefits arising from redevelopment of an unconnected site could not be used to justify taking Sainsbury’s land.

Sainsbury’s also relied on the idea that only off-site benefits that fairly and reasonably related to the development for which the compulsory purchase power was being exercised could be taken into account, and that a cross-subsidy was relevant only where there was a composite development rather than two unconnected sites. Sainsbury’s sought relief quashing or invalidating the Council’s decision and, ultimately, a declaration that the Royal Hospital site redevelopment opportunity was not a lawful consideration in deciding whether to make a compulsory purchase order for Raglan Street.

facts:
On 11 May 2004 a serious explosion occurred at premises operated by ICL at Grovepark Mills, Maryhill, Glasgow. The explosion caused substantial collapse of the factory building, killed nine people, and injured many others. It also caused extensive damage to neighbouring properties, including a shop owned by David T Morrison & Co Ltd trading as Gael Home Interiors (“Morrison”).

After the explosion, the police sealed off the surrounding area, including Morrison’s shop. Morrison was not allowed access to its premises until June 2004. When access was obtained, Morrison had to deal with damaged stock and the risk of asbestos contamination. ICL’s premises remained under the control of the Crown Office for a period; ICL sought access to investigate the cause of and responsibility for the explosion, and the Crown Office released ICL’s premises from its control on 12 July 2004.

Morrison maintained that there was continuing uncertainty and speculation about the cause of the explosion for some time after the event, and that it could not have obtained a reliable expert report on the cause until after mid-August 2004 at the earliest. In February 2006 the Crown Office announced an intention to bring criminal proceedings against two ICL companies. On 17 August 2007 those companies pleaded guilty to breaches of health and safety legislation. A public inquiry was announced in October 2007 and reported in July 2009, describing the explosion as an avoidable tragedy resulting from a number of failures by ICL companies.

On 13 August 2009 Morrison raised proceedings seeking reparation for damage to its property and for lost profits and other costs. ICL accepted that, apart from a time-bar point, it would be liable to make reparation to Morrison (quantum not agreed). ICL defended the proceedings on the basis that any obligation to make reparation had been extinguished by the passage of time before the action was raised.

In the courts below, the Lord Ordinary upheld ICL’s time-bar defence, reasoning that Morrison had sufficient knowledge from the date of the explosion and that an inference of negligence could be drawn from the circumstances. The Inner House reversed that decision and allowed a proof before answer on the time-bar issue, rejecting the view that the circumstances necessarily supported the inference relied on by ICL. ICL appealed to the Supreme Court, which addressed the correct approach to when time begins to run for such claims and allowed ICL’s appeal.
claims:
Morrison sought damages (reparation) from ICL for the damage to its shop and for consequential losses including lost profits and other costs. Morrison’s case was that the explosion-related damage to its property was caused by ICL’s wrongdoing, advanced on the bases of negligence, nuisance, and breach of statutory duty.

In response to ICL’s defence that the claim was brought too late, Morrison argued that the relevant five-year period had not started running on the date of the explosion because, although it knew immediately that damage had occurred, it was not aware—and could not with reasonable diligence have been aware—until a later date that the damage was attributable to ICL’s wrongdoing. Morrison contended that it could not have obtained a reliable expert report identifying the cause of the explosion until after mid-August 2004 at the earliest, and relied on the later criminal proceedings and the public inquiry report as part of the background showing that the cause and responsibility were not established immediately.

Morrison therefore maintained that its proceedings, raised on 13 August 2009, were in time because the start of the five-year period should be postponed to a date later than 11 May 2004, when it first became (or could with reasonable diligence have become) aware of the relevant causal connection between its loss and ICL’s alleged wrongdoing.
uk_statute_references_predicted: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974

facts:
Captain Ian Hugh Shepherd was a British citizen employed by British Airways as a long‑haul airline pilot. His flights all started or finished in the United Kingdom, usually at Gatwick or Heathrow, and his work pattern meant he was away from home for much of the year on trips averaging five to seven days for a return journey.

He married in 1968 and had a son (born 1972). Around 1987 he and his wife bought a house in Wokingham in their joint names with a mortgage, and it became the family home. In 1996 he had a relationship with an air stewardess which ended in August 1998. After that, he and his wife agreed to live separate lives while remaining in the same house; they did not divorce. When he was at Wokingham, his wife cooked his meals. In January 1998 he named his wife as the first person British Airways should contact in an emergency.

Before October 1998, when in the UK he stayed at the Wokingham house (convenient for Heathrow and Gatwick) and pursued hobbies including sailing, hang gliding, motorcycling, and amateur radio; he had a large radio mast at the Wokingham house.

Knowing he would have to retire on 22 April 2000 at age 55, he began planning for retirement overseas. In 1997 he contacted the UK tax authority for guidance on retiring abroad and received general guidance material. He understood that Cyprus was among countries where his pension could be paid without UK tax deduction, with tax instead payable in the country of retirement. On 5 May 1998 he applied to the Cypriot authorities for permanent residency and an immigration permit. On 17 September 1998 he wrote that he was considering moving abroad to minimise tax, had applied for Cyprus residency, and might move to Switzerland or Ireland in the meantime.

He visited Cyprus from 14 to 20 October 1998, stayed in a hotel, rented a car, and looked for accommodation near the airport. He chose a furnished penthouse flat in Larnaca (41, Eviathi Apartment), partly because he could access the roof for radio antennae. On 19 October 1998 he signed a one‑year tenancy agreement at a modest monthly rent and paid local taxes and utility bills. The tenancy was renewed from 1 February 1999 to expire on 24 April 2000. He said he rented initially to see if he liked living there and because renting was easier while working full time.

After taking the flat, he joined clubs in Cyprus (including a yacht club and a gliding club) but retained memberships of UK associations. He reduced the radio mast at Wokingham and moved radio equipment to Cyprus; all outgoing radio transmissions from October 1998 to April 2000 were made from Cyprus, with thousands of contacts recorded. He also had a woman friend in Cyprus whom he visited.

After October 1998, his time continued to be dominated by work travel. His remaining time was split between the UK, Cyprus, sporting activities, and holidays in Europe. He and his wife travelled together to Switzerland from 31 July to 9 August 1999 to visit her parents. In May 2000 his wife visited Cyprus for four days and he showed her the flat; later she and their son used the flat for holidays when he was elsewhere.

Financially, his salary was the household’s sole income. He maintained a joint UK bank account with his wife and a UK savings account in his own name. His salary continued to be paid into the joint UK account, from which mortgage payments and household outgoings for the Wokingham house were paid. For many years (including after October 1998) £500 per month was paid by standing order into his wife’s separate account for housekeeping, and she regularly wrote cheques on the joint account for personal spending and house outgoings. Both had access to credit cards linked to the UK accounts. These arrangements did not change in October 1998 and continued until April 2000. He opened a Cyprus bank account before the end of November 1998, but his salary still went to the UK joint account. The mortgage was fully paid when he retired in April 2000. The Wokingham house was not sold and his wife and son continued to live there.

He remained on the UK electoral roll until 2000. Correspondence (including flight rosters, tax correspondence, and bank/credit card statements) continued to be sent to the Wokingham address, and he asked that correspondence continue to go there. He did not inform his UK bank that he had moved to Cyprus.

British Airways wrote to him at the Wokingham address on 19 January 2000 confirming compulsory retirement on 22 April 2000 and asking for any change of address after termination; he acknowledged receipt on 2 April 2000 but did not provide a new address. Although he retired on 22 April 2000, his last working day was 6 April 2000. In April 2000 he visited Holland to buy a car for his wife.

On 7 February 2000 Cyprus granted him an immigration permit, conditional on acquiring permanent residence within one year. His first pension payment (31 May 2000) was paid into his Cyprus bank account. After retirement he stopped the £500 standing order but continued to support his wife, transferring from Cyprus an amount equal to half his pension each month.

From June 2000 he undertook a round‑the‑world sailing cruise until October 2002, visiting the UK once or twice a year to see family.

In January 1999 he wrote from Cyprus stating he was resident there, had decided to move before retirement and commute to Heathrow, expected to spend fewer than 90 days a year in the UK before retirement and little time after, and intended to claim non‑resident status. In September 1999 he filed a UK tax return for the year ended 5 April 1999 stating he was married.

Cyprus accountants wrote in February 2000 that they had been appointed to prepare Cyprus tax assessments for his claimed Cyprus residency from October 1998 to 31 December 1999 and would handle his Cyprus tax affairs from April 2000; they said there was no Cyprus tax liability until retirement.

In 2002 the UK tax authority made enquiries. Cyprus accountants stated that he opened a file with Cyprus tax authorities on 22 April 2000 when he began receiving his pension; although he had been resident in Cyprus since 1998, Cyprus did not accept tax assessments for October 1998 to 31 December 1999 because his employment income for services rendered outside Cyprus was exempt if not payable in Cyprus. Cyprus authorities also indicated he had lived in Cyprus only 68 days in the period October 1998 to 31 December 1999 and accepted his claim for Cyprus tax treatment from 2000 because he stayed in Cyprus for a very limited period in 1998 and 1999.

For the UK tax years in issue, the tribunal found (on the balance of probabilities) that in 1999/2000 he spent 180 days flying on duty (counting arrival/departure days), 80 days in the UK (excluding arrival/departure days), 77 days in Cyprus (including arrival/departure days), 8 days sailing, and 20 days visiting Europe. The tribunal also found that, although he sometimes stayed with his parents in London, on most occasions when in the UK he stayed at the Wokingham house. It further found that he and his wife remained good friends, evidenced by continued financial support and shared activities.

The determination under appeal concluded he was ordinarily resident in the UK for 1998/1999 and 1999/2000; it was agreed he was resident and ordinarily resident in the UK until October 1998, so the dispute effectively concerned 1999/2000. The tribunal ultimately concluded he remained resident and ordinarily resident in the UK at least until 5 April 2000 and dismissed the appeal.
claims:
The appellant appealed against the tax authority’s determination that he was ordinarily resident in the United Kingdom for the years 1998/1999 and 1999/2000. At the hearing he accepted that he was resident and ordinarily resident in the UK until October 1998 (so that 1998/1999 was not in dispute), and the dispute focused on whether he was resident and ordinarily resident in the UK in 1999/2000.

He contended that in October 1998 he became resident in Cyprus and, for 1999/2000, he was not resident and ordinarily resident in the UK and was not resident in the UK for employment income purposes. He argued that in October 1998 he deliberately set up a separate home in Cyprus and that after that date there was a material change in the character and quality of his presence in the UK: he ceased to be resident and became a visitor, coming to Wokingham only when necessary for work.

He maintained that by acquiring and leasing the Cyprus flat he adopted Cyprus as part of the regular order of his life and lived there with sufficient continuity; Cyprus was said to be his base even though he continued to visit the UK. He also argued that his continued presence in Cyprus years later supported his intention in 1998.

He further argued that after October 1998 his presence in the UK was for temporary purposes only and not with the intention of establishing residence, and therefore his UK residence should be assessed without taking into account any living accommodation available to him in the UK.

In practical terms, he sought a decision that he was not resident and not ordinarily resident in the UK for 1999/2000, so that the determination treating him as ordinarily resident (and resident) in the UK for that year should be set aside.

facts:
The appellant was a mother who was the parent with care of a child and was awarded family credit. After the award, she was told that she had to cooperate with the Child Support Agency and was sent standard forms requiring her to provide information/authorisation so that action could be taken to pursue child maintenance from the child’s father. She did not return the forms and did not respond to a subsequent standard warning notice about the consequences of non-compliance. A reduced benefit direction was then made against her family credit, and an adjudication officer directed a reduction in her family credit.

The appellant later returned the required forms, but her replies were not accepted and the reduced benefit direction remained in place. She made a late appeal to an appeal tribunal and asked for a paper hearing. The tribunal considered written material including a submission from the Secretary of State’s representative, copies of relevant forms, and a short letter from the appellant’s solicitors, and decided an oral hearing was unnecessary.

In its reasons, the tribunal noted that although the appellant said she did not know the father of the child, the child’s surname had been registered as different from the appellant’s surname. The tribunal also found that the appellant feared violence from the man she was living with, but that she said he was not the father of the child. The tribunal confirmed that the reduced benefit direction applied.

On appeal to the Commissioner, it was accepted that the tribunal had not been provided with complete papers. In particular, it was accepted that the tribunal did not see a letter from a Housing Directorate (dated December 1997) indicating that the appellant was at risk of domestic violence, and that this document should have been included (and possibly other letters as well).

The evidence before the Commissioner (including letters from the appellant, the Housing Directorate, and two firms of solicitors) referred to serious injury to the appellant, an injunction, involvement of the police and welfare authorities, and the need for the mother to move to avoid harm. The Commissioner found that this evidence was at least partly connected with the requirement that the appellant provide the name of the child’s father. The Commissioner concluded there were reasonable grounds to anticipate a real risk of harm to the appellant if she were required to, or did, name the father, and therefore the reduced benefit direction should not have been made. The Commissioner directed that the reduced benefit direction (and any subsequent related directions) be withdrawn retrospectively and that the benefit reductions be rescinded and refunded.
claims:
The appellant challenged the reduced benefit direction applied to her family credit. Her main argument on appeal was that the tribunal failed to consider evidence of actual violence she had sustained from the child’s father, which she said had been reported to the Child Support Agency. Through solicitors, she also argued that relevant documents held by the Child Support Agency were missing from the papers considered by the tribunal.

In a letter, the appellant stated that the Child Support Agency was aware she had obtained an injunction against the child’s father with a power of arrest following a serious injury to her. In substance, she contended that requiring her to cooperate by providing information/authorisation (including naming the father) exposed her (and/or her child) to a risk of harm or undue distress, and that she therefore should not have been required to provide the authorisation and should not have been subjected to a reduction of benefit.

The relief she sought was that the tribunal’s decision be overturned and that the reduced benefit direction be removed, with the consequence that the reduction in her family credit (and any subsequent reductions flowing from it) should be undone and repaid.

facts:
The case concerned the calculation of the mother’s housing costs for child support purposes following the parents’ separation. The parents had a joint repayment mortgage requiring monthly payments of £548.95 due on the 3rd of each month. After they separated in June 2001, the father continued to pay the full £548.95 each month until December 2001, and then stopped making payments. The mother paid half of the monthly amount in January 2002. From February 2002 she negotiated an arrangement with the lender under which the lender agreed not to take enforcement action provided she paid £200 per month, and she paid £200 per month under that arrangement while the property was being sold.

In divorce proceedings it was agreed that the property would be sold and the proceeds divided between the parents, with deductions from the father’s share to be paid to the mother, including an amount reflecting half of the mortgage interest payments she made from 16 December 2001 until the sale. The property was sold in June 2003.

The mother claimed child support maintenance in January 2002. Her housing costs were initially treated as £548.95 per month, but were later adjusted to £200 per month. The father sought a further adjustment to £100 per month on the basis that, under the divorce agreement, he would ultimately reimburse the mother for half of what she had paid. That adjustment was refused. The father appealed to an appeal tribunal but was unsuccessful. The tribunal, while dismissing the appeal, held that the correct housing costs figure was the full contractual mortgage amount of £548.95 per month.

On further appeal, it was common ground that the dispute about the housing-cost figure made no practical difference to the amount of child support maintenance payable in this case, because the father had the much lower income and his protected income position meant that moderate changes to the mother’s assessed income did not affect his liability.

The Commissioner concluded that the tribunal had erred in law by failing to treat the mother’s housing costs as only her share of the contractual mortgage liability in the circumstances of this case. The Commissioner set aside the tribunal decision and substituted a decision that the mother’s housing costs should properly have been assessed at £274.48 per month (half of £548.95) from 23 April 2003, while noting that this made no difference to the maintenance assessment.
claims:
The father (as appellant) challenged the calculation of the mother’s housing costs used in the child support calculation. He sought a reduction in the mother’s assessed housing costs from the figure being used (which had been adjusted to £200 per month) to £100 per month. His argument was that because the divorce arrangements provided that, on sale of the home, deductions would be made from his share of the proceeds and paid to the mother to reflect (among other things) half of the mortgage interest payments she had made, he would in effect be repaying her for half of what she paid; therefore, he contended, only half of her monthly payments should be treated as her housing costs.

In the alternative, he also pursued the point that the tribunal was wrong to treat the mother’s housing costs as the full contractual mortgage payment of £548.95 per month.

He maintained that it was important that the record be corrected even though it was accepted that the outcome would not change the amount of child support maintenance payable in this particular case.
uk_statute_references_predicted: Child Support (Maintenance Assessment and Special Cases) Regulations 1992

facts:
The claimant, a man aged 76, applied on 20 October 2004 for housing benefit and council tax benefit for a privately rented flat. In his application he disclosed only modest means: his state retirement pension, a small private annuity, and savings in various accounts totalling a little over £1,000. The local authority (the housing benefit authority) awarded him full housing benefit and council tax benefit from 25 October 2004 by decisions dated 4 and 24 December 2004, and he continued to receive those benefits.

A routine review visit on 22 September 2006 revealed that the claimant also had an additional, previously undisclosed, building society savings account in his own name with a balance of £16,063.30. The claimant signed a review form completed by the visiting officer which recorded that balance as his capital. Further enquiries showed the account had been opened on 22 November 2004 with an initial cheque deposit of £17,658.82, and the balance had remained above £16,000 thereafter. During 2006 the claimant made withdrawals of £700 (March), £800 (June) and £950 (August), which he paid into his ordinary bank account.

On 15 October 2006 the council issued a decision letter stating that because he had more than £16,000 in capital he was not entitled to housing benefit or council tax benefit. That letter did not specify the date from which entitlement was terminated. Shortly before, the claimant had written to the council asserting that the undisclosed account was “a trust fund for my sons from the settlement of the estate of my late sister-in-law.”

On 7 December 2006 the council issued a further letter stating that his claim was cancelled back to 25 October 2004 on the basis that he had capital in excess of £16,000 since he first claimed, and it set out alleged overpayments of housing benefit and council tax benefit for specified periods.

The claimant appealed. At the tribunal hearing on 22 February 2007, the claimant’s explanation (described as imprecise and lacking detail) was that the money represented part of what had been left to his sons by their aunt, who had died in Australia about 15 years earlier. He said his ex-wife had asked him to look after it when she was ill; although the sons were adults and entitled to the money, they wanted a separate sum kept aside for their mother’s medical or funeral expenses. There was no contemporaneous evidence showing the creation of a trust over the money, and no clear explanation why the money was placed into an account in the claimant’s sole name rather than held by the sons or their mother. The tribunal chairman found the claimant’s explanations unconvincing and noted gaps and discrepancies; documents produced appeared to have been assembled after the event. The fact that the account was opened in the claimant’s sole name and that he withdrew sizeable sums in 2006 (later described by him as “loans”) counted against his account.

However, the tribunal chairman also recorded as a fact that a 1991 letter from the claimant’s ex-wife suggested he might take over administration of the sons’ inheritance, and that this did not lead to anything until the undisclosed account was opened in November 2004 with the arrival of £17,658.82. The Commissioner concluded that the tribunal had failed to make a clear finding on the material issue of the nature and origin of the £17,658.82 deposit and whether it was money belonging to the claimant’s sons or money belonging to the claimant from another source. Without determining that issue, the tribunal’s conclusion that the money belonged beneficially to the claimant was unsafe. The Commissioner also noted that if the money only arrived at the end of November 2004, there was no basis for a decision that removed entitlement back to 25 October 2004 on the ground of capital only shown to have been possessed later.

The Commissioner set aside the tribunal decision and remitted the case to a fresh tribunal for a complete rehearing and redetermination of entitlement, directing that the new tribunal should investigate where the claimant obtained the £17,658.82 cheque used to open the account and consider further contentions and evidence the claimant sought to submit. The Commissioner also directed that the council’s statements about “overpayments” in the 7 December 2006 letter were insufficient to amount to a separate effective determination of recoverability, leaving it to the council to decide whether to make a further formal decision on that issue.
claims:
The claimant challenged the council’s decision that he was not entitled to housing benefit and council tax benefit because of capital over £16,000 in the undisclosed account, and the council’s cancellation of his claim back to 25 October 2004.

His central argument was that the money in the undisclosed building society account was not his own capital but was held for his sons: he asserted it was a trust fund derived from the settlement of the estate of his late sister-in-law (their aunt). He maintained that he had been asked by his ex-wife to look after the money when she was ill, and that although the sons were adults entitled to it, they wished a separate sum to be kept aside for their mother’s potential medical or funeral expenses. On that basis, he contended that the funds should not be treated as his beneficial capital for benefit entitlement purposes and that his entitlement to housing benefit and council tax benefit should continue (or be reinstated) rather than being terminated and backdated to the start of his claim.

In the appeal proceedings he also sought to rely on additional contentions and evidence beyond what had been before the original tribunal, which the Commissioner directed the new tribunal to consider on rehearing.
uk_statute_references_predicted: Social Security Contributions and Benefits Act 1992

facts:
Mr Y made a criminal injuries compensation claim in 1998 arising from stalking and harassment incidents said to have occurred between July and November 1997. After he appealed the initial award, a Criminal Injuries Compensation Appeals Panel decided on 25 September 2002 that he was entitled to £5,500. This was a reduction from the tariff award because the Panel concluded that only 30% of his presenting mental health problems were attributable to the relevant crimes, finding that he had suffered from depression and panic attacks for several years before the incidents, was receiving medication, described himself as very nervous before the incidents, and could not hold down a job.

On 19 October 2010 Mr Y, through solicitors, applied for a medical re-opening of the compensation decision, asserting a deterioration in his mental condition. The application was not supported by medical evidence, but his solicitor asked the Criminal Injuries Compensation Authority (CICA) to commission a psychiatric assessment. Internal correspondence showed that in August 2011 CICA undertook to fund a psychiatric assessment, but its medical contractor could not provide a female psychiatrist locally. Alternatives were proposed: assessment by a male psychiatrist with a female chaperone, or by a female psychiatrist at consulting rooms about 50 miles away. On 26 September 2011 Mr Y’s solicitor wrote to the contractor stating Mr Y was content to be assessed at home by a male psychiatrist. It appeared this may not have been communicated to CICA, because in a letter dated 24 June 2013 CICA said it had received no communication after July 2011 and stated that on 29 January 2012 it had written to Mr Y’s solicitor withdrawing the earlier undertaking to commission an assessment.

On 28 July 2012 CICA refused to re-open the case, stating there was no evidence of a material change in Mr Y’s condition. Mr Y appealed to the First-tier Tribunal. The Tribunal directed a hearing on the issue of medical re-opening. In November 2012 Mr Y’s then solicitor told the Tribunal that if it decided the case should be re-opened on medical grounds, Mr Y requested a direction that the previously indicated psychiatric assessment should take place.

A hearing on 6 June 2013 was adjourned after Mr Y raised CICA’s August 2011 undertaking to fund an examination. The adjournment directions required CICA to write within 21 days setting out its up-to-date position on funding a psychiatric examination. Mr Y said CICA’s representative had undertaken at that hearing to fund a fresh assessment if it was shown CICA had previously promised to do so, but this was not reflected in the Tribunal’s directions and the Upper Tribunal considered it more likely Mr Y had misunderstood what was said. On 24 June 2013 CICA wrote that, having reviewed the case, it still considered a psychiatric report was not required.

On 6 August 2013 a different First-tier Tribunal judge (Judge Walker) issued case management directions. The directions noted that, because the application was made more than two years after the final decision, re-opening would not occur unless the decision-maker was satisfied on the basis of evidence presented that the renewed application could be considered without extensive enquiries. Judge Walker considered this placed the onus on Mr Y to produce convincing evidence and stated that he did not think it mattered whether CICA had agreed to arrange an examination because it had not taken place and the parties were no further on; he also expressed the view that even if CICA had agreed to commission a report, it ought not to have done so.

Judge Walker directed Mr Y to obtain and supply his GP records. Mr Y said he could not afford to obtain them, and the Tribunal later directed CICA to obtain records for June 2011 to 2014; earlier records were already held by CICA and supplied to the Tribunal. Mr Y provided a GP letter dated 7 October 2013 stating he had suffered from anxiety and panic attacks since 2002, initially precipitated by stalking episodes, and that since then he had found it difficult to leave the house. In September 2013 Mr Y’s solicitor again asked CICA to proceed with the psychiatric assessment initially offered and then withdrawn; CICA replied that it would not arrange an assessment.

The First-tier Tribunal had a complete run of Mr Y’s GP records, including correspondence with external practitioners. The records showed ongoing anxiety, panic attacks and depression over many years, including entries from 2001 onwards and manuscript records showing consultations for panic attacks in 1998, 2000 and 2001. The records also included medical letters from January and February 1997 (before the reported stalking/harassment period) referring to frequent and severe panic attacks and diagnosing a panic disorder. During September 1997 a psychiatrist recorded panic attacks as frequent as three times a day without referring to stalking or harassment; stalking was first mentioned in a psychiatrist’s letter dated 4 November 1997.

The First-tier Tribunal dismissed Mr Y’s appeal, finding his medical condition had not materially changed since the 2002 award. It also found that, on the evidence before it, it could consider the case without extensive enquiries and there was no need to direct a psychiatric examination.

Mr Y sought judicial review in the Upper Tribunal. Permission was granted on two grounds: possible legal misdirection in construing the medical re-opening provisions, and whether the Tribunal had exceeded its case management role by effectively preventing CICA from commissioning a psychiatric assessment. Permission was refused on a separate complaint that he had been unfairly dealt with because he had an existing medical condition and was homosexual. The Upper Tribunal decided the judicial review without a hearing and dismissed the proceedings, concluding that any misunderstanding about the additional condition for older cases was immaterial because the Tribunal’s finding of no material change in condition was open on the evidence, and that Judge Walker’s earlier views about the psychiatric assessment did not cause unfairness because CICA had already withdrawn its offer and the Tribunal was not obliged to direct an assessment.
claims:
Mr Y sought to have his compensation case medically re-opened on the basis that his mental condition had deteriorated since the final award. In connection with that, he sought (or sought to secure) a psychiatric assessment funded by CICA, relying on CICA’s earlier undertaking in 2011 to commission such an assessment and contending that he had agreed to be assessed by a male psychiatrist at home.

In his appeal to the First-tier Tribunal, his then solicitor indicated that if the Tribunal decided the case should be re-opened on medical grounds, Mr Y requested a direction that the previously indicated psychiatric assessment should take place.

In the judicial review proceedings, Mr Y advanced two main challenges to the First-tier Tribunal process and decision: (1) that the Tribunal had misdirected itself in law in its approach to the medical re-opening requirements for an older application, in particular by treating it as necessary for him to show that the re-opening application could be considered without extensive enquiries; and (2) that at an earlier stage the Tribunal had gone beyond legitimate case management by effectively preventing or discouraging CICA from commissioning a psychiatric assessment, thereby unfairly depriving him of the opportunity to persuade CICA to fund such an assessment.

Mr Y also argued that he had been unfairly dealt with because he had an existing medical condition and because he was homosexual, but permission to pursue that ground was refused.

facts:
Scaffolding North East Limited held a restricted operator’s licence for four vehicles. It went into liquidation on 13 August 2014 owing HMRC £260,000. Its sole director and shareholder was William Collard. Cheryl Gray had previously described herself in correspondence as company secretary and later described herself as general manager.

Before Scaffolding’s licence was revoked, there was an allegation that it had been using an unauthorised operating centre at Birks Road, Heddon on the Wall, Newcastle. A preliminary hearing about that issue was listed for 4 August 2015. No one from Scaffolding attended. It then became apparent that Scaffolding had gone into liquidation and its licence was revoked in-office on 13 August 2015.

On 17 August 2015, SNE Newcastle Limited applied for a restricted operator’s licence for four vehicles. The vehicles it proposed to specify were the same four vehicles that had been specified on Scaffolding’s licence, and the proposed operating centre was the same Birks Road site previously used by Scaffolding. Newcastle’s sole director was Cheryl Gray and William Collard held 49% of its shares. Newcastle used the same correspondence addresses and telephone numbers as Scaffolding. In its application it answered “no” to a question asking whether, within the last twelve months, it had purchased the assets or shareholding of any company that holds or has previously held an operator’s licence, and it did not identify the link between Scaffolding and Newcastle through Mr Collard.

The Office of the Traffic Commissioner wrote to Newcastle on 27 August 2015 asking it to confirm what links it had to Scaffolding. On 8 September 2015, Ms Gray emailed stating that Newcastle had “overtook” Scaffolding, that she was the owner and director of the new company, that she had purchased the vehicles and stock from Scaffolding, and that Newcastle now had no links to Scaffolding.

On 15 December 2015, vehicle KD08 JWZ was stopped while displaying an operator licence disc in the name of Scaffolding. The driver said he was employed by Newcastle, that Newcastle owned the vehicle, and that he had taken instructions that day from “William Collard, the boss.” After this stop, Ms Gray emailed requesting an interim licence for Newcastle. John Maddison later telephoned stating he would hand deliver a letter and an interim licence application, but that interim application was never delivered.

On 16 December 2015, a traffic examiner produced an environmental report on the suitability of 20 Birks Road as an operating centre and concluded it was unsafe on road safety grounds.

On 17 December 2015, SNE Hire & Sales Limited applied for a restricted licence for eight vehicles. The same four vehicles previously specified on Scaffolding’s and Newcastle’s applications were included. The application stated Ms Gray was the sole director, but it was signed by John Maddison as “director.” Although the application was for a restricted licence, it named Mr Maddison as transport manager. The accompanying advertisement was in the name of John Maddison trading as SNE Hire & Sales.

A covering letter from TT Law stated Hire & Sales supplied scaffolding equipment, had recently “took over” Scaffolding’s business after Scaffolding went into liquidation, and urgently needed a licence due to a substantial order. It described Mr Maddison as Hire & Sales’ managing director and asserted that Scaffolding’s assets had been bought from liquidators by a third party and that Scaffolding’s previous officers were not involved in Hire & Sales.

The Hire & Sales application contained inaccurate answers. It answered “no” to a question asking whether any person named had been involved in a company that had gone into liquidation owing money, despite Ms Gray’s involvement with Scaffolding and Mr Collard being a shareholder of Hire & Sales. It also answered “no” to questions about whether any person named had ever held an operator’s licence or had a licence suspended, curtailed or revoked, despite Scaffolding’s licence having been revoked and Mr Maddison having been a director of City Scaffolding (Northern) Limited, whose operator’s licence was revoked after it went into liquidation.

Newcastle was called to a public inquiry on 9 February 2016. Hire & Sales was also called to a public inquiry on the same date. The call-up letter to Hire & Sales highlighted problems with its application and noted that bank statements relied on for financial standing were in Newcastle’s name and that both applications listed the same vehicles.

On 4 January 2016, Ms Gray emailed explaining that when the Hire & Sales application was signed Mr Maddison was not yet a named director, but it was later decided he should be and paperwork was sent to Companies House; she stated he had been a director of City Scaffolding for about two months and claimed he had not been advised that its licence had been revoked or suspended. She also referred to bank statements being held in the “holding company” name, which was in fact Newcastle. Mr Maddison was appointed a director of Hire & Sales on 7 January 2016.

On 7 January 2016, Mr Maddison hand delivered a letter dated 6 January 2016 seeking to clarify issues about both Newcastle and Hire & Sales “in the spirit of openness and transparency.” It said Newcastle’s application would be withdrawn due to the negative environmental report and the vehicle stop. It acknowledged the Traffic Commissioner would be concerned because Ms Gray was director of both companies and because of the unauthorised vehicle use. It enclosed a further interim authority request for Hire & Sales, sought to amend Hire & Sales’ application to a standard national licence, provided a transport manager form for Mr Maddison, and provided a bank statement showing funds for eight vehicles (with assurances about ring-fencing, relying on transfers from accounts in the names of Newcastle and Ms Gray). It acknowledged the original application was not fully complete and that Mr Maddison had attended a public inquiry relating to City Scaffolding.

Despite concerns about links between the entities and the unsatisfactory application, the Traffic Commissioner granted Hire & Sales an interim restricted licence for four vehicles, stating concerns persisted about the history of directors/shareholders such that he could not be satisfied on repute.

At the conjoined public inquiry on 9 February 2016, Ms Gray appeared as sole director of Newcastle and as a director of Hire & Sales; Mr Maddison appeared as a director of Hire & Sales and nominated transport manager. Evidence was given that Newcastle’s application was withdrawn due to environmental issues. It was accepted there were common themes between the companies and that Newcastle’s unauthorised vehicle use affected Hire & Sales. It was said the same vehicles were listed because the Newcastle application would not proceed and the vehicles would instead be listed for Hire & Sales.

Ms Gray gave evidence about Scaffolding’s liquidation, stating VAT returns had not been submitted by previous accountants, leading to the HMRC debt; attempts to reach an arrangement failed and liquidation followed. She said Mr Collard was the largest creditor. She said Hire & Sales purchased Scaffolding’s assets including websites and telephone numbers, and denied Mr Collard’s involvement in Hire & Sales though he dealt with contractors. She said the decision to apply through Hire & Sales was made before the 15 December 2015 stop, and claimed she genuinely believed Newcastle had an interim licence at the time the vehicle was used; she accepted it was her fault for allowing vehicles out and said the disc from the revoked Scaffolding licence should have been removed. She accepted that after Scaffolding’s licence was revoked the vehicles continued to operate up to 15 December 2015 without authorisation.

Ms Gray also said both Newcastle and Hire & Sales were set up in November 2014 as part of a structure in which SNE Scaffolding Services would employ workers and hold contracts, Hire & Sales would hold stock, Scaffolding North East would run simultaneously with Scaffolding Services, and Newcastle would be the holding company. She said Newcastle’s application was made in anticipation of Scaffolding’s liquidation to avoid a gap in operations. She said Scaffolding had used an unauthorised operating centre because the authorised one was close to houses and noisy, and Birks Road was offered as more suitable.

Mr Maddison gave evidence that he was managing director of Hire & Sales and nominated transport manager. He described prior involvement with City Scaffolding, saying he became managing director shortly before it was liquidated and claimed he was unaware of financial difficulties; he attended liquidation meetings and a public inquiry relating to a later application. He said he answered “no” on the Hire & Sales form about revocation because he had not been told City Scaffolding’s licence was revoked and because he had been advised by a Road Haulage Association contact that after five years it need not be disclosed. He described systems he had introduced at Hire & Sales after the interim licence was granted.

On 15 February 2016 the Traffic Commissioner refused Hire & Sales’ application and terminated its interim licence. He found Newcastle’s proposed operating centre unsuitable and found Ms Gray’s explanation showed Newcastle was a device to allow Scaffolding’s business to continue after liquidation while avoiding its debt to the public purse. He found Ms Gray’s email claiming no links to Scaffolding was untruthful because Mr Collard held 49% of Newcastle. For Hire & Sales, he accepted financial standing was met but concluded the application failed on good repute. He found Ms Gray had freely explained Hire & Sales was also a device to allow Scaffolding’s business to continue after wiping away its debt, and that vehicles had been used unlawfully throughout 2015. He found the untruthful statement about links and other adverse findings applied equally to Hire & Sales. He also found Mr Maddison failed to declare his involvement in City Scaffolding and its revoked licence, lacked due diligence in not checking discs and authorisation when he joined, and gave unsatisfactory evidence.

Hire & Sales appealed to the Upper Tribunal. The Upper Tribunal dismissed the appeal and ordered the interim licence terminated forthwith. It held the Traffic Commissioner was entitled to find that Ms Gray had described Newcastle and Hire & Sales as devices to continue Scaffolding’s business after liquidation and debt write-off, and that the entities were inextricably linked as successive phoenix operations. It rejected arguments that deficiencies in the call-up letter caused unfairness. It accepted that one criticism of Mr Maddison—being “significantly out of date” as a transport manager—was unfairly reached on limited questioning, but held this did not justify allowing the appeal given the other findings supporting refusal on good repute.
claims:
Hire & Sales appealed against the Traffic Commissioner’s refusal of its application for a standard national operator’s licence and against the termination of its interim licence.

In the appeal, Hire & Sales (through its solicitor) argued that the Traffic Commissioner had been unduly harsh in finding that Ms Gray had explained Hire & Sales (and Newcastle) was a “device” to allow Scaffolding’s business to continue after liquidation while avoiding Scaffolding’s debt to the public purse.

Hire & Sales also argued that the call-up letter for its public inquiry was inadequate and caused unfairness because it did not refer to possible links between Hire & Sales and Scaffolding (even though links to Scaffolding became a main basis for the adverse good repute finding), and it did not flag that the Traffic Commissioner would explore Scaffolding’s failure to attend the earlier hearing. It further argued that discussion at the inquiry about the timing of liquidation, applications, and continued vehicle operation was ambiguous and related to Newcastle rather than Hire & Sales, and that this too should have been identified in the call-up letter. It also argued that if the Traffic Commissioner considered Mr Collard’s presence necessary, that should have been stated in the call-up letter.

Hire & Sales additionally contended that the Traffic Commissioner’s statement that the “applicant company” had used vehicles unlawfully throughout 2015 was wrong because the unauthorised use was by Newcastle, not Hire & Sales.

Finally, Hire & Sales challenged the Traffic Commissioner’s assessment of Mr Maddison as unfairly “damning,” arguing he had not been called to the inquiry separately as transport manager to consider his good repute, that he was faced with historic matters, and that it was unfair to conclude he was “significantly out of date” based on his evidence about checking driving licences when he had also indicated awareness of online checks.

Overall, Hire & Sales sought to have the refusal decision overturned so that its operator’s licence application could succeed and the interim authority not be terminated.

facts:
The appellant is an Egyptian national born in January 1987. He first visited the United Kingdom briefly in 2011 and re-entered in early 2012 with entry clearance as a visitor. Apart from a brief visit to Egypt, he remained in the UK from 2012 onwards. He married a Polish national, Ewelina Wrzesniewska, on 28 March 2013 in an Islamic ceremony and later registered the marriage at the Egyptian Consulate on 5 April 2013. He was issued with an EEA residence card as the family member of an EEA national on 15 January 2014.

On 27 February 2015 immigration officers attended premises at Denzil Road to investigate another Egyptian national’s marriage to a Polish national. The appellant was encountered there. The respondent then decided to set removal directions on the basis that the appellant’s marriage to his wife was a sham (a marriage of convenience) and therefore an abuse of rights.

The appellant’s account was that his wife had travelled to Poland for about three weeks in February 2015 to visit her sick mother, and that during her absence he stayed with a friend for company; it was at that friend’s address that immigration officers attended. He said he was treated rudely, requested but was not provided with an interpreter, asked to call his lawyer but was not allowed, and was questioned when not properly awake. He disputed aspects of the immigration officers’ record of what he said, including that he did provide his full address but could not remember the postcode.

The appellant said his relationship began after he met his wife at a birthday party, with friends helping them communicate because they did not share a common language. He said they began living together after the marriage. In oral evidence he accepted that when he returned to the UK in 2012 he intended to remain permanently, that he applied for a visit visa because it was the available route to enter, and that he lied to secure entry. He said he later learned that to stay lawfully he would need to marry or study, could not afford study, and therefore decided he had to marry.

The appellant explained that an address at George’s Drive appeared on the consular marriage certificate because it was his sister-in-law’s address used for correspondence and security, and because he and his wife were unsure where they would settle. He also said he had used the Denzil Road address for correspondence and for official purposes (including a driving licence), despite saying he never lived there. He said he moved to various addresses, including Stonebridge Park and later Inca Drive, and that at the time of the February 2015 visit he lived with his wife but knew his address and not its postcode.
