The appellant produced limited documentary material in support of the relationship, including marriage documents, some joint bank statements (from an account originally in his sole name), letters addressed to each of them at the same addresses, a TV licence in his wife’s name, payslips and a P60 said to relate to his wife, a letter from a friend, and a small number of photographs. He said records of calls and messages were lost when his phone broke.

The respondent relied on evidence from an immigration officer (IO Hale) about the February 2015 visit and on digital/open-source investigation evidence (Mr Toleman). IO Hale said he attended Denzil Road with another officer, showed identification, obtained consent to enter, and questioned the appellant after waking him. IO Hale said he suspected the appellant was not lawfully in the UK, cautioned him (recorded as “C+2”), and asked questions. IO Hale said the appellant could not give his address beyond “New Eltham,” and that when asked to show contact with his wife the appellant handed over his phone showing a contact “Ewelina Lovely”; IO Hale considered the texts not to show direct personal contact and noted the last call to that contact was in September 2014. IO Hale said he called the number and spoke to a man who turned out to be the wife’s brother-in-law, who said he had not had contact with her for over six months. IO Hale said he did not offer an interpreter because the appellant’s English appeared sufficient.

The respondent also relied on checks said to show limited recorded travel by the appellant’s wife to the UK (two trips by air in 2014 totalling six days, both originating in Poland), and on a prior marriage interview (August 2013) with the wife’s sister and brother-in-law referring to the wife visiting the UK in April 2013 with her baby. The respondent relied on Facebook material said to be the wife’s account, containing photographs and personal information, and on online checks suggesting the employer named on the wife’s payslips had no internet presence and that a similarly named company had been dissolved.

The appellant disputed the Facebook material, denied his wife had children, and suggested the Facebook account had been fabricated. He could not explain why the wife’s brother-in-law had referred to her visiting the UK with a baby. He said his wife travelled to Poland by car with friends. He said the relationship deteriorated after the respondent’s decision and enforcement visit; he said it began breaking down in late 2015 and that his wife moved out in March 2016 and refused to communicate until his immigration status was resolved.

The First-tier Tribunal dismissed the appeal, finding the respondent had reasonable grounds to suspect a sham marriage and that the appellant had not rebutted the allegation. On appeal to the Upper Tribunal, the decision was re-made. The Upper Tribunal found, on the balance of probabilities, that the appellant entered into a marriage of convenience. It reached that conclusion without needing to rely on evidence obtained during the February 2015 questioning. The Tribunal considered the appellant’s evidence limited and found significant concerns about the marriage documentation (including the repeated use of an address the appellant said was false), the lack of clear evidence about the joint account conversion and use, doubts about the payslips (including that the company appeared dissolved before the last payslip), and the poor quality and scarcity of photographs. It also found conspicuous gaps in expected evidence of a genuine relationship, including lack of evidence of communications, joint household documentation, witnesses supporting the relationship, and—strikingly—any evidence from the wife.

The Tribunal accepted the respondent’s Facebook evidence as a genuine account belonging to the wife and found the alternative Facebook page produced by the appellant not credible, concluding it was created to support the appeal. It also found the travel evidence and other material supported the conclusion that the wife was resident in Poland during the claimed relationship and marriage. The appeal was dismissed and no anonymity direction was made.
claims:
The appellant challenged the respondent’s decision to set removal directions on the basis that his marriage to an EEA national was a sham. He maintained that he did not enter into a marriage of convenience and argued that it was not for him to prove the marriage was genuine; rather, the respondent bore the burden of proof and had failed to give adequate reasons for the decision.

He also contended that the removal decision breached his and his wife’s rights under EU free-movement arrangements and breached his rights under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

In addition, although not part of his written grounds, he argued before the First-tier Tribunal that evidence obtained during the immigration officers’ questioning on 27 February 2015 should not be admitted, or should be given reduced weight, because the questioning was not properly conducted in accordance with the applicable PACE-related direction and codes. His case on this issue was that the questioning amounted to an interview under caution to establish an offence or breach and that the immigration officer failed to administer the required criminal caution.

On appeal to the Upper Tribunal, he sought to overturn the First-tier Tribunal’s dismissal on the basis that the judge failed to deal with his PACE submissions, failed to give adequate reasons, applied the wrong test for a marriage of convenience, and made factual errors. The relief he sought was that the removal decision be set aside and his appeal allowed (i.e., that he not be removed on the basis of an alleged sham marriage).

facts: The decision concerns a self-assessment tax return in which Derek William Hankinson claimed that he was not resident in the United Kingdom. Following that return, a discovery assessment was made in relation to his tax position. The case before the Upper Tribunal addressed whether that discovery assessment was valid and whether the relevant statutory requirements for making it were satisfied. The Upper Tribunal concluded that the statutory requirements were satisfied and dismissed the appeal.
claims: The claimant (taxpayer) appealed against the discovery assessment. His position, as reflected in his self-assessment return, was that he was not resident in the UK, and he challenged the validity of the discovery assessment on the basis that the statutory conditions for making such an assessment were not met. He sought to have the discovery assessment set aside or treated as invalid. The Upper Tribunal rejected these arguments and dismissed the appeal.

facts:
Tempertech (Wales) Limited manufactured toughened glass from two factories in South Wales. It had about 50 employees and annual turnover of around £2 million. Jeff Edwards founded the business in 1989 and was its managing director.

For about four years the company employed Paul Irvine as general manager. Mr Edwards entrusted Mr Irvine with running the business, including sales. On 28 April 2006 Mr Irvine resigned with effect from 1 June 2006, telling Mr Edwards he intended to work self-employed outside the glass industry. Mr Edwards went on annual holiday around 20 May 2006 and returned on 1 June 2006. When he visited the factory on his return, he learned Mr Irvine would not be at work on 2 June and that five other key staff had resigned, including the production supervisors at each factory. This meant the company lost both management layers immediately below Mr Edwards.

Mr Edwards then discovered that Mr Irvine had set up a rival toughened-glass business, Glass Solution (Wales) Limited, which began trading on 5 June 2006 and had been incorporated on 9 May 2006 while Mr Irvine was still employed by Tempertech. The new business operated from premises about 40 miles away. Earlier, in April 2006, Mr Edwards and Mr Irvine had visited premises of another business (Omega Glass) and Tempertech had unsuccessfully bid for machinery from liquidators; Mr Edwards believed Mr Irvine used confidential information from his employment to outbid Tempertech and acquire the machinery for his new company.

While Mr Edwards was on holiday, Mr Irvine recruited Tempertech employees, telling them Tempertech was close to insolvency and redundancies were imminent. Mr Edwards also discovered Mr Irvine approached Tempertech’s customers. Mr Irvine obtained the business of Tempertech’s principal customer, Solar Windows, which accounted for about £700,000 of annual turnover. Solar Windows also refused to pay Tempertech invoices totalling £150,000 issued during VAT period 05/06, alleging poor quality. Tempertech pursued recovery of the debt; it was paid intermittently by instalments, with the final payment made shortly before the tribunal hearing.

Mr Edwards said Mr Irvine’s actions took him by surprise because he trusted him and relied on him to run the business. On returning from holiday, Mr Edwards took urgent steps to save the company: meeting employees to reassure them, working to retain remaining customers, and taking charge of production due to the loss of his management team. He also assessed finances: the company owed about £1.5 million to the bank in loans, about £100,000 to suppliers, and about £140,000 to the tax authority for National Insurance and VAT. Mr Edwards met the bank urgently; it indicated it would support the company through the period but did not formally extend the £25,000 overdraft.

For VAT period 05/06, Tempertech submitted its VAT return on time but did not pay the VAT due by the deadline of 30 June 2006. On 23 June 2006 Mr Edwards wrote to the tax authority explaining the situation and warning the company would not be able to pay by the due date, and sought an arrangement to pay by instalments. An instalment arrangement was agreed and Tempertech adhered to it, with one payment left at the time of the hearing.

Mr Edwards also began High Court proceedings against Mr Irvine and obtained an interim injunction on 26 June 2006; Tempertech was seeking damages against Mr Irvine and his company.

The tax authority imposed a default surcharge of £2,251.48 for period 05/06. The company had a history since 2000 of eight default surcharges and liability notices, mostly liability notices. The most recent prior surcharge was for period 11/05 (£1,117) arising from an under-declaration and late return; there was also a mis-declaration penalty that was reduced to zero after mitigating circumstances were put forward, and bailiffs were instructed to recover amounts due under assessments.

The 05/06 VAT return showed outputs of £477,295 (higher than the adjacent 02/06 and 08/06 periods but below the average of earlier periods) and inputs of £221,361 (much lower than 02/06 and 08/06), resulting in VAT due of £45,029 (much higher than the other two quarters in 2006). Mr Edwards accepted the company had financial difficulties toward the end of 2005, which he had thought were due to production problems, but he later believed Mr Irvine had been undermining the business in anticipation of setting up his rival company.

The tribunal found that the June 2006 events were different in nature and scale from the earlier financial problems: the sudden loss of key management, the loss of the principal customer, the customer’s refusal to pay invoices with immediate cash-flow impact, and damage to workforce morale and customer confidence. It found Mr Edwards had no prior knowledge of Mr Irvine’s actions; that Mr Edwards took urgent reasonable steps to keep the business operating and kept the bank informed; that his focus on production led to neglect of supply-side matters contributing to lower input tax and higher VAT liability in 05/06; and that he did not ignore VAT responsibilities because he filed the return on time, warned the authority before the deadline, and arranged and complied with an instalment plan. The tribunal concluded the failure to pay on time was a direct consequence of Mr Irvine’s destabilising actions, which left the company in a perilous financial position and could not reasonably have been foreseen by a prudent business person exercising due diligence.
claims:
Tempertech appealed against the imposition of the default surcharge of £2,251.48 for VAT period 05/06. It sought cancellation of the surcharge on the basis that it had a reasonable excuse for not paying the VAT by 30 June 2006.

Tempertech’s case was that its non-payment was caused by exceptional events in June 2006: its general manager, without the managing director’s knowledge, set up a rival business, recruited away key staff, and diverted the company’s principal customer, who also withheld payment of substantial invoices. Tempertech argued these actions threatened the survival of the business, created an immediate cash-flow crisis, and required the managing director to focus urgently on stabilising operations and customer and workforce confidence. It maintained that these circumstances were fundamentally different from earlier financial difficulties in late 2005.

Tempertech also relied on the steps it took to deal responsibly with its VAT obligations despite the crisis: it submitted the VAT return on time, notified the tax authority in advance that it could not pay by the due date, and sought and then complied with an instalment arrangement to clear the VAT debt. On that basis, it asked the tribunal to allow the appeal and set aside the surcharge.

facts:
Cargo Gateway Ltd appealed against HM Revenue and Customs’ refusal to approve it to use Simplified Import VAT Accounting (SIVA), a scheme relating to VAT payable on importation where payment is deferred and where approval removes the need to provide security if there is said to be no risk to payment. HMRC initially refused the application on 13 April 2007. Cargo Gateway requested a review on 1 June 2007, and HMRC issued a review decision by letter dated 27 June upholding the refusal.

In the review decision HMRC stated that SIVA could only be used where the trader satisfied HMRC that there was no risk regarding payment of the deferred import VAT. HMRC gave two reasons for not being satisfied: (1) Cargo Gateway had insufficient liquidity, and (2) it had not met a criterion of having a 12‑month history of international trade operations. At the hearing HMRC did not seek to maintain the second reason and accepted that, as a matter of fact, Cargo Gateway did satisfy the 12‑month history criterion.

HMRC’s remaining justification was that Cargo Gateway did not have sufficient liquidity to demonstrate it would always be able to meet obligations to pay deferred VAT when due. The tribunal considered arguments about the position of agents: Cargo Gateway acted as an agent importing in clients’ names (acting “directly”), and therefore did not have personal liability for clients’ tax. The tribunal noted HMRC’s position that approval involved trust and that deferment could be withdrawn if an agent did not ensure payment, while the tax would still be collected from the client.

The tribunal found there could still be risk to the revenue if an agent were approved, because HMRC might not have a direct relationship with the agent’s client and might not be able to judge the client’s financial capability at the time deferment occurred. The tribunal also noted an additional risk that the agent might import goods on its own behalf, increasing potential exposure.

Cargo Gateway also suggested it would have money on hand from clients who had put it in funds before payment was due. The tribunal considered that using one client’s money to cover another client’s obligations where that other client was slow to pay would create a risk of cash-flow problems for the agent.

HMRC’s decision relied on the view that Cargo Gateway needed sufficient readily available assets to cover potential liabilities. HMRC referred to Cargo Gateway’s latest available unaudited accounts (year ending 28 February 2006), which showed tangible fixed assets of £12,543, which HMRC considered fell far short of the sums that could be at risk. The tribunal concluded HMRC’s decision was within a reasonable range, even if cautious, and dismissed the appeal.
claims:
Cargo Gateway sought to overturn HMRC’s refusal to approve it for SIVA.

Cargo Gateway argued that because it acted as an agent importing in clients’ names and had no personal liability for clients’ import VAT, there was no risk to the revenue from approving it for SIVA since the client remained liable for the VAT.

Cargo Gateway also argued that it would always have money on hand from clients who had put it in funds before the payment deadline, and therefore there was no risk to the revenue even in cases where clients had not put it in funds in time.

In response to HMRC’s stated reasons for refusal, the issue ultimately pursued at the hearing was HMRC’s assessment of insufficient liquidity/insufficient readily available assets to cover potential deferred VAT liabilities. HMRC accepted that the asserted lack of a 12‑month international trade history was factually incorrect, but maintained the refusal was still justified on liquidity grounds. Cargo Gateway’s appeal, in substance, challenged HMRC’s conclusion that it presented a risk of non-payment sufficient to justify refusing SIVA approval.

facts: The complainant made a request to Winchester City Council (WCC) for information relating to Tree Preservation Orders (TPOs). In dealing with the request, WCC stated that it had provided the complainant with all the information it held. The Information Commissioner considered whether WCC held any further relevant information and concluded that WCC had, in fact, provided all the information it held. The Commissioner also found that WCC did not provide its response within 20 working days.
claims: The complainant sought disclosure of information relating to Tree Preservation Orders (TPOs) from WCC. The complaint to the Information Commissioner, as reflected in the decision, was effectively that WCC had not provided the requested information in full (i.e., that further information should have been disclosed).

facts:
The application was made by 61 employees of London General Transport Services Limited for permission to appeal against an order of the Employment Appeal Tribunal dated 30 November 2000. The Employment Appeal Tribunal had allowed the employer’s appeal from part of an Employment Tribunal decision promulgated on 5 November 1997.

The dispute arose from the privatisation in November 1994 of part of the London bus services. The employer had previously been part of London Transport. Privatisation was carried out by selling the employer’s shares to a private company used by the employer’s management for a management/employee buy-out. The Transport and General Workers Union was the only trade union recognised by the employer. Before August 1994, London Transport and the employer had for many years negotiated collective agreements with the union.

In the period leading up to privatisation, the employer’s management involved in the buy-out met with the union, and the union supported the buy-out. On 12 August 1994 the employer and the union entered into an agreement known as the Framework Agreement, which was conditional on the buy-out being successful. The Framework Agreement contemplated changes to employees’ terms and conditions, including those of the applicants. When implemented in November 1994, the changes resulted in a deterioration in employees’ remuneration.

The union informed the employer that a majority of staff had consented to the Framework Agreement. Staff were asked to sign a document agreeing to the changed terms and conditions. All but one of the applicants refused to sign. One employee, Mr Couchman, did sign, but the Employment Tribunal later held that he had not agreed to the variation of his terms.

Two petitions were presented by staff at Stockwell Garage. The first, dated 7 November 1994, recorded dissatisfaction with the new terms and conditions and stated that the signatories would continue to work under protest. The second, dated 17 November 1994, stated that the petitioners did not vote for the new terms and conditions and asked for a ballot; it appeared that ballots had previously been held when collective agreements were entered into.

In the Employment Tribunal, the employer contended that the Framework Agreement had become part of the individual contracts. The tribunal considered whether the Framework Agreement had been incorporated into the applicants’ contracts, including whether the union acted as agent for the employees and whether incorporation occurred by custom and practice. The tribunal was not satisfied that the evidence established union agency for this purpose, and it was not satisfied that the history of negotiations with the union was sufficient to show that the Framework Agreement’s fundamental changes were incorporated into individual contracts through collective bargaining. The tribunal also considered acquiescence and found that applicants who signed one or other Stockwell Garage petition clearly indicated they did not accept the new terms and were continuing to work under protest.

On the employer’s appeal, the Employment Appeal Tribunal held that the Employment Tribunal had erred in law on the burden of proof, stating that a neutral approach was correct to determine the terms of employment. It criticised the tribunal for requiring strict proof of incorporation by custom and practice, held that the tribunal had asked the wrong question when assessing whether agreements negotiated with the recognised union became contractual terms, and found error in the tribunal’s distinction between practices sufficient to effect changes and those sufficient to effect fundamental changes. It also found fault with the tribunal’s conclusion that petition-signers did not accept the new terms, and remitted the matter to the same tribunal.

The Court of Appeal judge considered the employees’ application for permission to appeal and concluded that the points raised were properly arguable and raised an issue of general importance concerning incorporation of collectively bargained terms into individual contracts. Permission to appeal was granted, with directions for amended grounds and case management steps.
claims:
Before the Employment Tribunal, the employees complained that the employer had made an unlawful deduction from their wages by implementing the Framework Agreement changes, which reduced their remuneration, without those changes having become part of their individual contracts.

In seeking permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal, the employees argued that the Employment Appeal Tribunal was wrong to overturn the Employment Tribunal’s approach and conclusions. In particular, they contended that the Employment Appeal Tribunal erred regarding (1) the onus of proof in relation to whether a term was incorporated into individual contracts by custom and practice, and (2) the question of whether the employees had accepted the new terms of employment. They also argued that the Employment Appeal Tribunal improperly interfered with findings of fact made by the Employment Tribunal, rather than confining itself to errors of law.

The relief sought in the application was permission to appeal against the Employment Appeal Tribunal’s order allowing the employer’s appeal and remitting the case; permission to appeal was granted.

facts:
A chartered accountant, Mr Graham I Born, was appointed as arbitrator on 30 November 1999 in an arbitration between United Tyre Company Ltd and Ego Computers Ltd.

On 3 December 2001 Mr Born issued his substantive award (save as to costs) and raised an invoice for his fees. He had previously raised an interim invoice on 30 September for £2,500 plus VAT. The invoice required to be paid to take up the award dated 3 December 2001 was £44,900 plus VAT. This invoice included charges said to comprise 282 hours at £150 per hour, 170 hours of secretarial assistance at £30 per hour, and room hire for five days at £500 per day.

The dispute was described as complicated and involving detail. In the outcome, United Tyre Company Ltd appears to have succeeded only on a small matter involving £15,000, against an amended claim of over £140,000, so costs issues were likely to arise.

United Tyre Company Ltd paid Mr Born’s fee to take up the award on 4 December 2001, expressly reserving a right to apply to court to determine reasonable fees (initially referring to the wrong basis for such an application, which Mr Born did not correct at the time).

On 8 February 2002 Mr Born notified the parties that his costs award was available on payment of further fees. The costs award was short (about two pages) and ordered United Tyre Company Ltd to pay one-tenth of Ego Computers Ltd’s costs of the reference and Ego Computers Ltd to pay nine-tenths of United Tyre Company Ltd’s costs of the reference. Mr Born issued a further fee note stating that preparing this costs award took him 20 hours at £150 per hour plus four hours of secretarial assistance at £30 per hour. United Tyre Company Ltd paid the additional fees on 23 February 2002 and the costs award was issued.

On 20 March 2002 United Tyre Company Ltd first requested a breakdown and sought Mr Born’s file notes. On 21 March 2002 Mr Born responded that he was functus officio and indicated his belief that an undefined time limit had expired. On 11 April 2002 United Tyre Company Ltd replied that it was unaware of any time limit.

On 15 April 2002 Mr Born provided a general breakdown listing units of time spent. It indicated a minimum charging unit of a quarter of an hour and included substantial time spent, including making a précis of trial bundle documents before trial, reviewing files, reading Ego Computers Ltd’s skeleton argument (10 hours claimed at a weekend), preparing a draft award (five days claimed), and attending/hearing argument (five days claimed).

United Tyre Company Ltd did not complain again until 24 June 2002, stating it had considered the position with its clients and taken instructions. It identified concerns including letters taking up to two hours to prepare, drafting the award taking five days, reading the skeleton taking ten hours, and the requirement for 170 hours of secretarial assistance. It asked for the documentary basis (“print-out”) underlying the typed list of time.

On 28 June 2002 Mr Born rejected the complaints in a brief letter and stated he did not have a print-out. It was later said (in the context of the court proceedings) that documentation from which the typed list was prepared had been destroyed when the typed list was produced.

On 26 July 2002 United Tyre Company Ltd wrote in more detail, raising particular difficulties including: charging in 15-minute units rather than 6-minute units; allegedly excessive secretarial assistance (said to be partly overhead); room hire costs where one room was said to be Mr Born’s usual room; the time recorded for the hearing said not to match start/finish times; and allegedly excessive time reviewing evidence and trial bundles, many said to contain invoices. It proposed two options: applying for the fees to be assessed, or accepting a £15,000 plus VAT refund in full and final settlement.

There was no direct response from Mr Born. Mr Born retired from his partnership on 2 August 2002. On 15 August 2002 his former firm wrote that he had retired and that a reply would follow after the current senior partner returned from annual vacation.

On 7 October 2002 the firm replied, stating briefly that the matters raised were misconceived and factually incorrect, without explaining why, and asserting that any application for assessment would have been hopelessly out of time.

On 10 October 2002 United Tyre Company Ltd responded that it was usual for the court to permit an assessment to continue where sensible negotiations had taken place, and said it had been attempting to reach agreement.

On 31 October 2002 the firm reiterated its view that any application would be hopelessly out of time and rejected the suggestion that sensible negotiations had taken place.

On 21 November 2002 United Tyre Company Ltd again asked for authority supporting the “out of time” assertion and stated it considered the correspondence since February showed an unhelpful attitude. It also asserted that its client had been charged for time that was not chargeable and said that if a court agreed it would report the matter to relevant professional bodies.

On 3 January 2003 the firm replied that Mr Born and the firm had reviewed the matter and had nothing to add.

There was then a substantial delay until 14 May 2003 when United Tyre Company Ltd issued a court claim seeking review/adjustment of the arbitrator’s fees. The claim was initially issued under the wrong basis but was later corrected. The delay from January 2003 to issue was said on the evidence to be attributable to solicitors and counsel.

In the High Court, the parties agreed to have tried as a preliminary issue whether United Tyre Company Ltd was entitled to have the arbitrator’s fees determined/assessed despite the delay in bringing the claim. Mr Born argued that the delay should bar the claim and also that he had altered his position because he had retired and his fees had been distributed among partners. The judge rejected the suggestion of prejudice and held that, although there had been unreasonable delay and legitimate criticism could be made of United Tyre Company Ltd and its advisers, the claimant had not lost its entitlement to an assessment because there was no real prejudice and because it had given notice at a fairly early stage of its intention to challenge the fees.

Mr Born sought permission to appeal that decision. The Court of Appeal refused permission, holding there was no real prospect of showing the judge had erred in principle or exercised his evaluative judgment outside the permissible range.
claims:
United Tyre Company Ltd sought a court determination and adjustment of Mr Born’s arbitration fees and expenses, including repayment of any amount shown to be excessive. Its position, as reflected in the correspondence and the proceedings, was that the fees charged were unreasonably high and included items and time said to be unjustified.

In particular, United Tyre Company Ltd challenged (among other matters) the scale of the main invoice (£44,900 plus VAT) and the further charges for the costs award, and raised concerns about: the time said to be spent preparing letters (up to two hours); the time claimed for drafting the award (five days); the time claimed for reading a skeleton argument (ten hours); the extent of secretarial assistance (170 hours); the use of 15-minute charging units; room hire charges where one room was said to be the arbitrator’s usual room; the accuracy of the time recorded for the hearing days; and the extent of time spent reviewing trial bundles said largely to contain invoices. It sought underlying documentation supporting the time breakdown.

United Tyre Company Ltd indicated it would apply to court if the matter could not be resolved and proposed a compromise under which it would accept a £15,000 plus VAT refund in full and final settlement.

In the court proceedings, the immediate relief it pursued (and which was addressed as a preliminary issue) was permission/entitlement to proceed with an assessment/determination of the arbitrator’s fees notwithstanding the delay in issuing the claim. It maintained that it had reserved its position when paying to take up the award and had given early notice of its intention to challenge the fees, and that the claim should not be barred merely because it was brought late.

facts:
Stephanie Lawrence and her four children (and the children’s father) came to the attention of Pembrokeshire County Council’s Child Protection Team around 1999. Over the next three years there was sporadic and inconclusive involvement by members of that team. In April 2002 the Council placed the children on the Child Protection Register on the basis that they were at risk of physical and/or emotional harm from Mrs Lawrence and/or the children’s father. The children remained on the Register for about 14 months and were removed from it in June 2003.

In December 2004 the Ombudsman upheld a number of Mrs Lawrence’s complaints of maladministration by the Council and recommended that the Council pay her £5,000 in recognition of distress, damage to her reputation, and the time and trouble she had taken in pursuing her complaints. The Council paid that sum, and it was noted that it would be set off against any damages she might recover in these proceedings.

Mrs Lawrence brought proceedings arising out of the conduct of social workers employed by the Council in relation to the decision to place (and keep) the children on the Child Protection Register. She alleged that the Council’s actions wrongly interfered with family life and caused her psychiatric injury. At first instance, the judge struck out her negligence claim and entered judgment for the Council on that claim. The Council accepted that she had an arguable claim based on interference with family life, but contended that it was brought outside the applicable one-year time limit; whether time should be extended had not yet been decided. The appeal concerned only whether her negligence claim should have been struck out.
claims:
Mrs Lawrence’s pleaded complaints were the same under both heads of claim. She sought relief against the Council on the basis that the Council’s child protection actions—placing her children on the Child Protection Register and keeping them there—wrongly interfered with her family life with her children and caused her psychiatric injury.

She advanced an alternative claim in negligence for personal injury, alleging that the Council (through its social workers) owed her a duty of care when exercising child protection functions in relation to her children and that the Council’s conduct breached that duty, causing her psychiatric harm.

On appeal, her central argument was that, because the right to respect for family life had become enforceable in domestic law, the common law should be developed so that public bodies and their child protection professionals owe a duty of care to parents when investigating suspected parental abuse and/or taking protective steps such as registration. She argued that the statutory remedy for interference with family life should not be the only remedy and that the common law should be brought into line with the protection of family life, including in relation to limitation and remedies.

She also argued that the previous refusal to recognise such a duty was too heavily based on an assumed conflict between the interests of child and parent, and that any conflict of interests did not necessarily mean there must be a conflict of duties; she contended that professionals could take account of both sets of interests without undermining child protection.

As a subsidiary point, she sought to distinguish her case from earlier authority by saying it concerned a local authority and social workers (and the direct role of social workers in registration decisions), rather than healthcare professionals.

facts:
The claimant, CXF, was born on 10 August 1998. He has diagnoses including autistic spectrum disorder, severe to profound learning disabilities, speech and language impairment, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. 

Since 22 June 2016 he has been detained as a patient for treatment. Because of his complex needs and challenging behaviour, there are limited suitable specialist residential placements. As a result, from 4 July 2016 he has been detained at Cawston Park Hospital in Norfolk, about 120 miles from his family home in Bedfordshire.

From August 2016 onwards, the clinician responsible for his care granted him daily leave of absence to go on bus trips, sometimes up to three times a day. A condition of this leave was that he be escorted by two members of hospital staff on each trip. The stated purposes of the leave were leisure, treatment, and relaxation.

The claimant’s mother travels weekly by car from Bedfordshire to visit him and return. During visits she accompanies him on his bus trips and helps him engage in activities such as shopping, walks on the beach, and visits to local attractions. Although there was some dispute about the importance of her presence on the trips, it was not disputed that the bus trips, the associated activities, and the claimant’s face-to-face contact with his mother are therapeutically beneficial.

The cost of the mother’s weekly visits was found to be substantial for her and to cause real financial hardship. Until the claimant turned 18, these expenses were reimbursed by the local authority as part of assistance provided to him as a child in need. That funding stopped when he turned 18, and thereafter his mother bore the costs herself from her social security benefits.

In the judicial review proceedings, the claimant challenged the refusal of the defendants to fund his mother’s travel costs. The first defendant was the local authority for the Bedfordshire area where the claimant’s family home is and where he was ordinarily resident before detention. The second defendant was the clinical commissioning group for the Norfolk area where the hospital is located. Neither defendant was funding the claimant’s hospital care and treatment at Cawston Park Hospital; that was funded by the clinical commissioning group for the Bedfordshire area, which was originally a party but the claim against it was later discontinued.

At first instance, the High Court dismissed the claim, deciding that the relevant duty relied on by the claimant was not triggered because, on the facts, he remained detained and had not ceased to be detained or left hospital when on escorted leave for short trips. The Court of Appeal dismissed the claimant’s appeal on the same basis. The court was told shortly before the appeal hearing that arrangements were being made to move the claimant to a residential placement much nearer to his family home, expected early the next year.
claims:
The claimant sought judicial review of the refusal by each defendant to fund his mother’s travel costs for weekly visits to him at the hospital.

His case was that when he went on escorted day trips under leave of absence, he should be treated as having ceased to be detained and as having left hospital for the purposes of the duty to provide after-care services. On that basis, he argued that the services involved in taking him on those trips were after-care services, and that the duty could extend to funding his mother’s transport costs so she could visit and accompany him on the trips.

He advanced two main arguments on the meaning of the relevant wording: (1) that in the statutory scheme “detained” means detained in a hospital, and (2) that a person cannot be both detained in a hospital and absent from it; therefore, when granted leave of absence, the person is not detained during that absence (even if kept in custody). He argued that whenever a detained patient leaves the hospital premises on such leave, the patient thereby ceases to be detained and leaves hospital.

He also contended that it was not necessary for him to have been formally discharged from hospital for the duty to arise, and that the duty could apply during periods of leave.

In the alternative issues identified as arising if his primary interpretation succeeded, he contended (or sought determinations) that: funding for his mother’s transport costs could in principle fall within the scope of after-care services; that on the facts there was a duty to provide such funding; and that responsibility for the duty lay with the defendants he had sued (though the second defendant disputed that it was the correct clinical commissioning group if any duty existed).

facts:
The case concerned K, a boy aged 16 months. The local authority had been involved with the family for decades, with long-standing concerns including neglect, inconsistent parenting, exposure to domestic violence, and the father’s misuse of alcohol. K became subject to a child protection plan in June 2014 for emotional abuse and neglect.

K’s parents, MH (mother) and JO (father), were married for over twenty years and had five children. The three youngest children (including K) were the subject of earlier public law proceedings begun in June 2013 and concluded in May 2015 with a 12-month supervision order for K. Two other siblings were made subject to care orders and placed with their older sister, SO.

At the final hearing in May 2015, MH’s evidence was that she had not been in a relationship with JO since July 2014. She had gone into a refuge in August 2014 and said she did not want a relationship with him. On the last day of that hearing, the parents signed an agreement that they would refrain from being in a relationship, that JO would not be allowed into the family home, and that MH would inform the local authority of any face-to-face contact and any change in the nature of their relationship.

On 3 June 2015 the local authority learned MH was pregnant (about 11 weeks). This triggered the current proceedings. MH accepted JO was the father but denied they were in a continuing relationship. In early June 2015 the local authority received information from SO that JO had visited MH’s home on 5 June 2015 and consumed a bottle of vodka there. When the social worker visited MH on 9 June 2015, MH confirmed the pregnancy and that JO was the father, but denied being in a relationship and denied allowing him into the property on 5 June. During that visit the social worker telephoned JO; he confirmed he had visited but denied drinking alcohol while there, saying he had consumed alcohol on the way.

Following this, the local authority asked MH to agree to K staying with SO while the matter went to court. MH refused and made threats to kill SO and to harm herself, causing concern about her state of mind and about risks to K. MH agreed to stay with her cousin FF with K, and FF and her partner signed a written agreement, but MH refused to sign.

Earlier professional assessments were before the court. A psychiatric assessment in September 2014 described JO’s alcohol use as deeply ingrained, with poor coping mechanisms and no prior treatment, and expressed the view he would not be able to address his alcohol addiction within 26 weeks. MH was described as anxious, lacking confidence and self-esteem, with limited coping mechanisms, overwhelmed by caring for three children, and ambivalent about separating from JO; she was said not to have a formal mental illness but to need assessment of cognitive functioning. A cognitive assessment found MH had capacity to instruct a solicitor but had low intellectual functioning with a full-scale IQ of 73. A parenting assessment dated 5 March 2015 concluded MH could cope with no more than one child and would need considerable support.

On 11 June 2015 an interim care order was made for K and he was placed with SO. On 22 July 2015 SO told the local authority she could not care for K; she and her partner had their own child and were also caring for K’s two older siblings. K was placed with short-term foster carers on 22 July 2015 and remained there. MH had contact twice weekly. JO’s fortnightly contact was inconsistent. K had weekly contact with his older siblings.

There was a reported incident over the weekend of 25–26 July 2015 of JO attending MH’s home drunk. This led MH to apply for a non-molestation order. During the proceedings MH engaged with the Parents as First Teachers programme, and from July 2015 also engaged with the Freedom Project and a counselling service.

A viability assessment of MH’s cousin TB as a potential carer in September 2015 was negative. At a hearing on 1 September 2015 it was indicated SO’s position had changed and she might be willing to care for K long-term; on 4 September she confirmed in writing she wished to care for him. The local authority was concerned she had been pressurised and did not support placement with her. The children’s guardian reported SO said she could care for K but considered SO had divided loyalties and was probably at the limit of her parenting capacity given the children already in her care.

In the current proceedings it became accepted by both parents that they had lied to the court at the May 2015 final hearing. They accepted there had been a sexual encounter in March 2015 leading to the pregnancy, and that they did not disclose this at the May hearing. They also accepted social services learned of the pregnancy from health professionals rather than from them; MH accepted she knew she was pregnant in April and did not disclose it because she feared K would be removed.

Both parents accepted JO came to MH’s property on 5 June 2015, though they said he only came to the garden gate. JO accepted he had consumed a bottle of vodka on the way there. The court was not persuaded JO had said he went into the house during the 9 June telephone call with the social worker, but considered it of little significance whether he went inside or not.

The parents also accepted JO attended the property over the weekend of 25–26 July 2015 and that he was drunk, though they disputed he entered the house. It was not disputed that on 27 July 2015 JO attended the home drunk, knocked on the door asking to speak to MH, and the police were called.

A contact note of 16 June 2015 recorded MH telling a contact worker that she and JO had been seeing each other at weekends when her son was not at home. MH denied saying this but accepted the rest of the record was accurate; the court found her denial not credible. Considering the evidence as a whole, the court found on the balance of probabilities that the parents had had more contact and sustained more of a relationship than they admitted, had concealed contact from professionals and the court, and had deliberately concealed it at the May hearing.

The court found MH was unlikely to remain separate from JO when vulnerable and that the risk of significant harm to K from domestic violence potentially remained regardless of whether JO was inside or outside the home. The court also found alcohol remained a significant risk factor for JO, relying on his admissions about drinking before the 5 June incident, the role of alcohol around the March encounter, the July incident when he was drunk, his own acceptance he still had to address his drinking, and the guardian’s evidence that he smelled strongly of alcohol at court on 1 September.

As to MH’s parenting, the court noted that concerns remained in May 2015 and that contact notes still recorded negatives as late as September 2015 about basic care (such as timely nappy changing and responding to K’s emotional needs when MH was upset or under strain), despite the contact being intensively supported and coached. The court accepted the guardian’s evidence that the combination of MH’s parenting difficulties and her inability to act protectively in relation to domestic violence, linked to her inability to separate from JO, created a very real likelihood of future emotional harm if K were returned to her care.

The court considered three options: return to MH, placement with SO, or adoption. It rejected return to MH as unrealistic because the risks could not be safely ameliorated, given the parents’ ongoing enmeshment, the likelihood of continued relationship and domestic violence risk, MH’s limited benefit from counselling/therapeutic work, and lack of significant improvement in parenting. It also rejected placement with SO as unrealistic, finding concerns about her commitment, divided loyalties, and capacity given existing responsibilities, and noting she had not made an application to be considered. The court concluded K needed stability and permanency within a timescale that did not allow further waiting, and that adoption was the only realistic option.

The court therefore made a care order and a placement order, endorsing a plan for adoption. It also noted the guardian’s concern about exploring direct sibling contact with prospective adopters, and the local authority’s indication it would pursue this.
claims:
The local authority applied for a care order and a placement order for K, seeking a final care order with a care plan of adoption.

The local authority alleged that K had suffered, or was at risk of suffering, emotional harm and neglect arising from the parents’ domestic violence, the father’s alcohol misuse, and the parents’ dishonesty with professionals and the court. It also alleged K was at risk of physical and emotional harm and neglect due to MH’s vulnerable mental health and inability to parent safely and adequately. Although the parents accepted the threshold for intervention was met, they disputed aspects of the factual basis as drafted and disputed the local authority’s and guardian’s assessment of future risk; the local authority therefore sought specific findings about disputed matters, particularly concerning the continuation and concealment of the parents’ relationship and associated risks.

MH opposed the local authority’s plan and sought K’s return to her care with support from the local authority. JO supported K being returned to MH’s care and did not put himself forward as K’s carer. In the alternative, both parents asked the court to consider placing K with his older sister SO alongside his siblings.

The children’s guardian supported the local authority’s applications for care and placement orders, agreeing that adoption was in K’s best interests. The guardian also raised an issue about post-adoption arrangements, asking that the local authority actively investigate the possibility of direct sibling contact with prospective adopters.

facts:
Bluefin Insurance Services Ltd (trading as Laythorn Blackham Insurance Brokers Ltd) acted as insurance broker for Betbroker Ltd in arranging a directors’ and officers’ liability insurance policy taken out in 2007 with Chartis Europe Ltd/AIG Europe Ltd. Betbroker was the policyholder. Wayne Lochner was a director of Betbroker and, under the policy, was an “insured person” (as was his spouse). Betbroker entered administration on 22 August 2008 and the policy expired on 8 September 2008.

In March 2008 Aberdeen Asset Management (on behalf of its investors) invested about £500,000 in Betbroker Plc. Later, Aberdeen Asset Management alleged that its investment was made in reliance on dishonest misrepresentations said to have been made by Betbroker’s directors, including Mr Lochner, at meetings in January and February 2008, and it also alleged breach of personal covenants given by Mr Lochner and other directors as part of the fundraising. Proceedings were commenced on 7 September 2011. The claims were disputed but were ultimately compromised on terms that resulted in a loss to Mr Lochner.

The policy allowed any insured to notify the insurer during the policy period of circumstances reasonably expected to give rise to a claim. Mr Lochner asserted that, before the policy expired, he informed Bluefin in August 2008 of a possible claim against him and other directors, but that Bluefin failed to pass that notification to the insurer. The insurer later refused cover for Mr Lochner on the basis that it had not received any notice of a claim or relevant circumstances before the policy expired.

After the proceedings began in 2011, Mr Lochner’s solicitors sent Bluefin a copy of the proceedings and asked Bluefin to obtain confirmation from the insurer that the claim would be covered. The insurer maintained its refusal.

On 4 July 2012 the Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS) notified Bluefin that Mr Lochner had made a complaint against it. Bluefin responded on 27 July 2012, disputing the complaint on its substance, and also challenged FOS’s jurisdiction on the basis that Mr Lochner was not eligible to complain.

On 3 May 2013 an ombudsman (Derry Baxter) issued a decision limited to jurisdiction, concluding that FOS could investigate because Mr Lochner was eligible to complain as a “consumer.” The ombudsman reasoned that the relevant question was whether Mr Lochner was acting outside his employment when bringing the complaint; that the policy benefits at issue would go to him as an individual rather than to the former company; and that because he was complaining on his own behalf and not on behalf of the company, he was acting outside his trade, business, or profession.

Bluefin brought judicial review proceedings on 2 August 2013 challenging that jurisdiction decision. Permission was initially refused on the papers but later granted on renewal. The High Court ultimately held that Mr Lochner was not acting for purposes outside his trade, business, or profession when making the complaint, because the complaint was wholly concerned with insurance cover for liabilities arising from alleged wrongful acts committed in his capacity as a director, and therefore quashed FOS’s jurisdiction decision.
claims:
Bluefin sought judicial review to quash FOS’s decision of 3 May 2013 that it had jurisdiction to investigate Mr Lochner’s complaint. Bluefin’s case was that FOS had no jurisdiction because Mr Lochner was not an eligible complainant, specifically not a “consumer” for the purposes of bringing the complaint.

Bluefin argued, first, that whether Mr Lochner was a consumer was a jurisdictional threshold issue for the court to determine (a “precedent fact”), because if he was not a consumer FOS’s compulsory jurisdiction was not engaged.

Alternatively, Bluefin argued that even if the issue was for FOS in the first instance, the ombudsman made legal errors in concluding that Mr Lochner was a consumer and the decision should be quashed on ordinary judicial review grounds. Bluefin contended that FOS adopted the wrong approach by focusing on Mr Lochner’s status when bringing the complaint rather than by reference to the underlying relationship and events giving rise to it (at least by the time of the act or omission complained of). Bluefin also contended that FOS wrongly treated the fact that Mr Lochner complained in his personal capacity (and not on behalf of the company) as sufficient to make him a consumer, which Bluefin said was a non sequitur and effectively collapsed the definition of consumer into “natural person.”

Bluefin’s substantive position was that Mr Lochner’s complaint was inextricably linked to his trade, business, or profession because it concerned alleged failures in handling notification under a policy that protected him against liabilities arising from alleged wrongful acts committed in his role as a director during business fundraising, and the relief sought through the complaint was compensation for loss arising from that business-related liability.

In a further alternative, Bluefin argued that FOS’s conclusion that Mr Lochner was a consumer was irrational.
