facts:
There were three related High Court actions and a case management conference with multiple applications by both sides. During the hearing it emerged that Sheikha Hind had started proceedings in Kuwait in May 2015 against Mr Al Baho which at least duplicated some of the relief sought in the English actions. Mr Al Baho had also brought defamation proceedings in Kuwait against Sheikha Hind, which were struck out; similar defamation proceedings he had brought in England had been discontinued in 2013. After discussion in court, Sheikha Hind was willing to undertake to stay or dismiss the Kuwaiti proceedings so far as they overlapped with the English relief.

The underlying dispute concerns the June 2009 sale of two adjoining London flats (numbers 61 and 62 Porchester Gate) for a documented price of £1.9 million. The flats were registered in the names of two Gibraltar companies, Rosork Holdings Ltd and Fairlann Trading Ltd. The shares in those companies formed part of the estate of Sheikh Salem, who had bought the flats and transferred them to the companies in 1989. Sheikh Salem died intestate domiciled in Kuwait, and his estate devolved under Kuwaiti law. To enable disposal of the property, 12 of 15 heirs executed a power of attorney dated 19 March 2008 appointing Mr Pinnell (then an English solicitor) to represent them and the Kuwaiti estate. Relying on that power of attorney, Mr Pinnell obtained letters of administration in Gibraltar, assumed control of the vendor companies, and directed the sale to Gulf Heritage Properties Ltd, a company controlled by Mr Sajwani.

Mr Meerza and Mr Mehra (property brokers/estate agents) claim a £300,000 commission said to have been agreed with Mr Al Baho (also said to be acting as agent for Sheikha Salem); that commission claim is disputed and was not part of the summary judgment issues addressed at this hearing.

Sheikha Hind’s case is that Mr Al Baho was retained to assist with the sale by introducing a buyer and therefore owed fiduciary duties to the estate, including not to make a profit at the estate’s expense and not to take bribes/secret profits from third parties. She alleges the property was sold at a substantial undervalue (said to be worth about £3 million or not less than £2.5 million). She alleges Mr Al Baho received an extra £600,000 connected with the sale: either as a bribe/secret profit from the purchaser to obtain the property at a reduced price, or as a payment procured by Mr Al Baho on the false basis that it was authorised by the vendors.

Contracts were exchanged on 9 June 2009 and completion took place on 23 June 2009. The completion statement showed the gross price as £1.9 million with deductions, including a 2.5% payment of £47,500 described as payable to Mr Al Baho. After Gulf and Mr Sajwani served their defence, it was revealed that an additional £300,000 was payable on completion by two bankers’ drafts in the names of Rosork and Fairlann, which was not accounted for to the Gibraltar vendor companies.

Sheikha Hind discovered that Mr Al Baho obtained those bankers’ drafts and then incorporated two English companies in August 2009 with identical names to the Gibraltar vendors (Rosork Holdings Limited and Fairlann Trading Limited). Mr Al Baho was initially sole director and then resigned shortly afterwards; the companies were later struck off. Mr Al Baho opened HSBC accounts in the names of “Rosork Holdings Limited” and “Fairlann”; about £300,000 was credited to those accounts, reflecting conversion of the drafts into sterling. The Rosork account was emptied and closed in 2009. The Fairlann account made various payments in October 2009, including payments to BC Penthouse Ltd and to persons involved in construction works for a penthouse at Bryan Court, and was closed in December 2009.

The penthouse at Bryan Court was ultimately vested in BC Penthouse Ltd (BCP), a joint venture vehicle said to be wholly or partly owned by Mr Al Baho. Evidence was relied on that the building works to create the penthouse were done at Mr Al Baho’s behest. A person (Mr Jorge Holtz) asserted he was the beneficial owner of BCP but BCP did not participate in the proceedings. Unilateral notices were lodged against the title to Bryan Court and the penthouse. In August 2012 BCP sold the penthouse for £1,572,629; under an undertaking the net proceeds (stated as £576,628.34) were held by MA Law pending the outcome of the proceedings.

There was also an HSBC account in Sheikh Salem’s name with a balance of £19,645.31 which was closed in May 2012 and paid to Mr Al Baho. HSBC said it paid out on the basis of written authority from the then named administrator (Sheikha Salem). Sheikha Salem denied giving permission for Mr Al Baho to receive those monies.

Gulf and Mr Sajwani admitted making the £300,000 payments by bankers’ drafts in the names of Rosork and Fairlann, but denied dishonesty and denied the payments were a bribe; they said they did not know what Mr Al Baho would do regarding the “clone” companies. The court treated those issues as matters for trial.

Procedurally, there was dispute about Sheikha Hind’s standing to sue on behalf of the estate in earlier actions because she did not have letters of administration in England and Wales when those actions were started; she later obtained a grant in March 2012. The judgment records that the defendants did not initially object to her title to sue and only later sought to put it in issue. The judgment also records that Sheikha Hind obtained assignments of any causes of action the vendor companies might have, so she could sue either as assignee of the companies’ causes of action or as administrator depending on the true beneficial ownership analysis.

At the hearing Mr Al Baho attempted a late jurisdiction challenge based on parallel Kuwaiti proceedings; the court dismissed it as tactical and abusive, noting his prior participation and earlier submission to the English jurisdiction. The court accepted Sheikha Hind’s undertaking to stay or dismiss the Kuwaiti action so far as it reflected the relief sought in England.

Mr Al Baho did not serve a defence or evidence addressing the substantive allegations. BCP also did not acknowledge service or defend, despite the court being satisfied it had been validly served and was aware of the proceedings.
claims:
The claimants sought case management and substantive relief including: permission to amend the pleadings so that a draft amended and consolidated particulars of claim would stand across the actions; summary judgment (or alternatively default judgment) for Sheikha Hind against Mr Al Baho, Mr Pinnell and/or BCP; payment out of security for costs lodged in court; and dismissal of various defendant applications.

On the merits, Sheikha Hind’s claims arise from the 2009 sale of the Porchester Gate flats. She alleges Mr Al Baho was retained to assist with the sale and thereby owed fiduciary duties to the estate. She contends he breached those duties by obtaining secret profits and/or bribes connected with the sale and by profiting at the estate’s expense. She alleges an additional £600,000 was received by Mr Al Baho in connection with the transaction (either as a bribe/secret profit from the purchaser to secure the property at a reduced price, or as an unauthorised payment procured by him on a false basis). She also alleges the property was sold at a substantial undervalue.

Sheikha Hind sought monetary recovery in relation to the additional £300,000 revealed to have been paid by bankers’ drafts and not accounted for to the vendor companies, and she also sought recovery of other sums said to have been taken from the sale proceeds at the direction of Mr Pinnell and Sheikha Salem, including £47,500 described as commission paid to Mr Al Baho and a further £88,339 identified in the evidence as paid out of the sale proceeds.

Sheikha Hind further sought proprietary and/or accounting relief in relation to the Bryan Court penthouse proceeds held by MA Law. Her case was that monies obtained by Mr Al Baho in breach of fiduciary duty were used to acquire and develop the penthouse, and that the net proceeds held by MA Law represented profit from misuse of estate monies. She sought a declaration that those monies belonged to the estate and that Mr Al Baho should account for them; alternatively she contended they were held on constructive trust for the estate. She also pursued relief against BCP in respect of those proceeds.

In argument on the interim relief application, Sheikha Hind contended it was not necessary at that stage to prove the £300,000 was a bribe because Mr Al Baho would be liable for breach of fiduciary duty in any event; however she maintained that if it were a bribe she could recover it and also pursue damages for breach of fiduciary duty without giving credit for the bribe against those damages. She ultimately sought payment of the £300,000 (and also the £47,500 and £88,339) as interim payments pending final determination.

Separately, in response to the emergence of parallel Kuwaiti proceedings, Sheikha Hind (through counsel) offered an undertaking to stay or dismiss the Kuwaiti proceedings so far as they duplicated the relief sought in England.

As against BCP, Sheikha Hind sought judgment because BCP had not acknowledged service or defended, and she sought an order enabling the monies held by MA Law (the net proceeds of the penthouse sale) to be paid out to her for the benefit of the estate.

facts:
HE is the father of AE, a 24-year-old woman. The family are Muslims, but after HE and AE’s mother separated, AE and her brother lived with their mother, who became a Jehovah’s Witness; AE was then brought up as a Jehovah’s Witness.

AE has a congenital heart problem and had surgery as a child, knowing further surgery would be needed in adulthood. On 13 February 2001 AE signed a pre-printed advance medical directive, witnessed by two ministers of her church. In it she consented to emergency treatment and surgery but expressly refused transfusion of blood or primary blood components in any circumstances, stating that this refusal was absolute and not to be overridden by relatives, and that the directive would remain in force unless she revoked it in writing.

On 29 November 2002 AE was seen by a doctor at a hospital in the Midlands town where the family lived. She had aortic valve disease. The notes recorded her as a Jehovah’s Witness and indicated planned surgery using measures to stimulate blood production without blood products.

On 20 April 2003 AE became seriously ill and was rushed by ambulance to London. HE reported that as she left she said to her brother, in the presence of her maternal aunt, “I don’t want to die.” AE was admitted on 21 April 2003 to the adult intensive care unit of a London teaching hospital (the first defendant), under the care of Dr B. Dr B stated that on admission AE was in extremis with overwhelming septic shock secondary to bacterial endocarditis. During severe sepsis she sustained significant peripheral circulatory damage with extensive necrosis of her hands and feet, likely requiring debridement or partial amputation, which would be impossible without significant blood loss.

On admission AE’s mother told the hospital AE was a Jehovah’s Witness and should not receive blood or blood products. Dr B described extensive discussions with the mother and other family members explaining that refusal would greatly increase the risk of death, that trivial haemorrhage could be fatal, and that emergency valve surgery would be impossible. The mother and her relatives remained adamant that the hospital should follow the advance directive despite the increased risk of death, and treatment continued accordingly.

AE was sedated and remained unconscious. With aggressive intervention her condition was stabilised for a time, with steps taken to minimise blood taken for testing and to stimulate haemopoiesis with erythropoetin and iron. Her condition later deteriorated. By 2 May 2003 Dr B reported continued sepsis (from the heart or gangrenous feet), falling haemoglobin, rising blood lactate, and an impending terminal decline. He stated it seemed inevitable she would die within 24 hours on current treatment, though blood transfusion might slow or reverse deterioration; survival was not assured even with transfusion.

On 1 May 2003 Dr B had a further discussion with the family. Dr B reported that AE’s mother and brother remained adamant AE would not wish to receive blood products even given impending death, while AE’s father, grandmother and fiancé insisted to the contrary. HE stated the consultant confirmed AE must receive a blood transfusion immediately to live and that transfusion would give her a substantial chance of survival, otherwise she would most certainly die within about 36 hours.

The hospital considered it could not override the advance directive without court intervention. An urgent application was made on 2 May 2003. The hospital was not represented at court due to late notice, but provided Dr B’s statement and documents. The Official Solicitor attended at short notice and agreed to act as AE’s litigation friend because AE was sedated, unconscious, and incapable of managing her affairs.

HE asserted that AE had rejected her Jehovah’s Witness faith since December 2002, was betrothed to marry a Turkish Muslim man and had agreed as a condition of marriage to revert to Islam; she had stopped attending Jehovah’s Witness meetings from early January 2003; and during a recent two-day hospital admission before her collapse she did not mention refusing blood transfusion or the directive. HE also relied on AE’s statement “I don’t want to die,” and said she would have consented to transfusion if conscious, particularly because her fiancé had recently arrived from Turkey and she wanted to be with him.

The judge concluded there was doubt as to the continuing validity and applicability of the advance directive and declared AE lacked capacity to decide about treatment. The court declared it lawful, in AE’s best interests, for the hospital and its staff to administer such treatment, including blood transfusions, as the treating medical staff judged to be in her best interests.
claims:
HE sought urgent court intervention to allow doctors to give AE life-saving treatment including blood transfusions, which the hospital said it could not provide because of AE’s earlier advance directive refusing blood.

HE asked the court to order (or declare) that the hospital proceed with any medical intervention required to keep AE alive, including blood transfusion, stating this was her last chance of survival and time was running out.

In support, HE argued the advance directive should not be relied upon because it predated a change in AE’s faith and circumstances. He contended AE had rejected her Jehovah’s Witness faith from December 2002, had agreed to revert to Islam as a condition of marrying her Muslim fiancé, and had acted consistently with that decision by ceasing to attend Jehovah’s Witness meetings from early January 2003. He also relied on the fact that during a recent hospital admission before her collapse AE did not mention refusing blood transfusion or the directive, and on her reported statement shortly before transfer to London that she did not want to die.

HE’s position was that, given these matters, AE would have consented to a blood transfusion if she were conscious, and that the directive was no longer valid or effective (or at least was sufficiently in doubt) so that the court should authorise treatment in her best interests.

facts:
The dispute arose from alleged subsidence damage to the plaintiffs’ house at 12 The Avenue, London NW6, which the plaintiffs said they first noticed in May 1989. The plaintiffs were the freehold owners and occupiers of number 12, a semi-detached property adjoining number 14.

Number 14 was divided into flats and, over the years, there had been several dealings in the freehold and leasehold interests. The plaintiffs joined 15 defendants because they alleged that each had, or had previously had, an interest in the whole or part of number 14.

The plaintiffs alleged that the damage to number 12 was caused by tree roots from trees on the property at number 14, described in their pleading as “a number of trees, namely, a large sycamore tree, fruit trees and a black poplar tree.” The fifth defendant, Mr Michael Dodson, was the leasehold owner of the garden flat at number 14 together with part of the rear garden, separated by fencing from the remainder of the garden over which other lessees had rights. In Mr Dodson’s demised garden there was a single tree, a pear tree. In the remainder of the rear garden of number 14 there were a poplar tree, a flowering cherry tree and a sycamore tree, none particularly close to number 12. There was also a sycamore tree in the small front garden of number 14 close to number 12. There were also several trees in the rear gardens of number 12 and number 10.

Before proceedings, the plaintiffs’ solicitors carried out Land Registry searches and made enquiries of solicitors acting for a number of leaseholders (including Mr Dodson) to identify who held leasehold interests over time and to see lease terms relevant to responsibility for trees. At that stage, the plaintiffs had not identified any particular tree as the cause. The leaseholders’ solicitors stated their clients’ position that the areas where the trees were situated were not within their demises and referred the plaintiffs to the freeholders; they refused to provide further information.

The action was started by writ dated 26 October 1995 and was renewed three times due to difficulty locating some defendants; four defendants were never served. A statement of claim was served on 27 March 1996. Defences were initially limited to issues about the defendants’ interests in the property, with causation issues deferred pending further particulars identifying, among other things, the precise location of the sycamore and poplar trees.

Limited defences were served in September and November 1996 by several defendants including Mr Dodson. Mr Dodson’s limited defence stated that he could not address responsibility for the relevant trees until further particulars were served, but it also disclosed that he was assignee of a lease of the garden flat and part of the garden and annexed the lease, which defined the garden for which he was responsible. It also stated the lease had been granted by a particular company and expressed a belief about a later freehold owner; it annexed a tenancy agreement for the garden flat and stated another defendant had lived there but had no legal interest. Despite this information, the action continued against other defendants.

Further and better particulars were not served until 1 May 1997. Although the plan attached showed the pear tree, the parties’ attention focused on the sycamore and poplar trees, and the plaintiffs’ response to a request for particulars did not indicate that the pear tree was important.

At some stage, a person believed to hold the freehold was added in separate proceedings that were consolidated; the plaintiffs obtained judgment against him without trial, though there was doubt about his ability to satisfy it.

In June, July and September 1997, the plaintiffs agreed with all effective defendants other than Mr Dodson that proceedings against them would be discontinued on terms that the plaintiffs pay their costs (sometimes agreed, sometimes to be assessed), and consent orders were made.

Expert meetings took place between the plaintiffs and Mr Dodson. On 17 December 1998 the experts signed an agreed statement: they agreed the pear tree was not solely responsible for the damage but possibly made some contribution; if it were established that the pear tree had encroached and caused damage, its contribution would be 7% of the total relevant costs, though they disagreed on what the total relevant costs were.

On 18 December 1998 Mr Dodson paid £5,000 into court. On the last day for acceptance, the plaintiffs accepted that sum as “full and final satisfaction of all the causes of action” in respect of which they claimed. By then, Mr Dodson was the only remaining effective defendant. The trial date (12 January 1999) was used to argue the plaintiffs’ application for a special costs order rather than to try the substantive claim.
claims:
After accepting Mr Dodson’s payment into court, the plaintiffs sought a special order for costs against him. They asked that Mr Dodson be ordered to pay not only the plaintiffs’ costs of the action against him, but also the costs the plaintiffs had incurred in bringing the action against the other 14 defendants and the costs the plaintiffs had paid to some of those other defendants when the plaintiffs discontinued against them.

In support of that request, the plaintiffs argued that it had been reasonable to institute proceedings against all defendants and to continue those proceedings for as long as they did. They relied in particular on the lack of information provided pre-action by Mr Dodson and other defendants about title and lease responsibilities, which the plaintiffs said affected their ability to identify who was responsible.

The plaintiffs also sought to distinguish other decisions relied on by the fifth defendant by contending that, unlike cases involving several liability, this case involved defendants originally sued jointly or in the alternative, and they contended this supported the court making the special costs order they sought.

facts:
The proceedings arose out of a dispute between Nigel Witham Ltd (the claimant) and Mr Robert Lesley Smith and Miss Jacqueline Isaacs (the defendants) concerning the claimant’s entitlement to fees and other sums in relation to work connected with the refurbishment of hotels.

After a five-day trial, the court’s principal judgment resulted (after adjustments for VAT and interest) in a net position that the claimant owed the defendants £1,683. The defendants were treated as the overall successful party because, looking at the outcome as a whole, the claimant did not establish that the defendants owed it further money.

The claimant advanced two substantial heads of claim—(i) a claim for legal costs by way of fees and (ii) a claim for sums said to be due as a consequence of a suspension—both of which failed entirely. The claimant’s entitlement to a percentage fee was found to be considerably less than claimed and close to the figure advanced by the defendants. The claimant also pursued a variations claim which stood at £61,745.50 by the end of trial, but recovered £24,748, again closer to the defendants’ figure of £16,468.

The defendants had brought counterclaims that survived until the start of trial, including a counterclaim alleging negligent cost estimates produced by the claimant during the contract and a counterclaim concerning listed building consent. By closing submissions, only the listed building consent counterclaim was pursued, and it was valued at £1,000. The negligent cost-estimates counterclaim was abandoned late (in closing submissions). The defendants had twice sought permission to introduce a second expert (a quantity surveyor) to address the cost-estimates issue; permission was refused. Despite that refusal, the defendants’ architectural expert sought to rely on a report by independent quantity surveyors (Jackson Rowe), which the court ruled inadmissible on the first day of trial. The court considered there were inherent difficulties with the cost-estimates counterclaim because the criticised figures were estimates and the ultimate cost would depend on contractor tenders; the court also regarded as unrealistic the first defendant’s evidence that he would have terminated the claimant earlier had he known the likely out-turn cost, given contemporaneous documents showing the defendants knew early on that the full scheme might exceed budget and wanted to understand the whole-scheme cost to decide what to proceed with.

On costs, the defendants produced a schedule showing gross costs of solicitors (£73,762.50), counsel (£16,425), and experts (£33,246.35), total £123,433.85, excluding (a) costs of an architect’s report (Mr Calcroft) commissioned by previous solicitors but not relied on and considered irrelevant, and (b) the Jackson Rowe report. The court ruled that neither of those two expert-report costs was recoverable.

There was extensive correspondence about mediation/ADR. The court found the defendants did not refuse to mediate; they consistently said mediation was possible but premature until the claimant properly set out its claim. The court considered that stance not unreasonable given the claimant’s delay in setting out details and later radical amendments after proceedings began. The court also considered it unlikely that early mediation would have settled the dispute, noting the claimant’s uncompromising attitude in communications.

The defendants made a settlement offer of £10,000 plus the claimant’s costs in October 2007, open for acceptance until 2 November 2007, and the defendants ultimately did better than that offer. The court nevertheless held it would be unjust for the defendants to recover 100% of their costs after 2 November 2007 because they should not recover costs of the abandoned counterclaim, particularly given its late abandonment.

The court ordered that the defendants recover 85% of their costs (reflecting a 15% reduction for the abandoned negligent-estimates counterclaim), with interest on that 85% from 2 November 2007. The court also ordered an interim payment on account of costs, calculated by taking the defendants’ total costs at about £123,000, applying the 15% reduction, making a further reduction to reflect non-recoverable settlement-conference costs, and awarding 40% of the resulting figure: £41,200, payable by 6 February 2008.
claims:
The claimant sought to recover money from the defendants said to be due under the parties’ arrangements for the hotel refurbishment work. In particular, the claimant advanced two substantial heads of claim: (1) a claim for legal costs by way of fees, and (2) a claim for sums said to be due as a consequence of a suspension. The claimant also pursued a claim for a percentage fee at a higher level than the defendants contended for, and pursued a variations claim which by the end of trial was put at £61,745.50.

In addition, in the post-judgment costs dispute, the claimant (through submissions on costs) sought to reduce the amount of costs recoverable by the defendants. The claimant relied principally on the defendants’ late-abandoned counterclaim alleging negligent cost estimates, arguing that this unsuccessful counterclaim justified a percentage reduction in the defendants’ recoverable costs. The claimant also argued for further reductions on the basis that the defendants’ counterclaim led to additional expert costs (because the case proceeded with separate experts rather than a single joint expert), that the claimant had been successful on the variations claim, and that the defendants had unreasonably delayed mediation until late in the dispute. The claimant also relied on the parties’ earlier without-prejudice offers in support of its position on costs.

facts:
Mr and Mrs Khan owned and lived at 68 Dennis Lane, Stanmore. Their neighbour to the right, Mrs Helen Sheila Kane, owned 62 Dennis Lane and had trees on her land, including a Lawson cypress hedge (referred to as H1) running close to the boundary and an oak tree at the front of her property (T1). An extension had been built on the right-hand side of 68 Dennis Lane around 1982, close to the boundary with 62 Dennis Lane. Mrs Kane and her late husband bought 62 Dennis Lane in April 1982.

Before buying 68 Dennis Lane, the Khans obtained a survey in November 2000 which noted mature trees and shrubs (including oak and weeping willow) and advised insuring particularly against subsidence and related risks. The Khans purchased 68 Dennis Lane in July 2001.

In September 2006 the Khans noticed cracking damage to their house. They notified their insurer, which appointed loss adjusters (Carmichaels). Carmichaels inspected and advised further investigation and monitoring before repairs. Structural consultants (PBA) were engaged around April 2007. PBA began monitoring movement at various crack locations and carried out investigations including trial pits on the right-hand side of the property. Arboricultural consultants reported in July 2007 that the Lawson cypress hedge on Mrs Kane’s land had the potential to be a significant factor in the damage and recommended removing a section to achieve at least 5 metres clearance from the Khans’ property, while maintaining the retained section. They also recommended that two front oak trees—one on Mrs Kane’s land (T1) and one on the Khans’ land (T2)—should not be allowed to exceed their current dimensions as an action to avoid future risk.

Further investigations included boreholes in June 2008 near the front right-hand corner of the Khans’ house. Roots recovered from one borehole at 1 metre depth included a conifer root consistent with cypress-type roots; at 2 metres depth ash roots were identified.

Carmichaels’ representative said he wrote to Mrs Kane in September 2007 and May 2008 about the damage and the need for cooperation in tree management, but those letters were addressed to a non-existent address (66 Dennis Lane) and to “Owner/Occupier.” Mrs Kane said she did not receive them. In June 2009 the Khans’ solicitors wrote to Mrs Kane (though the letter was confusingly addressed), after which Mrs Kane contacted her insurer.

In June 2009 PBA reported increased and new damage and carried out further investigations at the front of the property. The Khans’ solicitors asserted that the cypress hedge was the most likely cause of damage to the right-hand side and requested that the nuisance be abated by felling those trees. The Khans’ arboricultural expert reported that the cypresses were most likely the material cause of damage to the right-hand side and recommended felling all cypress trees within 5 metres of the right-hand side of the building. In early July 2009 the cypress trees adjacent to the right-hand wall of the Khans’ house were removed.

In October 2009 the Khans’ arboricultural expert issued an addendum stating that, after removal of the cypresses and in light of further investigation and survey results, it was clear that one or both of the front oak trees (T1 on Mrs Kane’s land and T2 on the Khans’ land) were a material cause of damage, and recommended felling both. In December 2009 Carmichaels wrote to Mrs Kane stating that approval had been granted to fell the oaks and sought her approval for felling T1. Both oaks (T1 and T2) were subsequently felled.

The claim originally included Harrow Council (owner of land to the left of the Khans’ property), but that part of the proceedings was settled. Proceedings were issued in March 2011 and later amended to include a claim against Mrs Kane for damage to the right-hand side of the Khans’ property said to have been caused by the cypress hedge (H1) and the oak tree (T1).

Experts divided the right-hand side damage into Areas A, B and C. The engineering experts agreed that Area A (the rear extension/office) was caused solely by the cypress hedge H1. They agreed Area C was caused by the two oaks T1 and T2, contributing equally. They disagreed on Area B (part of the sitting room): one view was that H1, T1 and T2 all influenced it; the other was that it was principally caused by T1 and T2. The court preferred the evidence that H1 also influenced Area B, and found that H1’s influence on the right-hand side was established in both Areas A and B.

On foreseeability, the court found that a reasonably prudent landowner ought generally to be aware of a risk of subsidence damage caused by tree roots, particularly on clay soils, but that general awareness alone was not enough to make damage from any particular tree foreseeable. The court found that, given the location, size, dominance and condition of the Lawson cypress hedge H1 very close to the Khans’ property, a reasonably prudent landowner would have appreciated a real risk of subsidence damage from H1. By contrast, the court found that a reasonably prudent landowner would not have appreciated a real risk of subsidence damage from the oak tree T1 on the evidence.

The court found Mrs Kane failed to take appropriate steps to eliminate the foreseeable risk posed by H1 before damage occurred, and held her liable in nuisance for damage caused by H1, but not for damage caused by T1. The court also found contributory negligence by the Khans at 15% because they did not communicate directly with Mrs Kane about the risks and damage for a prolonged period.

The Khans claimed remedial repair costs, loss adjusters’ fees, and general damages for distress and inconvenience. The court held that costs relating to investigation of an underpinning scheme were recoverable. Using an apportionment that attributed 29.3% of the relevant damage to H1, the court assessed damages attributable to Mrs Kane for H1-related damage and then reduced the award by 15% for contributory negligence, resulting in an award of £17,269.84 (with interest and costs to be agreed or determined later).
claims:
Mr and Mrs Khan brought a claim alleging that their house at 68 Dennis Lane suffered subsidence-related damage caused by encroaching tree roots from neighbouring land. After settling their claim against Harrow Council (relating to trees on the left-hand side), they pursued Mrs Kane as the neighbouring owner to the right.

Against Mrs Kane, the Khans alleged that the Lawson cypress hedge on her property (H1) and her front oak tree (T1) caused damage to the right-hand side of their house. They pleaded causes of action in nuisance and negligence and asserted that the risk of subsidence damage (and/or its continuation) was, or ought reasonably to have been, foreseeable to Mrs Kane. In support of foreseeability, they contended that it was reasonably foreseeable to a person owning or controlling multiple trees that roots could cause damage to property, that this was common knowledge reinforced by media reporting, and they relied on examples of newspaper articles and on the fact that Mrs Kane had buildings insurance.

They sought abatement of the alleged nuisance by tree works: in June 2009 they asserted the cypress hedge was the most likely cause of the damage and requested that the nuisance be abated by felling the cypress trees, and their expert recommended felling all cypress trees within 5 metres of the right-hand side of the building.

They claimed monetary compensation including: (1) the cost of remedial works to repair the damage to the property; (2) loss adjusters’ fees said to relate to investigating the damage and arranging remedial works; (3) general damages for distress and inconvenience; and they also sought recovery of fees incurred in relation to an underpinning scheme which did not proceed.

They resisted the defence allegations of contributory negligence and failure to mitigate, contending that they were entitled to rely on professional advice and that any blameworthiness on their part was significantly less than Mrs Kane’s, given her control of the hedge close to their property.

facts:
The appellant arrived in the United Kingdom and claimed asylum in January 2010. Her asylum claim was refused and her appeal was dismissed by the First-tier Tribunal in a decision dated 19 April 2010. She later made fresh representations. On 8 September 2015 the respondent refused her asylum claim again.

The appellant appealed that refusal. In a decision dated 26 April 2017 the First-tier Tribunal dismissed the appeal. In doing so, it did not accept much of the appellant’s account and rejected her claim to be a Somali citizen from the Ashraf clan, and rejected her account that her first husband had died.

Permission to appeal to the Upper Tribunal was granted on 13 July 2017. It was noted that the First-tier Tribunal had failed to take into account, among other matters, evidence from the appellant’s Somali Ashraf husband and evidence said to show the appellant was not entitled to lawful residence in Kenya. The respondent filed a notice dated 2 August 2017 maintaining that the First-tier Tribunal’s findings were open to it.

At the Upper Tribunal hearing, the respondent conceded that the First-tier Tribunal decision contained important gaps and material inconsistencies and should be set aside.

The Upper Tribunal identified that the First-tier Tribunal had failed to take into account or give adequate reasons for rejecting important evidence, including: evidence from the appellant’s second Somali Ashraf husband that he could verify she is Somali Ashraf based on accent, dialect and culture; evidence from the appellant and her second husband concerning the appellant being told her first husband had died and that, at the time of the second marriage, the religious officiant ensured the first husband was deceased; medical evidence that the appellant had undergone type 3 female genital mutilation (said to be more common in Somalia than Kenya); evidence about the position of the appellant’s vaccination scar being consistent with early childhood in Somalia rather than Kenya; the conclusion of a language analysis report that the appellant speaks a variety of South Somali found in Kenya and certain parts of southern Somalia (including the Gedo area), which was consistent with her account that she was born in Gedo and lived there until being taken to Kenya to live in refugee camps at age 4 in 1993; and country background evidence about the situation of Somalis in Kenya.

The Upper Tribunal also found internal inconsistencies in the First-tier Tribunal’s findings on pivotal issues: it found the appellant was of Somali extraction but had lived in Kenya throughout her life, yet elsewhere appeared to accept she and her mother may have lived in Mogadishu; and it reasoned that the appellant would not be returned to Somalia as a lone woman due to lack of evidence her first husband was dead, while also appearing to accept that she had met, married, and was having a baby with her second husband who supported her in the UK.

Further, the Upper Tribunal found the First-tier Tribunal’s conclusion that the appellant was Kenyan and could lawfully reside in Kenya was unsupported and inadequately reasoned. The language analysis report indicated it was equally likely she was from Kenya or Somalia’s Gedo region. The First-tier Tribunal treated the absence of evidence that Kenya would refuse her admission as a basis to be satisfied she was Kenyan, without giving reasons for rejecting the appellant’s evidence (supported by her second husband) that she had only temporary residence in Kenya and no lawful basis to live there, and without addressing relevant country background evidence.

The Upper Tribunal concluded the First-tier Tribunal had materially erred in law, set aside its decision, and remitted the case to the First-tier Tribunal for a complete rehearing with fresh findings of fact.
claims:
The appellant’s protection claim was that she is a citizen of Somalia and would face a risk of persecution because she is from the Ashraf minority clan and because she would be returned as a lone woman.

In pursuing her appeal against the refusal decision of 8 September 2015, she maintained that she is Somali (from the Gedo region) and that her circumstances and supporting evidence corroborated this, including evidence from her second husband about her Somali Ashraf identity and cultural/linguistic markers, evidence relating to her first husband’s death and the circumstances of her remarriage, medical evidence concerning type 3 female genital mutilation, evidence about a vaccination scar consistent with early childhood in Somalia, and language analysis findings consistent with her account of origins in southern Somalia and later residence in Kenya as a child in refugee camps.

She also advanced the position that she did not have a lawful basis to reside in Kenya and that relevant country background material supported her account about the position of Somalis in Kenya.

Before the Upper Tribunal, the relief sought (and ultimately obtained) was that the First-tier Tribunal decision dismissing her appeal be set aside due to errors in its credibility assessment and reasoning, and that the appeal be remitted for a fresh hearing and fresh findings of fact.

facts:
Mr R H Syed was employed by the Department of Social Security (later the Department for Work and Pensions) from 4 May 1993 in the substantive grade of Administrative Officer (AO). In May 1997 he moved to the visits section of the Ealing District office of the Benefits Agency. He was a member of the Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS). The PCS branch secretary covering the Ealing office was Mr Ford, who worked at the Acton office.

From 1996 there was a dispute between the union and management about proposals to reorganise the grading of work done by visiting officers. The union’s position was that duties properly graded at Executive Officer (EO) level were being carried out by AO staff without AO staff being paid at the higher rate.

After lengthy negotiations, management issued a notice dated 1 December 1999 stating that agreement had been reached with the union side to re-grade certain “new claimant visiting” work to EO grade, with implementation to take effect on 1 February 2000. Before implementation, the union (through Mr Ford) sought back pay for affected AO staff who had been doing EO-grade work. The back payment sought was referred to as a Higher Duty Allowance (HDA).

On 5 June 2000 management agreed to make back payments only as far back as 5 April 1999. The union pressed for back payments earlier than 5 April 1999, but management would not agree. By letter dated 19 October 2000 (misdated 1999), Mr Ford wrote to the Area Director, Mr Whitehead, registering disagreement with management’s refusal to pay HDA for the period before 5 April 1999 and indicating that complaints of unlawful deductions from wages would be made to the Employment Tribunal.

Mr Syed presented a complaint to the Employment Tribunal on 20 December 2000. Other AO employees also presented complaints, which were stayed pending the outcome of this appeal.

It was common ground in the proceedings that collective agreements reached through the negotiating machinery were incorporated into the individual contracts of employment of affected staff.

The Employment Tribunal heard a preliminary issue on whether Mr Syed’s unlawful deductions claim was time-barred. The Tribunal treated the claim as including (in addition to the back-pay issue) further alleged shortfalls identified in Mr Ford’s written submission. The Tribunal dismissed the first element (relating to backdating of HDA prior to 5 April 1999) as out of time and did not make findings or determinations on the further alleged shortfalls. On appeal, the Employment Appeal Tribunal upheld the Tribunal’s approach to the first element but held that the second and third elements had not been adjudicated and therefore remitted those elements for a full merits hearing before a fresh Tribunal, with permission for Mr Syed to amend his originating application to plead those elements in detail.
claims:
Mr Syed brought a complaint of unlawful deductions from wages against his employer.

As presented to the Tribunal (and as expanded by Mr Ford’s written submission), the claim was said to relate to a series of alleged deductions/shortfalls comprising:

1) A claimed difference in earnings for the period 12 May 1997 to 1 April 1999, linked to the contention that AO staff (including Mr Syed) had been performing EO-grade visiting duties and should have received higher pay/Higher Duty Allowance, including back pay for the period before 5 April 1999.

2) A claimed shortfall in earnings arising from pay progression for the period 12 May 1997 to 18 December 2000.

3) A claimed shortfall in his contributions to the Principal Civil Service Pension Scheme, said to follow from the alleged pay shortfalls.

In relation to the pre–5 April 1999 back-pay issue, the union (on behalf of affected staff including Mr Syed) sought back payments earlier than 5 April 1999 and, when management refused, indicated that unlawful deductions complaints would be pursued in the Employment Tribunal.

Before the Employment Tribunal, Mr Syed’s case also included an argument directed to time limits: he relied on the details of his pay as at 30 November 2000 and contended that his claim had been lodged within three months of that date.

On appeal, Mr Syed sought to overturn the dismissal of his unlawful deductions complaint as time-barred. The Employment Appeal Tribunal rejected the appeal so far as it concerned the first element (pre–5 April 1999 HDA back-pay), but allowed the appeal in part because the Tribunal had not determined the second and third elements; those elements were remitted for rehearing, and Mr Syed was given permission to amend his originating application to set out the second and third elements (including merits and timeliness) with particularity.

facts:
The claimant, Ms Lamya Nageh, was employed by David Game College Ltd from 1 July 1997. Mr David Game was the principal of the college. Over time she was promoted to Senior Course Co-ordinator and then to Director of Admissions and Head of GCSE.

On 21 November 2007 she raised a grievance complaining about a variety of matters arising out of her employment. She last attended work around 7 February 2008 and thereafter remained absent due to stress and depression.

While she was absent, the respondents appointed Dr Ian Moores (principal of an associated college) to investigate her grievance. Dr Moores issued a written adjudication on 19 January 2009 rejecting her complaints and/or not dealing with some of them. In his covering letter he invited her to raise any points in writing by a stated deadline of 30 January 2009 and asked that any response be sent by recorded delivery.

The claimant did not say she complied with that deadline or the recorded-delivery requirement. She maintained that she responded at length by letter dated 16 February 2009. Dr Moores said he never received that letter; the Employment Judge noted that the claimant’s copy bore an incorrect postcode. No finding was made at the pre-hearing review as to whether the letter was sent or received.

There was then no further correspondence or contact between the parties until 5 January 2010, when the claimant wrote to Mr Game complaining she had heard nothing further from him or Dr Moores. In that letter she asserted that during the period she had been waiting for a response and resolution, the respondents had terminated her salary, taken over her office, appointed another staff member to her position and job role, removed her from staff lists and materials, and “wiped [her] out” without speaking to her. She also stated that she continued officially to remain employed.

In response, Dr Moores wrote on 13 January 2010 denying receipt of any reply from her and stating that her employment had ended by reason of prolonged and unexplained absence. It was common ground that her employment had terminated, but the parties disagreed as to when and how. The claimant’s position was that the effective date of termination was 13 January 2010.

In April 2010 the claimant presented tribunal proceedings. Some allegations related to or arose on dismissal. Others pre-dated dismissal and largely pre-dated 7 February 2008, but she also complained about how the grievance process was conducted and about events during her absence, including the alleged failure to respond to her 16 February 2009 letter, the alleged failure to contact her after that date, and the alleged actions of taking over her office, forcing it open and emptying her personal property, appointing someone else to her role, and removing her from staff lists and materials.

The respondents contended that all pre-dismissal claims were out of time. A pre-hearing review was listed to determine, among other things, whether the claim should be struck out for having no reasonable prospect of success because of time limits. At that pre-hearing review the Employment Judge concluded there had been no contact between the parties from January/February 2009 to January 2010 and treated the claimant’s continuing-act argument as resting essentially on lack of contact alone. She declared that the claimant had no reasonable prospect of success in arguing that the pre-dismissal discrimination claims comprised a continuing act/act extending over a period, leaving the claimant to pursue (if she wished) an argument for an extension of time.

On appeal, the Employment Appeal Tribunal held that the Employment Judge had taken too narrow a view of the claimant’s case. The claimant’s pleaded case for the relevant period was not merely lack of contact, but that she was ignored while being replaced and removed from the workplace and staff materials, and only told her employment had ended after she made contact. The declaration was set aside and the matter was remitted for further case management consideration.
claims:
In her tribunal claim (issued April 2010), the claimant advanced pre-dismissal complaints of race discrimination, sexual harassment, discrimination on grounds of religion and belief, and detriment for making protected disclosures. Many of the alleged incidents were said to have occurred before she stopped attending work in February 2008. She also complained about the handling of her grievance and about the respondents’ conduct during her absence.

As pleaded and particularised, her complaints for the period after the grievance outcome included that the respondents (in particular Mr Game) failed to respond to her letter dated 16 February 2009, failed to contact her at all after that date, and—without contacting her—took over her office, forced it open and removed her personal property, appointed another staff member to her position, and removed her from staff lists, literature and materials. She alleged these matters amounted to unlawful treatment falling within her discrimination and whistleblowing causes of action.

On the jurisdiction/time-limit issue, the claimant’s argument was that the pre-dismissal discrimination and whistleblowing complaints were not out of time because they formed a continuing act (or an act extending over a period) running from around January/February 2009 to January 2010. She relied on the proposition that, even while off sick, discriminatory treatment could continue through the way an employer maintained contact or through a lack of contact, and she contended that the respondents’ lack of contact (in the context of the other alleged actions taken against her while she was absent) formed part of an ongoing discriminatory state of affairs.

In the appeal, she sought to overturn the Employment Judge’s declaration that she had no reasonable prospect of succeeding on the continuing-act argument. She contended the Employment Judge had wrongly narrowed her case to “lack of contact” alone, had not properly addressed that lack of contact could contribute to a continuing act in the circumstances alleged, had given inadequate reasons for rejecting that argument, and had erred by not recognising that Mr Game was effectively behind the actions taken by the corporate respondent.

facts:
R W Westworth Limited is a groundworks contractor established in October 1998 by Mr and Mrs Westworth. During the review period 28 December 2007 to 27 December 2008, the company experienced cash-flow difficulties, worsened by the failure of a major local customer who owed the company over £100,000.

Although both Mr and Mrs Westworth were directors, neither spent much time on office administration. Mr Westworth worked on the construction side of the business and Mrs Westworth had family commitments. From around Christmas 2007 (about the start of the review period) until April 2009, the company retained a consultant whose business was to supply support and consultancy to the construction industry. He worked almost full time for the company, spending about six hours a day in its office. The annual cost of his services was £60,000. The consultant was given, and exercised, authority and assumed responsibility for strategic decisions relating to day-to-day cash management and he dealt with all correspondence from HMRC. He was not authorised to sign cheques (which were signed by Mr or Mrs Westworth), but he decided when payments should be made, prioritised creditors, and could delay sending cheques that had already been signed if he thought it was in the company’s interest.

During the review period the company made multiple late payments of amounts due under PAYE. The late payments covered months 9 to 12 of 2007–08 and months 1 to 8 of 2008–09, with delays ranging from 5 to 22 days. HMRC reviewed the company’s compliance for the review period and cancelled its registration for gross payment status under the Construction Industry Scheme on the basis of failure of the compliance test due to these late PAYE payments. It was accepted that the company satisfied the business and turnover tests, and that the number of late payments was such that they could not be disregarded under the limited tolerance for late payments.

HMRC accepted there was reason to expect the company would comply on time in the future and did not rely on future compliance as a further reason to oppose the appeal. The dispute therefore focused on whether the company had a reasonable excuse for the late PAYE payments throughout the whole review period. The tribunal found that the company’s continuing reliance on the consultant was the real cause of the late payments, and that given the directors’ lack of experience and expertise in accounting, administration and taxation matters, it was reasonable for the company to retain the consultant and to expect him to ensure compliance, particularly given his role and remuneration. The tribunal concluded that a time limit on the excuse was not appropriate on these facts and allowed the appeal.
claims:
The company appealed against HMRC’s cancellation of its gross payment status under the Construction Industry Scheme. The company’s case was that, despite the late PAYE payments during the review period, it should be treated as meeting the compliance requirements because it had a reasonable excuse for the failures.

The company argued that it reasonably relied on the consultant it had engaged to provide management and administrative services. It contended that the consultant had assumed responsibility for day-to-day cash management and dealings with HMRC and effectively controlled the timing of payments, so the company’s reliance on him explained and excused the late PAYE payments.

The relief sought by the company was that the cancellation decision be overturned (so that it would retain or regain gross payment status), on the basis that the reasonable-excuse condition was satisfied for the late payments throughout the review period.

facts:
Barclays Bank plc operated a pension arrangement (the Barclays Bank UK Retirement Fund) for former employees of Barclays Bank plc and its subsidiaries. The appeal concerned a subset of about 13,500 pensioners (including widows and widowers) who had retired or agreed to retire before 31 December 1988.

For many years the Barclays group provided certain tax-related services free of charge on a concessionary basis through a group company specialising in such services (Barclays Bank Trust Company Limited and its subsidiary Barclays Personal Taxation Service (BPTS)). Initially these services were offered to widows of pensioners and later extended to pensioners. Communications to staff and pensioners described these services as a privilege and not part of terms and conditions of service.

In 1988 Barclays decided to withdraw the concessions, which led to strong resistance from pensioners and the trade union, threats of legal action, and negative media coverage. In March 1989 Barclays reinstated the concessions for those who had retired or accepted early retirement before 31 December 1988 and their widows/widowers, while stating that continuation would depend on future performance.

In 1997 Barclays considered selling BPTS (“Project Chatham”). Internal documents assessed the cost of providing the tax services and explored options for dealing with the pensioner concession. Barclays considered that fair treatment suggested either continuing the service or offering compensation, and that withdrawal without compensation risked renewed hostility, adverse publicity, and possible court action. A compensation approach was developed, including a sliding scale based on factors such as age, whether the person used the service, and the complexity of their tax affairs. The Executive Committee agreed to sell BPTS and discussed compensation levels and communications strategy.

On 11 September 1997 Barclays wrote to the affected pensioners explaining that, due to the intended sale, the free tax service would no longer be available, that Barclays would try to arrange favourable terms with a purchaser, and that Barclays intended to make one-off “goodwill” payments to those eligible, with details to follow after discussions with the tax authority about tax treatment. Pensioner reaction was reported as relatively muted, attributed in part to an expectation of compensation.

Barclays did not reach agreement with the tax authority on the tax treatment; the authority indicated in October 1997 that the payments would be taxable and maintained that view. By letter of 18 December 1997 Barclays informed pensioners of the compensation payments and that they would be paid on 23 March 1998. A further letter in March 1998 reminded pensioners of the payments, advised they need not enter them on that year’s self-assessment form, and stated that if the payments were held taxable the bank would meet any basic rate liability up to 23%.

Most payments were made in the week commencing 23 March 1998 through the pensioners’ payroll, without deduction of tax or national insurance contributions. Barclays later notified the tax authority that provisional payments totalled £6,486,850 to 13,521 recipients.

In June 2001 the tax authority confirmed its view that the payments were taxable and instructed Barclays to meet PAYE obligations by submitting a supplementary return. On 4 August 2003 the tax authority issued determinations for PAYE for the tax years ending 5 April 1998, 1999 and 2000, in amounts of £2,065,594.71, £201.66 and £316.88. The determinations were issued exclusively to the Trustees of the Barclays Bank Pension Fund, not to Barclays Bank plc.

Evidence from Barclays’ pensions manager indicated the payments were motivated by a combination of moral duty and a commercial desire to avoid hostility from pensioners and trade unions, and that the amounts were calculated carefully on a planned basis by reference to the complexity of recipients’ tax affairs. The tribunal found as a fact that the payments were made to compensate for the loss of the tax-related services and were not made in consideration of past services.

A procedural issue arose because the PAYE determinations were made on the Trustees rather than Barclays Bank plc. Although Barclays initially suggested the Trustees could be treated as responsible because the Trustees’ payroll was used, the tribunal concluded on the facts that the Trustees were not the party liable for PAYE in respect of these payments and therefore the appeal succeeded on that basis. The tribunal also addressed the substantive tax characterisation in case it was wrong on the procedural point.
claims:
Barclays Bank plc and the Trustees appealed against the PAYE determinations for 1997/98 to 1999/2000 relating to the one-off payments made to the affected pensioners and their widows/widowers.

They sought to have the determinations set aside on two main bases.

First, they argued that the determinations were made on the wrong party: the determinations were issued only to the Trustees, whereas (on the tax authority’s own case) any PAYE liability would fall on the employer, which was Barclays Bank plc. Because no determination was made on Barclays Bank plc, the Trustees contended they had no liability and the appeal should succeed on that ground.

Second, on the substantive issue, they contended that the payments were not taxable as benefits provided under a non-approved retirement benefits scheme. Their case was that the payments were compensation for the withdrawal of a long-standing, concessionary, non-taxable tax-return service and were not connected with retirement or past service in the relevant sense. They argued that the legislation in question was aimed at ongoing pension-type arrangements and not a one-off goodwill payment made for reasons unconnected with retirement or past service.

They further argued there was no “scheme” or “arrangement” under which the payments were made, characterising the payments as a unilateral act rather than something arising from a deed, agreement, or bilateral arrangement. They also argued that the payments were not “relevant benefits” and were not made “in connection with” past service, pointing to the basis of calculation (age, usage of the service, and complexity of tax affairs) rather than length or value of employment service.

They also advanced a substitution-type argument: because the payments were made in lieu of a non-taxable concessionary service, the payments should take the same non-taxable character as the benefit they replaced.

Overall, the relief sought was that the PAYE determinations for the three years be overturned and that no PAYE be payable in respect of the payments.
