facts:
The London Borough of Lambeth is the freeholder of 1–51 Bodley Manor Way, London SW2 2QH, a development of three blocks of purpose-built flats about 40 years old. Ms Gerlinde Gniewosz holds a long lease of Flat 21 (a one-bedroom flat) as assignee under a lease dated 12 April 2004.

In June 2018 Ms Gniewosz applied to the First-tier Tribunal for determinations about the reasonableness of service charges demanded for the years 2013/14 to 2018/19. She challenged many items, but the Upper Tribunal appeal concerned only one item: an advance service charge demand in 2018/19 for replacement of part of the roof.

The roof area in issue is the front, south-facing roof over Ms Gniewosz’s kitchen and bathroom, also covering a shared staircase and part of one other flat. The parties agreed the roof is seriously defective and needs replacement; it had been covered with a tarpaulin held down by sandbags for two years. The original roof was zinc. The landlord proposed replacing it with glass-reinforced plastic (GRP). The total cost was said to be £5,659.64, and Ms Gniewosz’s share had not yet been fixed but was said to be likely no more than 2.5%. A consultation process was carried out before the service charge was demanded.

Under the lease, the flat is demised excluding structural walls and the roof and associated structural elements. The tenant covenants to pay a rateable and proportionate part of the reasonable expenses incurred by the landlord in repair, maintenance, improvement, renewal and insurance of the building and provision of services. The landlord’s obligations include maintaining, repairing, redecorating, renewing, amending, cleaning, repointing and painting, and at its discretion improving, the structure of the building including the roofs.

Before the First-tier Tribunal, it was agreed that a new roof was needed; the dispute was whether replacement should be in zinc or GRP. It was agreed zinc would be more expensive, and that zinc would last about 40 years whereas GRP would last about 20 years. The First-tier Tribunal concluded that, ignoring estate regeneration plans, using GRP rather than zinc would breach the landlord’s covenant; it relied on views about quality, lifespan and appearance, and it did not determine Ms Gniewosz’s other objections once it found breach of covenant.

On appeal, the Upper Tribunal held that the First-tier Tribunal did not sufficiently explain the legal basis for finding breach of covenant and had not applied the correct test for whether the proposed works would comply with the repairing obligation. It also held that the First-tier Tribunal’s aesthetic judgment was based on inadequate evidence. The Upper Tribunal set aside the decision and remitted the roof charge issue to the First-tier Tribunal for a rehearing, where all of Ms Gniewosz’s objections (including value for money and other concerns) would need to be considered, and where regeneration plans could be relevant to the reasonableness of choosing one material over another if there was no breach of covenant.
claims:
Ms Gniewosz, as the applicant before the First-tier Tribunal, sought a determination that the service charge demand for the proposed roof works was not payable and/or not reasonable.

Her principal claim on the roof item was that replacing the existing zinc roof with GRP would not be permitted under the lease and would be a breach of the landlord’s covenant relating to the roof. She argued that the proposed works had to fall within the landlord’s obligations to repair, renew or improve, and that the appropriate characterisation was “renewal”; on that basis she contended that renewal required replacement with like-for-like materials, and that substituting GRP for zinc was a lower-quality and less attractive alternative and therefore outside what the lease permitted, so the cost could not properly be charged to her.

In addition, she raised further objections to the GRP proposal and the associated charge, including that a like-for-like metal roof would be better value for money than GRP; criticisms of the content of the consultation notice; objections to the timing of the works (saying it should have been done when other roof renewals were carried out a few years earlier); an argument that the works should be aggregated with replacement of other roofs on the estate; concerns about the sufficiency of warranties and guarantees and the likelihood of poor workmanship; and concerns about potential non-compliance with building standards and planning policies.

On appeal, while maintaining opposition to GRP, she did not pursue the argument that only like-for-like replacement could comply with the lease as a decisive point, and accepted that the distinction between repair and renewal was not crucial. She argued that the First-tier Tribunal had in substance applied the correct approach by considering the character and age of the building and what a reasonable occupier would expect, and that it was entitled to reach its aesthetic conclusions given the material before it and the expertise of the tribunal panel. She also relied on the landlord’s witness evidence that zinc would have been recommended if not for regeneration plans, as supporting her position that GRP was not suitable.

facts:
The case concerns the Oakfield estate in Weybridge, Surrey, a residential estate of 44 properties laid out from 1928 onwards. The estate’s original layout has largely been preserved by covenants imposed on first sales of properties which restrict development so that no more than one dwellinghouse may be erected on each plot. 

Mr Anthony Stephen Martin is the registered proprietor of Oak House, 11 Oakfield Glade, which sits on the largest plot on the estate (about 40 metres wide). The house dates from about 1930 and has been extended at the rear. The plot has a large garden, mature boundary planting, and a detached garage/workshop near the southern boundary served by an existing driveway. The property is centrally located on Oakfield Glade, opposite the junction with Oakfield Close. A public footpath runs between 11 and 13 Oakfield Glade.

Mr Martin wishes to divide his plot into two roughly equal parts and build a new detached house on the southern half of the garden while retaining the existing dwelling. The proposal involves demolishing the existing detached garage and using the existing access drive to serve the new house. Planning permission was granted on 13 December 2017 for the new house, and a further permission was granted on 18 July 2018 for a house of the same size and layout but with a modified façade. The proposed building was described in planning terms as a detached two-storey house with additional accommodation in the roof and a submerged basement.

There are 26 objectors (owners of other houses on the estate) who are entitled to the benefit of the one-dwelling-per-plot restriction affecting 11 Oakfield Glade. Two other objectors withdrew. There had already been High Court litigation between the parties which confirmed that the restriction remained enforceable, and a declaration to that effect was made on 20 September 2017.

The Tribunal inspected the estate and viewed 11 Oakfield Glade and surrounding properties, including views from neighbouring gardens and upper floors. The estate is bounded by York Road, Oatlands Drive, and Queen’s Road, with private internal roads including Oakfield Glade (gated at both ends) and Oakfield Close/North Common. Most houses are inter-war Arts and Crafts style, and many have been significantly extended. The Tribunal noted that while rear gardens are generous, the street scene along Oakfield Glade is of houses relatively close to the road and to each other.

The Tribunal considered evidence about the likely effects of the proposed development on neighbours’ outlook, privacy, greenery, and the estate’s character. It found that existing mature boundary vegetation around 11 Oakfield Glade would largely remain and that only modest sections might be removed during construction, with protective measures planned. It assessed impacts on specific neighbours: it considered that 13 Oakfield Glade would not become materially less private; that 11 York Road would be separated by substantial distance and screening; and that 10 and 12 Oakfield Glade would experience some change in outlook but not to a meaningful extent.

The Tribunal also considered short-term impacts during construction, including noise, dust, mud, increased traffic and heavy vehicles (including for basement excavation), and potential damage to verges and roads. Based on comparable nearby works, it assumed construction would take about 18 months. It concluded that disturbance would be significant for the closest neighbours, particularly regarding parking and access impacts.

The objectors also raised concerns that allowing this development would set a precedent leading to further erosion of the estate’s one-house-per-plot pattern. The Tribunal noted that there had already been departures from the one-dwelling principle on peripheral parts of the estate (including additional houses created from parts of gardens, conversion of one building into flats, and subdivision of a plot), but it found these had not damaged the integrity of the estate’s core pattern. It assessed the realistic scope for similar further development in the estate’s central core and concluded that granting this modification for 11 Oakfield Glade would not materially undermine the overall scheme or materially alter the context for future applications.

The Tribunal allowed the application and determined that compensation should be paid for temporary disturbance to certain nearby owners: £2,000 each to the owners of 8, 9, 12 and 15 Oakfield Glade; £4,000 to the owners of 10 Oakfield Glade; and £3,000 to the owners of 13 Oakfield Glade. No compensation was awarded to other objectors. Mr Martin had offered various conditions aimed at limiting disruption and protecting vegetation and design, but the Tribunal declined to impose additional conditions beyond what it intended to include in its order and the requirement that the determined compensation be paid.
claims:
Mr Martin applied to modify the restrictive covenant affecting 11 Oakfield Glade so that, instead of limiting the plot to one dwellinghouse, it would permit the construction of one additional detached house in the garden while retaining the existing house.

In support of the application, Mr Martin’s case was that building an additional house on the garden land was a reasonable use of the land and that the restriction prevented that use. He relied on the existence of planning permissions for the proposed new house (including a permission granted on appeal in December 2017 and a later permission with a modified façade). He contended in substance that the proposed development would not cause material harm to neighbouring occupiers’ amenity or reduce the value of neighbouring properties, and that the estate’s character would not be significantly harmed by the addition of a single substantial dwelling on the largest plot.

Mr Martin also sought to address objectors’ concerns by offering to accept modification subject to proposed conditions, including: making good any damage to roads/verges caused during construction; limiting contractors’ parking on common parts of Oakfield Glade during construction; restricting removal of boundary/perimeter landscaping except as required by the building footprint; tying the permitted development to the specific approved design; and limiting post-completion access to the existing route by the public footpath.

As relief, Mr Martin sought an order modifying the restriction to allow the additional house to be built on the plot at 11 Oakfield Glade. The Tribunal ultimately granted the modification but required payment of compensation to certain neighbouring owners for temporary disturbance caused by the building works.

facts: The decision concerns an appeal by Firefly UK Ltd (also described as J R Smith & Partners trading as Interlink Express) against the Commissioners of Customs and Excise. The appeal related to a decision imposing a default surcharge. The matter was heard in public in London on 13 October 2004 before a tribunal chaired by Peter H Lawson. Representatives attended and were heard: Mr R Smith for the appellant and Mr J Holl for the respondent. The tribunal heard the appeal and announced its decision at the hearing. The parties stated that they did not require the decision to be recorded in a written document beyond the direction issued. The tribunal found that the appellant had established a reasonable excuse for the default and therefore allowed the appeal. No order was made as to costs.
claims: The appellant appealed against the respondent’s decision to impose a default surcharge, advancing a “reasonable excuse” appeal. The relief sought was that the default surcharge decision be overturned on the basis that there was a reasonable excuse for the default. The tribunal accepted that the appellant had established a reasonable excuse and allowed the appeal.

facts:
The appeal concerned an assessment for £36,118.60 relating to 18,059.30 tonnes of inert soil and stones located in an area within the Easter Hatton Landfill site. The material appeared to have accumulated over a period of time.

A tax-free approval area within the site was first recognised on 15 November 2000. The initial approval covered 8 November 2000 to 30 November 2001, was limited to 100,000 tonnes, required any renewal application to be made two months before expiry, and stated that material could only be stored for up to three years, after which tax would have to be accounted for.

Following a visit by the tax authority to the premises on 5 February 2007, an officer noted that the tax-free area agreement had expired and that no request had been made for renewal. The authority’s letter of 2 March 2007 (sent with the assessment) set out the subsequent history: on 28 March 2003 a new agreement was issued to cover 1 December 2001 to 30 November 2003, with an accompanying warning that it would expire on 30 November 2003 and tax would become due on any material remaining after that date. On 14 October 2003 the site contacted the authority seeking an extension. On 14 January 2004 a meeting took place to discuss the continuing need for a tax-free area. Although the three-year storage limit had expired, the authority agreed on an exceptional basis to issue a further agreement to facilitate restoration, influenced by the lack of accurate figures for the amount of waste in the area as at 30 November 2003 because proper records of movements into and out of the area did not exist at that time. The new agreement was dated 15 January 2004 and covered 1 December 2003 to 30 November 2006. It again stated that renewal applications had to be made two months before expiry and repeated the three-year storage limit and that tax would become due on material remaining after that time. On 12 October 2004 an officer visited the site, inspected it, discussed the agreement, and later wrote on 29 October 2004 confirming record-keeping requirements.

After the 5 February 2007 visit, the appellant wrote on 12 February 2007 seeking a further extension. It was accepted by the authority that when ownership of the company changed in April 2004, certain information was not passed to the purchaser and current operator, including the terms of the tax-free area agreement, and that the appellant’s current management was not aware of the terms of the 2004 agreement.

In the 12 February 2007 letter the appellant explained that the original intention had been to carry out capping in 2006, but capping was delayed because permission was sought to delay Phase 1 capping while a pilot trial of a technology called LANDair commenced in June 2005; assessment and discussions continued into 2006; a decision was made in May 2006 not to proceed; and it was then too late in the year to tender and carry out capping works during 2006. The appellant said these delays meant the normal three-year period was insufficient. The appellant also said the new landfill manager had misinterpreted the position, believing material had three years from the time of deposition, and that if the 30 November 2006 expiry date had been appreciated an application would have been made in time. The appellant stated there had never been any intention to dispose of the material and it had always been stored for use in restoration work, and that it would be used up between March and July 2007 to restore Phase 1.

The authority’s assessment letter of 2 March 2007 merely noted receipt of the 12 February letter without addressing the specific request for an extension. A review letter dated 19 April 2007 maintained the authority’s approach that, with expiry of the agreement, tax had to be paid.

In the appeal, it was made clear in the appellant’s grounds and evidence that capping of Phase 1 was completed in May 2007, that all the material in question had been used during that work as tax-free restoration material, and that none remained in the tax-free area. It was also accepted that the appellant’s record-keeping under the newer regime was meticulous, contrasting with earlier deficiencies noted by the authority.

The Tribunal observed that the authority’s position was that it was unlikely a new agreement would have been issued, apparently based on the fact that the material had been on site for six years. The Tribunal also noted that the authority had previously issued new agreements in circumstances where earlier agreements had expired or where extension requests were made late.

The Tribunal concluded that the authority had not exercised discretion properly (or at all) in issuing the assessment, because it did not deal with the specific renewal request and proceeded mechanically on the basis of lapse of time. The Tribunal noted that by the time of the review the authority knew the material was about to be consumed in restoration work, and that removal from the site was impracticable. The Tribunal considered that the purpose of the regime was control of landfill and that this purpose had been achieved, and that due to the lapse of time the appellant could not recover the tax from others on what were exempt deposits. The Tribunal viewed the assessment as effectively a penalty for not renewing the permission in time and discharged the assessment.
claims:
The appellant appealed against the assessment of £36,118.60 on the inert soil and stones in the former tax-free area.

As framed, the appellant’s grounds of appeal focused on the contention that the company had a reasonable excuse for missing the deadline to apply for an extension/renewal of the tax-free area agreement. The appellant’s position was that the failure to renew in time arose from a change of ownership in April 2004 in which key documentation and information about the agreement’s terms were not passed to the new operator, leading current management to be unaware of the expiry date and to misunderstand how long material could be held.

The appellant also relied on the factual circumstances said to justify an extension: the material had always been stored for use in restoration rather than disposal; delays in planned capping/restoration were caused by a pilot trial of an alternative technology begun in June 2005, continued assessment into 2006, and a decision in May 2006 not to proceed, leaving insufficient time to tender and complete capping in 2006; and the material would be (and in evidence was said to have been) fully used in restoration works by May 2007, leaving none remaining in the tax-free area.

In substance, the appellant sought that the assessment be set aside, and had asked the authority (in the 12 February 2007 letter) for a further extension of the tax-free area approval to allow restoration to proceed and the stored material to be used for that qualifying purpose.
